options.detail: A terminal arrow makes the discard look like control flow at the end of a chain. It is visually distinct from ordinary methods, but `->` already carries return/arm meaning; using it in expression chains risks overloading a high-value token.
options.code:
send(event)
    .retry(2)
    -> drop("telemetry best effort")

comparisons.note: Uses `let _ = expr` or `drop(expr)`; no required reason string.
Discard is an audited terminal method or an explicit marker-scoped suppression.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust uses `let _ = expr` to make ignored `must_use` results explicit.
decisions.recommendation: Use `.drop("reason")` plus `#Suppress(MustUse)` (Option A): one discard vocabulary, method-chain friendly, and marker casing matches Jet.

log.text: Owner corrected scoped spelling to `#Suppress` and requested method-chain variants; ballot rebuilt around method discard syntax.
Ballot cleanup: rec key fixed, detail deduplicated, naming corrected.
Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.title: How does interpolation select the Debug hook instead of the default Display hook?
decisions.gist: Debug formatting needs a selector that signals "compiler-known protocol hook, not a field or method call." The key constraints that the current ballot underweights: (1) all `#`-markers are PascalCase and `#` infix means "pinned number" — Option B's `{value#debug}` violates both unless explicitly amended; (2) don't create a format mini-language by a different route; (3) the selector must compose cleanly in multi-value interpolations. The owner asked for non-member-looking operators; this ballot adds a casing conflict and an infix contract problem that must be resolved before any option is ratified.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: the ballot now has six non-member-looking selectors. `{value#debug}` marks Debug as a compiler-known interpolation feature, not a field or method. Adversarial pass: `#` inside interpolation is new and could invite a mini-language. Patch: selector set is closed (`#debug` only unless a future decision adds another), formatter round-trips it exactly, and unknown selectors produce Jet diagnostics.
decisions.story: Nora writes a CLI tool. Normal output should be clean and user-facing, but a debug log needs the full structural representation with variant names and field labels. She wants one interpolation selector that is obvious at the call site and cannot be confused with a field or method.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Try a method operator with different sigils that could identify it as a non-member/feature rather than a field. Give me multiple options.
Agent answer: Updated with six method/operator-style selectors. New rec: `{value#debug}`. Marks Debug as a compiler-known formatting feature, not a field or method. Restrict to a tiny closed selector set, formatter round-trips it, sema errors on unknown selectors.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): `#` INFIX CONTRACT: S76 + VERSION-# established that `#` in infix position "introduces a pinned number" ([T#N], pkg#1.2.0). `{value#debug}` breaks this contract — debug is not a number; needs explicit ratification in syntax-decisions.md. D-CASING1 CONFLICT: every #-marker is PascalCase; `{value#debug}` (lowercase) violates D-CASING1; `{value#Debug}` (corrected) looks like applying an attribute marker in expression position. OPTION E PARSING BUG: `{a | b | debug}` is ambiguous — parser cannot distinguish `debug` as a variable from a selector without reserved-word treatment. MINI-LANGUAGE RISK IS SYMMETRIC: reserving `#repr`/`#pretty` by decision creates the same format-spec mini-language as Option A, just slower. MISSING OPTION H: `{value:Debug}` — PascalCase protocol name after `:`; consistent with D-CASING1, no new sigil, unambiguous in interpolation context.

Sprint-readiness sweep: story and inWild filled so the ballot is complete for owner decision.

options.name: `{value@Debug}` — PascalCase selector suffix (ratified)
options.detail: Inside interpolation, suffix the value expression with `@Debug` to select the Debug hook: `{value@Debug}`. Bare `{value}` remains Display. This honors the owner correction away from `:Debug`, keeps selector casing PascalCase, avoids a format mini-language, and mirrors Jet marker-suffix visual grammar without making `Debug` look like a field or method.

options.name: `{#Debug value}` — marker-style prefix selector
options.detail: Use Jet's marker visual language inside interpolation: a PascalCase `#Debug` prefix names the protocol hook, then the value follows. This avoids member-call shape and avoids Rust's `:?` mini-language hint. Tradeoff: `#` inside interpolation becomes a new selector form even though `#` elsewhere marks declarations/blocks/types, so this must stay a closed interpolation-only grammar.

options.name: `{Debug user}` — protocol-name prefix selector
options.detail: Put the PascalCase protocol name first with no sigil: `{Debug user}`. It reads like "render this value with Debug" and cannot be mistaken for a field or method. Tradeoff: interpolation grammar must treat a leading PascalCase name plus following expression as a selector form, so `{Point x}`-style expressions need a clear parse rule or teaching error.
options.code:
print("user={Debug user}")
print("plain={user} debug={Debug user}")

// Display can be explicit if desired:
print("user={Display user}")

comparisons.note: Rust interpolation uses `{}` for Display and `{:?}` for Debug, a compact convention developers already know.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust: Rust interpolation uses `{}` for Display and `{:?}` for Debug, a compact convention developers already know.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: use `{value@Debug}` for Debug interpolation; bare `{value}` stays Display.

log.text: Owner ratified A with amendment: use `@Debug` suffix instead of `:Debug`; option text updated.
Owner kept A but rejected old B/C; ballot now has two new Jet-cohesive selector syntaxes.
Ballot cleanup: rec key fixed, detail deduplicated, naming corrected.
Adversarial pass complete: options hardened, challenges documented in detail field.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation (adversarial pass + recommendation fused), rec moved to A.

decisions.comment: use @Debug suffix on the variable instead of :Debug

decisions.title: What is the marker name for the replay-soundness function marker?
decisions.gist: D-REPLAY1=A ratified a function marker that rejects any reachable un-mockable `#(Time/Rand/Net/Io)` via inverse propagation. This is a low-stakes rubber-stamp of the NAME, matching the `#Pure`/`#Test` convention.
decisions.explainer:
Pure naming; no semantics at stake. PascalCase `#`-marker (D-CASING1) on a function. Blast radius: Syntax.rs keyword, parser, one ui snapshot, examples.

Recommendation: A — `#Replayable` matches the property-reading marker family and states what the guarantee buys without over-claiming.

options.name: `#Replayable`
options.detail:
Names the guarantee.

Matches the `-able` 'property of this fn' convention; says exactly what it buys.
options.code: #Replayable fn settle(order: Order, clock: Clock) -> Receipt { ... }

options.name: `#Deterministic`
options.detail:
Names the underlying property.

Accurate but over-claims (effect-free ≠ fully deterministic) and is longer/more abstract.
options.code: #Deterministic fn settle(...) -> Receipt { ... }

options.name: `#Replay`
options.detail:
Bare noun.

Terse, but reads as a command/mode, not a property the fn HAS.
options.code: #Replay fn settle(...) -> Receipt { ... }

comparisons.note: Temporal-style workflow engines use replayability as the contract for deterministic reruns.

decisions.bestCurrent: Workflow engines: Temporal-style workflow engines use replayability as the contract for deterministic reruns.
decisions.recommendation: Use `#Replayable`. It names the user goal directly: this function is safe to record and replay.

decisions.title: Which backing implementation powers the opt-in `Gc<T>` traced handle? (I6 owner gate)
decisions.gist: D-OPTGC1=A ratified `Gc<T>` as a library-only opt-in traced handle (ownership stays default). This is an I6 external-dependency approval gate: the collector either needs an owner-approved crate or a hand-rolled stdlib implementation. Per I6 any external dep is runtime-side only, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation.
decisions.explainer:
`Gc<T>` is an expert opt-in (I1: never the default). The collector is real machinery — mark/sweep with a root set + tracing. I6 governs the backing exactly like Cranelift/regex/wasmtime. Blast radius: a stdlib module + `.jet/lock` pin if a crate is approved. Does not touch `Source/`.

Recommendation: A — A pure-Rust stdlib mark-sweep is the I6 end-state with zero gated dep and no native-ize debt; effort is never a deterrent.

options.name: Hand-roll pure-Rust mark-sweep in stdlib (no external dep)
options.detail:
A small tracing mark-sweep in stdlib, std-only, no crate.

I6: nothing to native-ize — this IS the end-state; no gated dep, no lock pin. Most up-front work, which philosophy says is not a deterrent.
options.code:
import mem.gc
node@ Gc<Node> = gc.alloc(Node.{ value: 1, next: none })

options.name: Adopt a pure-Rust GC crate (e.g. `gc`/`broom`) runtime-side
options.detail:
Vetted pure-Rust tracing-GC crate as a runtime-side bootstrap, gated like Cranelift.
I6: owner-gated, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation to replace by Epoch-3. Faster to a working `Gc<T>` but adds a dep we must remove.

options.name: Defer until a concrete use-case
options.detail:
Keep `Gc<T>` reserved/unimplemented with a 'no GC backend yet' diagnostic until a real program needs it.
No dep/code now; cost: leaves a ratified feature a stub when the use-case (cyclic graphs) is already known.

comparisons.note: Go has a production tracing GC integrated into the runtime, but it is always part of the language cost model.

decisions.bestCurrent: Go: Go has a production tracing GC integrated into the runtime, but it is always part of the language cost model.
decisions.recommendation: Hand-roll an opt-in pure-Rust mark-sweep library. Jet preserves ownership by default and pays GC cost only where cyclic graphs need it.

decisions.title: Which crypto primitive backend powers `crypto.seal/open` + `sign/verify`? (I6 owner gate)
decisions.gist: D-CRYPTOENV1=A ratified the seal/open + sign/verify envelope. This is an I6 external-dependency approval gate for the underlying AEAD/signature primitives. Pure-Rust is preferred for the native-ize end-state.
decisions.explainer:
Hand-rolling primitive crypto is a footgun (constant-time, audited impls). A vetted backend is required; I6 governs which: runtime-side only, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation. Differentiator is the backend's I6 posture. Blast radius: a stdlib `crypto` module + `.jet/lock` pin.

Recommendation: A — RustCrypto is pure Rust with no C/asm, the closest of the three to the I6 end-state and simplest to re-implement first-party.

options.name: Pure-Rust RustCrypto (aes-gcm/chacha20poly1305/ed25519-dalek)
options.detail:
Audited pure-Rust crates, gated runtime-side like Cranelift.

I6: pure Rust, no C/asm — closest to the native-ize end-state, easiest to re-implement first-party.
options.code:
import crypto
box@ Bytes = crypto.seal(key, plaintext)?
sig@ Bytes = crypto.sign(privkey, msg)
crypto.verify(pubkey, msg, sig)?

options.name: `ring` (C/asm, BoringSSL-derived)
options.detail:
Battle-tested, fast.
I6: pulls in C + assembly, needs a C toolchain, pins a non-Rust core — furthest from the end-state.

options.name: libsodium via FFI
options.detail:
Bind system libsodium through the stdlib FFI-bridge pattern.
Widely audited, misuse-resistant — but an external C library + system dep (nixpkgs-interim), heaviest to native-ize, worst non-Nix story.

comparisons.note: RustCrypto offers pure-Rust AEADs, hashes, signatures, and traits with broad audit attention and no C toolchain.

decisions.bestCurrent: RustCrypto: RustCrypto offers pure-Rust AEADs, hashes, signatures, and traits with broad audit attention and no C toolchain.
decisions.recommendation: Use RustCrypto behind Jet’s misuse-resistant envelope. Jet can expose fewer knobs than Rust while keeping pure-Rust portability.

decisions.title: Should the leading enum-variant dot also apply in value position when the expected type is known?
decisions.gist: D-ENUMDOT1=A ratified the leading dot on enum-variant patterns in match arms (`.Circle(r)`). This decides whether that dot extends to VALUE position when the expected type is known (`c@ Color = .Red` alongside `Color.Red`). A coherent but separate extension the owner flagged for an explicit ruling.
decisions.explainer:
Today value-position is `Color.Red` (S30); the dot was added only to match arms (S31). Extending it mirrors dot-construction (`.{ }`, D-DOTCTOR) — type-directed authoring (Blueprint north-star). The dot resolves only where the expected type is known (annotated binding, return, typed arg). Blast radius: parser expression grammar, expected-type elaboration, every enum literal in canon/examples.

Recommendation: A — Extending the dot mirrors dot-construction and the owner's type-directed anti-repetition direction, while keeping `Color.Red` where no expected type exists.

options.name: Extend the dot to value position (both spellings)
options.detail:
`.Red` allowed anywhere the expected type is known; `Color.Red` stays valid everywhere.

Mirrors dot-construction and the match-arm dot; type-directed, less repetition. Rule: 'use the dot when the type is known.'
options.code:
c@ Color = .Red
fn default() -> Color { .Red }
paint(.Red)
x@ = Color.Red   // no expected type -> qualified form

options.name: Keep the dot match-arm-only
options.detail:
Value position stays `Color.Red`.

Smallest surface, no new ambiguity — but the dot means 'inferred member' in patterns yet is absent in the symmetric value case.
options.code:
c@ Color = Color.Red
match shape { .Circle(r) -> ... }

options.name: Require the dot everywhere; retire `Color.Red`
options.detail:
`.Red` the single spelling where the type is known; drop `Color.Red`.
One canonical spelling (I8-pure) but breaks the no-expected-type case and churns every `Type.Variant` literal.

comparisons.note: Swift allows `.case` when the enum type is known, making assignments and calls concise without losing type context.

decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift allows `.case` when the enum type is known, making assignments and calls concise without losing type context.
decisions.recommendation: Extend dot to value position. Jet already chose dot for inferred enum patterns; value-position parity gives Swift’s ergonomics with one inferred-member rule.

decisions.title: Should Jet pursue refinement types (e.g. PositiveInt proved > 0), and if so as a construction-time subset or a full SMT-backed prover?
decisions.gist: The decision has two forks that should be separated before the owner votes. Fork 1 (mechanism): does Jet add a new `refine` keyword, or extend the ratified `distinct` type (D-DIST1) with an attached invariant clause — these both deliver smart-constructor invariant checking, and I8 says choose one. Fork 2 (power): does the compiler check only at construction (no prover), check linear arithmetic with a bounded pure-Rust prover (I6-clean, no SMT, delivers D-OOBPROOF1=A), or defer to a full SMT solver. The current gist frames the decision purely as "how much proving" — but the I8/mechanism question is equally important and comes first. The expert/beginner split: beginners need "forgot the check = compile error" (all options except A deliver this); experts need "arithmetic on refined values does not require re-checking at every expression" (only the prover options deliver this). Option B gives beginners the compile-time guarantee but gives experts worse ergonomics than the status quo for arithmetic-heavy code.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: B loses real theorem-prover power compared with C. B can validate constructors, literals, and local flow narrowing; it cannot prove arbitrary arithmetic, universal properties, cross-function postconditions, or eliminate bounds checks from a proof. Adversarial pass: a small subset can become a dead-end half-feature. Patch: phrase B as the stable predicate surface/invariant discipline, so a later solver tier can reuse the same predicates instead of replacing them.
decisions.story: I'm writing a billing function and I type fn charge(cents: PositiveInt). A caller passes a value computed from user input. The compiler stops me at the call site: it can't prove the value is positive, and it points me at the one constructor — PositiveInt.new(n) returns PositiveInt ? String — so I write let amt = PositiveInt.new(raw)? once at the boundary. From there it flows through three layers of my code untouched, and nobody re-checks it. When I later guard with if amt > 0 the compiler already knew; when I forgot a guard last week, require() would have blown up at runtime — now it's a compile error with a fix-it pointing at the constructor.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: What are the tradeoffs of option B instead of C? What is lost by going with B over C?
Agent answer: B gives construction-checked refined values, literal checks, and flow narrowing. C can prove `a + b` remains PositiveInt, prove indexing is in bounds, eliminate runtime checks, and verify function postconditions over all inputs. What is lost with B: proof-preserving arithmetic, universal proofs, cross-function theorem reasoning, and check elision. Best sequencing: ship B as the surface; let future C reuse those predicates if a solver/prover tier is owner-approved.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): D-OOBPROOF1=A INCOHERENCE: D-OOBPROOF1 was ratified 2026-06-28 and uses `fn sum(arr: [Int], i: UInt where i < arr.len)` — a relational predicate between two bindings. Option B's construction-time model cannot check `i < arr.len` at construction time (arr is not in scope when i is constructed). If D-REFINE1=B ratifies without relational predicates, D-OOBPROOF1=A stays blocked. `refine` vs `distinct` (I8): D-DIST1/D-DIST3 (ratified) already provide a nominal wrapper; `refine` adds the same pattern with a predicate — I8 demands one mechanism. MISSING OPTION F: Presburger arithmetic (linear integer arithmetic, complete, decidable, pure-Rust, I6-clean) proves `a + b > 0` from `a > 0 && b > 0` and `i < arr.len()` from call-site context — the I6-clean middle path between B and C. `where` keyword: S45 explicitly rejected `where` clauses; using it for `refine T = Base where pred` introduces a rejected keyword in a new position.

options.name: Extend `distinct` with `#Invariant(pred)` + pure-Rust LIA prover — no new keyword (recommended)
options.detail: No new `refine` keyword (I8: `distinct` already provides nominal wrappers). Extend the ratified `distinct` type to carry an `#Invariant(predicate)` clause: `PositiveInt :: distinct Int { #Invariant(it > 0) }`. The compiler generates a smart constructor `.new() -> T ? Error` lowering to `require()/T?E`. Implement a pure-Rust Presburger/linear integer arithmetic (LIA) decision procedure (~3-5K lines, I6-clean, no external crate): proves (a) smart constructor invariants, (b) arithmetic preservation (`PositiveInt + PositiveInt -> PositiveInt` proven from `a>0 && b>0 => a+b>0`), and (c) relational predicates (`i < arr.len`) needed for D-OOBPROOF1=A (already ratified, currently blocked). Non-linear predicates fall back to construction-time checking with a clear diagnostic: "this predicate requires construction-time validation; arithmetic preservation not provable with linear arithmetic." Flow narrowing (`if x > 0` narrows `x: Int` to `PositiveInt`) is a separate sub-ballot — do not bundle.

options.name: Construction-time only — no LIA prover (D-OOBPROOF1=A stays blocked)
options.detail: Add `#Invariant(pred)` to `distinct` but implement only construction-time checking — no prover. Smart constructor `.new() -> T ? Error`. Arithmetic on refined values widens to the base type; caller must re-validate. Literal arguments checked at compile time. D-OOBPROOF1=A (bounds-check elision via `i < arr.len`) is a relational predicate between two bindings — cannot be checked at construction time without `arr` in scope. If B is ratified, D-OOBPROOF1=A has no delivery path.

options.name: Defer refinement types to Epoch 6
options.detail: No refinement syntax now. Prerequisites for reconsideration: Jet has shipped at least one numeric workload where the invariant-duplication cost of `require()` is concretely documented, AND D-OOBPROOF1=A has an alternate delivery path. Without those, defer is equivalent to closing the card indefinitely.

comparisons.note: Liquid Haskell proves rich predicates with SMT-backed refinements, but the model is expert-only.

Bolts refinement types onto GHC and discharges proof obligations to an external SMT solver (Z3). Predicates are written in special comments; the solver proves arithmetic/measure facts. Exactly the model option C describes — and exactly the external-solver dependency I6 forbids us from vendoring.

subtype PositiveInt is Integer with Dynamic_Predicate => PositiveInt > 0. Plain Ada checks the predicate at construction/assignment AT RUNTIME (raises Constraint_Error) — this is essentially option B's construction-time model. SPARK then adds an optional separate prover pass to discharge them statically (option C). The Ada/SPARK split is the clean precedent for shipping B first and treating C as a layered, optional research tier.

No real refinements; simulates them with a phantom 'brand' and a user-written guard that asserts the brand. The type only means anything because one constructor is the sole place that mints it. This is a no-solver pattern very close to option B's smart-constructor discipline — proof its construction-time core is viable without any prover.

Has no refinement types at all; the idiom is exactly Jet's status quo — a newtype wrapping a fallible constructor (NonZeroU32::new returns Option). The ecosystem reaching for newtype+constructor (and never getting compiler-proved arithmetic) shows option A is a coherent, shippable resting point, and that B is the natural, low-cost step beyond it.

decisions.bestCurrent: Liquid Haskell: Liquid Haskell proves rich predicates with SMT-backed refinements, but the model is expert-only.
decisions.recommendation: Extend `distinct` with `#Invariant(pred)` + pure-Rust Presburger/LIA prover (I6/I8-clean) — no new keyword, delivers D-OOBPROOF1=A (Option A). Construction-only (Option B) leaves D-OOBPROOF1=A blocked with no delivery path.

decisions.title: Should Jet pursue machine-checked formal verification, and if so as a bounded foundational checker, a full proof-carrying-code engine, or not at all?
decisions.gist: A request to attach machine-checked proofs to functions and refuse to ship if the proof fails. The decision currently conflates three distinct capabilities under 'Option B': (1) exhaustive enumeration of finite domains — genuinely machine-proven, I6-safe, and unique; (2) randomized sampling of infinite domains — already provided by D-TEST1 property tests, a duplicate mechanism; and (3) build-time contract enforcement — blocked by the current comptime scope. The honest question is narrower: should Jet add exhaustive-enumeration-only build-gate checks for truly finite types (the one thing B can do that D-TEST1 cannot), or should the Epoch 3 investment go to lightweight require/ensure contracts that every expert verification tool already reads as input and that beginners can understand without a quantifier DSL?
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: B cannot do what full proof tools do. B gives bounded/exhaustive finite-domain checks and randomized contracts through Jet-owned test/comptime machinery. C can prove universal properties: constant-time behavior, overflow absence for all inputs, functional correctness, and proof-carrying APIs. Adversarial pass: B risks being marketed as proof when it is only evidence. Patch: diagnostics and docs must call it bounded verification; C remains a separate expert prover tier, likely Epoch 6, with external solver errors translated into Jet diagnostics.
decisions.story: I'm writing a constant-time comparison for a password check. I write the function, mark it #Verify(constant_time), and `jet build` either proves the timing is input-independent and ships, or refuses with a diagnostic pointing at the branch that leaks. I never install a solver, never learn Dafny, and a teammate who's never heard of formal methods can read the marker and know exactly what's guaranteed. The day my logic stops being checkable by the bounded checker, Jet tells me plainly instead of silently downgrading to 'probably fine'.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: What are the tradeoffs of going with B over C? What could experts do with C that they can't do with B?
Agent answer: B can exhaustively check finite domains and sample large domains through Jet's own comptime/test engine. C can prove universal properties over infinite/huge domains: real constant-time claims, no overflow for all inputs, functional correctness against pre/postconditions, and proof-carrying APIs. What B preserves: zero solver in the compiler, no default build tax, no solver error leakage, and a direct extension of #Test.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) E0710 collision: the proposal reuses E0710, already assigned to effects-bound violations in syntax-decisions.md — assign a new code before ratifying. (2) `? VerifyError` in function signatures is wrong: #Verify is a build gate, not a runtime type; the return type must not change. (3) D-TEST1 overlap: the "large domain → sample" case duplicates what #Test fn already does; honest scope of #Verify is exhaustive-only. (4) Comptime engine scope gap: ratified comptime scope is "bindings only, no fn annotations" — evaluating arbitrary user functions exhaustively at build time requires an unapproved extension. (5) No enumeration cap defined: behavior at U16×U16 (4B cases) is unspecified. (6) Missing Option E (require/ensure contracts): simpler Epoch 3 step, already the foundation of every production verification language, cleaner I8 story.

options.name: `require`/`ensure` contracts + `#Verify` exhaustive finite-domain checker (recommended)
options.detail: Ship `require` (precondition) and `ensure` (postcondition) as first-class function contract annotations: checked eagerly in debug/test builds, treated as property-test generators by `jet test` (same engine as D-TEST1, no I8 cost — contracts are typed sugar over the existing test engine). No quantifier DSL, no enumeration engine beyond what D-TEST1 already provides. For finite-domain exhaustive proofs: add `#Verify(forall x: U8, y: U8 => predicate)` that exhaustively enumerates finite Cartesian products at compile time up to a build-time cap (default 1M; configurable). Domains exceeding the cap are a type error at the `#Verify` site — never silent fallback to sampling (that's D-TEST1's job). Assign a fresh diagnostic code from E08xx or E09xx (not E0710, which is already taken by effects-bound violations). Drop `? VerifyError` from function signatures — a failed `#Verify` is a build error, not a runtime type.

options.name: Decline — testing + property testing + #Unsafe audit is the floor
options.detail: No contracts, no #Verify. Constant-time and invariant claims are handled by #Unsafe("reason") audited regions plus property-style #Test blocks. Honest ceiling: Jet can never *prove* a property without an external solver; crypto/safety-critical users reach for SPARK/Dafny/F* and FFI the result in.

options.name: Defer to Epoch 6
options.detail: No contracts or verification now. Revisit in Epoch 6 when the solver/proof infrastructure and real production verification workloads exist. Choosing defer blocks the `require`/`ensure` foundation that every production verification language ships first — do not defer without an explicit plan for what fills the expert-guarantee story in the interim.
options.code:
// Only #Test and #Unsafe audit now.
// Epoch 6 revisit: require/ensure contracts + #Verify + optional SMT tier

comparisons.note: Dafny gives machine-checked pre/postconditions and proofs, but it is a verification language.

Verification-aware language: you write requires/ensures specs and Dafny discharges them via Z3 at compile time; verification is mandatory and the solver is core, not opt-in. Jet can't adopt this default-on model — it would put an SMT solver in every build (I6/beginner-path violation). Closest to Option C but without the expert gate.
comparisons.code:
method CtEq(a: array<byte>, b: array<byte>) returns (r: bool)
  requires a.Length == b.Length
  ensures r == (forall i :: 0 <= i < a.Length ==> a[i] == b[i])
{ ... }  // Z3 proves the ensures or the build fails

comparisons.note: Subset of Ada with contracts proved by an external prover (GNATprove/Why3); proof is opt-in per unit and layered (stone->gold->platinum). This is the closest precedent for Jet's Option C: a safe language where formal proof is an explicit, gated tier over normal compilation rather than the default — exactly the 'never in the default path' shape.

Bolt-on verifiers, none in rustc itself: Kani is a bounded model checker (finite unrolling — directly the Option B flavor), Prusti/Creusot are deductive SMT-backed (Option C flavor). All are separate opt-in tools you install and invoke, never part of `cargo build`. Validates that the foundational/bounded subset and the heavy prover can be cleanly separated, and that the prover lives outside the core toolchain.

Full dependently-typed proof assistants: maximal power (functional-correctness proofs, used for HACL* verified crypto), maximal cost — proofs are part of the source and the checker IS the compiler. This is beyond even Option C; cited to mark the far end of the gradient and why Jet would never embed a proof assistant in Source/ (it would BE an external proof kernel, the sharpest I6 collision).
comparisons.code:
let ct_eq (a b: bytes) : Pure bool
  (requires length a == length b)
  (ensures fun r -> r <==> equal a b) = ...
(* the F* typechecker discharges this; the proof ships with the code *)

decisions.bestCurrent: Dafny: Dafny gives machine-checked pre/postconditions and proofs, but it is a verification language.
decisions.recommendation: `require`/`ensure` contracts as the Epoch 3 foundation + `#Verify(finite-domain)` exhaustive checker for truly provable finite-type cases (Option A). `require`/`ensure` forward-composes into Option C's eventual proof language without redesign.

decisions.title: Should Jet express resource/time budgets as types and statically warn when a called function exceeds them — and if so, in what form?
decisions.gist: A render-frame loop wants a 16ms CPU budget that the compiler can enforce. But sound static timing/cost inference (WCET) is research-grade and undecidable in general — you cannot prove a wall-clock bound from source. The honest split: decline it as a type, ship a foundational #Budget that is really an effect/capability ceiling (forbid known-expensive effects in a hot region), or commit to full RAML-style cost inference as a post-Epoch research track.
decisions.explainer: Real timing budgets are a runtime property of a specific machine, inputs, and cache state; proving a 16ms bound at compile time is the worst-case-execution-time (WCET) problem, which is undecidable in general and, where tractable, requires whole-program loop-bound annotations and a hardware cost model (Ada/SPARK + aiT, RAML's amortized analysis). None of that is an Epoch-3 feature, and none of it composes with I8 without inventing a parallel mechanism. The pragmatic insight: most frame-budget blowups in practice come from doing forbidden *kinds* of work in a hot path — heap allocation, IO, syscalls, unbounded loops. Jet already has the exact machinery to forbid effect categories in a region (#(…) bounds, #Caps(…) ceilings, E0740/E0741). A #Budget region is therefore not a timing proof at all — it is an effect ceiling with a cost-oriented name that bans Alloc/Io/Net and flags unbounded loops, giving real, sound guarantees (no allocation in the render path) without claiming a millisecond it cannot honor. Full cost inference (option C) stays an honest research item; the runtime deadline path (option A's pointer to D-DEADLINE1) is the sanctioned way to get actual wall-clock enforcement today.
decisions.story: I'm writing render_frame for a 60fps game and I keep blowing my 16ms budget because some helper deep in the call graph quietly allocates and hits the filesystem to lazy-load a texture. I want the compiler to tell me — at the call site, before I ship — that this hot path is doing something it must never do, instead of finding it in a profiler at 11fps.

options.name: Decline budgets-as-types — sanction the runtime path (D-DEADLINE1)
options.detail: Do not add any budget type or marker. A wall-clock budget is a runtime fact, so enforce it at runtime: the existing latency/deadline-propagation card (D-DEADLINE1) carries a deadline on #Context and cancels work past it, and ordinary profiling catches regressions. The compiler makes no timing claim it cannot prove. Honest about undecidability; smallest surface; risks leaving the 'no alloc in the hot path' guarantee that game/audio devs actually want unserved.

options.name: Foundational #Budget marker — a cost-oriented effect ceiling (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship #Budget(name) as a region/function marker that is a thin policy layer over the existing effect ceiling (#Caps / #(…)). A budget profile names forbidden effects (default: Alloc, Io, Net, Fs) and requires every loop in the region to have a statically known bound. Reuses E0741's machinery; new diagnostics E0746 (forbidden effect in budget) and E0747 (unbounded loop in budget). It is NOT a timing proof — it proves the region does no expensive *kind* of work and has no unbounded iteration, which is the sound, decidable core devs can rely on. Composes with effect ceilings under I8 (one mechanism: effect bounds), not a parallel system. Names the limit honestly: a budget is a no-alloc/no-IO/bounded-loop contract, not 16ms.

options.name: Full static cost-bound inference (RAML-style, post-Epoch research)
options.detail: Commit to real comptime cost inference: a #Budget(16ms) (or abstract cost units) that the compiler discharges by inferring an amortized worst-case cost bound for each function and proving the called set fits. This is automatic amortized resource analysis (RAML) plus a hardware/instruction cost model — research-grade, requires loop-bound annotations or a termination/ranking analysis, an LP solver in comptime, and is undecidable in general (only sound on an annotated, restricted fragment). Highest value if it lands, but it cannot ship in Epoch 3, would pull a solver into the I6-clean compiler, and risks promising millisecond bounds the model can't honor across machines. Keep as a flagged research track that option B's effect ceiling forward-composes into.

comparisons.note: Real-time systems express priorities/deadlines; full static cost inference is rare and niche.

The hard-real-time world separates the two halves Jet must not conflate: the *language* (Ravenscar profile) statically forbids dynamic constructs in critical tasks — no unbounded allocation, no unbounded loops, restricted tasking — which is exactly option B's effect/capability ceiling. The actual *16ms timing proof* is done by a separate external WCET tool (aiT) over the binary with a CPU model, never by the type system. This is the prior-art case for declining timing-as-a-type while shipping the restriction profile.
comparisons.code:
-- Ravenscar restricts the language for the hot path (≈ option B):
pragma Profile (Ravenscar);   -- no dynamic alloc, bounded tasking
-- The 16ms bound is proven OUTSIDE the type system, by aiT WCET analysis on the binary.

comparisons.note: Two contrasting points. EVM proves cost only by *running* with a runtime gas counter that aborts when exhausted — dynamic, not static — mirroring option A's runtime-deadline path; even there the static bound is undecidable so it's metered live. Koka shows the decidable, sound thing you CAN infer: it infers *effect rows* (which effects a function has), not costs — confirming that effect membership is tractable and composable while cost magnitude is not. Jet's #Budget(B) leans on the Koka-style effect inference it already has, and leaves the EVM-style magnitude question to runtime.

decisions.bestCurrent: RTSJ / Ada: Real-time systems express priorities/deadlines; full static cost inference is rare and niche.
decisions.recommendation: Use a foundational `#Budget` marker, not full cost inference. Jet can connect budgets to effects/deadlines now and leave exact proofs to research.

decisions.title: Should Jet support reversible/constraint-solved values — write `width = parent.width - padding*2` and let the compiler solve for `padding` given a target `width` — and if so, as a general language feature or only as a scoped UI-layout library?
decisions.gist: A forward expression is normally a one-way function: you give inputs, you get an output. Reversible computation flips that — you state a relationship once and the system solves for whichever side is unknown, like spreadsheet goal-seek or a layout engine resolving sizes from constraints. The question is whether Jet adopts this as a general semantic capability, ships a narrow linear-constraint solver scoped to UI layout, or declines it and keeps plain functions + the reactive stack as the only paths.
decisions.explainer: General reversibility is a deep semantic change: an `=` would stop meaning 'bind this computed value' and start meaning 'assert this relationship, solve for the hole', which collides head-on with I8 (one canonical meaning) and forces a constraint solver into the language core. Any real solver (Z3-class SMT, or even a robust Cassowary linear solver) is a substantial dependency — in the compiler that violates I6, and even as stdlib it is heavy. The honest split: the *foundational, shippable* slice is a bounded LINEAR (Cassowary-style) solver delivered as a library scoped to UI layout, where the problem is well-posed, the math is tractable, and it slots into the reactive-UI stack already queued for Epoch 3 (D-REACTUI1) — this is a layout engine, not a language primitive, and `=` keeps its meaning everywhere. The *general* version (solve arbitrary forward constraints over arbitrary types) is open-ended research with no bounded solver and unclear semantics; it belongs post-Epoch if ever. Declining is defensible: plain functions already invert by hand, and reactive `derived` already propagates layout forward.
decisions.story: I'm building a settings panel. I write `panel = VStack.{ padding: 16 }` and a row inside it, and I want the row to fill the panel minus the padding. Today I compute that by hand: `row.width@ = panel.width.get() - 32`, and if the panel resizes I re-derive it. What I *want* is to state the relationship once — `row.width == panel.width - panel.padding*2` — pin the row's minimum, and let the layout pass solve the rest, the way Auto Layout does, so I never hand-thread which value drives which.

options.name: Decline — plain functions + reactive derived are the sanctioned paths
options.detail: Do not add reversibility or a solver as a language feature. Inverting a relationship stays an explicit, user-written function; layout that must react to inputs uses `core.reactive` (`derived`) to propagate forward. Keeps I6 (no solver dependency anywhere in the compiler), keeps I8 (`=` means one thing — bind a computed value), and keeps the surface small. Cost: layout authors hand-thread direction and hand-write any inverse; there is no goal-seek.

options.name: Foundational subset — bounded LINEAR constraint solver, library-scoped to UI layout (Epoch 3)
options.detail: Ship `core.layout`: a Cassowary-style incremental solver for LINEAR equalities/inequalities over numeric layout values, with weak/medium/strong/required priorities and `@suggest` edits — exactly the Auto Layout model. It is a library, not a language primitive: `=` keeps its meaning; the solver only runs inside an explicit `layout.solve.{ … }` region over declared layout values, and it ties into the reactive-UI stack (D-REACTUI1). Bounded math means a tractable, std-only implementation is realistic (no SMT). Scope is deliberately narrow — linear, numeric, layout — so it does not become a general reversibility back door (I8 honored: the one canonical job is 'resolve a layout').

options.name: Full general reversible computation / constraint solving (post-Epoch research)
options.detail: A first-class `@reversible` annotation turns a forward expression into a relation the compiler can solve in either direction over arbitrary types — goal-seek for the whole language. Requires a general solver (SMT/Z3-class), which is a hard I6 violation in the compiler and a heavy stdlib dependency, plus a deep semantic shift: `=` inside a reversible region asserts a relationship with a hole rather than binding a value (I8 tension — two meanings for one symbol). No bounded solver, undecidable in general, error/diagnostic story unsolved (rustc must never see it — I2). Powerful, but open-ended research with no clear Epoch-3 landing.

comparisons.note: The proven model for Option B: an incremental LINEAR solver with required + weak/medium/strong priorities and editable 'suggested' values. Scoped to layout, fast, well-understood, std-implementable. This is the sweet spot Jet's layout library would target.

The Option C end of the space. Janus programs run backward by construction (every statement reversible); MiniZinc/Z3 solve arbitrary constraints via a heavy external solver. Both show the cost: a solver dependency and a programming model where statements are relations, not assignments — exactly the I6 + I8 + semantic-depth problems C inherits.

decisions.title: How should Jet track taint, PII, secrets, and audited release without becoming a full IFC research language?
decisions.gist: Extend `#Tainted` to a closed label set (`.Input`, `.PII`, `.Secret`, `.Credential`) with one taint engine and an audited declassify gate. This ballot ratifies the label taxonomy only — four follow-on ballots are required before implementation: `declassify` syntax (I7 registration), `#Sanitizer(.Kind)` specificity, sink policy declaration mechanism, and interprocedural scope. Bare `#Tainted` (D-TAINT1) must be designated sugar for `#Tainted(.Input)` with a teaching-error migration to avoid the I8 coexistence hole.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: the cohesive best-in-class shape is one taint mechanism, not separate #Pii/#Secret systems and not a full Jif lattice by default. Values carry a small set of labels (`#Tainted(.Input)`, `#Tainted(.PII)`, `#Tainted(.Secret)`) that flow through existing taint propagation and are checked only at sinks. Experts get control through sink policies, org labels, audit reports, and required declassify reasons. Adversarial pass: label sets can explode and become compliance theater. Patch: built-in labels stay closed in the language; org labels live in policy; diagnostics fire at sinks, not at every assignment; full principal lattices are deferred unless Epoch 6 explicitly funds them.
decisions.story: A signup form stores an email. The web package marks it `#Tainted(.PII)`. Passing it to `log.info` fails until the developer redacts or declassifies with a reason. Security can grep every declassification and can add an org label like `.HIPAA` without changing the language.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: How can we give full control while keeping the system as small as it can be without cutting functionality? Can we turn #Tainted into something like `#Tainted(.PII)`?
Agent answer: Updated D-IFC1 around `#Tainted(.Kind)`. Best system: one taint mechanism, label set on values, built-in labels first (.Input, .PII, .Secret, .Credential), audited `declassify("reason", .Kind)`, sink policies, later org labels through policy. Devil's advocate: labels can explode and become compliance theater. Patch: closed built-ins in language, org labels only in policy, no principal lattice in Epoch 3, diagnostics at sinks only, declassification reports generated from semantic graph.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): Five concrete implementation blockers: (1) `declassify` syntactic form is undefined — must be I7-registered as a keyword or redesigned as a three-argument core library fn. (2) .Kind label type is unresolved — value-position dot requires a known expected type (D-ENUMDOT2=A); where is it declared and how does a caller use it? (3) Bare #Tainted (D-TAINT1, ratified + implemented) and `#Tainted(.Kind)` (Option B) coexist as two spellings for overlapping semantics — I8 violation with a safety hole (sink policy filtering .Input does not catch bare #Tainted). (4) `#Sanitizer fn` (D-TAINT-SAN, ratified) strips all labels, breaking label-aware declassification — a SQL sanitizer must not strip .PII. (5) Sink policy declaration mechanism is entirely absent from the ballot.

options.name: `#Tainted(.Kind)` closed label taxonomy + audited declassify gate (taxonomy decision only) (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify the label taxonomy: one taint engine, four built-in labels (`.Input`, `.PII`, `.Secret`, `.Credential`), an audited declassify gate (static string reason required), per-label sink policies (Db/Exec/Net for `.Input`; Log/Fs/Net for `.PII`/`.Secret`). This decision ratifies ONLY the label taxonomy and opt-in scope. Four follow-on ballots are required before implementation: (1) `declassify` syntactic form — keyword or three-arg core library fn, must be I7-registered; (2) `#Sanitizer` specificity — whether `#Sanitizer fn` strips all labels or becomes `#Sanitizer(.Kind)` to preserve other labels; (3) sink policy declaration mechanism — how core library fns declare their denied-label set; (4) interprocedural scope — whether labels propagate through unannotated fn parameters. Bare `#Tainted` (D-TAINT1, ratified + implemented) becomes sugar for `#Tainted(.Input)` with a teaching-error migration; I8 gap is closed by this designation.

options.name: Label-propagating distinct-type wrappers via D-DIST1 machinery
options.detail: Define `PII<T>`, `Secret<T>`, `Input<T>` as generic distinct wrapper types (D-DIST1/D-DIST3). The label IS the type; propagation is enforced by the existing type-checker without a new sema pass. Passing `PII<String>` where `String` is expected raises E0127 (distinct-type mismatch) with no new diagnostics. Declassification is an audited method: `email.declassify("support trace") -> String`. Costs: no multi-label without a union type; generic fns over `T` must propagate label type through signatures.

options.name: Defer rich information-flow to Epoch 6
options.detail: Keep today's one-bit #Tainted/sanitizer model (D-TAINT1, ratified and implemented). In Epoch 6, revisit the full label/policy/declassify system with real compliance workloads. Ship no new label taxonomy until then.

comparisons.note: Full principal lattice. Very expressive, but annotation-heavy and not mainstream.
Strong declassify discipline validates Jet’s audited release gate, but dynamic current-label semantics are too invasive for normal Jet.
Practical industry model: sources, sinks, sanitizers, labels. Jet can make this compile-time and type-aware instead of external analysis.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jif: Jif supports label-based information-flow control with principals and declassification, but its surface is heavy.
decisions.recommendation: Ratify `#Tainted(.Kind)` label taxonomy now; four follow-on ballots before implementation (Option A). This decision ratifies the label set and taint-engine scope only — not the syntax of declassify, #Sanitizer specificity, sink policy, or interprocedural propagation.

decisions.gist: D-VISDEFAULT1 already approved a file-scope marker. This card decides the marker spelling and whether the exception is a new private keyword or the existing per-item `pub` model inverted. It is one syntax choice; it does not reopen private-by-default as the language baseline.
decisions.story: Maya owns `core.http.server`. Almost every function in the file is public API. She wants one line at the top so the file reads like an API surface, while `parse_header_fast_path` stays private without being moved to another file.

comparisons.note: Swift supports file-scoped access and explicit public API boundaries.
`public`/`internal`/`private` are per declaration; no file-wide flip. Clear, but noisy for API-heavy files.
comparisons.code:
public func listen(_ port: Int) -> Server { ... }
private func parseHeaderFastPath(...) -> Header { ... }

comparisons.note: Visibility is per item (`pub`, `pub(crate)`); modules give structural grouping. No file-wide public default.
comparisons.code:
pub fn listen(port: i64) -> Server { ... }
fn parse_header_fast_path(...) -> Header { ... }

comparisons.note: Section labels (`@public`, `@private`) exist, but item position changes visibility. Jet already rejected that kind of positional surprise.

options.name: #PubFile + `priv` exceptions (recommended)
options.detail: One marker at the top flips this file to public-by-default. `priv` is the single exception keyword inside that file. Reads literally and keeps the exception local. Follow-up needed only to register `priv` in Syntax.rs and teaching errors.
options.code:
#PubFile

fn listen(port: Int) -> Server { ... }      // public
fn route(path: String) -> Route { ... }     // public
priv fn normalize_path(p: String) -> String { ... }

options.name: #PublicFile + `private` exceptions
options.detail: Same semantics, more English. `private` is longer and introduces a second visibility word beside `pub`, but it is self-explanatory for beginners.

options.name: Section labels `pub:` / `priv:`
options.detail: Lets one file mix public and private sections. Rejected as recommendation because item position becomes semantic: moving a helper above or below a label changes exports. That is the exact readability trap the file marker avoids.

decisions.recReason: `#PubFile` is short, direct, and consistent with Jet marker casing. `priv` is the smallest readable opposite of existing `pub`. Section labels are too position-sensitive.
decisions.title: What is the file-scope public-by-default marker, and how do private exceptions read?
decisions.explainer: S18 stays private-by-default. The approved marker is an opt-in escape for files that are mostly public API. The owner needs to pick two visible words: the file marker and the explicit-private exception inside that file. Avoid section markers here: S18 already rejected grouped visibility because moving an item across a line silently changes its export status. Also avoid `@` markers: D-ATTR1 retired `@` as an attribute prefix; Jet markers use `#PascalCase`/`#Name(...)`.
decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift supports file-scoped access and explicit public API boundaries.
decisions.recommendation: Use `#PubFile` with `priv` exceptions. Jet keeps private-by-default globally while giving API-heavy files a clear opt-in.

decisions.gist: Expose Cassowary-class layout as typed constraint values. Two open language gates must be resolved first: whether comparison operators may return non-Bool on closed built-in types, and whether core.layout.Var enters the compiler's closed type family. If both gates ratify, the ideal design is a static `layout { }` block (beginner face) desugaring to first-class typed constraint handles (expert layer), with axis-typed variables (`HVar`/`VVar`/`LengthVar`) that make cross-axis constraints compile errors. This is strictly better than Apple Auto Layout: readable authoring, inspectable/named/removable constraints, axis safety at compile time, and a structured conflict diagnostic rather than a runtime dump. If the language gates are declined, a method-only builder (Option A) is the safe fallback consistent with all ratified decisions.
decisions.story: Elena is building a settings panel. She wants the label column to be at least 80px wide, the input column to fill the rest, and a 16px gap between them. She writes these as constraints rather than calculated values so the layout adjusts automatically when the panel resizes.

comparisons.note: Auto Layout expresses UI constraints as linear equations and inequalities over anchors, the strongest production layout solver model.

options.name: `layout { }` block + typed-axis variables — gated on two language gates (recommended)
options.detail: A `layout { }` block desugars to first-class typed `Constraint` handles (each line is a named, removable, prioritizable handle). Layout variables are axis-typed: `HVar` (horizontal), `VVar` (vertical), `LengthVar` (unsigned scalar). Cross-axis constraints (`label.left >= label.height`) are compile errors — statically safe, zero-runtime-overhead axis checking; no existing constraint system offers this. Static layouts (all values comptime-known) can be solver-evaluated at compile time, emitting zero runtime solver. Expert escape: capture handles, adjust priorities, call `solver.suggest()`. GATE 1 (required): comparison operators may return non-Bool on specific closed built-in types — required for `>=`/`==`/`<=` on Var types to produce `Constraint`. GATE 2 (required): `core.layout.Var` and `core.layout.Length` enter the compiler's closed type family. If either gate is declined by the owner, fall through to Option B (method-only builder, unblocked today).

options.name: Method-only builder — no language gate (unblocked today)
options.detail: All constraints are explicit method calls: `Constraint.gte(a, b)`, `Constraint.eq(a, b)`. No comparison-operator overloading; no new compiler type family. Compatible with all ratified decisions (D-SIMD2, D-VECARITH1). Verbose relative to infix, but every constraint is a named, typed, inspectable value. Axis typing (G) can be added as a type-level distinction on top. The correct base layer for Option A's sugar if the language gates are later approved.
options.code:
c1 :: Constraint.gte(label.width, 80.px).named("label min")
c2 :: Constraint.eq_sum([label.width, Length(16.px), input.width], form.width)
solver.add([c1, c2])

options.name: Defer constraint solver to Epoch 6
options.detail: Ship only stack/grid/form presets for the UI stack now. Full Cassowary-based solver, constraint handles, and `layout { }` blocks defer to Epoch 6. Beginner presets cover common form/grid layouts without any solver dependency.
options.code:
Form.columns(label_min: 80.px, gap: 16.px)
// Epoch 6 revisit: full Cassowary solver + layout {} blocks

decisions.recReason: Infix operators on layout vars are the most ergonomic and don't require new syntax. Option B is good for tooling (inspectable constraints) but verbose. Option C needs a new compiler-blessed block (new syntax surface without clear I8 advantage over A).
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: best current practice is Cassowary/Auto Layout: linear constraints, priorities, edit variables, and conflict explanation. Jet can improve with typed `Constraint` values: math-like authoring for layout vars, but every constraint remains a named/removable/inspectable value. Adversarial pass: infix constraints can look like general operator overloading. Patch: only `core.layout.Var`/`Length` get blessed builders; ordinary user types still cannot overload operators.
decisions.bestCurrent: Apple Auto Layout: Auto Layout expresses UI constraints as linear equations and inequalities over anchors, the strongest production layout solver model.
decisions.recommendation: `layout { }` block desugaring to typed axis-safe Constraint handles — F+G combined (Option A) — gated on two owner decisions. If either gate is declined, Option B (method-only builder, no language gate) is the unblocked fallback.
decisions.title: What is Jet’s constraint-layout API surface?
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: Consider the best approach currently in any language, then improve on it from a functionality & ergonomics perspective.
Agent answer: Updated. Best current model is Cassowary/Auto Layout: linear constraints, priorities, edit variables. Jet improves with typed Constraint values: math-like authoring, every constraint inspectable, removable, named, prioritized, and traceable. Devil's advocate: math operators look like global operator overloading. Patch: only core.layout.Var/Length comparison/arithmetic builders are blessed; no general user operator overloading.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): PRIMARY BLOCKER: `>=` returning `Constraint` instead of `Bool` requires comparison-operator return-type overloading — explicitly not covered by D-SIMD2 or D-VECARITH1. This is a language-level gate, not an API choice, and must be balloted separately before Option B can be implemented. MISSING FEATURES: no conflict-resolution story — the defining pain point in all constraint systems. core.layout.Var carries no axis type, allowing cross-axis constraints that are geometrically nonsensical. STRINGLY-TYPED: `form.var('label_width')` conflicts with U13 preference — name should be inferred from the :: binding. OPTION G (typed-axis model) is the "better than any existing language" angle the ballot is missing.

decisions.gist: D-RENDERTGT1 approved a backend seam. This card decides the minimum trait between Jet UI and platform renderers: layout phases, event delivery, and paint calls. It is internal API shape, not user syntax.
decisions.story: Sophie is implementing the web backend for Jet's UI. She needs to implement the Backend trait. She wants to know: what methods does she have to implement, what data types do they pass around, and how do events flow back to Jet code?

comparisons.note: Flutter separates layout, paint, and hit testing through renderer objects.

options.name: Three-phase measure-layout-paint trait (recommended)
options.detail: Backend trait has three required methods: measure(node, constraint) -> Size (phase 1), layout(node, frame) (phase 2, sets final positions), paint(node, painter) (phase 3, draws to backend surface). Events flow in via a separate on_event(event) method. This is the universal model used by Flutter, SwiftUI internals, and Yoga.

options.name: Two-phase layout-paint trait (simplified)
options.detail: Combine measure+layout into a single layout(node, available: Size) -> Rect phase. Simpler to implement but less powerful: intrinsic size information is lost after layout, making some responsive layouts impossible. Better for simple backends (TUI, fixed-size targets), worse for CSS-flexbox-style adaptive layouts.

options.name: Event-driven reactive trait
options.detail: Backend is fully event-driven: the UI framework pushes layout/paint requests as events to the backend, and the backend responds. No synchronous method calls. Aligns with async runtime and signal model but introduces significant complexity in the protocol — backends must process events in order and cannot ask the framework questions synchronously.

decisions.recReason: Three-phase is the proven industry model (Flutter, Yoga, SwiftUI internals). Backends can implement C (simplified) on top of A by merging measure+layout, but A cannot be recovered from B. The measure phase is essential for intrinsic-size-aware layout (text reflow, content-sized containers).
decisions.explainer: Group this with layout/reactive UI. The owner is choosing architectural contract, not syntax. The trait must support native widgets, browser DOM, and future custom renderers without leaking one platform into the Jet UI model.
decisions.bestCurrent: Flutter: Flutter separates layout, paint, and hit testing through renderer objects.
decisions.recommendation: Use a three-phase measure-layout-paint trait. Jet gets Flutter-grade backend portability while keeping layout decisions explicit and testable.

decisions.gist: D-NATIVEUI1 approved Phase 1: thin Jet wrapper over native platform widgets. This decides which platform to build first and whether to build all three simultaneously.
decisions.story: Derek is building a Jet desktop app. He's on macOS. He wants to ship to Windows users too. He needs the native UI backend to exist so his app can render native widgets on both platforms from the same Jet code.
decisions.comparisons: Qt: cross-platform C++ widget toolkit, all platforms simultaneously. GTK: Linux-first, cross-platform with backends. wxWidgets: wraps native APIs per platform, all platforms. Electron: web tech, all platforms simultaneously. Flutter desktop: all platforms (macOS/Win/Linux) in one unified release. Tauri: web + native, all platforms.

options.name: macOS (AppKit) first, then Windows and Linux
options.detail: Build the macOS AppKit wrapper first (narrowest FFI surface, best macOS support). The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is defined and proven against AppKit before tackling Win32/GTK. Ship macOS, then add platforms. Risk: Windows users wait; API may be too AppKit-shaped.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: macOS only
use core.ui.native  // backed by AppKit on macOS

options.name: All three platforms simultaneously (recommended)
options.detail: Build AppKit, Win32/WinUI, and GTK backends in parallel. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) is kept platform-agnostic from day one. Jet's platform detection at compile time routes to the right backend. Flutter's desktop approach — commitment to parity from the start prevents API drift. Higher up-front cost but the right shape from the start.

options.name: Linux (GTK) first for CI/headless testing
options.detail: GTK is available in CI headless environments (Xvfb). Build GTK first to establish the testing infrastructure and Backend trait API with automated tests. Then port to AppKit and Win32. Best for testing rigor; not ideal for the majority macOS/Windows developer audience.
options.code:
// Phase 1a: GTK on Linux (CI-first)
use core.ui.native  // backed by GTK on Linux

decisions.recReason: Flutter's lesson: committing to cross-platform from the start produces a better API than porting a single-platform API later. The Backend trait (D-RENDERTGT2) provides the seam; parallel implementation keeps all three honest against the same contract.

decisions.gist: Partition inference requires a `Browser` effect (or equivalent named call-graph rule) as its engine — the current D-EFF4 closed set has no such entry. The JS/WASM boundary is bidirectional (WASM→JS exports and JS→WASM callbacks) and interacts with the D-SIGNAL1 reactive graph. Before this decision can be ratified, D-WEBKIND1 (WASM target) and D-JSBIND1 (boundary types) must exist as ballot cards, and the inference engine must be defined precisely enough to snapshot-test.
decisions.story: Priya writes a dashboard. Her chart view responds to clicks in the browser, but CSV export and matrix transforms should run in WASM. She does not want to annotate a hundred helper functions; she wants Jet to send pure compute to WASM and keep browser API code in JS.

comparisons.note: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.

options.name: Infer from `Browser` effect + allow module-level target ceilings (recommended)
options.detail: Amend D-EFF4 with a `Browser` effect and use effects as the default partition engine: browser/DOM APIs imply JS; pure/compute code is WASM-eligible. Add the useful part of B as expert control: a module may declare `#Target(Wasm)` or `#Target(Js)` as a ceiling/default, and sema validates it against the inferred effects. This keeps beginner magic (no required module declarations) and gives large teams auditable module-level placement. Per-function `#Wasm`, `#Js`, and `#WasmExport` remain overrides. GATES: D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 still need ballots before implementation.

options.name: Module-level `#Target(Wasm)` / `#Target(Js)` declarations + sema validation
options.detail: Each module declares its default compile target in the header. All functions in the module inherit the default; per-function overrides allowed. Inference validates: a `#Target(Wasm)` module calling a Browser-effect function is a compile error. Explicit, auditable, and no language-gate dependency (no comparison-operator or compiler-type-family changes required). Less magic than Option A for beginners; more auditable for large teams. Does not require amending D-EFF4. Compatible with D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 being raised later.

options.name: Defer web partitioning to Epoch 6
options.detail: Do not decide the JS/WASM boundary now. D-WEBKIND1 and D-JSBIND1 are unraised cards that must precede a sound partition model. D-EFF4 may need amending. D-SIGNAL1=A reactive primitives have no boundary model. D-PLUGIN1's Component Model may or may not compose with the web-backend WASM target. Deciding D-WASM1 before these gates produces a model that will be revised within the same epoch.
options.code:
// No web target partition policy yet.
// Epoch 6 revisit after D-WEBKIND1, D-JSBIND1, and D-EFF4 amendment are settled.

decisions.recReason: Effects already encode the information. Inference gives beginner magic and keeps target details out of normal Jet code; explicit markers remain possible later for exports, not partitioning every helper.
decisions.title: For the web backend, how does Jet partition JS DOM code and WASM logic while preserving expert control?
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: pure inference is not enough for experts. Best shape is inferred default plus explicit markers and a partition report. Compared with Next/SvelteKit, Jet should keep the magic boundary inference but add typed bridge/audit reports. Compared with wasm-bindgen, Jet should require less manual glue and own all diagnostics. Adversarial pass: override markers can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema rejects browser handles in WASM, checks bridgeable types/effects, emits a build manifest, and snapshots boundary diagnostics.
decisions.bestCurrent: SvelteKit / Next.js: Modern web frameworks infer client/server splits from imports and boundaries, minimizing manual export markers.
decisions.recommendation: Use effect inference by default plus module-level `#Target` controls (Option A). Pure B makes every beginner choose a target; hybrid A gives magic out of the box and expert visibility where teams need it.
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: We must ensure full expert control & auditability. Reconsider this ballot with devil's advocate, make it best in the world.
Agent answer: Updated. New rec: C, not pure inference. Default is inferred from effects and browser API use; experts can pin #Wasm, #Js, #WasmExport, then inspect `jet build --target web --explain-partition`. Devil's advocate: overrides can create unsound crossings. Patch: sema checks all boundary types/effects, rejects browser handles in WASM, emits a bridge manifest, snapshots boundary diagnostics.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): INFERENCE ENGINE GAP: D-EFF4 (ratified) closed the effect vocabulary at ten effects with no Browser/Dom entry; Option C inference has no implementation foundation without amending D-EFF4 or introducing a parallel ad-hoc tracking pass (I8 violation). Option F (add Browser effect) is the I8-coherent path. PURE ≠ WASM: #Pure (empty effect set) ≠ "WASM candidate" — wasm32-wasip2 allows Net/Fs effects in WASM; correct inference rule is "no Browser effect in transitive closure," blocked on D-WEBKIND1. CALLBACK BRIDGE MISSING: #WasmExport covers WASM→JS direction only; JS→WASM callbacks are absent from all options, gated on D-JSBIND1. D-PLUGIN1 COHERENCE: D-PLUGIN1=B (WASM Component Model) and this web-backend WASM model are two distinct incompatible WASM compile targets — neither ballot acknowledges the other.

log.text: Owner asked why not module-level declarations; Option A now includes module-level `#Target` as expert control while keeping inference default.
