decisions.gist: Rich reflection is already approved. This card decides whether `T.reflect()` returns one typed handle with methods, a variant description you pattern-match, or trait-gated reflection. The goal is derive authors reading fields, methods, generics, and markers without raw AST access.
decisions.story: Victor writes a `Codable` derive. For each field he needs the Jet field name, type, visibility, default marker, and rename marker. He should not parse source text or inspect generated Rust; he should ask the reflected type handle.

comparisons.note: Swift exposes reflection through `Mirror`, a single value describing children/labels/types.

options.name: One `TypeInfo` handle with typed metadata values (recommended)
options.detail: `T.reflect()` returns `TypeInfo`. It has methods like `.fields() -> [FieldInfo]`, `.methods() -> [MethodInfo]`, `.type_params()`, `.markers()`, `.implements(Trait)`. Each info value exposes typed methods, not open dictionaries.

options.name: Variant description tree
options.detail: `T.reflect()` returns a `TypeDescription` enum. Users dispatch on `.Struct`, `.Enum`, `.Primitive`, etc. This is precise, but every simple field loop starts with boilerplate.

options.name: Reflection as a trait
options.detail: Only types implementing `Reflect` expose metadata. This fits trait vocabulary, but makes reflection availability another derive/trait condition and conflicts with the goal that compiler-known type facts are always available to comptime derives.

decisions.recReason: One typed handle matches the ratified reflection direction and gives derive authors the shortest correct path. It exposes sema facts, not AST internals.
decisions.title: What shape does the typed reflection API return to comptime code?
decisions.explainer: D-METAREFLECT1 chose one reflected type handle, not AST injection. D-CTCODEGEN1 says generated code re-enters lexer/parser/sema, so reflection must expose sema-approved facts only. That means no raw parser nodes, no Rust types, and no untyped `Any` blob that makes derive authors guess. Examples use ratified Jet spellings: `comptime`, `::` bindings, `if subject == { }` style dispatch when needed.
decisions.bestCurrent: Swift: Swift exposes reflection through `Mirror`, a single value describing children/labels/types.
decisions.recommendation: Return one typed `TypeInfo` handle. Jet can make Swift-style reflection compile-time-only and strongly typed for derives.

decisions.gist: `#Reactive` is already the opt-in scope marker. This card decides the library vocabulary underneath it: mutable sources, derived values, and side-effect scopes. It should be one small API, not a second language.
decisions.story: Fiona writes a counter widget. `count` changes on click, `doubled` updates from `count`, and the label rerenders when either value changes. She should see exactly which values are mutable and which are derived.

comparisons.note: SolidJS has primitive signals, memos, and effects with fine-grained dependency tracking.

options.name: `Signal<T>` + `Computed<T>` + `Effect` (recommended)
options.detail: Three names for three jobs. `Signal` is mutable, `Computed` is read-only derived state, `Effect` is the runtime value created by `#Reactive`. Familiar from Preact/Solid/Vue while staying explicit.

options.name: `Cell<T>` + `derived` + `watch`
options.detail: More plain-English, spreadsheet-flavored names. Good beginner readability, but `Cell` already has meanings in Rust/interior mutability and spreadsheets; `watch` is less clearly a retained effect value.
options.code:
count :: Cell(0)
doubled :: derived(() => count.get() * 2)
watch(() => label.set_text(doubled.get().to_string()))

options.name: One `Reactive<T>` value with `.map()` / `.effect()`
options.detail: Fewer type names, but blurs mutable source, derived value, and effect lifetime. Harder diagnostics because every misuse is on one overloaded concept.
options.code:
count :: Reactive(0)
doubled :: count.map((n: Int) => n * 2)
doubled.effect((n: Int) => label.set_text(n.to_string()))

decisions.recReason: Three concrete types make dependency graph roles visible and keep diagnostics simple. `#Reactive` remains the only reactive syntax; the library handles graph mechanics.
decisions.title: What are the primitive `core.reactive` types under `#Reactive`?
decisions.explainer: Reactive code has three jobs: hold changing state, compute a value from other reactive reads, and rerun an effect when dependencies change. `#Reactive { }` should desugar to the effect job only; ordinary library types do the rest. Avoid syntax-shaped examples like `let` or operator lambdas that Jet has not ratified. This card is API naming, not new syntax.
decisions.bestCurrent: SolidJS: SolidJS has primitive signals, memos, and effects with fine-grained dependency tracking.
decisions.recommendation: Use `Signal<T>`, `Computed<T>`, and `Effect`. Jet should adopt the clearest fine-grained reactive triad and let `#Reactive` wire capture.

decisions.gist: M:N green threads are decided. This card chooses the runtime implementation behind blocking-looking socket/file APIs. It is not user syntax: user code keeps `task { }`, channels, and ordinary reads/writes.
decisions.story: Gary runs a chat server with 50,000 open TCP connections. Most sockets are idle. `socket.read()` should park the Jet task and free the OS thread until the socket is ready, without Gary learning epoll, kqueue, or IOCP.

comparisons.note: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.

options.name: Own platform-native backends (recommended)
options.detail: Implement Linux io_uring/epoll, macOS/BSD kqueue, and Windows IOCP behind one runtime trait. No external event-loop dependency. Highest ceiling and matches Go/BEAM shape: one scheduler, native pollers, task parking, timers, cancellation, and metrics under Jet control.

options.name: Own portable poller first
options.detail: Start with epoll/kqueue/IOCP readiness only; defer `io_uring` batching. Still no external dependency and simpler to test, but leaves Linux peak throughput on the table.

options.name: Use libuv through C FFI
options.detail: Battle-tested portability. Requires explicit owner approval for a runtime external C dependency and a system-library story. Good fallback if owned backends stall, but not the best Jet identity.

decisions.recReason: Owning native backends gives Jet the highest performance ceiling, no foreign event-loop dependency, and full observability/control for the task-scope/task runtime. It keeps the user surface unchanged while letting experts tune the runtime.
decisions.title: Which OS readiness backend parks M:N tasks on I/O?
decisions.explainer: The scheduler needs one park/wake layer per platform. The decision is between owning native backends, owning a lowest-common-denominator poller, or depending on libuv. I6 matters: compiler Source has zero external crates, and runtime-side deps still need owner approval. The E3 goal is better-than-Go networking, so the backend must support task-per-connection scale, O(ready events) wakeups, low allocation pressure, and runtime observability.
decisions.bestCurrent: Go: Go parks goroutines on epoll/kqueue/IOCP through platform-native netpollers, enabling high concurrency.
decisions.recommendation: Build own platform-native backends. Jet needs Go-class scaling as the floor and a higher ceiling through native pollers, structured cancellation, deadlines, and runtime metrics.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a structured select combinator for channels, timers, task handles, and I/O events?
decisions.gist: Select must provide a single, coherent construct that specifies what to wait for AND what to do when each arm fires. The open questions before any option is implementable: what type does the wait produce, how does the builder's lifetime bind to the taskgroup scope, and what label replaces the keyword-conflicting `as:`. A if-fused form that reuses ratified if-subject arm syntax may resolve all three without new surface.
decisions.explainer: Owner question answered: syntax should be cohesive with task scopes and avoid a second `case` mini-language. A scoped fluent builder keeps ownership under the nursery/taskgroup and lets losing waits deregister safely. Adversarial pass: fluent chains can get long and hide arm identity. Patch: formatter keeps one wait arm per line, every arm has an explicit result tag, and reusable select sets can become values later without new syntax.
decisions.story: I am writing a WebSocket hub. For each connection I need to react to whichever happens first: a client message, a broadcast channel message, a heartbeat timer, or server shutdown. I want one structured wait that cleans up the losing waits automatically.
decisions.inWild:
taskgroup g {
    ev :: g.select()
        .recv(inbox, as: .Message)
        .read(conn, as: .ClientData)
        .after(ms: 30_000, as: .Heartbeat)
        .cancelled(as: .Shutdown)
        .wait()?
    handle(ev)?
}
decisions.detail:
Owner Q: I like A but don't like the syntax. Please provide an updated ballot with more cohesive options and much better syntax.
Agent answer: Updated. New syntax recommendation: fluent scoped select, `g.select().recv(...).read(...).after(...).wait()?`. Avoids `case`/block syntax, keeps ownership under the taskgroup, gives each event an explicit result tag. Devil's advocate: fluent chains can get long. Patch: formatter keeps one arm per line, each arm has a stable typed result.

Adversarial pass (2026-06-28): (1) `as:` label is syntactically invalid — KW_AS is a reserved keyword in Syntax.rs; every Option A example needs a different label. (2) Option A's return type is unspecified — a blocking design gap that if-fused Option F resolves by inheriting match's existing type rules. (3) .cancelled() in Option A conflicts with D-DEADLINE1=A's #Context propagation — two mechanisms for the same cancellation event. (4) Select-vs-race boundary must be drawn explicitly (I8): if `select` can race task handles, `race(handles)` is redundant. (5) Option E's Epoch 6 target is a category error; E6 = CI/docs, not language surface features; correct target is E3 after D-NURSERY1 ships.

options.name: If-fused select: `if g.select() { .recv(ch) -> val: ...; }` (recommended)
options.detail: Reuse the ratified if-subject arm syntax (S68, D-IF1, D-MATCHARM1=A, D-MATCHARM2=B) directly as the select surface. `g.select()` is the match subject; each arm names the event source and binds the result inline. Arm handlers are co-located with their declarations. Return type is the union of the arm handler return types — exactly what match already computes (no new type rule needed). Taskgroup `g` owns registration; losing arms deregister when any arm fires. No new language statement (avoids the parser cost the current ballot assigns to the `select { }` block option). No reserved-word collision (`as:` is not used — arm binding is direct in the match form). Extensibility: any type implementing a `Selectable` trait is a valid arm source. Gate: D-NURSERY1 must ship first (taskgroup/nursery primitive must exist).

options.name: Fluent `g.select().recv(...).after(...).wait()?` builder
options.detail: No new language statement; scoped to the taskgroup. Four blocking design gaps must be resolved before implementation: (1) Return type of `.wait()` — pre-declared user enum, compiler-synthesized tagged union, or match extension; (2) `as:` label must be renamed (`as` is KW_AS, reserved); (3) Builder lifetime relative to taskgroup must be specified; (4) Select/race boundary must be drawn (which sources belong here vs `race/any/all`). These resolutions tend to converge toward the if-fused form (Option A).
options.code:
ev :: g.select()
    .recv(inbox, tag: .Message)    // "as:" renamed — KW_AS is reserved
    .read(socket, tag: .Data)
    .after(ms: 50, tag: .Timeout)
    .wait()?

options.name: Defer select to after D-NURSERY1 ships
options.detail: Do not add a select API until the taskgroup/nursery primitive is implemented and the runtime's event polling model is operational. Fallback: `race/all/any` over helper tasks, which incurs task-allocation overhead and is less ergonomic. The correct defer target is Epoch 3 after D-NURSERY1 ships — not Epoch 6 (which is CI/docs, not language surface).

comparisons.note: select is central to channels, cancellation, timers, and server loops. It is powerful but a distinct language statement.
tokio::select! handles futures and channels, but macro/future ceremony leaks into user code.
receive expresses actor mailbox selection; great for actors, less general for typed channels, timers, and native I/O under one model.
comparisons.code: receive Msg -> handle(Msg) after 5000 -> timeout end

decisions.bestCurrent: Go select proves event choice belongs in the core concurrency toolbox; Tokio select proves the same need for async runtimes.
decisions.recommendation: If-fused select using the ratified if-subject arm syntax — no new language statement, return type resolved, no keyword conflicts (Option A). Option B (fluent builder) has four unresolved design gaps that converge on the same design anyway.

decisions.title: What spelling should Jet use for the scoped task group?
decisions.gist: The model needs a lexical scope that owns child tasks, but the word `nursery` may be too borrowed and obscure. This decision chooses the final user-facing spelling.
decisions.explainer: `nursery` is precise in Trio, but it is not obvious to most programmers and does not read like Jet systems-language product copy. The concept should survive; the word should be challenged. The spelling should make three facts visible: this is about tasks, it is a group/scope, and child work is owned until scope exit. The choice must not introduce a second spawn model or imply actor supervision unless that is really what it does.
decisions.story: I am new to Jet and I see a block that spawns three API calls. I should understand from the keyword that this block owns a group of tasks and waits/cancels them at the end, without knowing Trio history.

options.name: `taskgroup g { ... }` (recommended)
options.detail: One keyword that says exactly what the construct owns: a group of tasks. It is plain, searchable, close to Swift TaskGroup terminology, and avoids importing Trio jargon. It keeps `task { }` visually related to the scoped form. Downside: compound keyword is less pretty than a short word.

options.name: `task group g { ... }`
options.detail: Most readable English and clearly related to `task`. Downside: two-word keyword phrase adds parser/teaching weight and can look like a declaration rather than a control construct.

options.name: `scope g { ... }`
options.detail: Short and general. Downside: too vague; Jet will have many scopes, and this hides that the construct owns concurrent tasks.

options.name: `nursery n { ... }`
options.detail: Best-known term in structured-concurrency literature through Trio. Downside: obscure to non-Trio users, not self-describing, and product-language mismatch for Jet.

options.name: `with tasks g { ... }`
options.detail: Reads naturally and emphasizes a scoped region. Downside: adds or overloads `with`; less direct as a named API receiver for combinators.

comparisons.note: TaskGroup is mainstream and directly names the idea: a group of child tasks with scoped lifetime.
Nursery is semantically strong but jargon-heavy outside Trio.
coroutineScope is accurate but tied to coroutine vocabulary Jet is intentionally hiding from beginners.

decisions.bestCurrent: Swift TaskGroup has the clearest mainstream name; Trio nursery has the strongest semantics but weaker product language.
decisions.recommendation: Use `taskgroup g { ... }` unless the owner prefers another spelling. It keeps the task relationship obvious and avoids Trio-specific vocabulary.

decisions.title: Should workspace resolution write a separate `.jet/workspace.lock` or fold into unified `.jet/lock`?
decisions.gist: Workspace member discovery needs one durable lock location. A separate workspace lock duplicates package locking; a unified `.jet/lock` keeps one source of reproducibility truth.
decisions.explainer: D-WORKSPACE1/B chose `pack.jet payload:` instead of a new `workspace.jet` file, so the lock should follow the same I8 logic: one package/workspace graph, one lock. The only reason to split is if workspace member discovery has a different lifecycle from dependency resolution. Splitting creates two files CI must validate and two stale states users must debug.
decisions.story: Mara opens a monorepo and runs `jet test`. She wants one lockfile checked into review that tells CI exactly which payload members and dependencies were used, without learning whether a change belongs in package lock or workspace lock.
decisions.inWild:
# pack.jet
[payload]
members = find("./packages")

# recommended lock result:
.jet/lock   # contains dependency pins plus normalized payload-member graph

options.name: Fold workspace graph into unified `.jet/lock` (recommended)
options.detail: One `.jet/lock` file stores dependency pins, payload member paths (normalized), sparse-subtree metadata, and comptime member-expression inputs. Matches D-WORKSPACE1=B: no new workspace file, no new lock file. CI validates one lock with `jet fetch --locked`. Consistent with Cargo (one Cargo.lock for the whole workspace) and pnpm (one pnpm-lock.yaml). When the member expression is a comptime `find()`, the lock records the discovered paths so future builds are hermetic without re-evaluating the expression.
options.code:
# pack.jet
[payload]
members = find("./packages")

# .jet/lock  (one file covers everything)
[workspace]
members = ["packages/a", "packages/b"]  # normalized from find() at lock time

[deps]
core = "1.4.2"

$ jet fetch --locked  # validates both sections

options.name: Separate `.jet/workspace.lock`
options.detail: Workspace member discovery gets its own lock file, distinct from `.jet/lock` which covers dependencies. Isolates member-list churn from dep pins, but creates two sources of truth and two failure modes under `--locked`. Reviewers must understand which lock to check for which change.
options.code:
.jet/lock           # dependency pins
.jet/workspace.lock  # member paths

options.name: Defer member-expression locking — explicit lists only for now
options.detail: Support only explicit member lists (no `find()`/comptime discovery) until D-CTMARKER1/D-CTEFFECT1 implementation lands. Avoids choosing lock shape for computed members now. Blocks the full D-WORKSPACE1=B surface.
options.code:
# only explicit members for now
[payload]
members = ["packages/a", "packages/b"]
# Epoch 3 revisit: find() members + .jet/lock recording

comparisons.note: One Cargo.lock records the whole workspace dependency graph, not a separate workspace lock.
One pnpm-lock.yaml includes workspace package graph and dependency resolution together.

decisions.bestCurrent: Cargo/pnpm: one lockfile covers the complete workspace graph.
decisions.recommendation: Fold workspace member graph into unified `.jet/lock` — one reproducibility file, one CI gate (Option A). I8: one lock mechanism covers both dependency pins and payload-member discovery.

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: What is the ratified syntax and access gate for labeled stored-reference fields?
decisions.gist: Stored reference fields let structs carry zero-copy views into owner values; owner selected marker syntax `#Ref(Label)`.
decisions.explainer: The recovered #100 concern is not an unresolved dangling-reference bug. E2-M5 hardened stored refs. The remaining issue is governance: `ref[label] field: T` is user-typeable, documented by diagnostics, and absent from syntax-decisions.md. I7 requires every keyword/sigil to have a decision ID. This ballot either ratifies that syntax, replaces it, or removes it until a better tier-2 stored-reference model exists.
decisions.story: Earl builds a parser over a large input buffer. He wants tokens and slices to point into that buffer without allocating new strings, while the compiler still proves the buffer outlives every view.

options.name: Ratify `ref[label] field: T` behind `use core.mem` (recommended)
options.detail: Purpose: this is for structs that store a view into another value, e.g. parser tokens pointing into an input buffer, graph edges pointing into arena-owned nodes, or zero-copy packet/header views. The normal Jet memory model lets functions borrow during a call, but v1 intentionally disallows storing/returning references in beginner code. `ref[label] field: T` is the expert-tier opt-in that exposes that power while naming the owner relationship. It does not make unsafe memory possible by itself; sema must still reject dangling/escaping views. Gate it behind `use core.mem` so beginners never encounter stored-reference vocabulary accidentally.

options.name: `#Ref(Label)` field marker, no import gate (ratified)
options.detail: Stored reference fields use normal Jet marker syntax on the field: `#Ref(arena) name: T`. The label names the owner relationship sema must prove. No `use core.mem` gate is required per owner choice; safety still comes from sema rejecting dangling or escaping views. This gives experts zero-copy stored views that call-time `&`/`~` capabilities cannot express, while avoiding a new bracket keyword form.

options.name: Remove labeled ref fields until tier-2 references are redesigned
options.detail: Delete or hide current syntax and diagnostics until a full tier-2 stored-reference model is designed. Avoids ratifying a syntax that may need to change when the broader owned/borrowed reference system (post-v1) is specified. Breaks existing examples and tests that use `ref[label]`.
options.code: // no stored reference fields until tier-2 reference model is designed

comparisons.note: Rust encodes stored-reference relationships with lifetimes; Jet intentionally has no lifetime syntax in v1.
Swift mostly avoids stored borrowed references in safe user code; ownership features are explicit advanced syntax.

decisions.bestCurrent: Rust proves stored references need explicit relationship tracking; Jet should keep that explicit but hide it behind an expert gate.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: use `#Ref(Label)` on the field, with no `use core.mem` gate (Option B as amended).

log.text: Owner amendment applied: stored-ref fields use `#Ref(Label)` syntax.
Owner asked purpose/control question; ballot expanded to explain zero-copy stored views and why call-time capabilities are insufficient.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.comment: Use syntax `#Ref(Label)` instead of `ref[label]`; no import gate.

decisions.title: Reopen C FFI syntax or keep S59/D-CFFI2-SYN?
decisions.gist: C FFI syntax is already ratified. This decides whether `#Lang_C`-style blocks are better enough to reopen that surface.
decisions.explainer: C FFI syntax is already ratified. This decides whether `#Lang_C`-style blocks are better enough to reopen that surface. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A systems programmer binds a small C header. They want the boundary to read clearly as C interop without importing C syntax into normal Jet code.

options.name: Keep C FFI, but spell blocks `#Extern module` (ratified)
options.detail: Keep the ratified C FFI model (`use c.<lib> as alias`, generated bindings, same safety gates) but update the marker spelling to Jet-canonical `#Extern module`, per owner comment. This preserves one C-binding mechanism while aligning with PascalCase marker syntax; `@extern` becomes retired teaching syntax.

options.name: Add `#Lang_C { ... }` C-FFI block
options.detail: A marker block visually names the foreign language. Risk: looks like a syntax island and may imply raw C declarations parse inside Jet braces (they do not). I8 concern: `#Lang_C { }` and `@extern module` both declare C bindings — two mechanisms for one job. Only justified if user research shows `@extern module` is consistently misread.

options.name: Docs-only: teach "C binding block" terminology without new syntax
options.detail: Keep current syntax; rename the docs section and examples to use "C binding block" as the teaching term. No syntax change, no I8 cost. Correct if the issue is terminology, not syntax.
options.code:
// docs: "C binding block"
@extern module libc { fn puts(s: *U8) -> Int }

comparisons.note: Existing ratified decisions are the baseline; reopening needs a clear safety/readability win.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Ratified owner amendment: keep the existing C FFI model, but spell the binding block `#Extern module`, not `@extern module`.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a compact counted-loop header with semicolon-separated parts?
decisions.gist: The question is not `for` as an alias; it is whether loop setup, bound, and increment need a compact header form.
decisions.explainer: Jet already chose one `loop` keyword and no visible semicolons. This decides whether Odin-style `for`/`;` loop headers are worth reopening. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: Hank writes a byte scanner. He wants one line to name the index, set its bounds, and say how it advances. A beginner should still understand which part starts the loop, which part stops it, and which part changes each turn.
decisions.inWild:
loop i in 0..len step 4 { scan(bytes[i]) }

loop i := 0; i < len; i += 4 { scan(bytes[i]) }

options.name: Keep range + `step` as the compact counted loop (recommended)
options.detail: Preserve the ratified shape: `loop i in start..end step n`. It already gives a one-line iterator variable, range, and increment for the common counted-loop case, without making semicolons user-visible. More complex state changes stay in the loop body where they are explicit.

options.name: Add a semicolon header under `loop`
options.detail: Keep Jet's `loop` keyword, but allow a C/Odin-style counted header: initializer; condition; afterthought. Semicolons would be legal only inside this header, not as statement separators. This gives experts compact control over non-range increments, but it creates a second counted-loop mechanism beside `loop i in range step n`.

options.name: Add a named-header form without semicolons
options.detail: Use labels inside the loop header instead of punctuation: `from`, `while`, and `step` name the same three jobs. This keeps visible semicolons out of Jet, but adds new contextual words and still overlaps with the current range form.

options.name: Expert-only counted loop marker
options.detail: Keep beginner loops unchanged and put arbitrary counted headers behind an explicit expert marker, e.g. `#Counted loop init; cond; step`. This surfaces the control when needed without making it the everyday loop form, but it is heavier and still spends semicolon syntax.

comparisons.note: One `loop` keyword; counted loops use inclusive ranges and `step`.
Initializer, condition, and afterthought share one header separated by semicolons.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Keep `loop i in range step n` as the compact counted-loop path (Option A). It already carries iterator, bounds, and increment in one line while preserving Jet's no-visible-semicolon rule. Option B is the direct answer if the owner wants full C/Odin header control.

log.text: Owner clarified the proposal: semicolon-separated loop header parts, not a `for` alias. Ballot rebuilt around compact counted-loop syntax.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Should Jet support switch/case fallthrough?
decisions.gist: Jet rejected C-style `switch`/`case` and uses multi-arm `if`. This decides whether fallthrough exists at all or grouped arms are the only path.
decisions.explainer: Jet rejected C-style `switch`/`case` and uses multi-arm `if`. This decides whether fallthrough exists at all or grouped arms are the only path. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A C programmer wants two HTTP status codes to share handling. Jet should make the shared handling obvious without hidden control flow from one arm into the next.

options.name: No fallthrough; shared handling via grouped arms (recommended)
options.detail: Jet's multi-arm if syntax (`400 | 404 -> handle_client()`) handles all cases where C fallthrough is used for shared logic — with no implicit fall-through, no hidden control flow, and exhaustiveness checked. Do not add `fallthrough`. Teaching: when a C programmer asks "how do I fall through?", the diagnostic or docs point to the grouped-arm form. This is unambiguously the safer, cleaner path.

options.name: Explicit `fallthrough` statement
options.detail: Allow an arm to jump into the next arm only when it writes `fallthrough`. Familiar to switch users who expect it, but adds a second control-flow edge (arms can now have two exits), complicates exhaustiveness analysis, and reintroduces a class of bugs (wrong arm order changes behavior silently). Only justified if a use case cannot be expressed with grouped arms — which has not been demonstrated.
options.code:
400 -> { log("client"); fallthrough }
404 -> handle_client()

options.name: Reopen `switch/case/default` with fallthrough semantics
options.detail: Bring back switch vocabulary, case arms, and optional fallthrough. Conflicts with S24/D-IF1 teaching policy, adds a third pattern-dispatch surface (I8), and brings C fallthrough's bug class back into the language. Not recommended under any circumstances — this is the pattern Jet's multi-arm if was designed to replace.

comparisons.note: Existing ratified decisions are the baseline; reopening needs a clear safety/readability win.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: No fallthrough — grouped arms (`400 | 404 -> ...`) cover all shared-handling use cases safely (Option A). C-style fallthrough is a well-documented footgun; Jet eliminated it intentionally.

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.title: Does Jet need general union types or `Any`, and how should dynamic cases be served?
decisions.gist: Jet already has enums, optionals, fallible values, generics, traits, and data values. This decides whether to add a general dynamic escape or keep unions closed and explicit.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has enums, optionals, fallible values, generics, traits, and data values. This decides whether to add a general dynamic escape or keep unions closed and explicit. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: A library author parses JSON and plugin messages. Some values are only known at runtime, but most app code should stay statically typed and beginner-safe.

options.name: No general `Any`; document the correct mechanism per use case (recommended)
options.detail: Jet already has: closed unions via enums (JSON parsing, plugin messages), polymorphism via traits/generics (algorithm abstraction), absence via T? and T?E, and data values (DataTree from D-SERDE2) for truly dynamic untyped trees. A general `Any` top type adds a second optional-like mechanism (I8) and a second polymorphism mechanism (I8), while weakening static guarantees for beginners. The correct path: a compiler diagnostic that recognizes "I need to hold anything" patterns and points at the right tool for the specific use case.

options.name: Closed union type syntax
options.detail: A type-level syntax for a fixed set of alternatives: `Int | String`. More compact than defining an enum for short-lived unions. Risk: overlaps with enum (I8: two ways to define closed unions), and pattern matching rules must extend to the union form. Only justified if enum definition for 2-3 variant unions is demonstrably too verbose in common code.

options.name: `Any` only at interop/dynamic-data boundaries (expert-gated)
options.detail: A boxed dynamic value (like DataTree but for arbitrary types) gated behind `use core.interop`. Required explicit downcast before use; compile error outside interop scope. The narrowest possible escape hatch for FFI/plugin/serde edges. Distinct from D (full Any): upcasting to Any requires explicit invocation; the beginner surface is untouched. Only justified if DataTree + enums provably cannot cover a critical interop use case.

comparisons.note: `any` is the default escape for JS interop and gradual migration; `unknown` is the safer closed form requiring narrowing before use.
comparisons.code:
function handle(x: any) { return x.foo }  // no error
function safe(x: unknown) { return (x as {foo: string}).foo }

comparisons.note: Pre-generics, `interface{}`/`any` was the only way to write generic containers and JSON boundaries; post-generics it shrank but never disappeared at FFI/JSON edges.
`Any`/`AnyObject` for heterogeneous collections and ObjC interop; app code is encouraged toward typed enums/protocols instead.
comparisons.code:
let items: [Any] = [1, "hi", UIView()]
let n = items[0] as? Int

comparisons.note: No std `Any` top type for years; `dyn Trait` for open polymorphism, `enum`/`serde_json::Value` for closed/dynamic data. `Box<dyn Any>` exists but is niche (type-id downcasts).
comparisons.code:
enum Value { Null, Bool(bool), Number(f64), String(String) }
// or trait objects: Box<dyn Display>

comparisons.note: `Any`/`Object` is the root of the class hierarchy — every reference type is implicitly an `Any`, which powers collections and reflection but erases static guarantees.
comparisons.code:
val list: List<Any> = listOf(1, "x")
val s = list[1] as String

comparisons.note: Dynamic trees via `Data`/`DataTree`; closed sums via enums (+ ratified `A | B` unions); open polymorphism via traits/generics; absence via `T?`; interop stays explicit.

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: No general `Any` — existing mechanisms (enums, traits, generics, T?, data values) cover all dynamic cases without a top type (Option A).

log.text: Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.
Owner question q5lq42z answered: cross-language Any survey, benefits/detriment analysis, devil's advocate pass. Comparisons facet expanded.

decisions.title: Keep Jet fallback control flow or add an Odin-style `or_` suite?
decisions.gist: Odin has a family of `or_` control operators; this maps each case to today's Jet and decides whether Jet needs another family.
decisions.explainer: Jet already has `?? return` for fallback/early return. This decides whether an Odin-style `or_return` spelling adds clarity or just a second way to mean it. The ballot is a proceed/reopen check so tomorrow's agents know whether to implement, document, or leave the existing design alone.
decisions.story: Mara writes a log shipper. Missing config should use a default, bad records should skip the current loop turn, a closed stream should break the loop, and startup failure should return from the function. She needs the error path to stay visible without learning four unrelated spellings.

options.name: Keep Jet's existing fallback/control suite (recommended)
options.detail: Do not add Odin-style `or_` words. Jet already covers the suite with one fallback operator plus control words: value fallback is `x ?? default`, early return is `x ?? return value`, loop break is `x ?? break`, loop continue is the ratified loop shorthand `x?continue`, and normal propagation remains `x?`. The only rough edge is documentation: the ballot now names the whole map so users are not left comparing only `or_return`.

options.name: Unify all local exits under `?? <control>`
options.detail: Keep `??` as the single fallback operator, but complete the control-word family so loop skip is `x ?? continue` instead of the special `?continue`. Then fallback, return, break, and continue all read as "use the value, or do this control action." This is the most Jet-shaped path if the current `?continue` shorthand feels like an exception.

options.name: Add explicit `or_*` keywords as teaching-only diagnostics
options.detail: Reserve/recognize `or_return`, `or_break`, `or_continue`, and `or_else` only to emit teaching errors that point at the Jet spelling. No accepted second spelling reaches formatted source. This helps Odin users migrate while preserving I8.

options.name: Accept an Odin-style `or_*` suite as real syntax
options.detail: Add `or_else`, `or_return`, `or_break`, and `or_continue` as accepted postfix forms. This is familiar to Odin users and very explicit, but it duplicates `??`, `?`, and `?continue` semantics with another family of spellings. It should only win if the owner chooses that readability over the one-path rule for error control.

comparisons.note: Uses `or_`-style postfix control helpers around optional/error-returning operations.
`??` is the fallback operator; `?` propagates; loop skip has ratified `?continue`.
comparisons.code:
value :: parse(raw)?continue
other :: parse(raw) ?? return fallback

decisions.bestCurrent: Jet ratified surface unless this ballot identifies a stronger beginner-safe, one-path design.
decisions.recommendation: Keep Jet's existing suite (Option A): it covers fallback, return, break, continue, and propagation without adding a second family. If the `?continue` exception bothers us, Option B is the cohesive Jet-shaped amendment.

log.text: Owner asked for the whole Odin-style `or_` suite; ballot expanded to map fallback/return/break/continue/propagation and added cohesive Jet alternatives.
Ballot tightened: collapsed to 3 options, Option A is the unified optimal recommendation, rec set to A.

decisions.bestCurrent: No ratified decision yet.
decisions.recommendation: Use a closed ABI-safe subset with generated adapters (Option A).

decisions.title: What types may cross the JS/WASM boundary?
decisions.gist: The web backend needs a stable ABI for values crossing between generated JS and WASM.
decisions.story: Nora builds a dashboard. UI events begin in JS, heavy filtering runs in WASM, and typed results return to the view without losing Jet safety.

decisions.gist: A11y-by-default should combine beginner magic with expert control: built-in components infer roles automatically, custom interactive components must declare or derive a typed role, and experts can override deliberately.

decisions.title: Retire S25 `||` comparison-distribution shorthand?
decisions.gist: Ratify that `||` no longer distributes comparisons; comparator value alternatives use single `|` (`x == 1 | 2`) in arm heads, while `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` remain boolean arm conditions.
decisions.explainer:
S25 was ratified on 2026-06-11 as “comparison distribution”: inside a boolean chain, a bare value to the right of a comparison reused the nearest comparison on its left. The old spelling used boolean operators, e.g. `status == 400 || 404` meant `status == 400 || status == 404`. This ballot retires that `||`/`&&` distribution rule.

Ratified shape: single `|` is the value/pattern-alternative separator against the comparator, e.g. `status == 400 | 404 ->` in an arm head. `||` and `&&` do not distribute comparisons; they combine full boolean expressions/guards. `==` and `!=` remain explicit boolean comparisons/guards in arm heads.
decisions.story: A reader sees `status == 400 || 404` and should not have to know that `404` secretly reuses `status ==`. Retiring S25 makes `||` a boolean operator only. The compact comparator-alternate form is still available where Jet pattern matching lives: `status == 400 | 404 ->` or, under an inferred comparator, `400 | 404 ->`.

options.name: Retire S25 `||` distribution (recommended)
options.detail: Delete comparison distribution from `||`/`&&`. Write full boolean comparisons in ordinary expressions. Keep single `|` for value/pattern alternatives against the comparator in arm heads, and keep `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` as boolean condition syntax inside arm heads.

options.name: Keep S25 expression shorthand
options.detail: Allow bare values in `||`/`&&` chains to reuse the nearest comparison. Compact, but `||`/`&&` would carry a Jet-only value-distribution rule instead of being boolean-only. Arm `|` alternatives and arm boolean guards still stay exactly as described above.

options.name: Retire S25 and design membership later
options.detail: Remove S25 `||`/`&&` distribution now, then separately decide whether Jet needs `in`/set/range membership sugar for common equality lists. This still preserves arm `|` alternatives and arm boolean guards.

comparisons.note: D-MATCHARM1/2 uses single `|` for alternatives against the comparator in arm heads and `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` for boolean arm conditions; retiring S25 keeps that compact arm syntax but removes hidden comparison reuse from `||`/`&&`.
Boolean operators combine Bool expressions only; repeated comparisons are explicit unless a separate membership operator exists.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified: retire S25 `||`/`&&` comparison distribution; comparator alternatives are single `|` (`x == 1 | 2`), not `||`.

log.text: Owner ratified A and clarified comparator alternatives are `x == 1 | 2`, not `x == 1 || 2`.
Clarified scope: ballot only retires ordinary-expression S25 shorthand; arm `|` alternatives and `&&`/`||`/`==`/`!=` boolean arm conditions are explicit non-goals.

Question answered and ballot expanded: S25 defined as comparison distribution with before/after examples.

#[Deserialize]

options.name: Codable/Encode/Decode only (recommended)
options.detail: Use Jet-native vocabulary. Delete Serialize and Deserialize syntax docs/tests until any post-Epoch 6 compatibility pass.
options.code:
#[Codable]
struct User { name: String }

options.name: Keep Serialize aliases
options.detail: Accept foreign-language trait names as aliases.
options.code:
#[Serialize]
struct User { name: String }

options.name: Split roles
options.detail: Use Codable for automatic derivation and Serialize for manual trait implementation, creating naming overlap.
options.code:
#[Codable]
impl User.Serialize { ... }

comparisons.note: Serialization vocabulary is user-facing product language; foreign aliases add little and teach another ecosystem.
comparisons.code: I8: one way to mean it. I4: every diagnostic needs snapshot coverage.

log.text: Raised from owner request for latest syntax guidance before reconciliation.

decisions.title: Counted loop separator: what replaces semicolons?
decisions.gist: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C retired semicolons from counted loop headers; pick the replacement separator.
decisions.explainer: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C kept compact counted loops but deferred the separator choice. The ratified S6-R law bans visible semicolons; we need a different separator for the three-part header (init; condition; afterthought).
decisions.story: Gerald is porting a tight inner loop from C and wants the three-part form. He knows Jet has no semicolons, so he needs to know exactly what punctuation to type between the init, condition, and step.

comparisons.note: Semicolons in for-loop header
Semicolons in for-loop header
No three-part for; use while
comparisons.code: var i = 0; while i < n { i += 1 }

options.name: Comma separator (recommended)
options.detail: Use commas between the three parts. Commas already appear in function call arguments and tuple construction; reusing them here keeps the punctuation vocabulary small. The header reads left-to-right with natural pauses.
options.code:
loop i := 0, i < n, i += 1 { process(buf[i]) }
loop i := len, i > 0, i -= 1 { drain(q[i]) }

options.name: Keyword separators (while/step)
options.detail: Use keywords: . Self-documenting but verbose; adds two reserved words or repurposes existing ones.
options.code: loop i := 0 while i < n step i += 1 { process(buf[i]) }

options.name: Retire three-part form entirely
options.detail: Remove the three-part header. All counted loops use range iteration  or manual . Porting C loops requires rewriting them as range loops.

log.text: Raised as follow-up to D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1=C (redesign counted loop separator).
Closed as superseded — D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 reversed to A (keep semicolons).

decisions.comment: Superseded: D-LOOP-SEMICOLON1 reversed to A — semicolons stay. No separator redesign needed.

decisions.title: Ratify the two language gates required for D-LAYOUT1 option A?
decisions.gist: D-LAYOUT1=A needs two compiler extensions: comparison ops that return Constraint on layout types, and axis-typed layout variables in the closed type family.
decisions.explainer: D-LAYOUT1 ratified option A (typed-axis layout block) conditionally on two compiler language gates. If both gates are ratified here, the full design ships. If either is declined, core.layout falls back to a method-only builder (D-LAYOUT1 option B), which is implementable today without any language change.
decisions.story: Sandra is building a form layout. She wants to write  and have Jet catch  (cross-axis mix) as a compile error. Both features require the compiler to treat layout variable types specially.

comparisons.note: Uses NSLayoutConstraint builder; no axis safety
frame/padding modifiers; no constraint model

options.name: Ratify both gates — ship full typed-axis layout (recommended)
options.detail: GATE 1: comparison operators (>=, ==, <=) may return Constraint (not Bool) when both operands are closed layout variable types (HVar, VVar, LengthVar). Like D-SIMD2's closed-operator blessing, this is limited to the compiler-provided family only. GATE 2: HVar, VVar, LengthVar, Constraint, and LayoutHandle enter the compiler's closed type family (recognized by core_type_known). Both gates are tightly scoped and follow existing precedent (SIMD/D-SIMD2, distinct types/D-DIST2).

options.name: Decline gates — use method-only builder
options.detail: Keep comparison operators Bool-only and keep the closed type family as-is. core.layout ships as a method-only builder (no layout {} block, no axis safety). Implementable today with no language change. Axis errors are runtime conflicts, not compile errors.

log.text: Raised as follow-up to D-LAYOUT1=A (two language gates required to implement full design).

decisions.title: External inherent method spelling
decisions.gist: Pick the syntax for adding methods to a type outside its definition block.
decisions.story: Betty is writing a geometry library. She defines Point in geometry/types.jet and wants to add a dist() method in geometry/ops.jet without reopening the original file. What does she write?

options.name: Keep S83 ~~: fn Point~~dist(self, other: Point)
options.detail: S83 ratified ~~ for ALL external defs. D-IMPLDOT1 retired it for trait-impls only. Keeping it here means two external connectors exist: ~~ for inherent methods, . for trait impls. Single unusual token users must memorize.

options.name: fn Point.dist(self, other: Point) — mirrors D-IMPLDOT1 (recommended)
options.detail: Uses the same . connector D-IMPLDOT1 chose for impl Point.Trait. One external-attach connector for everything: inherent methods, trait impls, forwarding. fn keyword + PascalCase type name prevents any ambiguity with a call (p.dist()) — a call cannot have a capital first segment.

options.name: extend Point { fn dist(self, other: Point) }
options.detail: Groups methods in a named block like Swift extension or Kotlin companion. Clear at a glance. Adds a second block keyword beside impl — users must now pick between extend Type {} and impl Type.Trait {}, two block forms that look similar.

options.name: No external inherent methods — trait impls only
options.detail: Conflicts with ratified philosophy.md which explicitly says inline and external are two entry points of one feature. Not recommended.
options.code: // blocked — users must define all methods in the struct body or use a trait

decisions.title: How comptime block exposes values for runtime splice
decisions.gist: Does a comptime {} block expose its computed values to runtime code via $name?
decisions.story: Earl is building a tiny VM. He wants to compute an opcode dispatch table size at compile time inside a comptime {} block, then use that constant in runtime code — checked at the call site — via a $TABLE_SIZE splice.

options.name: Block-local comptime bindings leak into the enclosing scope (recommended)
options.detail: Consistent with how comptime if already works (D-WHEN1): bindings defined in comptime if arms are visible after. The block is erased at codegen; only the serialized literals from $name splices appear in output. Scope leak is bounded to comptime bindings declared directly in the block body.

options.name: Explicit expose NAME inside block marks which values escape
options.detail: Most explicit about what crosses the build/runtime boundary. Introduces a second way to declare visibility inside a block (alongside comptime NAME).

options.name: $name stays comptime-only; block exposes nothing
options.detail: Conservative — comptime {} remains a build-time assertion/side-effect block only. $name keeps working inside derive bodies and comptime binding RHS but not in runtime code. The feature is mostly already shipped.

decisions.comparisons:
Zig:       comptime { const N = 64; }  // comptime vars always accessible in enclosing scope
Rust:      const N: usize = 64;          // top-level const, no block scoping
C++:       constexpr int N = 64;         // same — top-level
Nim:       const N {.compileTime.} = 64  // pragma-gated but still top-level
D:         enum N = 64;                  // compile-time constant, no block

decisions.title: UI tree node shape: typed enum vs dynamic record
decisions.gist: Should UI view-model nodes be a typed enum (Text, Box, Button) or a dynamic tagged record?
decisions.story: Dorothy is building a to-do app. She needs text labels, containers, buttons, and input fields. She wants the compiler to catch a typo in a node kind at build time, not at runtime.

options.name: Typed constructors: ui.text(), ui.box(), ui.button() (recommended)
options.detail: Each node kind is a distinct constructor. The compiler knows statically that ui.button() produces a button node and ui.text() produces a text node. No stringly-typed fields, no runtime kind-check. Consistent with closed-type direction.

options.name: Dynamic tagged record: ui.node({ kind: "text", content: "..." })
options.detail: A single ui.node() function accepts a record with a "kind" string field. Flexible for dynamic node creation but kind typos are runtime errors. Inconsistent with Jet's static-safety direction.

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:      Text("hello") / VStack { ... } / Button("ok") {}  — typed constructors, each is a distinct type
Flutter:      Text("hello") / Column(children:[...]) / ElevatedButton(...)  — same pattern
React JSX:    <Text>hello</Text> / <View> / <Pressable>  — tagged strings compiled to typed calls
HTML:         <div> / <span> / <button>  — string tags, no compile-time kind checking
Android XML:  android:layout_width="match_parent"  — string attributes

decisions.title: Style API shape: flat record vs builder chain
decisions.gist: Should ui.Style be a flat value record or a builder-method chain?
decisions.story: Walter is styling a submit button: red background, white text, 12px padding, 80px wide. He wants to define the style as a reusable constant and pass it to multiple buttons.

options.name: Flat value record: Style { color: rgb(255,0,0), width: px(80) } (recommended)
options.detail: Style is a pure value — comparable, hashable, passable as a constant. Consistent with Jet's value semantics: no mutable builder state, no object identity, no method chain side effects. A partial style (only some fields set) uses default values for the rest.

options.name: Builder chain: Style.new().color(rgb(255,0,0)).width(px(80))
options.detail: Familiar from many UI frameworks but introduces mutable builder state. A Style mid-chain is not a value — you cannot store it, compare it, or pass it without calling a terminating method. Inconsistent with Jet's value-oriented surface.
options.code:
// Not easily reusable as a constant:
SUBMIT_STYLE :: Style.new()
    .background(rgb(220, 38, 38))
    .color(rgb(255, 255, 255))
    .padding(px(12))
    .width(px(80))
    .build()   // or is this the value? when is it a value?

decisions.comparisons:
SwiftUI:     Text("hi").foregroundColor(.red).frame(width: 80)  — builder chain on the node, not style
Flutter:     TextStyle(color: Colors.red, fontSize: 16)              — flat struct
CSS:         { background: red; width: 80px; padding: 12px }        — flat key-value
Tailwind:    "bg-red-500 text-white p-3 w-20"                       — string class list
React:       {{ backgroundColor: 'red', width: 80, padding: 12 }}   — plain object
SwiftUI (StyleSheet): not idiomatic — styles via modifiers on views

decisions.title: Motion timing: injectable Clock vs global time signal
decisions.gist: Does core.motion.spring() take a Clock capability parameter, or does it read a global time signal?
decisions.story: Doris is building a loading spinner that animates with a spring. She needs to write a unit test that asserts the spinner reaches its target position after 300ms — without waiting 300 real milliseconds.

options.name: Injectable Clock: spring(target, clock, stiffness, damping) (recommended)
options.detail: Clock is passed in explicitly. Tests inject FakeClock.new() and call clock.advance(ms) for deterministic results. Production code passes the real system clock. Consistent with D-DET1 (all time/randomness is injectable). Flutter uses the same pattern (TickerProvider).

options.name: Global time signal: core.motion.time_signal() read internally
options.detail: Motion reads a module-level time signal automatically. Simpler call site but tests must stub the global, which requires framework-level mocking support (jest.useFakeTimers equivalent). Less consistent with D-DET1.

decisions.comparisons:
React Spring:   useSpring({ from: {x:0}, to: {x:1} })          — global RAF/time; not testable without mocking
Framer Motion:  useAnimate(), animate(el, {x:1}, {duration:0.3}) — global time; testing needs jest fake timers
SwiftUI:        withAnimation(.spring()) { state = 1 }           — global CADisplayLink; XCTest uses waitFor
GSAP:           gsap.to(el, {x:1, ease:"elastic.out"})          — global ticker; test with gsap.ticker.tick()
Flutter:        AnimationController(vsync: this, duration: ...)  — vsync injected via TickerProvider (close to option A)

decisions.title: A11y diagnostic gating mechanism
decisions.gist: How are accessibility diagnostics triggered — automatic on --release, explicit jet lint --a11y, or per-file #A11yStrict?
decisions.story: Hank's team ships a web app. He wants his CI to catch missing ARIA roles and unlabeled buttons before they reach users. But he doesn't want beginners running jet build to see a wall of a11y warnings on their first hello-world.

options.name: --release build flag enables a11y lints automatically
options.detail: Hank runs jet build --release for production and a11y lints fire automatically. But a beginner who runs jet build --release for their first deployed app also sees a wall of a11y errors on components they didn't write. Surprise on first real build.
options.code:
jet build --release
# output includes:
# W2930: button "X" has no accessible label (E2930)
# W2931: ui.text used as interactive element without role (E2931)
# 2 accessibility warnings — use --no-a11y to suppress

jet build              # no a11y lints (dev builds)
jet build --release    # a11y lints fire automatically

options.name: jet lint --a11y explicit separate step (recommended)
options.detail: A11y linting is an explicit step Hank adds to CI. It never surprises beginners. Consistent with existing lint profile pattern — same as running jet lint --unused or jet lint --style.
options.code:
# CI pipeline (Hank adds this step):
jet lint --a11y

# output:
# src/nav.jet:3: W2930: button "X" has no accessible label
# src/nav.jet:4: W2931: interactive text missing role
# 2 accessibility issues

# Beginner dev loop:
jet build     # no a11y lints — not surprised
jet run       # no a11y lints
jet lint      # base lints only
jet lint --a11y  # only when explicitly requested

options.name: #A11yStrict file-level opt-in marker
options.detail: Files with #A11yStrict at the top get a11y lints; others don't. Hank can enforce it on specific modules. Very granular but obscure — beginners don't know to add it, and it requires discipline across a large team.

decisions.comparisons:
ESLint a11y:    eslint --rule jsx-a11y/...  explicit plugin; CI adds --rule flags
axe-core:       separate npm run a11y  — entirely separate tool run
Lighthouse:     CI step: lighthouse --only-categories=accessibility
SwiftUI:        XCUIAccessibilityAudit  — explicit test call in test suite
Android:        AccessibilityScanner    — separate IDE plugin, not build-time

decisions.title: Method name inside impl Type.Display
decisions.gist: What is the method name inside impl Type.Display { }?
decisions.story: Doris is building a Color type for a design tool. She wants Color to print as "rgb(255, 0, 128)" when used in string interpolation. She writes impl Color.Display { } — what method name goes inside?

options.name: fn display(self) -> String (recommended)
options.detail: Method name matches the trait name exactly. No collision with any existing Jet built-in. Reads like the trait. Consistent with how fn restore matches the Rollback trait.

options.name: fn to_string(self) -> String
options.detail: Familiar from Rust/Java/Kotlin/Swift. But to_string is a common name users already write as helpers on their own types — high collision risk. Also implies conversion, not display.

options.name: fn format(self) -> String
options.detail: Evokes string formatting but in most languages "format" means formatting with arguments/patterns. A zero-argument fn format reads as if it takes a format string.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       impl fmt::Display for Color { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut Formatter) -> fmt::Result }
Swift:      var description: String { "rgb(...)" }   // CustomStringConvertible
Python:     def __str__(self) -> str
Java:       public String toString()
Kotlin:     override fun toString(): String
Go:         func (c Color) String() string

decisions.title: Field-level marker to exclude a field from Debug auto-derive output
decisions.gist: What marker hides a sensitive field from Debug auto-derive output?
decisions.story: Walter's User struct has a password_hash and a stripe_token. He never wants these in debug output, log files, or error messages. Debug auto-derives for all structs. What annotation hides a specific field?

options.name: #[Redact] field marker (recommended)
options.detail: General-purpose privacy marker. Not just for Debug — signals that this field contains sensitive data across all serialization, logging, and display contexts. PascalCase per D-CASING1. A single marker teaches one concept: "this field is sensitive."

options.name: #[Debug.skip] field marker
options.detail: Scoped specifically to Debug output. Clear intent but introduces a new dotted-name marker form not used anywhere else in Jet. Also, a developer might want a field to be skipped in JSON too — they would then need both #[Debug.skip] and a separate serialization marker.
options.code:
struct User {
    id:            Int
    email:         String
    #[Debug.skip]
    password_hash: String   // hidden from Debug but still in JSON?
    #[Debug.skip]
    stripe_token:  String
}

options.name: No v1 field exclusion — implement Display manually to filter
options.detail: Conservative. Users who need redaction override impl Type.Display themselves. No new marker. But Debug still leaks the field — you cannot hide a field from auto-derived Debug without a language mechanism.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust:           #[allow(dead_code)]  — doesn't hide from Debug
                derive(Debug) with manual impl — only way to hide
                serde:          #[serde(skip)] / #[serde(skip_serializing)]
Python:         override __repr__ manually — no field-level annotation
Swift:          no field-level skip; override debugDescription manually
Java:           @JsonIgnore (Jackson) — serialization only, not debug
Go:             omitempty tag — JSON only

decisions.title: User-type for-loop iterable hook: beginner .each/.to_list + expert Iterable protocol
decisions.gist: Beginners iterate custom collections with .each(fn) or .to_list() — no protocol required. Experts who want `for x in mytype` without copying implement Iterable + Iterator.
decisions.story: Betty built a BTree<T> for sorted data. As a beginner she writes `bt.each(fn(val) { print(val) })` or `for val in bt.to_list()` and it just works. When she needs zero-copy in-order walks, she adds `impl BTree.Iterable` and `for val in bt` becomes native.

options.name: Beginner .each/.to_list defaults + expert Iterable hook (recommended)
options.detail: Two tiers, one path. Default: any collection exposes `.each(fn(T))` for callback iteration and `.to_list() -> [T]` when a list is needed — no trait impl, no syntax surprise. Expert opt-in: `impl Type.Iterable { fn iter(self) -> Cursor }` plus `impl Cursor.Iterator { fn next(~self) -> T? }` enables `for x in mytype` without allocating a copy. Built-in `[T]`/`Map` keep `for` natively. Custom types without the protocol never silently copy — callers choose `.each` or `.to_list()` explicitly. Matches Jet's beginner-magic / expert-control split.

options.name: impl Type.Iterator only — type is its own cursor
options.detail: Single protocol on the collection. Simpler surface but fuses collection and cursor — two simultaneous `for` loops over the same value break (shared mutable state). Rejected for the expert tier when Iterable+Iterator is the safe pattern.

options.name: Defer v1 — .to_list() / .each() only, no for-in hook
options.detail: No iterable protocol in v1. Forces copies or manual `.each` forever. Rejected now that the dual-tier design gives beginners ergonomics without obligating experts to implement anything.
options.code:
for val in bt.to_list() { print(val) }   // only path
bt.each(fn(val) { print(val) })

decisions.recommendation: Beginner `.each`/`.to_list()` out of the box; expert `impl Iterable` + `Iterator` unlocks zero-copy `for x in mytype` (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       IntoIterator + Iterator — two traits; beginners use .iter()/.into_iter()
Python:     __iter__ + __next__ — experts implement; beginners use list()
Swift:      Sequence + IteratorProtocol — same split
Kotlin:     Iterable + Iterator — for-in requires Iterable
Jet (A):    .each/.to_list() without protocol; for-in with Iterable opt-in

decisions.title: User-type square-bracket indexing: beginner .get/.set + expert Index hook
decisions.gist: Built-in List/Map keep `m[k]` out of the box. Custom types use `.get(k)` / `.set(k, v)` by default; experts who want bracket syntax implement Index (+ optional IndexMut).
decisions.story: Earl built a SparseMatrix. Beginners call `m.get(3, 7)` and `m.set(3, 7, 42.0)` — explicit, always works. When he wants `m[3, 7]` sugar, he adds `impl SparseMatrix.Index` and bracket syntax lights up.

options.name: Beginner .get/.set defaults + expert Index hook (recommended)
options.detail: Built-in `[T]` and `Map` keep native `xs[i]` / `map[k]` with no impl. User-defined types without a protocol use named `.get(k) -> V?` and `.set(k, v)` — clear, fallible, no magic. Expert opt-in: `impl Type.Index { fn get(self, k: K) -> V? }` enables `mytype[k]`; optional `impl Type.IndexMut { fn set(~self, k: K, v: V) }` enables `mytype[k] = v`. D-SIMD2's closed built-in `[]` rule stays; only user types with an explicit impl gain brackets.

options.name: impl Type.Index + IndexMut required for all indexing
options.detail: Even built-ins would route through protocols — too much ceremony for beginners. Rejected: List/Map already have blessed `[]` and should not require impl blocks.
options.code: // Would force impl on every collection type — rejected

options.name: Defer — .get/.set only forever
options.detail: No bracket hook for user types. Rejected now that the dual-tier design keeps beginners on explicit methods while experts get brackets when they want them.

decisions.recommendation: Built-in `[]` for List/Map; `.get`/`.set` for custom types by default; expert `impl Index` unlocks `mytype[k]` (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Rust:       Index/IndexMut traits — opt-in for user types; Vec has built-in []
Python:     __getitem__/__setitem__ — always protocol-based
Swift:      subscript — explicit on each type
Kotlin:     operator get/set — opt-in
Jet (A):    built-in [] for List/Map; .get/.set default; Index opt-in for experts

decisions.title: Unit construction: dot-constructor spelling, not a literal-suffix hook
decisions.gist: No new literal-suffix protocol. #UnitFamily unit types construct with dot-construction like every other Jet value: `px.{100}`, `Em.{1.5}`.
decisions.story: Hank wants typed lengths in UI styles. He should write `width: px.{100}` — same dot-constructor family as `Point.{x: 3, y: 4}` — not CSS `100px` suffixes and not a hidden coercion protocol.

options.name: Dot-constructor on unit types — no literal-suffix hook (recommended)
options.detail: Close the literal-suffix hook item. D-QUAL3 #UnitFamily already provides typed units. Construction uses the ratified dot-constructor form (D-DOTCTOR1): `px.{100}`, `Em.{1.5}`, `Pct.{50}` when the target type is known from context (`width: Px = px.{100}`). No grammar suffix, no `from_int_literal` coercion protocol, no second mechanism. Consistent with struct/enum construction everywhere else in Jet.

options.name: Bless fn from_int_literal(n: Int) -> T coercion protocol
options.detail: Context-driven implicit coercion: bare `100` routes to different unit constructors depending on inferred type. Fights I8 (one path) and hides which conversion ran. Rejected in favor of explicit `px.{100}`.

options.name: CSS-style grammar suffix `100px`
options.detail: Tier-4 grammar extension. D-EXT1 already rejected user-defined literal suffixes. Would be a second construction path beside dot-constructors.
options.code: width :: 100px   // rejected — not Jet's constructor family

decisions.recommendation: Unit values construct with dot-construction `px.{100}`; remove literal-suffix hook from card #41 (Option A).
decisions.comparisons:
Jet structs:  Point.{x: 3.0, y: 4.0}  — same dot-constructor family
Jet enums:    Color.Red / .Variant     — leading dot
CSS:          width: 100px            — rejected suffix grammar
Kotlin:       100.px                   — extension property, not constructor
Rust:         Px::new(100)             — function, not dot-constructor

decisions.title: Add C-style ++/-- increment and decrement operators?
decisions.gist: Jet already increments with `x += 1`. Should Jet also accept `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, and `x--` on mutable integers?
decisions.explainer: S17 ratified compound assignment (`+=`, `-=`, …) as the update-operator family. The owner asked for C-style `++`/`--`. Under I8 there should be one mechanical path — unless the owner explicitly chooses familiarity over uniformity on this site. The ballot covers full C semantics, permanent rejection, and three partial shapes (postfix-only, prefix-only, statement-only). Operand policy mirrors S17: mutable `var`, `mut` parameters, `self.field` on `mut self`, and index sites; integer types only (trap-on-overflow per D-NUMOPS2). No user-defined operator overloading.
decisions.story: Carla is porting a C sprite engine. Her game loop has `tick++` and `while (--lives > 0)` scattered through the original. She wants Jet to accept the same tokens so she can translate line-for-line, but she also wants beginners reading her code to understand what changed.

options.name: Full C-style ++/-- on mutable integer lvalues (pre + post)
options.detail: All four forms. Prefix returns the new value; postfix returns the old value. Operand must be a mutable integer lvalue (same LHS policy as S17). Applies to `Int` and sized integer widths; not `Float`. Overflow traps like `+= 1` (D-NUMOPS2). Gives C/C++ transliteration fidelity; spends a second increment spelling (I8 tension).

options.name: Reject ++/-- forever — keep `+= 1` / `-= 1` only (recommended)
options.detail: No increment/decrement operators. S17 compound assignment is the single canonical update path (I8). Matches Rust, Swift, Zig, Go, and Python. Users coming from C see a teaching error pointing at `+= 1`. Owner request is satisfied by documenting the transliteration table in the cookbook, not new syntax.

options.name: Postfix only (`x++`, `x--`) — no prefix forms
options.detail: Only postfix increment/decrement. Value of `x++` is discarded (statement form) or typed as `Void` — no old-value expression semantics. Covers the most common C loop idiom (`i++` at end of body) without prefix `--lives` in conditions. Still a second path beside `+= 1` but avoids prefix/precedence puzzles in conditions.

options.name: Prefix only (`++x`, `--x`) — no postfix forms
options.detail: Only prefix forms; they return the updated value (usable in expressions). Matches the `--lives > 0` condition pattern and `++it` iterator style. No postfix old-value trap. Rejects `tick++` at statement end — users write `tick += 1` or `++tick` there.

options.name: Statement-position only — both pre and post, never inside expressions
options.detail: Lexer/parser accept `++x`, `x++`, `--x`, `x--` only as standalone statements (or loop-header afterthought if D-LOOP-SURFACE B is extended). Using them where a value is expected is an error. Cuts the classic footgun (`arr[i] = i++`) while still letting Carla write familiar statement lines. Expression increment stays `+= 1`.

comparisons.note: Full four-form family; prefix/postfix differ in expression value. Decades of familiarity; also decades of postfix confusion.
No `++`/`--`. Updates use `+= 1`, `-= 1`, or `+=` with any step. Deliberate removal from C lineage.
No `++`/`--` (removed in Swift 3). `+= 1` / `-= 1` only.

decisions.recommendation: Reject `++`/`--` (Option B). S17 already owns increment/decrement; adding C operators duplicates that job and reintroduces prefix/postfix value semantics beginners stumble on. Choose A only if C transliteration ergonomics outweigh I8 on this site.

log.text: Ballot raised from increment-operators.md plan. Five options: full C-style, reject, postfix-only, prefix-only, statement-only. Rec B on I8 + beginner clarity.

decisions.title: Should methods be ordinary functions or macro-like rewrite hooks?
decisions.gist: Methods stay ordinary functions; the two things people actually love about Jai macro-methods — guaranteed inlining and DSL power — get honest homes: @Inline contracts now, E4 metaprogramming later.
decisions.explainer: Jet already ratifies methods as one structural placement for functions: inline, impl block, or external `fn Type.method(self)` all mean the same program. Treating methods as macros would blur call semantics, make refactoring up/down the hierarchy less predictable, and conflict with R11 source-fragment re-entry. The useful Jai insight is not “every method is a macro”; it is that refactoring should preserve shape and that library hooks should feel direct where the compiler blesses them.
decisions.story: Carla moves `Player.heal` from inside `struct Player` to an external method so her gameplay file reads top-down. She needs the call `p.heal(10)` to keep meaning exactly the same thing, not start participating in code rewriting because the method moved.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: the original options only gatekept. What Jai users love is (1) zero-cost abstraction they can TRUST (macros inline by construction) and (2) DSL authoring power. (1) translates as inline contracts: @Inline is a checked promise — if the compiler cannot inline, that is a compile error, not a silent regression; jet expand --facts inline shows every decision. (2) is real but belongs in E4 where expansion is auditable through the derive/build-message machinery — deferring it there routes the desire instead of killing it. Macro methods in v1 would make every call non-local and poison tooling.

options.name: Ordinary methods + checked @Inline / @InlineAlways contracts (recommended)
options.detail: The performance kernel of macro-methods without macro semantics. @InlineAlways failing to inline is a compile error naming why. Blessed hooks (Iterable/Index/Display) stay sema-owned traits.

options.name: Document the closed compiler-hook set only
options.detail: Iterable, Index, IndexMut, Display power syntax; nothing else does. Mostly current law; adds no answer for the perf-trust kernel.
options.code: impl Store.Iterable { fn iter(self) -> It { ... } }

options.name: Macro methods (call-rewrite hooks) in v1
options.detail: A method can receive syntax and emit source. Non-local call semantics, tooling blind spots; the power is E4’s to deliver auditable-y.
options.code: macro fn query(self, block) -> Source { ... }   // E4 question

comparisons.note: Jai exposes broad compile-time execution and compiler message loops. It is powerful and fast for game/tool authors, but trusts project code heavily.
comparisons.code:
#run build_tables();
#modify Some_Type { /* compiler message loop territory */ }

comparisons.note: Rust keeps methods and macros separate. Proc macros generate tokens that the compiler parses and checks again.

decisions.title: What symbol family owns metadata, compiler control, and comptime splices?
decisions.gist: Two planes with an eye-checkable law: @ states a contract on the declaration below; # instructs the compiler (modes, items, effects, quantities, queries); $ stays splice-only.
decisions.explainer: The question is not which sigil is easier to type — it is whether a reader can tell, from the first character, what kind of statement they are looking at. The v5 proposal (docs/reference/syntax-comparison-proposal.md) draws a line a reader can check by eye: @ only ever precedes a declaration and states a checkable contract about it (@Pure, @MustUse, @Codable, @Pub); # never states a contract — it changes what compiles, when it runs, what is legal, or supplies a compile-time value (#Unsafe, #Comptime, #Test, #(Fs), [T#N], pkg#1.2.3, #Caller()). $ remains the splice sigil inside generated Jet only.
decisions.story: Maya is exploring Jet in the LSP. She types `#` before a function and expects completions for tests, safety gates, FFI, purity, and build markers. She types `$` inside an expression and expects compile-time values, not another attribute namespace.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01 after owner signaled comfort with @-attributes/#-directives (C++ framing). The line resolves every fuzzy case mechanically: @MustUse is a contract on callers, #Suppress changes legality in a scope; @Codable is a capability contract (derivation is implementation), #Derive is generation machinery you write; #Unsafe stays a directive even on items because it changes what is legal inside the body. Bonus: # stays rare and loud — #Unsafe/#Comptime scream instead of drowning in visibility/encoding markers. Tradition backs both instincts as-is: C’s #include/#pragma = machine instructions; Java/C#/Python @ = annotation on the declaration below. Grep law: rg '@\w' = every contract, rg '#\w' = every compiler instruction. Casing (PascalCase per D-CASING1 vs the v5 doc’s lowercase) is a separate knob — examples here keep the ratified PascalCase. Full worked law: proposal doc Sigil Law section + decision card D-META-PLANE.

options.name: One marker family: # for everything, $ splice
options.detail: One sigil to learn and grep; but # appears on every pub/codable item, diluting the alarm value of #Unsafe/#Comptime, and the attribute-vs-instruction distinction the reader still needs is no longer visible.

options.name: @ contracts / # directives / $ splices (recommended)
options.detail: The eye-checkable law: @ promises, # permits/controls. @ never appears inside a type or expression; # can (#(Fs), [T#N], #Caller()). ~ stays reserved.

options.name: $ as the compiler/comptime marker family
options.detail: Collapses "compute here" and "mark this item" into one sigil — the overload this whole family exists to avoid.
options.code: $Test "routing" { ... }   // and $name still a splice — muddled

comparisons.note: Jai leans on `#` directives for compile-time and compiler features.
Zig uses `@` for compiler builtins and `comptime` as a keyword. Search is good, but `@` becomes a second namespace every user must learn.
Rust uses `#[]` attributes; macros use `!`, creating a visible split between metadata and expansion.

decisions.title: What should the first-party CLI flag API look like?
decisions.gist: CLI args become the entry function’s typed signature: fn run(args: ServeArgs) — flags derived from fields, help generated from docs, subcommands are an enum. Zero parse ceremony, Go-flag simplicity kept.
decisions.explainer: What people love about Go’s flag package is that a small tool needs no framework: declare, run, get --help. Jet can beat it: the entry function already has a signature — let it take a typed args struct. Field names become flags, defaults become defaults, doc attributes become help text, an enum parameter becomes subcommands. The parser, help, completion, and man page all derive from the one struct the program was going to define anyway.
decisions.story: Nora writes a one-file asset packer. She wants `--input`, `--out`, and `--fast` parsed with good help text, and she wants tests to pass synthetic argv without mutating global process state.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: integrates the lifecycle-verbs proposal (jet <verb> -> fn <verb>(), syntax-comparison-proposal.md §36A / D-BUILDENTRY1). fn run() stays zero-arg for hello-world; adding a typed parameter opts into CLI parsing — magic default, one step to full control. Machinery is the same derive/reflection layer as Codable, no new syntax. Bad-flag errors are Jet diagnostics with what/why/fix. The explicit builder remains as the library floor for non-entry parsing (REPLs, plugins) — option A generates down onto it.

options.name: Typed entry signature: fn run(args: ServeArgs) (recommended)
options.detail: Flags from fields, help from @Doc, subcommands from an enum parameter. Hello-world keeps zero-arg fn run().

options.name: @[Cli] struct + explicit parse call
options.detail: Same derive, manual wiring: args :: cli.parse<ServeArgs>(io.args())?. Ships anyway as the layer under A; as the ONLY surface it keeps ceremony Go users came to avoid.
options.code: args :: cli.parse<ServeArgs>(io.args())?

options.name: Builder API only (status quo)
