options.detail: args.spec().flag("verbose", ...) — works, stringly, help text drifts from the code that reads the values.
options.code: spec :: args.spec().flag("verbose", "print extra detail")

comparisons.note: The stdlib flag package is tiny and predictable, but global registration can make larger CLIs awkward.
Derive-based CLI parsing gives excellent UX but uses macro-heavy generated code.

decisions.title: Should Jet add a Jai-style `Any` for expert reflection boundaries?
decisions.gist: No top type — but deliver what Any is actually USED for: heterogeneous varargs over a trait (...Renderable) so anyone can write print-like functions, plus reflect/Data handles for tooling.
decisions.explainer: In real Jai code, Any overwhelmingly serves one need: writing your own print/log/assert that accepts anything displayable. Jet already covers consumption via interpolation. The missing piece is authorship: a variadic parameter constrained by a trait — parts: ...Renderable — where each argument is monomorphized at the call site. Full static typing, no boxing, no top type, and the print-like function is three lines.
decisions.story: Owen writes an inspector panel for game entities. He wants to show arbitrary field values in tooling, but his gameplay APIs should still say `Health`, `Position`, or `Inventory`, not `Any`.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: the original options only said no. The kernel is trait-bounded heterogeneous varargs: each call site compiles a shape-specialized body (same machinery as generics), so log_all("sev ", 3, incident) type-checks every argument against Renderable and fails with a teaching error naming the odd one out. Tooling/serialization keeps reflect.Value + Data (option B’s handle, now folded in as the expert floor rather than a rival). General Any stays rejected — D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 stands.

options.name: Trait-bounded heterogeneous varargs + reflect handles (recommended)
options.detail: parts: ...Renderable monomorphizes per call site. Statically checked, zero boxing. reflect.Value/Data remain the tooling floor.

options.name: Expert core.reflect.Any handle only
options.detail: Library type carrying type info + value for reflection internals; construction gated behind reflection APIs. Covers tooling, not the print-authorship kernel.
options.code:
v :: reflect.value_of(incident)
print(v.type_name())

options.name: General Any top type
options.detail: Every value flows into Any. Repeats what D-DYNAMIC-TYPE1 closed; weakens the whole type system for one convenience.
options.code: fn log_all(parts: ...Any) { ... }

comparisons.note: Any is a type-info pointer plus value pointer. Useful for tooling/reflection, but weakens static guarantees if ordinary APIs accept it.
`Any` exists, but serious APIs prefer protocols/generics/enums to recover static meaning.

decisions.comment: Can we do A & B? also for A, we should be able to bind groups of traits, right? So we can require a specific set, not just one?

decisions.title: Should Jet adopt Jai-style dynamic-array type syntax?
decisions.gist: Keep [T] / [K,V] / [T#N] — but the real Jai kernel is the view/owning distinction: plan a labeled zero-copy View<T> riding the stored-ref machinery, instead of a second bracket spelling.
decisions.explainer: Jai’s [..]T reads well there because Jai has several array kinds to tell apart. Jet’s list family is already one-spelling-per-kind. What Jai users actually miss in Jet is not the bracket — it is the cheap non-owning VIEW: slicing without copying. Jet slices are inclusive copies by beginner law (safe, no dangling); the expert tier needs a real view type whose owner relationship the compiler tracks.
decisions.story: Iris ports a Jai particle system. She sees `particles: [..]$Particle` and asks for the Jet equivalent. The safest answer is a direct transliteration table, not new syntax.
decisions.inWild:
particles: [Particle] := []
particles.push(Particle.{ pos: .{0, 0}, vel: .{1, 0} })

ids: [Int#128] := fixed_ids()
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: option A now carries a plan instead of a bare no. View<T> is a library type over the stored-reference machinery (D-REF-SHORTHAND1 labels/inference): window :: incidents.view(0..9) is zero-copy, compiler tracks that it borrows from incidents, and the expand lens distinguishes copy-slices from views in hot loops. Beginner law unchanged: [a..b] copies. Bracket spelling [..]T stays rejected — .. already means inclusive range/step, $ means splice, and a second dynamic-list spelling violates I8.

options.name: Keep the family; add zero-copy View<T> on stored-ref machinery (recommended)
options.detail: One spelling per collection kind. Views are the expert zero-copy tier with tracked owners; copy-slices stay the safe default.
options.code:
head :: incidents[0..9]              // beginner law: inclusive copy
window :: incidents.view(0..9)        // expert: zero-copy, owner tracked
sum :: window.fold(0, (a, i) => a + i.severity)

options.name: Add [..]T as a dynamic-list spelling
options.detail: Jai familiarity; duplicate semantics for [T], visual collision with ranges and splices.
options.code: ids: [..]String = []

options.name: Reserve [..]T for future slice/view syntax
options.detail: Keeps the option open; but if View<T> as a library type suffices, reserved grammar is a promise nobody needs.
options.code: // reserved, unused

comparisons.note: Dynamic-array type uses a compact bracket marker distinct from fixed arrays.
Slices are `[]T`; fixed arrays are `[N]T`; capacity-owning collections are library types.
comparisons.code:
var slice: []u8 = buffer[0..];
var fixed: [16]u8 = undefined;

decisions.title: Should Jet add a Jai-style `shift` primitive for stream parsers?
decisions.gist: The shift kernel — linear consume-from-front parsing — lands as core.binary.Reader with ?-composed methods, plus parse-pattern take for text (D-PARSESTR1). No new operator, full autocomplete and bounds diagnostics.
decisions.explainer: What makes Jai shift-style parsers pleasant is that a parser reads top-to-bottom in consumption order with no index bookkeeping. That is a cursor API shape, not an operator: a Reader owns position, every read advances, every read is fallible with ?. For text, the same motion composes with string parse patterns: cursor.take_pattern("inc-{id:Int} ")? consumes and binds in one line.
decisions.story: Sam writes a binary asset loader. He wants compact code that consumes a header, count, and payload from a byte buffer without hand-managing indices.
decisions.inWild:
cursor := bytes.cursor()
magic :: cursor.read_u32_le()?
count :: cursor.read_u16_le()?
items :: cursor.take(count)?
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: option A upgraded from "methods if needed" to a designed core surface: binary.Reader (u8/u16/u32/u64 le/be, take(n), remaining, at_end) and text.Cursor (take_pattern, take_until, skip_ws), all fallible, all ?-composed — the linear read shape with bounds failures surfacing as ordinary Jet errors, not hidden truncation. Integrates D-PARSESTR1 (c8syntaxwave): one pattern syntax serves matching AND consuming. A shift operator stays rejected: domain punctuation for one idiom, hides failure behavior.

options.name: core.binary.Reader + text.Cursor with parse-pattern take (recommended)
options.detail: Consumption-ordered, fallible, discoverable. One pattern syntax shared with D-PARSESTR1.
options.code:
r :: binary.Reader.over(packet)
magic :: r.u32_be()?
len :: r.u16_be()?
body :: r.take(len)?

c :: text.Cursor.over(line)
c.take_pattern("inc-{id:Int} sev {sev:Int}")?
escalate(id, sev)

options.name: Builtin generic shift<T>(cursor) helper
options.detail: One blessed function instead of a designed surface; still needs the Reader type underneath, so it is A minus the API design.
options.code: magic :: shift<U32>(r)?

options.name: New shift operator/keyword
options.detail: Most compact, least general; syntax for one idiom, failure behavior hidden in punctuation.
options.code: magic :: r >> U32   // rejected shape

comparisons.note: Shift-style helpers make parsers compact by advancing a pointer/cursor as data is read.
Byte readers usually expose methods that advance internal position and return Results.

decisions.title: Should Jet support compact pointer-cast/deref chains like Jai?
decisions.gist: Keep casts and deref explicit inside `#Unsafe`; add docs for the Jai transliteration.
decisions.explainer: The Jai expression means: take a stored untyped pointer, cast it to pointer-to-bool, then dereference it. Jet already has raw pointer `*T` and postfix `p.*` under `#Unsafe`. The question is whether to add a compact cast/deref chain for reflection internals. Safety priority says no: every untyped pointer cast should be loud and gated.
decisions.story: Priya is implementing a debugger variable editor. A reflected slot tells her a field is Bool and gives a raw pointer. She needs to set the field, but only in audited tooling code.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: Jai’s chain is very readable to experts once learned and great in metaprogramming code. In Jet, the same compactness would normalize untyped pointer mutation. Keep it explicit, and make reflection APIs provide typed setters where possible so most code never casts.

options.name: Explicit cast + postfix deref inside `#Unsafe` (recommended)
options.detail: Current low-level model. Add docs/examples, not syntax.

options.name: Typed reflection setter API
options.detail: Avoid pointer syntax at call site; reflection library checks type before mutation.
options.code: slot.set_bool(true)?

options.name: Jai-style cast/deref chain
options.detail: Compact expert syntax, but hides two unsafe operations in one expression.
options.code: slot.value_pointer.(*Bool).* = true

comparisons.note: Type-info + pointer casts can be compact and expressive for reflection internals.
Raw pointer casts and dereferences are inside explicit unsafe blocks.

decisions.title: What spelling should visible uninitialized storage use?
decisions.gist: New option D: a lowercase `uninit` keyword in the initializer slot — bytes: [U8#1024] := uninit. Reads plainly, greps exactly, no punctuation soup; sema proves write-before-read regardless of spelling.
decisions.explainer: Visible uninitialized storage is a statement about the VALUE slot: "the initializer is: nothing yet." The most honest spelling puts that statement where the initializer goes. A keyword literal `uninit` is Jai’s --- with the mystery removed: newcomers read it aloud, rg 'uninit' finds every site, and the checker’s job (every path writes before any path reads) is identical under every option.
decisions.story: Leah fills a fixed buffer from a device packet. She needs storage before all fields are known, but she wants the compiler to reject any read before assignment.
decisions.inWild:
#Uninit header: PacketHeader
header.magic = cursor.read_u32_le()?
header.len = cursor.read_u16_le()?
process(header)
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: added option D and moved the recommendation to it. Against A (#Uninit/@Uninit marker): a marker states a contract about the DECLARATION, but uninit-ness is a property of the initializer — the attribute plane is the wrong plane, and the marker line separates the fact from the = it modifies. Against B (---): visual noise beside ->, --, -=, ranges; unreadable aloud; muscle memory is the only argument. Against C (Uninit<T>): type-level wrapper for a value-slot fact, infects signatures. D maps 1:1 for Jai users (--- -> uninit), costs one contextual keyword legal only in initializer position.

options.name: @Uninit marker on the binding
options.detail: Searchable and marker-consistent, but states a value-slot fact on the declaration line — wrong plane, and the fact sits away from the = it modifies.
options.code:
@Uninit bytes: [U8#1024]
bytes[0] = 1

options.name: Jai-style := ---
options.detail: Compact, Jai muscle memory; punctuation with no pronunciation, visually adjacent to ->, --, -=, ranges.

options.name: Library wrapper Uninit<T>
options.detail: Explicit but infects types and signatures with a storage-state detail.
options.code: bytes: Uninit<[U8#1024]> := Uninit.new()

options.name: Contextual keyword: := uninit (recommended)
options.detail: The initializer says "nothing yet" in a word. Greppable, teachable, legal only in initializer position; checker proves write-before-read, reads of possibly-uninit slots are compile errors.

comparisons.note: `---` means intentionally uninitialized. Very terse, but punctuation-heavy.
`undefined` is explicit but keyword-like and can leak into ordinary code.
`MaybeUninit<T>` is library-explicit and unsafe to assume initialized.

decisions.title: Should stored-reference fields use `#Ref(Label)` or capability-style `~Type`?
decisions.gist: Middle path the ballot lacked: stored refs spell &T like every other shared borrow, the owner label is INFERRED when unambiguous, and @Ref(label) is required only to disambiguate — beginner-short, expert-precise.
decisions.explainer: The binder note asked: why is #Ref(Label) so long? Because diagnostics need to know WHOSE storage the field borrows. But that label is only informative when there are multiple candidate owners. In the common case — one owner in the construction context — the compiler can infer it, and field: &Incident is both short and honest: & already means shared borrow at call sites; a stored & extends the same word to fields. Unlike ~ (write authority) nothing is conflated.
decisions.story: Earl stores token text as a view into an arena-owned source buffer. The field is not “mutable access to String”; it is “this String view belongs to source”.
decisions.detail: Reworked 2026-07-01: added option D (recommended). Inference rule: if exactly one candidate owner exists at the construction site, it is inferred and jet expand --facts refs materializes it; if several candidates exist, compiling without @Ref(label) is an error that lists the candidates — the teaching moment arrives exactly when the information matters. This is the magic-default/expert-control shape applied to lifetimes: the beginner writes &T, the multi-arena expert writes @Ref(arena), and nobody writes a label the compiler already knows. ~T stays rejected (conflates write authority); bare-&-always (old C) stays rejected because ambiguous cases would get folklore defaults instead of diagnostics.

options.name: #Ref(Label) always required
options.detail: Every stored ref names its owner even when there is only one candidate — the repetition the binder note complained about.

options.name: field: ~T
options.detail: Short but conflates stored-borrow with call-time exclusive WRITE access, and still has no owner label for diagnostics.
options.code: struct Owner { primary: ~Incident }

options.name: field: &T always, never labeled
options.detail: Short everywhere, but multi-owner cases lose the label diagnostics need — errors degrade to "somewhere, something outlived."
options.code: struct Index { hot: &Incident }

options.name: &T with inferred owner + @Ref(label) to disambiguate (recommended)
options.detail: One candidate owner: inferred, zero ceremony. Several: compile error listing candidates, fixed by @Ref(label). Expand lens always shows the resolved owner.

comparisons.note: Stored references name a lifetime relationship; mutable access is a separate `&mut` concept.
comparisons.code:
struct View<'a> { text: &'a str }
fn edit(x: &mut String) {}

comparisons.note: Borrowing/consuming annotations are access-mode concepts, separate from object storage identity.

decisions.title: What is Jet’s compile-time build entrypoint?
decisions.gist: Give Jet a build-time main: one explicit `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?`, selected by the build surface.
decisions.explainer: Jai’s `#run` is powerful because build code is just language code. Jet should import that power through a single auditable entrypoint instead of hidden module-level execution. Local `comptime {}` remains for value computation; the build entrypoint owns graph construction: targets, generated source, assets, toolchains, profiles, and package/workspace integration. Generated source still re-enters lexer -> parser -> sema (R11).
decisions.story: Marcus is building a game. He wants to pack textures, generate an enum from asset names, compile shaders, and then build the game binary with one command. His studio security team wants the same build to explain exactly what ran and what files/network endpoints it touched.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: a build-time main can become Cargo build.rs with better syntax: dependency code executes before users inspect it. Patch: one selected root entrypoint, BuildContext authority only, D-CTEFFECT1 tiers, dependency Tier 2 denied by default, generated-source re-check, lock/provenance, and jet explain-build. Do not let every imported module have hidden build hooks. STATUS CORRECTION 2026-07-01: an earlier edit claimed the lifecycle-verbs law (jet <verb> -> fn <verb>(); syntax-comparison-proposal.md §36A) was ratified — it is NOT; it is an open proposal, related open ballot D-JPK-DEVCOMPOSE1 (jet dev). Option B stands on its own merits and the owner direction recorded 2026-07-01 (a fn-main-equivalent build entry that maps cleanly to jet build); if the verb law later ratifies, B becomes one instance of it. D-BUILDPOLICY1 governs authority either way. Scope ladder (single file / package / workspace) is D-BUILDSCOPE1; generated-source home is D-BUILDGEN1.

options.name: `Build.entry` selects `#Build fn build(ctx) -> BuildPlan ?`
options.detail: One explicit build-time main. The marker makes the authority boundary visible; `Build.entry` makes selection explicit for tools and CI. Local `comptime {}` remains separate.

options.name: fn build(b: BuildContext) via the lifecycle verb map (recommended)
options.detail: Not name magic and not dependent on any unratified law: jet build runs fn build(BuildContext) when the root defines one, else the batteries default pipeline runs. The typed BuildContext parameter is the visible authority boundary. Aligns with the OPEN lifecycle-verbs proposal (jet run -> fn run(), jet dev -> fn dev()) without depending on it.

options.name: `comptime main` in any module
options.detail: Maximal #run feel. Rejected unless owner accepts hidden import-time execution risk.
options.code: comptime fn main(ctx: BuildContext) -> BuildPlan ? { ... }

options.name: No build entrypoint; only declarative `Build.{}` plus local `comptime {}`
options.detail: Safest and easiest to audit, but cannot replace Jai/Zig/Make-class orchestration.
options.code: build: Build.{ sources: ["src/main.jet"] }

comparisons.note: `#run` can execute arbitrary compile-time code and participate in build orchestration. It is fun and direct, but authority is broad by default.
`build.zig` is a programmatic build file with explicit steps. Strong model, but separate from ordinary source entrypoints.
`build.rs` runs before compilation and communicates through files/env instructions. Powerful but stringly and historically easy to abuse.

decisions.title: What authority does build-time code get by default?
decisions.gist: Build code gets pure and locked reproducible inputs by default; ambient effects require source audit plus policy.
decisions.explainer: Build metaprogramming is supply-chain code execution. Jet needs a policy model that is fun locally but enforceable in CI and enterprises. D-CTEFFECT1 gives the effect tiers; this decision fixes the build-system default: root builds may request authority, dependencies are denied ambient authority unless project/org policy grants it, and every granted capability is recorded in lock/provenance.
decisions.story: Alicia maintains a fintech service. She is fine with a root build script reading `schema/*.sql`, but she cannot allow a transitive dependency to read CI secrets or hit the network during build.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: too much policy can make game-dev builds feel bureaucratic. Too little policy loses enterprise adoption. The compromise is profile-sensitive: developer default allows pure + locked Tier 1 and prompts for Tier 2; CI strict/offline deny drift; enterprise can allowlist roots/domains/tools. The model must not rely on wrapper scripts.

options.name: Tiered policy with `BuildContext` authority only (recommended)
options.detail: Pure + locked Tier 1 by default. Tier 2 needs `#Impure("reason")`, CLI/project/org permission, and provenance. Dependencies get no Tier 2 unless explicitly granted.
options.code:
jet build --profile=ci --locked --deny-impure
jet audit-effects

options.name: Warn-only policy for impure build effects
options.detail: Fast and friendly, but CI can accidentally ship non-reproducible builds.
options.code: Warning [L3102]: build reads `$HOME/.token`

options.name: Pure-only build code
options.detail: Maximum reproducibility, but blocks shader compilation, bindgen, asset packing, and real-world package builds.
options.code: // ctx.exec, env, unpinned network: always errors

options.name: Jai-style unrestricted build execution
options.detail: Most fun and powerful locally; unacceptable supply-chain default for Jet.
options.code: #run { run_process("curl https://...") }

comparisons.note: Builds are sandboxed and inputs are explicit; reproducibility is excellent but general programming ergonomics are specialized.
Actions declare inputs/outputs and remote cache keys. Strong enterprise model; BUILD language is separate from app language.
Build scripts are easy but broad; policy/audit is mostly convention and sandboxing is external.

decisions.title: Native OS platform gating for #Extern backends (Phase 8 blocker)
decisions.gist: How does Jet source say "this function/module only compiles on Linux (or macOS, or Windows)" so a native GTK/AppKit/Win32 FFI backend doesn't break builds on the other two platforms?
decisions.story: Walter is shipping a desktop app. His `LinuxWindowBackend` calls into GTK via #Extern C FFI. He needs the compiler to leave that code out entirely when building on macOS (no GTK there) and swap in an AppKit-backed implementation of the same JetBackend trait instead — without a runtime crash or a linker error on the wrong platform.

options.name: Extend the existing #Target marker with OS variants (recommended)
options.detail: D-WASM1 already established #Target as "module-level target marker" with Browser/Wasm/Js as the first instances. Add Os.Linux / Os.Macos / Os.Windows as more instances of the SAME marker family, so there is exactly one marker for "what environment does this code run under" (web bucket or native OS) — I8 one-way-to-mean-it. Sema rejects mixing a web variant and an OS variant on the same item (two different axes, one marker, mutually exclusive values).

options.name: New dedicated #Os marker, separate from #Target
options.detail: #Target's existing job (web WASM/JS partitioning) is a genuinely different compilation axis from "which native OS." A distinct #Os(Linux) marker keeps the two concerns from ever being conflated in sema, at the cost of one more marker family to learn.

options.name: Manifest-level gating (pkg.jet / env.jet), no in-source marker
options.detail: No per-function marker at all — the whole file/package is included only when the target platform in pkg.jet's payload matches. Coarser granularity (whole file, not per-impl), and inconsistent with how every other conditional-compilation-flavored feature in Jet (#Reactive, #Extern, #Unsafe, D-WASM1's #Target) is an in-source marker, not a manifest switch.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust: #[cfg(target_os = "linux")] — attribute-based, same shape as option A/B.
Swift: #if os(macOS) ... #endif — source-level directive, same shape.
React Native: Button.ios.js / Button.android.js — filename convention, same shape as option C.
Zig: builtin.target.os.tag comptime check — comptime-if, closer to option A/B than C.

decisions.title: File-level + manifest-level default build target (web without --target=web every time)
decisions.gist: A .jet file (or its pkg.jet once it's a managed package) can declare "I'm a web app" so jet run/dev/build default to the web backend without --target=web typed every time.
decisions.story: Nate is iterating on a loose example file and is tired of typing --target=web on every jet dev invocation. Once he promotes the file into a real package, he wants that same intent to live in pkg.jet instead of the source file, since a packages target is project config, not a per-file concern.

options.name: #Target(Web) file-level marker + pkg.jet target: "web" field, CLI flag always wins
options.detail: Extends the EXISTING #Target(...) marker (today only #Target(Wasm)/#Target(Js), both already file/module-scope-only ceilings, never per-function) with a third value, Web -- distinct in meaning (default backend selection, not a partition ceiling) but same lexical form, no new marker family (I8). pkg.jet's payload gains a parallel target: "web" key. Precedence: --target=<x> CLI flag overrides pkg.jet target which overrides file-level #Target(Web) which overrides the native default. No automatic file-to-manifest migration tool for now -- a manual edit, or a later jetpack convenience, not blocking this decision.
options.code:
#Target(Web)
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

$ jet dev counter.jet                 // infers web from the marker
$ jet dev counter.jet --target=native  // flag still overrides

decisions.title: Explicit companion-HTML marker for jet build/dev --target=web
decisions.gist: Replace the silent <stem>.html filename convention with an explicit #Html("path.html") marker at the top of the .jet file, so the pairing is visible in the source and errors loudly if the file is missing.
decisions.story: Nate renamed a file mid-project and jet dev silently started serving the generic fallback page instead of his real one -- no error, just a confusingly plain-looking dashboard. He wants the source itself to say which HTML file it pairs with.
decisions.inWild:
#Target(Web)
#Html("dashboard.html")
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

$ jet dev app.jet   // uses dashboard.html, or a clear error if it's missing
decisions.detail: AMENDED 2026-07-01: option B added — manifest-level pairing for managed packages composes with the file marker; single-option ballots decide nothing.

options.name: #Html("path.html") file-level marker, same family as #Target(Web)
options.detail: Precedence when building for web: explicit #Html(...) wins; else the existing sibling <stem>.html convention (kept for backward-compat with 190-197's existing examples, none of which will be forced to add the marker); else the generic auto-generated page. A referenced #Html(...) path that doesn't exist on disk is a build-time error naming the missing file, not a silent fallback.
options.code:
#Target(Web)
#Html("dashboard.html")
use core.ui as ui
fn main() { ... }

options.name: pack.jet target field for managed packages, #Html(...) for single files — composed
options.detail: Once a project has a manifest, pairing belongs with the target declaration: executable { entry: "src/run.jet", html: "dashboard.html" }. Single-file apps keep the #Html marker (option A). Precedence: CLI flag > manifest field > file marker > sibling <stem>.html > generated page. Missing referenced file is a build error either way.

decisions.title: Can string interpolation run backwards as a parse pattern?
decisions.gist: The same "inc-{id}" syntax that formats output also destructures input in if-tables, with typed holes — scanf done right.
decisions.explainer: Today "inc-{id}" formats a string (interpolation). This proposal makes the same literal legal in pattern position: it matches the fixed text and binds each {hole} to a name. A typed hole like {id:Int} only matches digits and binds an Int. One syntax, both directions — most CLI/log/protocol parsing needs no regex library at all.
decisions.story: Dana writes a CLI that tails a log and reacts to lines like "inc-4411 sev 3". Today she chains starts_with + split + parse with three separate failure points and no compiler help. With parse patterns she states the line shape once and gets typed bindings or a clean non-match.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Colon collision — in format position {x:debug} the colon is a format spec; in pattern position {x:Int} it is a type. Direction disambiguates mechanically, but docs must teach it. (2) Greedy-match ambiguity ("{a} {b}" against "x y z") needs one fixed law: holes are non-greedy and stop at the next literal run; no backtracking regex engine hides inside, matching stays linear-time and predictable. Inputs needing real alternation/repetition graduate to the future re library. (3) A plain string arm without braces stays simple equality — no behavior change for existing code; {{ escapes a literal brace, as in interpolation.

options.name: String patterns with typed holes in if-table arms (recommended)
options.detail: {x} binds String, {x:Int} is a typed fallible hole; non-greedy holes anchored by literal text; else arm catches non-matches. No new sigils, reuses interpolation syntax and if-tables.

options.name: Library function only: parse(line, "inc-{id:Int}")
options.detail: Same power, no pattern-position grammar. Weaker: no multi-arm dispatch, results come back as a tuple/struct instead of scoped bindings.
options.code:
matched :: text.parse(line, "inc-{id:Int} sev {sev:Int}")?
escalate(matched.id, matched.sev)

options.name: Reject; wait for the regex library
options.detail: Regex covers everything but drags a second language with famously bad readability for the 90% simple cases.
options.code:
re :: regex.compile("inc-(\\d+) sev (\\d+)")?
caps :: re.captures(line)?

comparisons.note: scanf is the tradition: types in holes. Right idea, but stringly, unsafe, and divorced from printf's format in subtle ways.
Regex builders are powerful and type-safe but are a second language with real learning cost.
f-strings only format; the community keeps reinventing the reverse as third-party `parse` — proof of demand.

decisions.title: Do typed unit literals like 500ms and 19.99usd ride #unit?
decisions.gist: Numbers can carry their unit as a suffix; wrong-unit math dies at compile time instead of in production.
decisions.explainer: #unit already generates typed families (Usd, Ms). Today you construct one with Usd("19.99") or time.ms(500). A unit literal is a number followed by a unit suffix the compiler resolves to a unit type in scope. Not new types — a new spelling for existing ones. The Mars Climate Orbiter was lost to a lb/N mix-up; this class of bug becomes unrepresentable.
decisions.story: Greg tunes gameplay: jump cooldown 250ms, dash speed 4mps. He typos seconds where millis go. With bare Ints nothing catches it and the jump feels broken for a week; with unit literals the compiler rejects the assignment on the spot.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Lexer collision — float exponent 1e5 vs a hypothetical unit named e5. Law: exponent notation is reserved; a unit may not be named `e` followed by digits. (2) Suffix resolution must be scoped through imports (use core.time) so short names never squat globally and two domains can both define `pt`. (3) No implicit cross-unit conversion, ever: 1s + 500ms only compiles if the unit family declares the conversion; otherwise a diagnostic names the conversion fn. (4) Today `500ms` is a lex error, so zero existing code changes meaning.

options.name: Suffix literals resolved via in-scope #unit families (recommended)
options.detail: Any ratified #unit family gains literal spelling for free. Core ships time/size; user families get it identically — beats C++ where writing the literal operator is expert-only.

options.name: Constructor calls only (status quo)
options.detail: time.ms(500), Usd("4.99"). Explicit but noisy exactly where numbers are densest (games, embedded registers, timeouts).
options.code:
timeout :: time.s(30)
budget :: Usd("4.99")

options.name: Suffixes for core units only, not user families
options.detail: Keeps the lexer surface tiny but creates a two-tier system where core types are more ergonomic than user types — against the expert-parity philosophy.
options.code:
timeout :: 30s      // ok, core
budget :: Usd("4.99")  // user family, no literal

comparisons.note: std::chrono user-defined literals proved 500ms ergonomics; defining your own is arcane template machinery.
Units of measure are the gold standard: compile-time only, zero runtime cost, dimensional analysis.
No unit literals; Duration::from_millis(500) everywhere. Verbosity is the daily complaint.

decisions.title: Copy-with-update: does value.{ field: new } build an edited copy?
decisions.gist: Dot-construction on an existing value: copy it with the named fields replaced. No mutation, no field-by-field rebuild.
decisions.explainer: Incident.{ ... } constructs a new struct. This proposal lets the left side be a value: incident.{ severity: 3 } means "a copy of incident with severity replaced". The original is untouched — you get a new value. It reuses the already-ratified .{} shape, so there is nothing new to learn.
decisions.story: Sarah escalates an incident: same record, severity up, owner set. The struct has ten fields; today she rebuilds all ten by hand and the eight unchanged lines are pure noise that hides the two real edits — and breaks every time a field is added.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Grammar — Type.{} already parses; value.{} is the same postfix form on an expression, and sema already distinguishes type names from values, so no ambiguity. Chains work: get_incident().{ severity: 3 }. (2) Cost honesty — it is a copy; the expand/LSP lens shows the allocation for heap-holding fields, same as slice-copy policy. (3) @single_use interaction — copying a single-use value must be a compile error or the linearity guarantee dies. (4) Pairs naturally with fixed-by-default bindings: edit without mutation.

options.name: value.{ fields } postfix copy-update (recommended)
options.detail: Reads as "start from this value, change these fields". Reuses .{} exactly; changed fields are the only thing on the page.
options.code: escalated :: incident.{ severity: 3, owner: .Some(oncall) }

options.name: Rust-style spread inside construction
options.detail: Familiar to Rust users but adds a second construction element (..) and buries the source value at the end of the literal.
options.code: escalated :: Incident.{ severity: 3, owner: .Some(oncall), ..incident }

options.name: Reject; write update methods per type
options.detail: fn with_severity(self, s: Int) -> Incident per field is exactly the boilerplate Jet exists to delete.
options.code: escalated :: incident.with_severity(3).with_owner(oncall)

comparisons.note: Struct update syntax ..base — proven need, awkward position.
data class copy() is one of the most-used features in the language.
No native form — you mutate a var copy across multiple statements; a known ergonomic gap.

decisions.title: May lambda parameter types be inferred from the expected type?
decisions.gist: (i) => i.state == .Open — the parameter's type flows in from what the callee expects, so the annotation becomes optional.
decisions.explainer: Today every lambda spells its parameter types: (i: Incident) => .... But when filter expects fn(Incident) -> Bool, the compiler already knows i is an Incident before it reads the lambda. Inference here is local and one-directional (expected type flows in) — the same expected-type elaboration that already powers .{} construction and .Variant shorthand.
decisions.story: Tom came from TypeScript. He writes .filter, .map, .each fifty times a day and each one demands a type he and the compiler both already know. It is his single biggest "Jet feels heavier than TS" complaint — in a codebase where every other inference already flows from expected type.
decisions.inWild:
open :: incidents.filter((i) => i.state == .Open)
names :: open.map((i) => i.title)
totals :: by_owner.map((entry) => "{entry.key}: {entry.value}")
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Scope discipline — inference only where an expected type exists (argument position, typed binding). A lambda bound to a bare :: still needs annotations, and the diagnostic must say exactly that with the fix. (2) No Hindley-Milner creep: one-directional, no unification across multiple lambdas, no return-type-driven backsolving. This keeps error messages local and the mental model simple. (3) Annotations stay legal everywhere — teams that want them keep them; a lint profile can require them (I8: policy, not a second mechanism).

options.name: Infer parameter types in expected-type positions (recommended)
options.detail: Annotations optional where the context already fixes the type; required elsewhere. Matches every mainstream language users arrive from.
options.code: open :: incidents.filter((i) => i.state == .Open)

options.name: A + bare single parameter without parens
options.detail: i => i.state == .Open. Reads lighter; costs one more grammar form for the same semantics.
options.code: open :: incidents.filter(i => i.state == .Open)

options.name: Keep mandatory annotations (status quo)
options.detail: Maximal explicitness, but explicitness the compiler already has adds reading noise, not information — the LSP lens can always show the type.
options.code: open :: incidents.filter((i: Incident) => i.state == .Open)

comparisons.note: Contextual typing of callbacks — the exact model proposed here.
Closure params inferred from context; annotations rare in real code.
Closure params inferred; nobody asks for mandatory annotations back.

decisions.title: Trailing block argument: ui.button("Save") { save() }?
decisions.gist: When a call's last parameter is a function, the call may end with a braced block — UI trees and builders read as structure, not nested punctuation.
decisions.explainer: Today passing a lambda means parens-inside-parens: ui.button("Save", () => save()). A trailing block moves that last function argument outside the parens as a plain { } block. For APIs that take "a thing plus what to do" — UI children, task bodies, transaction bodies — the code starts to look like the tree it builds.
decisions.story: Priya builds a settings screen with the reactive UI stack. Three levels of nesting means six layers of (() => ...) punctuation; her code review comments are about parens, not UI. With trailing blocks the source is shaped like the screen.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Parser ambiguity — the rule must be airtight: a { directly after a call's ) (or after a bare callee in statement position) is the trailing zero-parameter lambda; Jet has no bare-block statements so the space is free. (2) v1 restriction: zero-parameter blocks only. Blocks with parameters (Kotlin it, Swift $0) invite implicit-name magic; lambdas with parameters stay in parens. This dodges the whole it/$0 debate. (3) Formatter must own one canonical layout or diffs churn. (4) This is the last piece of the no-JSX UI story: typed constructors + signals + trailing blocks reach SwiftUI readability with zero second language.

options.name: Zero-parameter trailing blocks (recommended)
options.detail: f(args) { body } and f { body }. Parameterized lambdas keep the (x) => form inside parens. Small grammar, most of the win.
options.code:
ui.button("Save") { prefs.save() }
tasks.spawn { queue.flush() }

options.name: Full Swift-style trailing closures with parameters
options.detail: Maximum fluency, but needs parameter-name conventions ($0/it or a header form) — a magic surface Jet has deliberately avoided.
options.code: incidents.filter { (i) => i.state == .Open }

options.name: Reject; lambdas always in the argument list
options.detail: One less grammar rule; UI/builder code keeps the punctuation tax forever.
options.code: ui.button("Save", () => prefs.save())

comparisons.note: Trailing closures are the backbone of SwiftUI's readability.
Lambda-outside-parens made Gradle/Compose DSLs possible; `it` is the part people regret.
Blocks are the original tradition: an entire ecosystem's ergonomics built on one call-with-body form.

decisions.title: @pre/@post function contracts on the signature?
decisions.gist: Declare what a function requires and guarantees; builds check it, comptime proves what it can, and the diagnostic quotes the violated clause.
decisions.explainer: A @pre is a claim about the arguments ("cents must be positive"); a @post is a claim about the result (result names the return value). They sit on the declaration, so callers read the contract without opening the body, the compiler enforces it, and the failure message is the clause itself — not a stack trace into someone else's function.
decisions.story: Miguel's payment function corrupts a balance when cents = -500 sneaks in from a malformed webhook. Today that is a 2am data-repair incident three calls away from the bug. With @pre it is an immediate, named boundary failure pointing at the webhook handler.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Conditions must be pure expressions (no effects), or the contract itself becomes program behavior — enforced by the same purity checker as @pure. (2) Release policy is the hard question. Stripping checks in release (C tradition) means safety evaporates exactly where inputs are hostile. Recommend: checks stay on by default in all builds; a build-policy/#suppress(Contracts) escape strips them per module for measured hot paths. Safe default, expert opt-out — the philosophy's exact shape. (3) Overlap with D-RANGETYPE1 is complementary, not duplicate: range types state a fact about one value's shape at the type; pre/post state relations between arguments and results. (4) Fits the @ contract plane perfectly — these are literally contracts.

options.name: @pre/@post checked in every build; policy strips per module (recommended)
options.detail: Safe by default; enterprises get provable boundaries; game/embedded strip measured hot paths explicitly and auditable-y.
options.code:
@pre(sev >= 0 && sev <= 10)
fn route(sev: Int) -> Route { ... }

options.name: Debug-only checks
options.detail: The C/assert tradition. Cheap, but contracts vanish exactly when inputs turn hostile in production.
options.code:
@pre(sev >= 0)   // compiled out in release
fn route(sev: Int) -> Route { ... }

options.name: Reject; assertions in the body
options.detail: require(cents > 0) works today but is invisible at the call site, invisible to docs, and invisible to the prover.

comparisons.note: Design-by-contract origin: require/ensure on the signature, 35 years of proof it aids reasoning.
comparisons.code:
charge (cents: INTEGER)
  require cents > 0
  ensure balance >= 0

comparisons.note: Pre/Post aspects, statically proven in SPARK — the enterprise/avionics gold standard.
comparisons.code:
procedure Charge (Cents : Positive)
  with Pre => Cents > 0, Post => Balance >= 0;

comparisons.note: No signature contracts; debug_assert! in bodies. Contracts RFC stalled for years — the gap is real.

decisions.title: Package-level effect budget in pack.jet?
decisions.gist: The manifest caps what the whole dependency graph may do — allow Net/Db, deny Exec/Env — and the compiler fails the build naming any dependency that exceeds it.
decisions.explainer: Jet already types effects per function (#(Net)). This lifts them to the package boundary: pack.jet declares which of the ten ratified effects the program may use, and if any dependency — transitively — needs one outside the list, the build fails and prints the dependency path to the offending function. Supply-chain review becomes a compile error instead of a human audit.
decisions.story: Elena runs platform security at a fintech. Policy: no third-party code may exec processes or read environment secrets. Today enforcement is quarterly vendor review and hope. With an effect budget it is one manifest block, enforced on every build, with CI proof.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Division of labor with the open build-authority ballots: D-BUILDPOLICY1 governs what code may do AT BUILD TIME; this governs the COMPILED PROGRAM. Both use the same ten-effect vocabulary (D-EFF4), so users learn one list. (2) Per-dependency grants are required or one noisy-but-trusted dep forces a global allow and the budget rots. Grants are recorded in the lock file — auditable diffs. (3) Precision risk: if stdlib over-reports effects (effect-polymorphic helpers), budgets become noisy and users cargo-cult allow-everything. The effect checker's precision is a prerequisite. (4) This is a differentiator no mainstream compiled language ships: Deno proved demand at runtime; Jet can prove it at compile time. AMENDED 2026-07-01 (magic/expert/audit lens): option D added and recommended — visibility should not require configuration; enforcement should. A remains D's enforcement half.

options.name: allow/deny lists + per-dependency grants in pack.jet (recommended)
options.detail: Whole-graph enforcement, named escape hatches, lock-file provenance. The enterprise story in one block.

options.name: Allow-list only, no grants
options.detail: Simpler, but the first legitimate exception forces widening the global list — budgets erode to allow-everything.
options.code: effects: { allow: [Net, Db, Log, Time] }

options.name: Report only: jet audit effects
options.detail: Visibility without enforcement. Useful day one, but reports get ignored; budgets that fail builds do not.
options.code:
$ jet audit effects
telemetry -> metrics-agent: Env (env.get in read_hostname)

options.name: Always-on provenance report + opt-in enforcement + per-dep grants (recommended)
options.detail: Beginner magic: with NO effects block, every build still prints a one-line effect summary and records per-dependency effect provenance in the lock — visibility costs zero config. Writing effects: { allow/deny } turns on enforcement (option A behavior). Experts get grants; auditors get jet audit effects on every project ever built, not just configured ones.

comparisons.note: --allow-net/--allow-env runtime flags proved developers want capability caps; runtime is too late and per-invocation.
SecurityManager tried dynamic sandboxing and was deprecated — dynamic checks at this granularity failed; static effects are the lesson.
Capability-security lineage: authority flows explicitly or not at all. Jet's effect types are the practical middle.

decisions.title: @persist: keep marked state across jet dev hot reloads?
decisions.gist: Mark a binding; hot reload swaps the code but that value survives — you never replay three minutes to reach the bug again.
decisions.explainer: The JIT dev tier recompiles code while the program runs. Normally module state resets on every reload. @persist tells the dev runtime to carry that value across the reload: edit the damage formula, the world keeps existing, you are instantly back in the fight. In release builds @persist is inert — it is purely a dev-loop contract.
decisions.story: Ken chases a boss-fight bug that only appears three minutes into a level. Every tweak today costs a full replay: ten iterations, half an hour of walking. With @persist on the world state, each code edit lands in the live fight in under a second.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Dev-tier only, stated in the contract: release semantics identical with and without @persist — no prod behavior riding a dev annotation. (2) Identity is module+name; rename loses the state (acceptable, predictable). (3) Type-shape migration: if the reloaded type layout changed, attempt a Codable-style re-decode; on failure reinitialize and print a one-line warning — never crash the session. (4) Wrong-by-default check: persisting ALL module state automatically (option B) would carry stale connection handles and OS resources across reloads — the footgun; opt-in is correct. (5) Depends on the JIT dev-loop card (E3 exit criterion); balloting the surface now lets the runtime work assume it.

options.name: @persist opt-in on module-level bindings, dev-only (recommended)
options.detail: Explicit, greppable, no prod meaning. Migration = re-decode or reinit+warn.
options.code:
@persist world := World.load("level3")
@persist session := DebugCamera.default()

options.name: Persist all module state by default; @fresh opts out
options.detail: Maximum magic, but carries sockets/files/handles across reloads by default — the footgun as default, against I8's bar.
options.code:
world := World.load("level3")   // silently persisted
@fresh conn := db.connect()?

options.name: Reject; state lives in an external store during dev
options.detail: Works today (save/load), but every project reinvents it and the friction kills the tight loop that makes hot reload worth having.
options.code: world := World.load(save_path)  // manual save/load dance

comparisons.note: Domain reload wipes state; the #1 iteration-speed complaint, with an ecosystem of workarounds.
Beta hot reload keeps memory as-is — fast but no typed migration story when layouts change.
comparisons.code: // recompile keeps the arena; layout change = UB

comparisons.note: Time-travel/hot-swap worked because state is a value separate from code — the architectural inspiration.

decisions.title: UFCS: may any free function be called as a method?
decisions.gist: url(incident) callable as incident.url() with no declaration — recommend REJECT: Jet's existing fn Type.name(self) already covers it with one spelling per call.
decisions.explainer: Uniform Function Call Syntax defines a.f(b) as sugar for f(a, b): every free function becomes a method automatically. The draw is chaining and discoverability. But Jet already ships extension declarations — fn Incident.url(self) makes url a method with one explicit line. Full UFCS would make every call spellable two ways.
decisions.story: Owen imports a geometry library of free functions and wants v.normalize().scale(2). Under the status quo the library author (or Owen, locally) writes fn Vec3.normalize(self) once and the chain works — without every other function in the program growing a second spelling.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass — this card exists to record the rejection with reasons: (1) I8 violation: two ways to write every call in the language; review styles fork immediately. (2) Grep integrity dies: finding uses of url means rg 'url\(' AND rg '\.url\(' forever. (3) Method resolution becomes scope-dependent: what x.f() means changes with imports — spooky action Jet has avoided. (4) The genuine benefits (chaining, discoverability) are already delivered by fn Type.name declarations plus LSP completion. A pipeline operator |> was considered as option C and adds a third call spelling — same objection, stronger.

options.name: Full UFCS
options.detail: Everything chains, nothing needs declaring. Two spellings per call, grep-hostile, import-sensitive resolution.
options.code: items.total()   // resolves to free fn total(items)

options.name: Status quo: explicit fn Type.name(self) extension declarations (recommended)
options.detail: One declaration line buys the chain; every call keeps exactly one spelling; extensions are greppable declarations.
options.code:
fn Vec3.normalize(self) -> Vec3 { ... }
unit :: v.normalize()

options.name: No UFCS, add pipeline operator |>
options.detail: x |> f |> g chains free functions without method-izing them — but is a third call spelling with the same I8 objection.
options.code: unit :: v |> normalize |> scale(2.0)

comparisons.note: UFCS origin; celebrated for chaining, criticized for resolution surprises.
Full UFCS: loved for fluency, notorious for "where is this defined?" archaeology.
Considered and rejected; extension traits chosen — the same one-explicit-declaration shape as Jet's fn Type.name.
comparisons.code: impl Vec3Ext for Vec3 { fn normalize(&self) -> Vec3 {...} }

decisions.title: Struct destructuring: .{ id, title } :: incident?
decisions.gist: Construction syntax runs backwards to pull named fields into bindings — the struct twin of the ratified [a, b, c] :: list destructuring.
decisions.explainer: .{ id, severity } :: incident binds local names id and severity from the fields of incident. .{ severity: sev } binds under a different name. The same shape works as a pattern in if-tables, where .{ kind: "page", .. } matches structs whose kind field equals "page" — the .. explicitly marks that other fields exist and are ignored.
decisions.story: Lena handles a webhook payload with eleven fields and needs three. Today that is three access lines (or three fields threaded through a signature). One destructuring line names exactly what the handler consumes — and the reader knows the other eight are untouched.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Grammar fits: fixed-list destructuring [first, second] :: xs is already ratified; .{ } in binding position is its struct twin and cannot collide with variant patterns (.Name vs .{). (2) The .. is mandatory for partial matches so partiality is visible — omitting it means "all fields named", and adding a field to the struct then breaks the full pattern loudly (a feature: exhaustiveness for data). (3) Formatter round-trip test required before ship (the serde-marker corruption lesson). (4) Nesting allowed one level (.{ owner: .{ email, .. }, .. }) but the formatter should discourage deep towers.

options.name: Bindings + if-table patterns with mandatory .. for partial (recommended)
options.detail: One shape in both positions; partiality always visible; renames via field: name.
options.code:
.{ id, severity: sev } :: incident
if event == { .{ kind: "page", target, .. } -> page(target) }

options.name: Binding position only, no patterns
options.detail: Smaller step; if-tables keep matching on whole values/variants only. Loses the webhook-dispatch win.
options.code: .{ id, severity } :: incident

options.name: Reject; field access lines
options.detail: Status quo. Fine at one field, noise at three, signature-threading at five.
options.code:
id :: incident.id
sev :: incident.severity

comparisons.note: Object destructuring is used in essentially every file; the proven daily-driver feature.
Struct patterns with .. — the exact partiality marker proposed here.
No struct destructuring — a gap users complain about; tuples only.

decisions.title: Range-constrained types: type Severity :: Int(0..10)?
decisions.gist: A nominal type that also carries a value range; construction is checked, so invalid states become unrepresentable at the boundary.
decisions.explainer: Extends the ratified nominal form type X :: Base with a constraint: type Severity :: Int(0..10) is an Int that provably holds 0–10. Constructing from a literal is checked at compile time; from a runtime value it is fallible (Severity(raw)?). Arithmetic widens to Int; converting back re-checks. "Parse, don't validate" as a type.
decisions.story: Rosa writes firmware for a 4-bit DAC: legal values 0–15. A percent-over-100 or index-out-of-range bug today ships to the field and bricks a unit. With range types the illegal value cannot even be handed to the register function — the boundary conversion is where it fails, loudly, in the webhook/CLI layer where it belongs.
decisions.inWild:
type Severity :: Int(0..10)
type Percent :: Float(0.0..100.0)
type DacLevel :: Int(0..15)

sev :: Severity(item.severity)?      // runtime: fallible at the boundary
bar :: Percent(73.0)                  // literal: checked at compile time
// dac.write(DacLevel(20))            // compile error: 20 outside 0..15
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Scope discipline is everything: ranges only in v1. Full predicate refinement types (type Even :: Int where self % 2 == 0) are a research tarpit that explodes inference and error messages — same deferral discipline as D-BUDGET1. (2) Complementary to D-PREPOST1, not duplicate: a range type states a fact about one value's shape once, at the type; @pre relates multiple arguments per function. Both earn their keep. (3) Arithmetic law must be boring: ops widen to the base type immediately; only construction narrows. No dependent-type arithmetic on ranges. (4) Ada proved this for 40 years of embedded/avionics; modern languages dropped it and the ecosystem reinvents it badly (NonZeroU8, runtime validators).

options.name: Integer/float ranges on nominal types (recommended)
options.detail: Comptime-checked literals, fallible runtime construction, ops widen to base. Small, proven, huge embedded/game/web payoff.
options.code:
type Severity :: Int(0..10)
sev :: Severity(raw)?

options.name: Ranges + arbitrary pure predicates
options.detail: type Even :: Int where (self % 2 == 0). Maximal power; inference and diagnostics complexity balloon. Defer.
options.code: type Even :: Int where (self % 2 == 0)

options.name: Reject; @pre on every consuming function
options.detail: Repeats the constraint at N call boundaries instead of stating it once where the data lives.
options.code:
@pre(sev >= 0 && sev <= 10)
fn route(sev: Int) -> Route { ... }

comparisons.note: Range types are bread and butter; four decades of embedded proof.
Nothing general — NonZeroU8 is a hand-carved special case; pattern types remain an RFC dream.
Literal unions fake small ranges; nothing for real numeric bounds.

decisions.title: Typed text literals: sql"..." and html"..." with safe interpolation?
decisions.gist: Prefixed strings produce typed values whose interpolations auto-parameterize (SQL) or auto-escape (HTML) — injection becomes unrepresentable, not just discouraged.
decisions.explainer:
sql"select * from t where id = {id}" is not a String — it is a Sql value carrying the query text and {id} as a typed bound parameter. db.query accepts Sql, not String, so concatenating user input into a query is a type error, not a code-review hope. html"

{title}

" escapes title on the way in. The compiler machinery is the ratified @tainted/@sanitizer model; this gives it a front door.
decisions.story: Jake, an intern, ships a search box in week two. String-concatenated SQL has been the #1 web vulnerability for 25 years across every mainstream language. In Jet the vulnerable spelling does not type-check, and the error names the sql"..." fix.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) The prefix set is CLOSED in v1: core defines sql and html only. User-defined prefixes are reader-macro territory — explicitly an E4 question, not smuggled in here. (2) sh"..." (shell) is deliberately excluded: argv-array APIs are the safe shape for exec, not string templating. (3) Cost: core db/ui APIs must take Sql/Html types; drivers written before this need a shim. (4) Prior art is strong: JS tagged templates made sql`...` the standard safe pattern; C# FormattableString feeds parameterized queries. Jet's twist is compile-time taint integration instead of library convention. AMENDED 2026-07-01: option D added and recommended — expected-type elaboration (the Blueprint north-star mechanism) deletes even the prefix for the 95% call-position case; A becomes D's fallback spelling for unexpected-type positions.

options.name: Closed core set: sql and html literals (recommended)
options.detail: Two prefixes, two typed values, injection dead in the two places it actually kills. Extensibility deferred to E4.
options.code:
rows :: db.query(sql"select * where sev >= {min_sev}")? page :: html"

{title}

"

options.name: Core set + user-defined prefixes via derive
options.detail: Libraries define css"...", re"...". Powerful, but user prefixes are effectively reader macros — E4's decision to make, not this ballot's.
options.code:
#derive Css.TextLiteral { ... }
style :: css"color: {c}"

options.name: Builder APIs only, no literal syntax
options.detail: Safe and shippable today, but the ergonomic tax means users fall back to string concat — the vulnerability survives on the path of least resistance.
options.code: rows :: db.select("incidents").where_gte("sev", min_sev).query()?

options.name: Expected-type elaboration: plain interpolated strings elaborate to Sql/Html where expected (recommended)
options.detail: db.query takes Sql; a string LITERAL with interpolations in that position elaborates to template + typed bound params — the same expected-type law as .{ } construction. No prefix to learn for the common call. Runtime String values and concatenation into Sql positions stay type errors naming the fix. Sql.raw("...") is the audited expert escape (greppable, lint-gateable). Prefixes sql"…"/html"…" remain only for bindings without an expected type.

comparisons.note: Tagged template literals — sql`...` is the ecosystem-proven prior art for exactly this.
comparisons.code: const rows = await db.query(sql`select * where id = ${id}`);

comparisons.note: FormattableString overloads let APIs receive the template + args and parameterize safely.
Nothing; parameterized queries are convention only, and sqli persists in the wild.
comparisons.code: db.Query("select * where id = " + input) // compiles fine

decisions.title: Chained comparisons: 0 <= sev < 10?
decisions.gist: Math notation for range checks; the middle operand is written and evaluated once.
decisions.explainer: 0 <= sev < 10 desugars to 0 <= sev && sev < 10 with sev evaluated a single time. Today a < b < c is a type error in Jet (Bool < Int), so the grammar space is free — no existing code changes meaning. Only same-direction chains are legal; mixed directions like a < b > c are rejected with a teaching error.
decisions.story: Casey writes range checks hourly. In x >= lo && x < hi the duplicated x is exactly where the typo hides (x >= lo && y < hi passes review twice a year). The math spelling has one x.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) C's footgun is the opposite behavior — (a<b)<c silently compares a Bool to an Int; Jet currently rejects, and this proposal keeps rejecting everything except monotone chains, so the footgun cannot return. (2) Single-evaluation of the middle operand must be specified (matters when it is a call). (3) Pairs with D-RANGETYPE1: the chain is the check you write when a range type is overkill. Tiny feature, permanent daily payoff, zero interaction with any other card.

options.name: Same-direction chains, middle evaluated once (recommended)
options.detail: <, <=, >, >= chains of any length, one direction per chain; == excluded (use table dispatch).
options.code: if 0 <= sev < 10 { route(sev) }

options.name: Reject; explicit && forever
options.detail: One less desugaring rule; the duplicated-operand typo class stays.
options.code: if 0 <= sev && sev < 10 { route(sev) }

comparisons.note: Has chained comparisons; universally liked, never a confusion source.
The tradition being fixed: a < b < c compiles and does the wrong thing silently.
Has them; scientific users treat the math notation as table stakes.

decisions.title: What operations does a nominal type inherit from its base?
decisions.gist: type Usd :: Decimal starts inert; named capability bundles (@numeric, @comparable, @printable) grant chosen base operations without hand-written operator boilerplate.
decisions.explainer: The value of type Usd :: Decimal is what it does NOT inherit: a CustomerId should not multiply. But hand-implementing +, -, and < for every currency type is boilerplate that pushes users back to raw Decimal — losing the safety they came for. Capability bundles are contracts that re-expose a curated slice of the base type's operations, with the nominal type preserved (Usd + Usd -> Usd; Usd + Eur still an error).
decisions.story: Hannah models Usd, Eur, and Btc. Six operator implementations per currency is eighteen identical functions of noise — so on a deadline she types raw Decimal everywhere, and six months later a Usd/Eur mix-up ships. The bundle line keeps her honest for free.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Bundles vs fine-grained with (+, -, <) list: the list is precise but is pseudo-syntax with unclear semantics for non-operator members; bundles are teachable, cover ~95%, and a type can stack several. Fine lists can come later if bundles prove too coarse — the reverse migration would be breaking. (2) Overlap declared: #unit families auto-grant numeric behavior; this card covers standalone nominal types that are not units (ids, handles, wrappers). One ratification should name that relationship. (3) Go's cautionary tale: named types inherit ALL base operators automatically — CustomerId * CustomerId compiles. Inert-by-default is the correct pole; bundles are the ergonomic bridge.

options.name: Named capability bundles: @numeric, @comparable, @printable, @codable_as_base (recommended)
options.detail: Curated, teachable grants; nominal identity preserved in every granted op; stackable.
options.code: @[numeric, printable] type Usd :: Decimal

options.name: Fine-grained grant list
options.detail: type Usd :: Decimal with (+, -, <, to_string). Maximum control, new pseudo-syntax, bikeshed magnet.
options.code: type Usd :: Decimal with (+, -, <, to_string)

options.name: Nothing inherited; hand impls only (status quo)
options.detail: Pure but punishing: the boilerplate tax drives users back to raw base types, defeating the feature's purpose.
options.code:
impl Usd.Add { fn +(self, rhs: Usd) -> Usd { ... } }
// x6 per type

comparisons.note: GeneralizedNewtypeDeriving — derive the base's instances per class; the direct ancestor of bundles.
comparisons.code: newtype Usd = Usd Decimal deriving (Eq, Ord, Num)

comparisons.note: The derive_more crate exists purely because std has no answer — third-party proof of the boilerplate pain.
Named types inherit every operator — CustomerId arithmetic compiles. The too-much pole.
comparisons.code: type CustomerId string // id1 + id2 compiles

decisions.title: How do errors gain context on the way up?
decisions.gist: A failure crossing three layers should say what the program was doing; recommend stdlib .context() on fallible values — no new syntax.
decisions.explainer: ? propagates the raw error. Three layers up, "file not found" no longer says WHICH file or WHY it was being read. Context wrapping attaches a human sentence at each meaningful boundary, and the final error renders the chain. The question is whether that deserves syntax or a method.
decisions.story: Sam's service fails at startup with "file not found". Which of the nine config/asset/cert files? He adds print statements to find out — the error should have carried its own story: "loading TLS cert (config/tls.pem) ← starting https listener ← startup".
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: syntax (option B: expr ? "msg") spends grammar budget on what a method spells fine, and couples the ? operator to string formatting. Rust settled this in the ecosystem: anyhow's .context() became the standard without any syntax. The one compiler-side piece worth ratifying: the diagnostic/panic renderer understands the context chain natively so the arrows come free. Interpolation inside .context is lazy — only evaluated on the failure path. AMENDED 2026-07-01: option D added and recommended — the trace is free magic the compiler already has the information for; .context stays the intentional layer. A is D minus the automatic trace.

options.name: Stdlib .context(msg) on fallible values + native chain rendering (recommended)
options.detail: No grammar change; lazily-evaluated message; renderer shows the chain with locations.
options.code: config :: fs.read(path).context("loading config {path}")?

options.name: Context operator on ?
options.detail: fs.read(path) ? "loading config {path}" — shortest spelling, but overloads the single most load-bearing operator in the language.
options.code: config :: fs.read(path) ? "loading config {path}"

options.name: Nothing; errors carry only their origin
options.detail: Every service team reinvents context wrapping badly, or debugs with print statements.
options.code: config :: fs.read(path)?   // "file not found" — which file? why?

options.name: Automatic propagation trace by default + .context() for human wording (recommended)
options.detail: Beginner magic: every ? crossing is recorded (dev/debug builds; cheap span push), so an unhandled failure prints the full propagation path with file:line — zero user code, Zig-style but with Jet spans and rendering. .context("loading config {path}") adds the human WHY at boundaries that deserve one; lazily evaluated. Release builds keep origin + explicit contexts only (policy can keep full traces). Auditors read failure paths without instrumenting anything.
options.code:
// no user code at all:
error: file not found (config/tls.pem)
  via src/tls.jet:14 load_cert
  via src/server.jet:41 start_https
  via src/run.jet:9 run

// plus intentional wording where it matters:
cert :: fs.read(path).context("loading TLS cert for {host}")?

comparisons.note: anyhow .context() — the ecosystem-proven shape this recommends adopting into core.
fmt.Errorf %w wrapping — same idea, stringly and verbose at every site.
comparisons.code: if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("loading config %s: %w", path, err) }

comparisons.note: Error return traces show WHERE errors passed, but carry no human WHY.

decisions.title: Generator functions: fn ticks() -> Stream<Int> with yield?
decisions.gist: Functions that produce values lazily, suspending at yield and resuming on demand; loops consume them like any sequence. E3 already promises coroutines — this ballot fixes the surface.
decisions.explainer: A generator runs until yield, hands the value to the consumer, and resumes where it left off when the next value is demanded. It turns state machines back into straight-line code: game behavior scripts, parsers, pagination, pipelines. The runtime is the E3 structured-concurrency/coroutine machinery; this decision is only about how it is spelled.
decisions.story: Marta scripts a cutscene: walk to the door, wait two seconds, speak, fade. As sequential code with yields it reads like stage directions. As a hand-rolled state machine it is an 80-line enum with a tick method — the reason Unity users cling to coroutines despite everything else.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Function-coloring risk is the classic objection — contained here because Stream<T> is an ordinary value implementing the Iterable hook; consumers are plain loops, no await/async split enters the language. yield is legal only inside fns returning Stream<T>, enforced with a teaching error. (2) Rust's decade of unstable generators is the cost-of-not-deciding cautionary tale; C#'s twenty years of IEnumerable/yield is the it-just-works proof. (3) Sequencing: E3's exit criteria already include "structured concurrency + coroutines" — deciding the surface now lets the runtime card build toward it instead of retrofitting. (4) Effects compose: a Stream producer's effects appear in its signature like any fn.

options.name: yield + Stream<T> return type, riding the E3 coroutine runtime (recommended)
options.detail: One keyword, one type; consumers are ordinary loops; no async/await coloring anywhere.
options.code:
fn ticks() -> Stream<Int> { yield 1; yield 2 }
loop t in ticks() { print("{t}") }

options.name: Library only: tasks + channels
options.detail: spawn a producer task, recv from a channel. Works, but a concurrency construct for what is often a single-threaded control-flow need — heavier to write, schedule, and reason about.
options.code:
ch :: channel<Int>(cap: 8)
tasks.spawn(^ch () => { ch.send(1); ch.send(2) })

options.name: Defer past E3
options.detail: Avoids surface risk now, but the coroutine runtime lands in E3 regardless — deciding late means retrofitting the spelling onto shipped machinery.
options.code: // hand-rolled state machine, 80 lines

comparisons.note: yield return / IEnumerable — twenty years of proof that generators without async coloring work.
comparisons.code: IEnumerable<int> Ticks() { yield return 1; yield return 2; }

comparisons.note: Generators are load-bearing across the entire ecosystem.
Generators unstable for a decade; ecosystem limps on hand-written state machines and async-stream macros.

decisions.explainer: Today a script that needs a library needs a pack.jet — a cliff exactly where beginners stand. An inline pin on the use statement (the already-ratified pkg#version pin) lets one file carry its own deps. The lock lives in the user-invisible cache keyed by file content; `jet lock script.jet` materializes a sidecar when someone wants committed reproducibility.
decisions.story: Nate writes a 40-line log analyzer for a friend. He sends ONE file. The friend runs jet run analyze.jet and it just works — deps fetched, locked, cached. No project, no manifest, no instructions.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Reproducibility — cache lock is per-file-hash; editing the file re-locks. For committed exactness, `jet lock` writes analyze.jet.lock beside the file; jet run prefers it when present. (2) Version drift — bare `use textkit` (no pin) in a script resolves latest-compatible and RECORDS the choice in the cache lock; the teaching hint suggests adding the pin. (3) Upgrade path — `jet init` lifts inline uses into a generated pack.jet deps block, so the script→package rung costs one command. (4) No install-time code execution (PM-I1) applies identically.

comparisons.note: PEP-723 inline script metadata made uv the fastest-growing tool in Python. Demand is proven.
cargo-script languished unstable for a decade; everyone feels the gap.
No single-file story at all; gorun and hacks fill the void.

decisions.title: U11 — Inline dependencies for single-file scripts?
decisions.gist: use textkit#1.4 inside a bare .jet file: jet run resolves, locks (cache keyed by file), and runs. Rung 0 stays manifest-free while gaining the whole registry.

options.name: use pkg#version inline, cache lock + optional sidecar (recommended)
options.detail: Zero ceremony, ratified pin syntax, committed reproducibility on demand, one-command upgrade to a package.
options.code:
use textkit#1.4
$ jet lock analyze.jet    // writes analyze.jet.lock for committing

options.name: Header manifest block (uv/PEP-723 style)
options.detail: A comment/data block at the top of the file listing deps. Works, but invents a second manifest grammar when use already exists.
options.code:
//! deps: { textkit: "1.4" }
use textkit

options.name: No inline deps; scripts with deps need pack.jet
options.detail: Keeps one dependency surface, but rebuilds the exact cliff rung 0 exists to remove.
options.code: // analyze.jet + pack.jet + .jet/ — three things to send a friend

decisions.explainer: A dev environment is tools + RUNNING THINGS. Nix needed devenv/process-compose bolted on; jetpack builds supervision in. A service is a typed struct: fields are its options (completion + docs in the editor), the supervisor owns lifecycle, health-checks, and logs. Core ships the common set (postgres, redis, mysql, nats, minio…); any package can define a Service.
decisions.story: Priya clones the repo, types jet dev. Postgres 16 comes up with the schema loaded, redis follows, the app starts against them. She never installed either, and `jet services logs postgres` answers her first question of the day.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Supervisor scope — project-scoped processes with sockets/data under .jet/, never system daemons; jetos system services are the system.* namespace, same Service type, different lifecycle owner. (2) Health — a service declares readiness (port/probe); jet dev waits for ready before fn dev(), killing the "app raced the database" class. (3) Magic/expert: beginners write two lines; experts define custom Service types (typed fields, readiness probe, shutdown hook) in ordinary Jet; auditors see every process a project can start by grepping services:. (4) State — service data dirs live under .jet/ and are GC-visible.

comparisons.note: services.postgres.enable = true proved the demand; it is the reason devenv exists apart from flakes.
The YAML sidecar Nix shells need for supervision — the bolt-on this absorbs.
The default answer everywhere else: container-heavy, slow on mac, another language.

decisions.title: U12 — Typed services in env modules with built-in supervision?
decisions.gist: services: { postgres: Service.{ version: 16 } } — jetpack supervises (up/down/health/logs), the editor completes options, and devenv/process-compose die as separate tools.

options.name: Typed Service structs + built-in supervisor (recommended)
options.detail: Core service set, user-definable Service types, health-gated startup, logs/up/down verbs.
options.code: services: { postgres: Service.{ version: 16, init: "schema.sql" } }

options.name: Untyped process list (process-compose style)
options.detail: processes: ["postgres -D .jet/pg"] — quick, stringly, no completion, no health contract.
options.code: processes: ["postgres -D .jet/pg", "redis-server"]

options.name: No supervision; document docker-compose
options.detail: Punts the #1 devenv feature to a tool Jet is supposed to replace.
options.code: $ docker compose up -d   # separate file, separate tool

decisions.explainer: Secrets are Nix's open wound: the store is world-readable, so agenix/sops-nix exist as third-party duct tape. Jet builds the answer in: a secrets file encrypted to team/machine keys (age-style) lives in the repo; secret("name") references an entry; decryption happens at env entry or service start, in memory, never written to the hangar; reading one from code requires the Secret effect, so the audit question "what can exfiltrate keys" is a grep.
decisions.story: Elena onboards a contractor. He gets repo access and his key added to secrets.recipients — one line, one re-encrypt. He never sees the production Stripe key travel over Slack, and when he leaves, removing the line rotates him out.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Never in the store — hangar artifacts must be secret-free by construction; secrets resolve at activation, not build; a build that tries to read one fails (Secret effect denied in build tier by default, D-BUILDPOLICY1). (2) The Secret effect joins the ratified ten as effect #11 or rides Env — separate is better for budgets (deny: [Secret] for the whole dep graph = D-EFFBUDGET1 integration). (3) Key management: age-style recipients file; CI gets a machine key; no vault dependency for the base tier, adapters (vault/op/kms) as providers for enterprises. (4) Magic/expert: beginners run jet secrets set and it works; experts swap the backend; auditors grep #(Secret) and the recipients file history.

comparisons.note: World-readable store made secrets a third-party problem: agenix, sops-nix — the duct tape this replaces.
Encrypted-file-in-repo with recipient keys — the proven model A adopts, minus the YAML.
The default everywhere else: plaintext .env, .gitignore, and prayer.

decisions.title: U13 — First-class encrypted secrets in env/system modules?
decisions.gist: secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: secret("stripe-dev") } — encrypted at rest in the repo, decrypted only into the entered environment, never in the store, reads effect-gated.

options.name: Built-in encrypted secrets + Secret effect gating (recommended)
options.detail: age-style file in repo, recipients management, activation-time decryption, effect-gated reads, provider adapters for vault/kms.
options.code: secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: secret("stripe-dev") }

options.name: Env-var passthrough only
options.detail: env_vars: { STRIPE_KEY: env("STRIPE_KEY") } — pushes the real problem back to .env files and Slack DMs.
options.code: env_vars: { STRIPE_KEY: env("STRIPE_KEY") }

options.name: External managers only (adapters, no built-in)
options.detail: Clean scope, but small teams get nothing out of the box — the anti-batteries choice.
options.code: secrets: { STRIPE_KEY: vault("kv/stripe#key") }
