decisions.explainer: Deployment artifacts are the third thing every project eventually needs (after build and env). The image namespace is already reserved (§5 unified-ecosystem). This gate fixes its surface: an image module names what goes in (a package target, env slices, files) and what comes out (oci, iso, vm). Because the hangar is content-addressed, images are layered and reproducible for free — nix dockerTools' killer feature with typed fields instead of function soup.
decisions.story: Sam finishes the web app and needs a container for the platform team. He writes four lines, runs jet image server, and gets a 12MB distroless image with exactly the binary and its closure — no Dockerfile, no apt-get layer archaeology, same lockfile provenance as the binary.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Scope discipline — kind: .Oci and .Iso in v1 (containers + jetos installers); VM/disk images later. (2) Contents law: closure of the named target only; adding ad-hoc files is explicit (files: [...]), so images stay minimal and auditable — jet audit image lists every path and where it came from. (3) No Docker dependency: OCI layout built directly from hangar objects; --push speaks the registry protocol. (4) Base-image escape hatch for the messy world: base: oci("debian:12") for teams mid-migration.

comparisons.note: dockerTools.buildLayeredImage — reproducible layered images are beloved; the interface is expert-only function soup.
The default: imperative layers, apt snapshots, non-reproducible by design.
Language-specific image builders proved "no Dockerfile" demand for Go/Java.

decisions.title: U14 — image.* namespace: OCI containers and ISOs from the same manifest?
decisions.gist: module image.server { from: packages.pulseops } → jet image server emits a distroless OCI image; image.installer emits a jetos ISO. One model, dockerTools without the arcana.

options.name: image.* modules, kind .Oci/.Iso, closure-only contents (recommended)
options.detail: Typed, reproducible, distroless by default, explicit file additions, registry push built in.
options.code: module image.server { kind: .Oci, from: packages.pulseops }

options.name: CLI-only: jet image --target pulseops --oci
options.detail: No declaration to review or reuse; flags rot into CI scripts.
options.code: $ jet image --target pulseops --oci --expose 8080

options.name: Defer images past jetpack v1
options.detail: Smaller v1, but every real deployment reinvents Dockerfiles on top of jet build meanwhile.
options.code: # Dockerfile again

decisions.explainer: One machine is system.*; many machines are a map of hostname to system value. Per-host differences are copy-with-update on a shared system module — no overlay/override spaghetti, just the language's own edit-a-copy form. jet push builds every host closure locally (or in CI), ships to each host's hangar over ssh, activates atomically, and rolls back any host whose health probe fails.
decisions.story: Elena runs 2 web nodes and a DB. She edits the nginx module once, runs jet push prod, watches web1 activate and pass health, then web2. The DB host is untouched — its closure hash did not change, so nothing shipped.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Sequencing honesty — this rides jetos Phase 2 (activation/generations); ratify the SURFACE now so system.* design accounts for it, implement after single-host jetos works. (2) Unchanged-host skip falls out of content addressing — deploys are incremental for free. (3) Failure law: health probe fails → that host rolls back to its previous generation and the rollout halts; no partial-fleet mystery states. (4) Secrets integrate per U13 (recipients include host keys). (5) Magic/expert: two hosts need four lines; experts get Rollout knobs; auditors get per-host generation history.

comparisons.note: The NixOS fleet tool this absorbs: hive.nix with per-node overrides.
Flake-based deploys with rollback-on-failure — the health-gate prior art.

decisions.explainer: The owner uses nix shells daily; so does every target user this tool must win. Parity is three flows: (1) ad-hoc tools — jet env -p nodejs ripgrep opens a subshell with those packages from the default source (nixpkgs via the inferred provider today); (2) repo shells — jet env in a repo with flake.nix/devenv.nix and no env.* modules realizes the foreign devShell, prompt and lock jet-side; (3) ephemeral runs — jet run nixpkgs@fastfetch. Export closes the loop: jet bridge flake writes a flake.nix shim exposing this repo's packages/env to Nix consumers.
decisions.story: Nate keeps his muscle memory: where he typed nix-shell -p ffmpeg he types jet env -p ffmpeg. His work repo is still all-Nix — jet env picks up its devShell unchanged. His Jet side project exports a shim so his Nix-die-hard friend consumes it with nix build. Nobody converted anything, and both tools work the whole time.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet env -p nodejs_22 ripgrep     # nix-shell -p, typed refs, jet prompt
$ jet env                           # flake.nix detected -> its devShell
$ jet run nixpkgs@fastfetch           # nix run parity, nothing installed
$ jet bridge flake                    # writes flake.nix shim for Nix users
$ jet env --pure                    # hermetic: only declared packages
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Mechanism honesty — phase 1 shells out to the nix binary (ratified stopgap: requires Nix installed; clear message otherwise); the UX contract is jet's and survives the core provider absorbing realization later, so muscle memory built now never breaks. (2) Detection order: env.* modules win over flake.nix when both exist; --flake forces foreign. (3) devenv.nix consumption limited to packages/env/services fields it can map — unmappable fields produce a named warning, not silence (no silent caps). (4) The exported shim is generated, never hand-edited, and CI-checkable for drift. (5) Lock: foreign inputs recorded in .jet/lock with their narHashes — one lockfile law holds.

comparisons.note: The flows being matched, verb for verb.
comparisons.code:
$ nix-shell -p nodejs ripgrep
$ nix develop
$ nix run nixpkgs#fastfetch

decisions.explainer: jet = language, jetpack = package engine are ratified canon. The OS name ships on ISOs, boot menus, and headlines — it is the most public name in the family and currently a placeholder. Candidates below keep the aviation canon and are checked for obvious collisions (a real trademark sweep is a pre-release task).
decisions.story: Six months from now someone writes "I daily-drive ____". The word in the blank is this ballot.
decisions.inWild:
MENU (aviation canon, original, no echoes):
  jetos       — literal, matches canon, zero surprise
  Airframe    — the structure everything mounts to; strong OS metaphor
  Jetstream   — fast, always-on current; consumer-friendly
  Flightdeck  — where the whole machine is commanded
  Avionics    — the systems layer of an aircraft; precise but technical
  Mach        — short, fast, memorable; collision: mach kernel
  Contrail    — what a jet leaves behind; generations metaphor, soft
  Tarmac      — where jets live between flights; grounded, humble
  Altimeter   — instrument; too narrow
  Slipstream  — riding the jet's wake; evocative, minor product collisions
decisions.detail: Filter applied: must read as an OS (a place/structure, not an action), survive "install ____", "____ generations", "____ switch", and not collide loudly (Mach = kernel history; Slipstream = several products; Runway = fashion/startup tools — excluded). Shortlist rationale: Airframe is the structural metaphor (the OS is what everything bolts to) and unclaimed in the OS space; Jetstream is the friendliest to consumers; Flightdeck says "control everything" which matches declarative machines; jetos costs nothing and can be renamed only with pain later — decide now.

decisions.explainer: The vision originally implied five file names (pack/env/workspace/host/fleet) and three commands (jet/jetpack/jetos). The owner called the confusion; the fix was already latent: modules are named declarations (U3) discovered by find() (U4), so the namespace states the role and the filename is the USER'S organizational choice. Same for commands: verbs resolve against declared modules, and unknown jet verbs dispatch to the jetpack/jetos binaries git-style — the one-way dependency arrow survives untouched because the compiler execs by name, links nothing.
decisions.story: A beginner learns exactly two names on day one: pack.jet and jet. Six months later she manages a fleet — and has still learned zero new file names and zero new commands, only new module namespaces her editor completed for her.
decisions.detail: Adversarial pass: (1) Revisions required — U10 (jetpack.toml/env.jet as REQUIRED names die; env.jet remains a blessed convention), D-WORKSPACE2 (workspace.jet folds into root pack.jet workspace block), D-PM4 (jet fronts jetpack verbs). (2) The ratified payload/env SEMANTIC separation survives fully — it moves from filenames to namespaces. (3) Verb collisions: jet run file.jet vs jet run nixpkgs@tool disambiguate by ref shape; a user fn named like a tool verb never collides because lifecycle verbs are a closed ratified set. (4) Discovery cost: tools index by module namespace, so "where is the env?" is jet list env, not a filename hunt. (5) Single-binary UX with multi-binary architecture is the D-TOOL-SPLIT industry finding.

comparisons.note: One file (Cargo.toml), one command (cargo, fronting rustc) — the shape that won Rust its tooling reputation.
External subcommand dispatch by binary name — the zero-coupling mechanism proposed here.
The cautionary tale: flake.nix, shell.nix, default.nix, configuration.nix, home.nix + nix/nixos-rebuild/home-manager.

decisions.title: U18 — The two-names rule: one reserved file (pack.jet), one command (jet)?
decisions.gist: pack.jet is the only file name the tool looks for; module namespaces (env.*, system.*, fleet.*) carry every role, discovered anywhere. jet is the only command; jetpack/jetos stay as engines it dispatches to. Revises U10, D-WORKSPACE2, D-PM4.

options.name: Two names: pack.jet + jet (recommended)
options.detail: One reserved file, one command; roles are namespaces; engines dispatched by name.
options.code: $ jet env    # -> execs jetpack enter, invisible to the user

options.name: Two files (pack.jet + env.jet required), one command
options.detail: Keeps the env filename mandatory for the ratified separation; one more name to learn for no semantic gain — the namespace already separates.
options.code: pack.jet + env.jet required; jet only command

options.name: Status quo: five files, three commands
options.detail: Every role visible in the filesystem, at the cost the owner already rejected: 5 names + 3 CLIs to learn.
options.code: pack.jet env.jet workspace.jet host.jet fleet.jet / jet jetpack jetos

decisions.ratificationNote: Owner amendment folded in: only pack.jet is a reserved filename; every role module (env.*, system.*, fleet.*, build) may live in any file the user chooses (e.g. build.jet) and is discovered by declaration via find(), never by filename. Implementation plans must carry this as an acceptance test.

decisions.explainer: Entering an environment and running project code are different intents with different risk. jet env [name] realizes the environment (base env.* plus an optional named overlay) and opens a shell — no project function ever runs from env entry. jet dev is the explicit execution verb: it realizes env(base + env.dev) because running needs the toolchain anyway, then runs fn dev() (fallback: fn run under watch/reload). jet test / jet build use env.test / env.build the same way. The danger direction is closed: code runs only when a verb whose MEANING is "run code" is typed.
decisions.story: Ken types jet dev. Postgres comes up seeded, the wasm toolchain is on PATH, fn dev() starts the server with hot reload — one command, and the same command works identically on his teammate's machine. In CI, jet test gets the env.test overlay with a throwaway database, no YAML.
decisions.detail: Owner direction 2026-07-01: entering a dev env is often just "give me the tools to work" — autorunning project functions from an entry verb is dangerous (clone untrusted repo, enter env, project code executes). Split ratifies the intent boundary. Residual hole closed with it: on_enter hooks and service definitions are also project-authored code — first jet env in a fresh repo shows a trust summary (hooks, services, sources) and requires confirmation, direnv-allow style; the grant is recorded and re-prompted when the env definition changes hash. jet dev inside an untrusted repo is explicitly running its code — that is the user's stated intent, no gate. Option A (auto-compose entry+run under one verb) kept below for the record; superseded by D. Owner addition 2026-07-01: --trust flag bypasses the gate in one shot (CI/scripts/known sources) and records the grant; expert/org tier: jet config trust add <pattern> pre-trusts sources by pattern so matching repos never prompt.

comparisons.note: processes + enterShell + scripts approximate this composition with three concepts; env.<verb> is one.
npm run dev — entry only, environment is your problem; the half-answer everyone has.
Solves enter-on-cd only; composition with a dev process is manual.

decisions.title: U19 — What exactly does jet dev do? (env.dev module vs fn dev entry)
decisions.gist: Owner-refined split: jet env enters the shell (tools only — NEVER executes project functions); jet dev explicitly runs fn dev() inside env(base + env.dev). Named env.<verb> overlays stay.

options.name: Compose: env overlay + entry fn, one verb
options.detail: jet dev = env(base+dev) -> services -> fn dev. env.<verb> generalizes to test/build. jet enter for shell-only.
options.code:
$ jet dev
$ jet enter dev

options.name: Separate: jet dev runs only fn dev; environments need jet enter first
options.detail: No composition magic; every session is two commands and CI scripts chain them — the glue Jet exists to delete.
options.code:
$ jet enter
$ jet dev      # two steps, every time

options.name: Compose, but rename the env overlay (env.local/env.serve) to avoid the double "dev"
options.detail: Same semantics as A with distinct names; costs the neat env.<verb> generalization symmetry.
options.code:
module env.local { ... }
$ jet dev   # env(base+local) -> fn dev

options.name: jet env enters (no execution) / jet dev runs fn dev inside env (recommended — owner direction)
options.detail: jet env [name]: shell with base env or named overlay; never runs project fns; first-entry trust gate covers hooks/services. jet dev/test/build: explicit execution verbs, each inside env(base + env.<verb>) when declared.
options.code:
$ jet env                # base env shell — tools only, nothing runs
$ jet env dev            # shell with the dev overlay — still nothing runs
$ jet dev                # EXPLICIT: env(base+dev) -> services -> fn dev()
$ jet test               # env(base+test) -> #test items

$ cd fresh-clone && jet env
// trust gate: env.dev declares 2 services, 1 on_enter hook, 3 sources
//   review: jet env --show   allow: jet env --trust
$ jet env --trust        # bypass the prompt when you trust the source
$ jet config trust add github.com/acme/*   # org tier: pattern-trusted sources, no prompts

decisions.title: Where does fn build live at each scale, and how do workspace builds compose?
decisions.gist: One build-entry model from a single file to a monorepo: where the entry lives at each rung, and who grants its authority.
decisions.explainer: D-BUILDENTRY1 picks the entry spelling; this decision fixes its home per scale and the grant chain. Owner direction (2026-07-01): effect/capability declaration must travel with the code so a lone .jet file works with no manifest; pkg.jet is where a project grants standing permission; the workspace is where an org caps everything. Composition: a workspace build runs member builds in dependency order; whether it may only observe/cap members or also contribute targets is part of this choice. Declaration stays one mechanism (code-site #Impure/effect tags, D-CTEFFECT1); permission and policy are the two layers above it — nothing is declared twice (I8).
decisions.story: Earl writes a one-file jam game that bakes a sprite atlas at build time. It grows into a package, then his studio pulls it into their 40-package monorepo. Earl's build fn should survive each move unchanged, and the studio's security lead needs one file that caps what every member build may touch in CI.
decisions.detail: Grant chain at a glance: single file = per-invocation grant (flag or interactive prompt); package = standing grant recorded in pkg.jet; workspace = ceiling that member grants cannot exceed. Each rung caps the rung below; jet audit reads all three without executing anything.

options.name: Entry lives in the unit's existing definition file at every rung
options.detail: Single file: fn build beside fn main. Package: fn build inside pkg.jet. Workspace: fn build inside workspace.jet. Zero new filenames; the grant chain (flag -> pkg.jet build: block -> workspace policy block) mirrors containment. Workspace fn build may add workspace-level targets and cap members, never mutate a member's plan.

options.name: Dedicated build.jet beside the manifest
options.detail: Package and workspace each get a build.jet next to pkg.jet / workspace.jet; single file keeps fn build in-file. Manifests stay purely declarative; build logic gets its own home. Cost: a fourth special filename (env.jet, pkg.jet, workspace.jet, build.jet) and a two-file story for small packages.

options.name: Any source file, selected by an explicit pointer
options.detail: pkg.jet points at the entry: build: .{ entry: tools.release_build }. Most flexible layout; auditors must follow the pointer instead of grepping one location, and two packages can spell the same thing two ways.

options.name: Package scope only (no single-file, no workspace entry)
options.detail: The Cargo build.rs shape: only packages get a build entry. A lone script cannot use build-time generation without first creating a package, and an org has no first-class ceiling — policy lives in external CI scripts.
options.code:
// jam.jet
fn build(b: BuildContext) ... // error: build entry requires a package manifest

comparisons.note: build.rs is package-only, ambient-authority, and has no workspace-level build or policy file; orgs bolt policy on with external tooling.
comparisons.code: // build.rs — full process authority, no grant chain

comparisons.note: build.zig is a dedicated per-package build program (option B shape); no capability layer, no workspace ceiling.
BUILD per package + WORKSPACE/MODULE at root — the two-rung shape of option A/B, but in a separate dialect from the app language.
One flake.nix serves every scale and evaluation is pure by default — the closest existing grant-chain model, in a specialized language.

decisions.title: Where does build-generated Jet source live, and how is it addressed?
decisions.gist: Build code emits real Jet modules (D-CTCODEGEN1). Decide the on-disk home, lock hashing, staging, and the additive-only rule.
decisions.explainer: D-CTCODEGEN1 already ratified the pipeline law: generated code re-enters lexer -> parser -> sema like hand-written source. This decision fixes the user-visible surface on top of it: where generated files land, whether they are committed, how b.generate() addresses them, whether a later generation round may observe an earlier round's output (bounded staging vs single round), and the additive-only law — generation may ADD modules but never mutate or shadow user-written source, so reading a file always tells the truth. That last rule is the deliberate break from Jai's #insert, whose output never exists anywhere a person or an LSP can open.
decisions.story: Doris generates a typed API client from openapi.json. She wants to open the generated file, set a breakpoint in it, and point a teammate at line 214 in review; her CI must prove the artifact byte-matches the spec hash recorded in the lock.
decisions.detail: All options share the ratified floor: re-entry through the front end, hash recorded in .jet/lock, diagnostics pinned to the trigger site with the generated fragment as optional context. Staging recommendation carried in each option: generation runs in bounded, deterministically ordered rounds; a cycle is a compile error naming the chain — no Jai-style loop-until-quiescent.

options.name: Derived state under .jet/generated/, never committed
options.detail: Generated modules are build products, addressed by module name and materialized under .jet/generated/<package>/. Real files: LSP go-to-def lands in them, debugger steps through them, jet explain-build diffs them. Lock records source-input and output hashes, so CI verifies without committing. Source tree stays clean; no drift class of bugs.

options.name: In-tree build/generated/, committing optional
options.detail: Files land inside the project at build/generated/; each project decides whether to commit them. Visible without any flag, but the committed/uncommitted split means two ecosystems and --locked must handle both.
options.code:
b.generate("api_client", src)?
// -> build/generated/api_client.jet   (gitignore or commit — project choice)

options.name: Checked-in generated/ required
options.detail: Go-generate model: generated source is always committed, reviewed in every diff. Maximum review visibility; the cost is a standing drift hazard (artifact vs input) that CI must re-verify anyway, plus generated noise in every review.
options.code:
b.generate("api_client", src)?
// -> generated/api_client.jet   committed; CI fails if regeneration differs

options.name: Virtual only — no files, dump on demand
options.detail: Generated modules exist only inside the compilation; a flag dumps them for forensics. This is the Jai/#insert and Rust-proc-macro feel: nothing to open, breakpoint, or review. Listed to reject.
options.code: // nothing on disk; jet build --emit-generated is the only window

comparisons.note: OUT_DIR + include! hides generated code; cargo-expand exists because nobody can otherwise read what a proc-macro produced.
go generate commits artifacts (option C): perfectly visible, drifts unless CI regenerates and compares.
Generated files are derived outputs under bazel-out/, addressable as labels — the option A shape with strong caching.

decisions.title: May build code read the whole checked program and enforce custom rules (ladder rung B)?
decisions.gist: Rung B of the D-METADEPTH1 ladder: read-only whole-program reflection plus first-class custom diagnostics, from the build entry only. No mutation, no macros — rung C stays frozen (c154).
decisions.explainer: D-METADEPTH1=A ratified that rung B (a read-only lint-style rejection pass) rises 'only by a future vote'. This ballot is that vote, scoped to the fn build arc. Grant if ratified: the build entry receives a post-sema, read-only snapshot of the whole program through the existing D-METAREFLECT1 TypeInfo surface scaled up (program -> packages -> types/functions), and a diagnostic-emission API whose signature structurally requires code + what/why/fix, so I4 quality holds by construction. Runs only at the selected build entry (D-BUILDENTRY1) — never at module import time, so no hidden execution and no action at a distance. Rung C (mutation, message loop, user macros) is untouched and stays frozen on c154 (e7).
decisions.story: Walter runs the platform team at a 40-team company on one Jet monorepo. Org rules — 'no panic reachable from a net handler', 'every Entity type has archive()' for GDPR export — live on a wiki and die in code review. He wants the build itself to enforce them with compiler-grade errors no team can miss, without granting anyone the power to rewrite code invisibly.
decisions.detail: Why this is the safe rung: reading the checked program cannot change what any file means — local reasoning survives, the LSP model survives, and generated diagnostics are the only output. The enterprise value is policy-as-code with the compiler's own error quality, in the language the team already writes. The adversarial cost to weigh: a build entry that fails builds on custom rules is a new way for a dependency to be annoying — mitigated because only the ROOT's build entry runs rules (dependencies' rules do not run for you) and D-BUILDPOLICY1 authority applies.

options.name: Stay at D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection + derives only)
options.detail: Status quo. Org rules remain external linters with their own parsers that drift from the language; the wiki stays the enforcement mechanism.
options.code:
// jet has no answer; Walter writes a tree-sitter script that re-parses Jet
// and breaks on every syntax release

options.name: Read-only program snapshot + structured diagnostics from the build entry
options.detail: The Roslyn-analyzer shape: typed read-only API, structured diagnostics, zero mutation. Scoped to the root build entry; dependency build code gets no rule execution in your build.

options.name: Full message loop / mutation (Jai rung)
options.detail: Build code observes AND rewrites every declaration. Maximal power; reading a file no longer tells you what it means, and the LSP cannot model the program without running the metaprogram. Stays frozen on c154 — listed so the ladder is explicit.

comparisons.note: Analyzers are the industry success story of rung B: typed read-only compilation API + structured diagnostics, shipped as packages, beloved in enterprise.
Custom lints require unstable compiler internals (clippy is in-tree); third parties are locked out — the gap Jet can close.
Userland custom rules over a stable AST — massive adoption, but stringly typed and per-file only; no whole-program view.
The message loop grants observe + rewrite together; there is no read-only tier to adopt without the mutation cost.

decisions.title: How should examples/features/ be organized? (258 examples, 44 duplicate numbers)
decisions.gist: One flat numbered directory collapsed — pick the shape: topic folders with plain names, topic folders with per-topic numbers, or a one-time flat renumber.
decisions.explainer: Golden tests discover examples by file stem and match expected/<stem>.out, so any reorganization is one mechanical commit: move files, make discovery recursive, mirror expected/. Nothing about the language changes — this is the daily navigation surface for you and every agent.

He wants jet run examples/features/net/http_server.jet and done.

258

100_counted_loop.jet

100_sized_floats.jet   # four examples, one number — ordering device already dead

gobyexample: plain names (channels, select, timeouts), curated index page
swift-book guided tour: prose-ordered chapters, code grouped by topic

decisions.title: Casing of the new @ contract plane: PascalCase like # markers, or lowercase?
decisions.gist: D-MARKER-FAMILY1 gave contracts the @ sigil but left casing open: @Pure/@Pre/@Persist or @pure/@pre/@persist. D-CASING1 mandated PascalCase for # markers only.
decisions.explainer: This batch itself is split: D-MARKER-FAMILY1 own examples are PascalCase (@Pure, @MustUse, @Codable — they are today PascalCase # markers moving over), but D-PREPOST1 (@pre/@post), D-PERSIST1 (@persist) and D-CAPBUNDLE1 (@numeric, @comparable, @printable, @codable_as_base) were ratified with lowercase spellings. Nothing can be implemented or renamed until one rule exists.
decisions.story: Walter writes his first contract. He knows #Test and #MustUse are PascalCase, so he types @Pre(amount > 0). If the plane is lowercase he gets an unknown-marker error on the spelling every # marker taught him.

options.name: PascalCase everywhere (recommended)
options.detail: Extend the D-CASING1 law to the @ plane: @Pure, @MustUse, @Codable, @Pre, @Post, @Persist, @Numeric, @Comparable, @Printable, @CodableAsBase. One casing rule for every marker in the language; markers moving from # keep their exact spelling.

options.name: Lowercase @ plane
options.detail: Contracts read as quiet prose annotations, visually distinct from SHOUTING # directives: @pure, @pre, @persist, @numeric. Cost: #Pure becomes @pure on the move — a rename AND a recase; two casing rules live forever.

options.name: Split: PascalCase derives, lowercase clauses
options.detail: @Codable/@Pure stay PascalCase (they name a capability), clause-like contracts with arguments go lowercase (@pre/@post). Matches how this batch was literally ratified; costs a judgment call per marker forever.

decisions.title: Which existing # markers move to the @ contract plane?
decisions.gist: D-MARKER-FAMILY1 states the law (@ = contract, # = directive) but only names three examples. This ballot fixes the exact move list so agents never guess per marker.
decisions.explainer: Clear moves under the law: #Pure, #MustUse, #Codable/#Encode/#Decode, and the maturity tags #Experimental/#Tested/#Hardened all state declaration promises. Clear stays: #Unsafe, #Test, #Bench, #Ref(Label), #Grant, #Target/#Js/#Wasm, #Extern/#Bindgen, #Uninit, #UnitFamily, #Layout (directives — the ballot names #Unsafe/#Test/#Ref itself). Genuinely ambiguous, needing your call: #Numeric (overlaps the new @numeric bundle from D-CAPBUNDLE1 — same job, two spellings unless merged), #PublishedSchema (a promise that also triggers snapshot machinery), #Redact (a promise about debug output that also drives codegen), and the serde field markers #Rename/#Skip/#Default/#Flatten (wire-format configuration, closer to generation machinery than contract).
decisions.story: Doris reviews a struct with #Codable, #Numeric, #Redact and #Rename("id") on it. Under the new law she should be able to read at a glance which are promises and which are compiler instructions — but only if every marker actually sits on its correct plane.

options.name: Minimal: only the three named families move
options.detail: #Pure -> @Pure, #MustUse -> @MustUse, #Codable/#Encode/#Decode -> @ plane. Everything else stays # until individually reopened. Smallest migration; leaves the maturity tags and #Numeric stating promises from the wrong plane.

options.name: Full application of the law (recommended)
options.detail: A plus: maturity tags -> @, #PublishedSchema -> @, #Redact -> @, and #Numeric merges into the D-CAPBUNDLE1 @numeric bundle (one mechanism, resolves that ballot open overlap). Serde field markers stay # (wire-format machinery, not promises). Every marker sits on its lawful plane; one migration pass, teaching errors on every old spelling.

options.name: Forward-only: nothing moves
options.detail: The @ plane starts with only the newly ratified markers (@pre/@post/@persist/bundles). Existing # markers keep their spellings; migration deferred to a later epoch sweep. Zero churn now; the law is immediately false for #Pure/#MustUse/#Codable — the ballot own canonical examples.

decisions.title: #Pure moved to @Pure — but #Pure also lives in TYPE position (callback bounds). What happens there?
decisions.gist: The @ plane law says @ only precedes declarations. `#Pure fn(Int) -> Int` is a live callback-type bound inside types, where @ never goes. The move list says Pure moves; the law says @ can’t go where #Pure lives.
decisions.explainer: D-MARKER-FAMILY1=B ratified: @ states a checkable promise and may only precede a declaration. D-MARKERMOVE1=B moved Pure to the @ plane. Neither addressed Parser/Types.rs:361: a function TYPE may be written `#Pure fn(T) -> U` to require a pure callback. Planning found the gap; parser work on the plane migration is gated on this answer.
decisions.story: Dot writes a numerics library and wants map() to accept only pure callbacks. She declares her own functions with @Pure now. When she writes the parameter type for map(), does the bound spell #Pure (old plane), @Pure (breaking the declarations-only law), or something else?
decisions.inWild:
fn map(items: [Int], f: #Pure fn(Int) -> Int) -> [Int] { ... }   // today

@Pure
fn double(x: Int) -> Int { x * 2 }   // after the move

map(nums, double)   // the bound and the declaration should visibly match
decisions.detail: Raised as gate G1 in docs/plans/epoch-3/marker-family.md. Blocking: parser work on the @ plane cannot start until the type-position surface is fixed.

options.name: Position split: @Pure on declarations, #Pure stays on callback-type bounds (recommended)
options.detail: The law stays exact: @ precedes declarations only. The type-position bound keeps its # spelling as wire-in machinery. Cost: one concept, two spellings, chosen by position — a taught rule, softened because you READ them in different places.

options.name: One spelling: @Pure allowed in the single type-position bound slot
options.detail: The law gains one carve-out: a contract marker may prefix a function TYPE to state a bound. One spelling everywhere Pure appears; the "declarations only" law becomes "declarations, plus contract bounds on function types".

options.name: Retire the type-position bound; purity is required at the parameter declaration
options.detail: No marker inside types at all. The parameter is itself a declaration, so the contract plane can annotate it. Grammar stays smallest; the bound moves left of the name instead of inside the type.

decisions.title: Which plane owns the remaining derive markers: #[Debug], #[Summarize], #[Comparable], user derives like #[Wire]?
decisions.gist: D-MARKERMOVE1=B moved only Codable/Encode/Decode among derive markers. The rest were not named. Default reading: they stay # (generation machinery, not promises) — confirm or move them.
decisions.explainer: The ratified two-plane law: @ states a checkable promise about the declaration; # is compiler machinery/directives. Codable moved because "this type round-trips" is a promise. #[Debug]/#[Summarize]/#[Comparable] and user derives (derive T.Wire bodies) generate code — the MARKERMOVE1 ballot itself frames user derives as directive machinery. Unaddressed, so the plane migration ships with a documented default that needs ratifying.
decisions.story: Walter just learned @Codable is a promise-plane contract. He types @Debug on his struct by analogy and gets a teaching error pointing back to #[Debug]. Is that the language he was promised, or should Debug have moved with Codable?
decisions.detail: Raised as gate G3 in docs/plans/epoch-3/marker-family.md. Non-blocking: the migration ships with the default (stay #) either way; this ballot ratifies or reverses it.

options.name: They stay # — derives are generation machinery (recommended)
options.detail: Only the three ratified movers (Codable/Encode/Decode) live on @. Everything that exists to GENERATE code, including all user derives, is # machinery. One teachable line: "@ promises, # generates."

options.name: All built-in derive markers move to @; user derives stay #
options.detail: Built-ins read as capability promises (@Debug = "this type is printable for debugging"). User derives stay machinery. Cost: the built-in/user line becomes the plane line — two kinds of derive spelling forever.

options.name: Case-by-case: promise-like derives move, mechanical ones stay
options.detail: Judgment call per marker (Comparable moves, Debug stays?). Maximal nuance, permanent ambiguity for every future derive.

decisions.comment: ALL derive markers INCLUDING USER DERIVES use @ - separation is ridiculous and defeats the purpose of separating anything at all. Use @ for all derive markers

decisions.title: U13 follow-up — which cipher backend encrypts the secrets file?
decisions.gist: D-JPK-SECRET1=A needs age-style crypto (X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305). Zero external crates in the compiler is I6. Pick the backend: FFI-bridge to a vetted crate, shell out to age/rage, or native std-only.
decisions.explainer: The ratified secrets design (encrypted file in repo, recipients list, memory-only decrypt) is cipher-agnostic — everything except the encrypt/decrypt step is already plannable and buildable. But the cipher itself needs X25519 key agreement plus ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD (and scrypt for passphrase keys, bech32 for key encoding), none of which exist std-only in Source/. I6 forbids external crates in the compiler, so the backend choice is an owner call, same shape as the tvix waiver (D-JPK16) and the FFI-bridge stdlib pattern.
decisions.story: Elena runs jet secrets set stripe-dev on a fresh laptop with nothing installed but jet. Option A/C: it just works — the cipher ships inside jet. Option B: jet prints a clear one-line message to install age first, exactly like the Nix-bridge stopgap message she has already seen.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet secrets set stripe-dev
  enter value: ****************
  encrypted to 3 recipients -> .jet/secrets  (never plaintext at rest)

$ jet dev
  secrets: 2 decrypted into the environment (memory only)

fn charge() -> Receipt ? Error #(Net, Secret) {
    key :: secrets.get("stripe-dev")?    // effect-gated read
}
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U13 — first-class encrypted secrets', 'I6 watch — OWNER BALLOT REQUIRED'. The plan builds all non-cipher scaffolding (secrets: field capture in ModuleEval, Secret effect in jet-sema, store format, jet secrets CLI, trust-gate integration, E0986–E0988) regardless of this outcome — only the encrypt/decrypt call is gated. Adversarial notes: (A) the FFI-bridge pattern (Archive.rs/Db.rs/CFFI.rs precedent) emits bridge template text and never touches jet's Cargo.toml, so I6's letter holds; the crate (e.g. age or x25519-dalek + chacha20poly1305) still enters the trust base and the Epoch-3 'replace external deps' mandate applies later. (B) is zero new code in the trust base and ships fastest, but secrets then fail on machines without age — acceptable for the Nix bridge, harsher for a batteries-included secrets story (philosophy: beginner experience ranks above effort). (C) is the only I6-pure end state and the Epoch-3 mandate arrives there eventually; X25519 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are small, well-specified, test-vector-rich algorithms, but hand-rolled crypto needs a real review gate before it guards production keys. A staged A-then-C or B-then-C is a legal answer — say so explicitly if chosen.

options.name: FFI-bridge a vetted crypto crate (house stdlib pattern)
options.detail: Emit bridge template text linking a vetted age-compatible crate (age, or x25519-dalek + chacha20poly1305); never added to jet's Cargo.toml, isolated exactly like Archive.rs/Db.rs. Works out of the box; crate joins the trust base; Epoch-3 native-replacement mandate still applies later.

options.name: Shell out to the age/rage binary (bridge-style stopgap)
options.detail: std::process::Command to age, mirroring the ratified nix-binary stopgap. Zero new code in the trust base, ships immediately; secrets require age installed, with a clear teaching message otherwise — the anti-batteries cost for a first-class feature.
options.code:
// std-only, no crate:
Command::new("age").args(["-R", "recipients", "-o", out]).spawn()?

$ jet secrets set stripe-dev
Error [E09xx]: the `age` tool is needed to encrypt secrets
 Fix: install age (https://age-encryption.org), or ask the owner to enable the built-in cipher

options.name: Native std-only X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305
options.detail: Implement the ciphers in plain Rust inside the driver. I6-pure, no trust-base growth, matches the Epoch-3 replace-external-deps mandate; both algorithms are small and RFC-test-vectored, but hand-rolled crypto guarding real keys needs an explicit review/audit gate before ship.

comparisons.note: The model U13 ratified: X25519 recipients, small file format, no vault. The question is only where its cipher runs.
Both shell out to or link age — precedent that either A or B is a normal shape for this feature.
Go ships X25519 + ChaCha20-Poly1305 in crypto/ — the option-C end state is a proven stdlib choice, not exotic.

decisions.title: U14 follow-up — which backend builds and pushes OCI images?
decisions.gist: D-JPK-IMAGE1=A promises 'OCI layout built directly from hangar objects, --push speaks the registry protocol'. That needs sha256 digests, gzip layers, and TLS for push — none std-only today. Pick: shell out to skopeo/nix, FFI-bridge a registry lib, or native.
decisions.explainer: The image.* surface (kind/from/expose/env_vars/files/base field-check and capture) builds now with no external need. The build step needs sha256 (layer + config digests) and gzip (layer compression) — both implementable std-only. The push step needs HTTPS/TLS to speak the OCI distribution protocol, which is the genuinely hard native piece. I6 makes any crate an owner call; the split between build (near-native-feasible) and push (TLS wall) is why this is a menu, not a foregone choice.
decisions.story: Sam runs jet image server --push ghcr.io/acme/pulseops:0.4.0. Option A: jet assembles the layout, then skopeo copies it up — works today if skopeo is installed, message otherwise. Option B/C: the whole path is jet's own, nothing external, and CI needs one binary.
decisions.inWild:
module image.server {
    kind: .Oci
    from: packages.pulseops
    expose: [8080]
}

$ jet image server
  -> hangar:.../pulseops-oci-...  (12.4 MB, 3 layers, reproducible)
$ jet image server --push ghcr.io/acme/pulseops:0.4.0
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U14 — image.* OCI containers + ISOs', 'I6 watch — OWNER BALLOT'. The plan lands field-check/capture (E0989/E0990) and the reproducible-layout test regardless; this ballot gates only the tar/digest/compress/push engine. Adversarial notes: (A) matches the ratified nix-binary stopgap pattern and the 'nixpkgs now, jetpack later' interim policy; the UX contract stays jet's so muscle memory survives a later native swap — but the ballot text explicitly promised 'no Docker dependency', and skopeo is a cousin of that dependency; the message must be as clear as the missing-nix one. (B) FFI-bridge (Archive.rs/Db.rs pattern) to an OCI/registry crate keeps Cargo.toml clean but pulls an HTTP+TLS stack into the trust base — the largest surface of the three. (C) split honestly: layout building (tar is already done std-only for archives, sha256 and gzip are small well-specified additions) is native-feasible now; push over TLS is the wall — a legal C variant is 'native build + option-A push until native TLS exists', and the recommendation is exactly that staging.

options.name: Shell out to skopeo / nix dockerTools (stopgap, bridge pattern)
options.detail: jet assembles inputs, skopeo (or nix dockerTools via the bridge) produces/pushes the image. Ships fastest, zero trust-base growth; requires the tool installed with a clear teaching message; leans on the very ecosystem the ballot said images wouldn't need.
options.code:
// push path only:
Command::new("skopeo").args(["copy", "oci:.jet/images/server", &format!("docker://{tag}")]).status()?

$ jet image server --push ghcr.io/acme/pulseops:0.4.0
Error [E09xx]: pushing needs the `skopeo` tool
 Fix: install skopeo, or push from CI where it exists

options.name: FFI-bridge an OCI/registry crate
options.detail: Bridge-template an OCI distribution client (e.g. oci-distribution) for build+push; Cargo.toml untouched, works everywhere jet runs; pulls an HTTP+TLS stack into the trust base — the biggest audit surface on the menu.

options.name: Native: std-only layout build now, native push when TLS exists
options.detail: sha256 + gzip + OCI tar layout in plain Rust (small, spec-pinned, reproducibility test-vectored) — jet image works offline with nothing installed. --push stages through option A's skopeo shell-out until a native TLS story lands; the gate is named, not hidden.
options.code:
// std-only build path:
let layer = tar::pack(closure_paths)?;            // existing archive code
let gz    = gzip::compress(&layer)?;              // new, RFC 1952
let digest = sha256::hex(&gz);                    // new, FIPS 180-4 vectors
write_oci_layout(&out, &[(digest, gz)], config)?;

$ jet image server           # fully native, reproducible digest
$ jet image server --push …  # skopeo until native TLS (named gate)

comparisons.note: dockerTools builds reproducible layered images without Docker — proof the no-daemon build is the right target; its interface is the function soup U14 replaces.
Language-native image builders that assemble OCI layouts and push directly — the option-B/C shape, proven in Go and Java.
The standard daemonless copy/push tool — the option-A engine and the C-variant push stopgap.

decisions.title: U18 follow-up — confirm pack.jet, reversing the shipped pkg.jet rename?
decisions.gist: TWONAMES1=A says the one reserved file is pack.jet. But the shipped code retired pack.jet FOR pkg.jet on 2026-06-18 (D-JPK-FILES, 'clean break, no alias'). Confirm the re-reversal to pack.jet, or amend the TWONAMES1 record to keep pkg.jet.
decisions.explainer: History, honestly: payload.jet -> pkg.jet was ratified and shipped 2026-06-18 (D-JPK-FILES; Syntax.rs:1140–1142 records 'the Jet package manifest is pkg.jet … Prior filenames (pack.jet, the U10 interim name) were retired (clean break, no alias)'). The 2026-07-01 vision and the ratified TWONAMES1 text both say pack.jet throughout. One of these must give: either the codebase renames again (every fixture, snapshot, doc, and user habit moves; the old-name teaching error now fires on the name we shipped two weeks ago), or the TWONAMES1 record is amended to read pkg.jet and the vision docs sweep. This is purely a spelling call — the one-reserved-file semantics are identical either way and no other U11–U19 work is blocked on it.
decisions.story: A user who created a project on June 20 has pkg.jet on disk. Under A, her next jet build prints a teaching error telling her to rename to pack.jet — one command, but the tool renamed its own file twice in a month. Under B, nothing changes for her, and the vision docs quietly correct their spelling to pkg.jet.
decisions.inWild:
// Option A — after migration:
$ jet build
Error [E1226]: `pkg.jet` is no longer the manifest name — Jet reads `pack.jet`
 Why: one reserved filename (U18); prior names were retired in a clean break
 Fix: rename `pkg.jet` to `pack.jet`

// Option B — nothing moves:
$ ls
pkg.jet   src/   .jet/
$ jet build      # works as today; vision.md re-spelled to pkg.jet
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U18 — the two-names rename' (and the 'pkg.jet -> pack.jet is a reversal' ambiguity flagged at hand-off). Option A migration, concretely: PAYLOAD_FILE constant in crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs flips to "pack.jet"; ~12+ fixture files rename; all pkg.jet-mentioning stderr snapshots re-bless; docs sweep (spec.md, epoch-5 plans, payload-env-separation.md); E1226 teaching error covers pkg.jet/payload.jet/jet.toml/jetpack.toml by name — the house clean-break pattern, third rename in the file's history. Option B is the zero-churn path: amend the TWONAMES1 ratification record + sweep vision.md/ballot prose to pkg.jet; cost is that the ratified ballot text, the owner's amendment note, and all U18 worked examples say pack.jet — amending a ratified record is its own precedent to weigh. Either way the U18 semantics (one reserved file, roles by namespace, find() discovery) land unchanged; only the string differs.

options.name: Confirm pack.jet (matches the ratified TWONAMES1 text)
options.detail: Rename shipped pkg.jet -> pack.jet: Syntax.rs constant, fixtures, snapshots, docs; E1226 teaches the move (clean break, no alias — house pattern). Cost: second rename in a month for early users; the ratified text stays exactly as written.
options.code:
// crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs
pub const PAYLOAD_FILE: &str = "pack.jet";   // was "pkg.jet" (D-JPK-FILES)

$ git mv pkg.jet pack.jet          # per repo, one command
$ jet build                        # old name -> E1226 teaching error

options.name: Keep pkg.jet (amend the TWONAMES1 record)
options.detail: Zero churn: the shipped name stands, no fixture/snapshot/user migration, no re-reversal optics. Cost: the ratified ballot text, the owner amendment, and every U18 worked example must be corrected to pkg.jet, and amending a ratified record sets its own precedent.

comparisons.note: Cargo.toml has never been renamed — the reserved-manifest name is the single most habit-forming string a toolchain owns; whichever wins here should be final.
deno.json vs deno.jsonc vs package.json compat — a live example of manifest-name wobble costing user trust.

decisions.title: U18 follow-up — canonical module body: module env.dev { fields } or ns.path: Type contributions?
decisions.gist: Vision and every U11–U19 ballot example write module env.dev { packages: [...] } — namespace in the declaration name, fields bare. Shipped code parses module dev { env.dev: Env.{ ... } } — plain name, namespaced typed contributions inside. TWONAMES1 ratified filenames/commands, not this grammar. Pick the one canonical form (I8).
decisions.explainer: Two grammars exist for the same semantic job. The shipped form (module <name> { ns.path: Type.{ fields } }) lets one module contribute to several namespaces and carries the U5 merge machinery; it is what ModuleEval evaluates today. The vision form (module env.dev { fields }) is what the owner ratified examples in six ballots show: the namespace IS the module path, fields sit bare, and discovery-by-declaration (the U18 amendment's find() acceptance test) reads the role straight off the declaration name. I8 says one way to mean it: both forms surviving as equals is the rejected outcome. Note the U18 amendment ('role modules … discovered by declaration') reads most naturally against form A, where the declaration name itself is the role.
decisions.story: Priya reads the U12 ballot, copies module env.dev { services: { postgres: Service.{} } } into her repo, and runs jet dev. Under A it works verbatim. Under B she gets a teaching error showing the module dev { env.dev: Env.{ ... } } wrapping — and learns the docs' own examples don't parse.
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md, 'Module body sugar' ambiguity flagged at hand-off; evaluator at crates/jet-driver/src/Jetpack/ModuleEval/ (form B is what tests exercise today), discovery at PackageManifest/Discovery.rs. Adversarial notes: (A) matches every owner-ratified worked example verbatim and makes the U18 find()-by-declaration test read the role off the module name; migration = parser accepts dotted module names as namespace roles + a teaching error rewrites form B; multi-namespace authors write two modules (module env.dev + module system.laptop) — arguably clearer, loses one-module-many-contributions. Contribution machinery survives underneath: env.dev: Env.{} becomes the desugared form of module env.dev {}. (B) zero code motion, keeps one module contributing to many namespaces, but every ratified U11–U19 example is then wrong-as-written and needs an owner-visible errata sweep — the docs teaching a spelling the parser rejects is the worst beginner outcome available here. (C) both-legal is listed for completeness and fails I8's bar on its face: two spellings for the same semantic job, doubled docs, doubled formatter/round-trip surface, and every future example forced to pick a dialect. Formatter round-trip + fmt STABILITY test required for whichever wins (house rule).

options.name: Canonical: module env.dev { fields } (vision/ballot form)
options.detail: Namespace is the declaration name; fields sit bare; form B becomes a teaching error that names the rewrite. Matches all ratified examples and the U18 discovery-by-declaration amendment; multi-namespace files write one module per role.

options.name: Canonical: ns.path: Type.{ } contributions (shipped form)
options.detail: Keep the evaluator as-is; one module may contribute to several namespaces; U5 merge machinery untouched. Every ratified U11–U19 worked example must be errata'd to the wrapped spelling — docs and ballots currently teach a form the parser would reject.

options.name: Both legal (sugar + desugared) — fails the I8 bar
options.detail: module env.dev { fields } desugars to the contribution form; both parse forever. Listed for completeness: two spellings for one semantic job, doubled formatter/docs/teaching surface — exactly the second-feature-same-job shape I8 exists to reject.

comparisons.note: One attrset grammar for every module — but roles live in option paths, not declaration names; the discovery-by-name idea A ratifies is the thing Nix lacks.
mod a::b { } is illegal — a module declares one path segment; Rust chose the B-shaped restriction and nobody writes dotted module names.
Block label carries the role (resource "aws_instance" "web") — the A shape: the declaration head states what the block is.

decisions.title: U18 follow-up — engine dispatch scope for this card: in-process crate or git-style exec now?
decisions.gist: TWONAMES1 prose says jet 'dispatches unknown verbs to jetpack/jetos by name, git-style, zero coupling — the compiler stays fully standalone'. Today Jetpack is a linked crate (jet::Jetpack::run, in-process). Decide whether U11–U19 ride the linked path with separation as a later rung, or binary separation lands first.
decisions.explainer: The user-facing contract (one command, verbs resolve against declared modules) is identical either way — this is an architecture-sequencing call, not syntax. Today Source/main.rs already has both mechanisms: jet env calls the linked crate in-process, and a git-style external jet-<cmd> PATH fallback exists (find_external, D-DX5). Full separation means the compiler binary stops linking jet-driver's Jetpack module and execs a jetpack binary for every engine verb: a real seam move (error-rendering, exit codes, --json plumbing, test harness all cross a process boundary) that touches every verb this card adds. The ratified text names the end state; it does not date it.
decisions.story: Nate types jet dev. Under A, nothing observable changes now — the verb runs in-process, fast, one binary to ship — and a later card moves the seam. Under B, jet execs jetpack dev; the compiler binary provably contains no package-manager code, and deleting the jetpack binary leaves a still-working compiler — the standalone claim is checkable today.
decisions.detail: Plan section: docs/plans/epoch-5/implementation.md §'U18 — the two-names rename', step 5 ('full … separation is a larger architectural item — do NOT block U11–U19 on binary separation'), and the third hand-off ambiguity. Adversarial notes: (A) matches the plan as written; all new verbs (services/secrets/image/switch/push/bridge/lock/config) route through the existing in-process dispatch; diagnostics stay one rendering path; the one-way arrow jetos->jetpack->jet holds at the module level even while linked; cost — 'the compiler stays fully standalone' remains a promise, not a property, and every verb added now is a verb to move later. (B) makes the ratified claim true immediately and forces the process-boundary contract (exit codes, --json diagnostics over the seam, engine-version skew handling) to be designed once, before eight new verbs pile onto the wrong side; cost — it front-loads a seam move onto the critical path of every U11–U19 gate, and the trust gate (U19) + service supervisor (U12) then need their first implementations written against the cross-process contract. Repo already builds two binaries (jet + jetpack per Cargo [[bin]]), so B is a wiring+contract change, not a new build system. Difficulty is not a factor (house rule); the question is purely which order produces the better seam.

options.name: In-process linked crate now; binary separation as its own later card
options.detail: All U11–U19 verbs ride jet::Jetpack::run as jet env does today; the D-DX5 jet-<cmd> PATH fallback stays for third parties. Separation becomes a named follow-on card with its own contract design. One diagnostics path, no cross-process plumbing in this card.
options.code:
// Source/main.rs — extend the existing arm:
"services" | "secrets" | "image" | "switch" | "push" | "bridge" =>
    exit(jet::Jetpack::run(raw[1..].to_vec())),

$ jet services logs postgres   # in-process, one binary shipped

options.name: Git-style exec separation now, before new verbs land
options.detail: Compiler drops the Jetpack linkage; engine verbs exec the jetpack binary by name (both binaries already build). The standalone claim becomes checkable; the process-boundary contract (exit codes, --json diagnostics, version skew) is designed once, first — on the critical path of every gate in this card.

comparisons.note: External subcommand dispatch by binary name — the mechanism the ratified text names, and what D-DX5 already implements for third-party jet-<cmd>.
cargo links its ops crates in-process and still fronts rustc as a separate binary — the A shape: one UX, seam moved where it pays.
Plugin verbs exec kubectl-<name> from PATH; core verbs stay linked — a proven hybrid identical to A + D-DX5 fallback.

decisions.title: Parse patterns: what do adjacent unanchored holes mean, and can a bare binding fail?
decisions.gist: D-PARSESTR1=A left two edges open: two {holes} touching with no literal text between them, and a parse pattern used as a plain binding outside an if-table, where no else arm exists to catch a non-match.
decisions.explainer: The ratified D-PARSESTR1 option A text reads: "{x} binds String, {x:Int} is a typed fallible hole; non-greedy holes anchored by literal text; else arm catches non-matches." That does not define (1) a pattern like "{kind}{id:Int}" where two holes are adjacent with no anchoring literal between them, or (2) whether a parse pattern is legal in bare binding position — "{host}:{port:Int}" against addr outside an if-table — and if so what a non-match does, since there is no else arm there to catch it.
decisions.story: Dana parses ticket ids shaped "INC4411" — prefix letters and digits abut, so the tempting pattern is "{kind}{id:Int}" with nothing between the holes. Later she wants a one-line bind of a known-good "host:port" config value without wrapping a single-arm if-table around it. Both lines compile or don't depending on this ballot.
decisions.detail: Raised from docs/plans/epoch-3/syntax-wave.md §17 (ambiguity 1); the plan currently builds against option A (E0147 unanchorable adjacent holes, E0148 refutable pattern with no else/fallible handling) and ships nothing until this is decided. Adversarial notes: (1) the ratified D-PARSESTR1 detail promises "no backtracking regex engine hides inside, matching stays linear-time and predictable" — any tie-break law (option B) must stay single-pass or it quietly reintroduces backtracking ("{kind}{id:Int}" with a lazy {kind} needs a retry loop unless the split rule is character-class driven); (2) a bare binding that panics on non-match would be the only refutable construct in Jet without a visible failure path — against the fallibility voice everywhere else (`?`/`??`); (3) option C keeps v1 smallest but makes the single-line config-parse case need a one-arm if-table, pure ceremony.

options.name: Adjacent unanchored holes are a compile error; bare binding is fallible via ? (recommended)
options.detail: Two holes with no literal text between them cannot be split deterministically — compile error naming the fix (add literal text, or type the boundary and use an anchored form). A parse pattern in bare binding position is legal and refutable: the statement carries ? (or ?? fallback) exactly like every other fallible operation, propagating on non-match. No panic path, no hidden backtracking.

options.name: Character-class split law for typed boundaries; bare binding fallible via ?
options.detail: Adjacent holes are legal when the right hole is typed: an untyped hole runs until the first character the next typed hole's type accepts (digits for Int), single pass, no backtracking. "{kind}{id:Int}" on "INC4411" gives kind="INC", id=4411. Two adjacent UNTYPED holes remain a compile error (no class to split on). Bare binding same as A. Buys the abutting-fields case at the cost of a subtle law docs must teach, and it silently mis-splits "AB12CD34" shapes.

options.name: v1 anchored-only, if-table-only
options.detail: Every hole must be anchored by literal text or a pattern edge on both sides, and parse patterns are legal only as if-table arm heads — no bare binding form in v1. Smallest surface, zero ambiguity, but the one-line known-good parse needs a ceremonial single-arm if-table, and the abutting-fields case is out entirely.

comparisons.note: The third-party parse library allows adjacent fields and resolves them by minimal match with backtracking — famously surprising splits on real input; the cautionary tale for option B done loosely.
comparisons.code: parse.parse("{kind}{id:d}", "INC4411")  # users must run it to find out how it splits

comparisons.note: scanf's %s%d is exactly the adjacent-hole problem: %s is greedy through non-whitespace, so the pair never matches — decades of bug reports say don't ship an implicit split law without a loud rule.
comparisons.code: sscanf(line, "%[A-Z]%d", kind, &id);  // works only via the character-class escape hatch

comparisons.note: No format-string parsing in std; the community's scan crates all either forbid adjacent captures or require a type-driven boundary — evidence A and B are the two honest designs.
comparisons.code: // no std equivalent; sscanf crate rejects "{}{}" as ambiguous

decisions.title: Typed text v1 scope: do plain literals elaborate, and do the sql"…"/html"…" prefixes ship?
decisions.gist: D-TYPEDTEXT1=D pinned elaboration to a literal "with interpolations" and said prefixes "remain" for no-expected-type bindings — leaving open whether a hole-free literal elaborates, and whether the prefixes ship in v1 at all.
decisions.explainer: The ratified D-TYPEDTEXT1 option D text reads: "db.query takes Sql; a string LITERAL with interpolations in that position elaborates to template + typed bound params — the same expected-type law as .{ } construction" and "Prefixes sql\"…\"/html\"…\" remain only for bindings without an expected type." It does not say whether a literal with NO interpolations also elaborates in an expected-Sql position, and — since option A's prefix surface was explicitly "deferred to E4" — whether the two prefixes ship in v1 or wait. Both calls change what a beginner's first db.query line looks like.
decisions.story: Sam's first query is db.query("select count(*) from users") — no holes at all. Does that line compile, or does Jet demand a prefix on the simplest possible query? Later Sam extracts the query to a named binding for reuse and hits the no-expected-type case: is the spelling sql"…", or an explicit type annotation q: Sql :: "…"?
decisions.detail: Raised from docs/plans/epoch-3/syntax-wave.md §17 (ambiguity 2); the plan currently builds option B's semantics and ships nothing until this is decided. Adversarial notes: (1) rejecting hole-free literals (option C) makes the SAFEST possible input — a fully static query — the one that needs extra ceremony, exactly backwards for the beginner tier; (2) D-BIND4's explicit-type binding q: Sql :: "…" already supplies an expected type, so the prefix and the annotation are two spellings for the same binding job — an I8 tension option A resolves by shipping zero prefixes and letting the annotation carry the no-expected-type case; (3) if prefixes ship (B), they are two fixed lexer-known names, never user-extensible in v1 — E4 owns extensibility per the ratified deferral.

options.name: Hole-free literals elaborate; no prefixes in v1 — annotation covers bindings
options.detail: Any string literal (with or without holes) in an expected-Sql/Html position elaborates to the typed value. The sql"…"/html"…" prefixes do not ship in v1: a binding without an expected type uses the existing D-BIND4 explicit-type form q: Sql :: "…", which supplies the expected type through the one law already ratified. Leanest surface, one spelling per job (I8); costs nothing the annotation can't express.
options.code:
rows :: db.query("select count(*) from users")?          // elaborates, no holes needed
by_id: Sql :: "select * from users where id = {id}"       // annotation supplies the expected type
row :: db.query(by_id)?

options.name: Hole-free literals elaborate; sql"…"/html"…" ship in v1 (recommended)
options.detail: Same elaboration law as A — any literal in an expected position elaborates. The two fixed prefixes also ship, only for positions without an expected type; user-defined prefixes stay E4. Matches the ratified "remain only for bindings without an expected type" most literally, and gives a greppable spelling for query constants without a type annotation. Cost: two spellings for the no-expected-type binding (prefix vs annotation) — the I8 overlap named in the detail.
options.code:
rows :: db.query("select count(*) from users")?          // elaborates, no holes needed
by_id :: sql"select * from users where id = {id}"         // prefix carries the type
row :: db.query(by_id)?

options.name: Only interpolated literals elaborate; hole-free needs a prefix
options.detail: Reads the ratified text narrowly: "with interpolations" is the trigger, so db.query("select 1") is a type error pointing at sql"select 1". Prefixes must ship (they're the only path for static queries). Maximally literal to the ratified sentence, but the simplest and safest call in the language gets the ceremony, and the error teaches a prefix where a plain literal was already injection-free.
options.code:
rows :: db.query("select count(*) from users")?           // Error: expected Sql, got String — write sql"…"
rows :: db.query(sql"select count(*) from users")?         // required spelling
total :: db.query("select * from t where id = {id}")?      // holes present: elaborates

comparisons.note: FormattableString overloads only bind to $"…" interpolated literals — a plain literal falls to the string overload silently. The exact option-C trap: the safe static query takes the unsafe path unless the user remembers the sigil.
comparisons.code:
ExecuteSql($"select {id}");   // parameterized
ExecuteSql("select 1");        // silently the raw-string overload

comparisons.note: Tagged templates (sql`…`) are the prefix design: it works, but every call needs the tag forever — there is no expected-type elaboration to make the common call sigil-free, which is exactly what option D bought.
sqlx's query! macro accepts a plain static literal with no marker beyond the macro itself and type-checks it — evidence that hole-free static queries should be the zero-ceremony case.

decisions.title: Variadics: may a ...vararg pack be bounded by MULTIPLE traits?
decisions.gist: Owner asked inside the ratified variadics decision: 'can @-varargs bind a set of traits, not just one?' Single-trait bounds are ratified; the multi-trait spelling is not.
decisions.explainer: D-VARIADIC ratified typed varargs with a single trait bound. The owner's inline comment asked about a set of traits. The final owner amendment chooses one list form everywhere for multi-trait bounds: generic parameters use `<T: [A, B]>`, and vararg packs use `...items: [A, B]`. The alternative is restricting packs to one trait forever and requiring a named combined trait for more.
decisions.story: Ruth writes a debug helper that prints and hashes every argument: each pack element must be both Printable and Hashable. One bound spelling exists for generics; does it work on the pack too?
decisions.detail: Raised from docs/plans/epoch-3/jai-adoptions.md ambiguity 4. Ratified with owner amendment: list-form trait sets everywhere; no `+` multi-bound spelling.

options.name: Reuse the unified trait-bound list spelling on packs (owner-amended)
options.detail: The pack element bound accepts exactly what a generic parameter bound accepts: one trait or `[A, B]`. One bound language everywhere (I8), using the owner-selected list form instead of `+`.
options.code:
fn audit(...items: [Printable, Hashable]) { ... }
// same law as: fn f<T: [Printable, Hashable]>(x: T)

options.name: Single trait only; combined needs a named trait
options.detail: Packs keep exactly one bound. Wanting two means declaring `trait Auditable: [Printable, Hashable]` and bounding by it. Smaller pack grammar; a naming ceremony for every combination.
options.code:
trait Auditable: [Printable, Hashable] {}
fn audit(...items: Auditable) { ... }

comparisons.note: Bounds compose with + uniformly across generics and impl-trait — the A shape.

decisions.comment: I want this to be a consistent list form everywhere, the + adds new syntax that users wont expect. The other places where users cocmbine traits should all be settled to [Trait1, Trait2]

decisions.title: Does core.mem gain a `cast_ptr<T>` primitive (the ratified pointer-chain example uses one)?
decisions.gist: D-POINTERCHAIN1=A's worked example calls mem.cast_ptr<Bool>(...) — an API that does not exist in core.mem today. Confirm the addition (name + gating) or point at an existing cast.
decisions.explainer: The ratified option showed Jet's answer to Jai's `slot.value_pointer.(*bool).*` using an explicit, `#Unsafe`-gated cast step spelled mem.cast_ptr<T>. core.mem has no such function; nothing else currently does typed raw-pointer reinterpretation. Shipping the ratified example requires either adding the primitive (I1: only usable inside `#Unsafe("reason")` regions) or re-spelling the example onto an existing mechanism.
decisions.story: Frank ports a Jai interop layer. He reaches the reinterpret step, greps core.mem docs for cast, and either finds cast_ptr with a clear unsafe-gate error when used outside a gate — or finds nothing and stalls.
decisions.detail: Raised from docs/plans/epoch-3/jai-adoptions.md ambiguity 5. Blocking only the pointer-chain example/doc deliverable; nothing else rides it.

options.name: Add mem.cast_ptr<T>, #Unsafe-gated (recommended)
options.detail: The primitive the ratified example already teaches. Registered in core.mem beside rawptr machinery; calling it outside an #Unsafe region is the standard gate error; golden example under lowlevel/.
options.code: flag_ptr :: mem.cast_ptr<Bool>(raw)   // only inside #Unsafe("…") { }

options.name: Re-spell the example onto existing rawptr machinery
options.detail: If an existing cast (e.g. rawptr reinterpret via read-as) already covers it, the ratified example text is corrected to that spelling and no API is added. Only valid if the existing path truly exists — verify before choosing.
options.code: flag :: raw.read_as<Bool>()   // hypothetical existing spelling — verify first

comparisons.note: ptr::cast<T> is safe to form, unsafe to deref — Jet gates the whole region instead.

decisions.title: Decode-time migration transparency: how do you ask a decoded value "were you migrated?"
decisions.gist: When old stored data is auto-upgraded during decode, how does a program find out it happened?
decisions.explainer: Jet already snapshots #PublishedSchema types and auto-applies `migration { }` blocks when decoding old data (D-MIGRATE1, D-MIGRATE2A-F). Today that upgrade is silent: the caller gets a fresh value and cannot tell it started life as an old version. D-SELFVER1=A rejected per-value history but ordered this narrower follow-up: a `DecodeResult { value: T, migration: MigrationStatus }` decode-time answer, zero overhead when nothing migrated, #PublishedSchema types only. (Raised as D-MIGRATE3 — the ordered name D-MIGRATE2 was already taken by the ratified migration-verb family D-MIGRATE2A-F. The struct name `DecodeResult` below is exactly as you prescribed; note it can read like a fallible Result at a glance — say the word if you want a different name, e.g. DecodeTrace.)
decisions.story: Betty runs a SaaS that has stored customer records as JSON for three years. She just shipped schema v3. Her nightly import decodes millions of records; migrations apply silently. Compliance asks her: "how many live records are still arriving in the v1 shape, and which customers do we need to re-export?" Betty has no way to answer — decode hides exactly the fact she needs.

options.name: Separate `decode_traced` — default decode untouched (recommended)
options.detail: One extra method beside `decode`: `json.decode_traced<T>(raw) -> DecodeResult<T> ?`, where `DecodeResult<T>` is a plain struct `{ value: T, migration: MigrationStatus }` and `MigrationStatus` carries `.migrated: Bool`, `.from` (source schema version), and `.steps` (applied migration names) — `.migrated` is false and the rest empty for fresh data and for non-#PublishedSchema types. `decode` stays exactly as it is — zero cost, zero API change for everyone not asking; one canonical way to ask (I8); same method on every codec (json/toml/yaml/csv) since they share the decode machinery. The honest cost: visibility is opt-in — a caller who reaches for plain `decode` silently misses the migration fact (Betty must know `decode_traced` exists), and the codec surface grows to two decode methods to learn.

options.name: `decode` always returns `DecodeResult` for #PublishedSchema types
options.detail: Decoding a #PublishedSchema type returns `DecodeResult<T>`; decoding a plain type returns `T`. Migration visibility is impossible to miss — but the return shape of the same function now depends on whether the type carries a marker: adding #PublishedSchema to an existing struct breaks every `decode` call site in the program (each must add `.value`). A beginner following a JSON tutorial hits the split the moment they adopt schema versioning.

options.name: Observer hook, no per-call value
options.detail: `schema.on_migration(fn (info) { ... })` registers a process-wide callback fired whenever any decode applies a migration; `decode` signatures never change. Good for metrics dashboards, useless for Betty's actual question — "was THIS value migrated?" — because the callback is disconnected from the call site that decoded it. Ambient global state also cuts against effect-visible design.

options.name: Decline — schema tooling only, no runtime answer
options.detail: Keep decode fully silent; point Betty at `jet schema status` (which describes the *code's* schema baseline, not the *data's*). Rejects the gap D-SELFVER1=A explicitly said is real. Listed for completeness.
options.code:
$ jet schema status
  UserRecord  v3 (published 2026-06-30)  2 migrations on file
# says nothing about which stored records are old — the gap stays.

decisions.comparisons:
Rust serde: nothing built in — teams hand-roll a `version: u32` field and match on it.
Protobuf: unknown/renamed fields resolve silently; no per-message answer.
Avro: reader/writer schema resolution is automatic and silent.
Django/Rails DB migrations: migrate the store once, so the question disappears — but Jet migrates lazily at decode, so the question is real and per-value.

decisions.title: Epoch 4 exit bar: how much of the build-graph vision ships before e4 is done?
decisions.gist: Pick the finish line for Epoch 4 (metaprogramming): the ratified fn-build MVP, that plus typed targets/actions, or full CMake/Bazel-class build-graph parity.
decisions.explainer: The five fn-build ballots are ratified (D-BUILDENTRY1=B, D-BUILDGEN1=A, D-BUILDPOLICY1=A, D-BUILDSCOPE1=A, D-METADEPTH2=B) with an executable plan (metaprogramming.md §15). The vision doc also holds back six build-graph decision bundles (§12: targets, actions, toolchains, cache, probes, lock) that were deliberately frozen "until the foundation ballots land." They have landed. This decision sets what "Epoch 4 done" means, and therefore which of those six bundles agents must develop into ballots for you now versus later.
decisions.story: Hank maintains a game studio's engine repo: Jet code, shader assets, a test suite, and a handful of C tools. He wants to delete the Makefile. The ratified MVP lets his fn build generate bindings and pick sources — but a test target, an asset-cook step with declared inputs/outputs, and "only rebuild what changed" are exactly the parts of Make he still needs. Where Epoch 4 stops decides whether Hank deletes the Makefile at e4 or waits.

options.name: MVP bar — ship §15 as ratified, all six §12 bundles wait for e5
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits when the five ratified ballots are implemented end-to-end (entry, generate, policy, scope, enforce) plus the explain-build/audit surfaces. BuildPlan stays the three lists. The six §12 bundles get balloted in Epoch 5 beside jetpack. Cleanest scope; but e4's own charter is Jai parity, and Jai ships targets — Hank keeps his Makefile another epoch, and every real project's asset/test steps live in Tier-2 `#Impure` shell-outs in the meantime, which trains exactly the habit the capability model exists to prevent.

options.name: Full parity bar — all six §12 bundles designed, ratified, shipped in e4
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits at CMake/Bazel-class parity: typed targets, declared-I/O actions, toolchain pinning, content-addressed action cache, typed probes, lock/provenance for all of it. "Never reach for Make" is true at e4 exit. The cost is decision-load and design risk, not effort: toolchain registries, remote-cache trust, and probe vocabularies are ecosystem decisions that will be better informed by jetpack's provider model (e5) — ratifying them first risks re-opening them, which is the one thing the ratification process is supposed to prevent.

options.name: MVP + targets/actions — Jai-parity bar; toolchains/cache/probes ride e5 (recommended)
options.detail: Epoch 4 exits on §15 plus two of the six bundles: D-BUILDTARGET1 (executable/library/test/bench/asset targets in BuildPlan) and D-BUILDACTION1 (declared inputs/outputs/argv actions — a step with no declared outputs is not a build step). That is the Jai benchmark e4 is named for, and it is what deletes Hank's Makefile: tests and asset cooks become graph nodes instead of #Impure shell-outs, so the capability story stays honest. Toolchains, cache, and probes are jetpack-shaped ecosystem bundles; they ballot in e5 where the provider model informs them — until then `jet build` is correct-if-slower (no action cache) and probes stay Tier-2 #Impure. Agents develop the two bundles into full ballots immediately; the other four are named and parked, not lost.

decisions.comparisons:
Jai: builds-as-programs with targets and compile options — the e4 charter's benchmark.
CMake/Bazel/Ninja: typed targets + declared-I/O actions + caching; nobody's v1 shipped remote caching.
Cargo: build.rs (ambient, no graph) — the anti-model Jet already rejected.
nob.h (binder idea): C build-as-program; covered by targets+actions, not by the MVP lists.

decisions.title: Single-file Tier-2 build grants: what does the user type to say yes?
decisions.gist: A lone script's fn build wants an ambient effect (exec, env, ...). Pick the CLI spelling that grants it for one run.
decisions.explainer: D-BUILDPOLICY1=A ratified the mechanics: Tier-2 build effects need BOTH a `#Impure("reason")` gate in source AND permission at run time — "a flag or an interactive prompt" for a manifest-less single file. The flag spelling was left open. There is already one ratified grant flag: D-CTEFFECT1's blanket `--allow-impure` (comptime Tier-2, diagnostic E3411 names it). This ballot decides whether that blanket stays the one grant path or is refined into per-effect grants — whichever wins becomes THE spelling (I8: one grant system, E3411's fix text updated to match). Effect names come from the ratified ten-effect vocabulary (D-EFF4: Net, Fs, Io, Db, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, Log, Gpu) — nothing new is minted.
