decisions.story: Walter has a 60-line `tool.jet` — no pkg.jet, just a script whose fn build probes pkg-config for a legacy C library before compiling. The probe is `exec`, a Tier-2 effect. His build fn already declares it and gates it with #Impure. Now he runs `jet build tool.jet` on his laptop (interactive) and in CI (no TTY, hermetic by default). What does he type?

options.name: Per-effect `--allow-<effect>` + TTY prompt fallback — supersedes the blanket (recommended)
options.detail: One flag per D-EFF4 effect, lowercase: `--allow-exec`, `--allow-env`, `--allow-net`, `--allow-fs`, ... Grants exactly what is named, for this invocation only, recorded in lock/provenance. No flag + TTY: one prompt listing the declared effects and the #Impure reason. No flag + no TTY (CI): fail, naming the flag to add (the §15.4 not-granted diagnostic). This REPLACES the blanket `--allow-impure` — E3411's fix text is rewritten to name the specific missing effect flag, so there is exactly one grant system (I8), and granting exec never smuggles in env. The honest cost: ten flags are more surface than one, and a build declaring three effects needs three flags in the CI line (or the pkg.jet rung). Tab-completable, greppable, reads instantly to anyone who knows Deno.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --allow-exec
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0

$ jet build tool.jet          # interactive, no flag
  fn build declares #(Exec) — "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
  allow exec for this run? [y/N] y

$ jet build tool.jet          # CI, no TTY: hermetic by default
Error: this build asks for `Exec`, which nothing has granted
  Fix: pass --allow-exec, or add a pkg.jet with a build: grant

options.name: Keep the ratified blanket `--allow-impure` as the only grant
options.detail: Status quo extended to build entries: one flag opens every effect the build fn declares. Nothing to ratify beyond scope; E3411 already teaches it; shortest to type. But coarse: Walter wants exec, and the same flag also opens env/net/fs if the script (or a future edit to it) declares them — the grant never names what it grants, so reviewing a CI line tells you nothing about what was opened. Provenance still records what ran, but the human said "whatever it wants."
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --allow-impure
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0
# next month someone adds b.env("TOKEN") to fn build —
# the same CI line silently grants that too.

options.name: One list flag `--grant exec,env` — supersedes the blanket
options.detail: Single flag, comma-separated effect list; replaces `--allow-impure` the same way A does. Same granularity as A in fewer characters; but it is a second spelling grammar (list parsing, ordering) instead of plain flags, doesn't tab-complete per effect, and diverges from the Deno convention users will pattern-match against. Everything else behaves like A (prompt fallback, CI failure naming the fix).
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet --grant exec
   impure   exec: "probe local openssl for the legacy C bridge"
   compiled tool 0.1.0

$ jet build tool.jet --grant exec,env,net   # grows into a mini-language

options.name: Prompt-only; no grant flags exist
options.detail: Interactive prompt is the only single-file grant path; CI must create a pkg.jet with a build: block (and `--allow-impure` is retired entirely). Maximally deliberate, but it breaks the ratified single-file story ("a lone script works with no manifest at every rung") the moment that script runs in CI — the exact place hermetic-by-default matters most would force manifest ceremony.
options.code:
$ jet build tool.jet            # laptop: prompt works
  allow exec for this run? [y/N] y

$ jet build tool.jet            # CI: dead end
Error: this build asks for `Exec`, which nothing has granted
  Fix: create pkg.jet with `build: .{ allow: #(Exec) }`   # manifest ceremony

decisions.comparisons:
Deno: `--allow-net`, `--allow-read=./data`, `--allow-env` — per-capability flags, the direct precedent; prompts interactively when a flag is missing.
Cargo: nothing — build.rs gets ambient everything, the anti-model.
Nix: sandbox on/off; no per-effect grants.
Jet today: blanket `--allow-impure` (D-CTEFFECT1/E3411) opens ALL declared Tier-2 comptime effects for a run; builds are hermetic unless it is passed.

decisions.title: Stored-ref disambiguation label: #Ref(label) or @Ref(label)?
decisions.gist: Two decisions ratified the same day contradict each other on one sigil: does the stored-ref owner label stay a # directive or move to the @ contract plane?
decisions.explainer: D-MARKERMOVE1 (=B, ratified 2026-07-01) explicitly lists `#Ref(Label)` under markers that CLEAR STAY on the # directive plane — it names #Ref itself as an example of a directive, alongside #Unsafe/#Test/#Bench. D-REF-SHORTHAND1 (=D, ratified the same day) chose an option whose own worked code sample spells the disambiguation label `@Ref(pool)` on the @ contract plane. Both are ratified; they cannot both be true once the marker-family @ plane actually ships (this card, c7markerfamily/#167). The label just names which in-scope value owns a `&T` field when inference is ambiguous — it is not, on its own, a promise about the declaration (the plane law's test), which reads closer to `#`'s job of supplying compiler-needed data, not stating a contract. This ballot exists purely to pick the one spelling that ships.
decisions.story: Walter is implementing the ref-shorthand card and hits the fork in the road: the marker-family law card says #Ref, the ref-shorthand ballot's own code sample says @Ref. He should not guess which ratified decision wins — a one-line owner call closes the gap and the exact same label (whichever spelling) gets typed into every stored-ref struct in the codebase from here on.

options.name: #Ref(label) — directive plane (recommended)
options.detail: Matches D-MARKERMOVE1's explicit text, which names #Ref(Label) as a clear-stays example in the same breath as #Unsafe/#Test/#Bench. The label supplies compiler-needed disambiguation data at a specific construction site — it is not a checkable promise about the type itself the way @Codable or @MustUse are (those hold regardless of any call site; a ref label only matters when inference is ambiguous). Zero rework needed in the marker-family card (already implemented this way); only the ref-shorthand card's own worked example needs a one-line respell in its ballot record.

options.name: @Ref(label) — contract plane
options.detail: Matches D-REF-SHORTHAND1's literal worked example. Requires reopening D-MARKERMOVE1's move list to add #Ref back in as a mover (it currently names #Ref as a non-mover on purpose, distinguishing it from the promise-shaped markers that plane law was built for). Creates a visible exception: the label is data supplied at a use site, not a standing promise about the declaration, so it reads against the @ plane's own stated test ("states a checkable contract") even though the sample code wrote it that way.

decisions.title: U20 — How does jetpack define and run refs with no pkg.jet, no flake, no nixpkgs equivalent? (ad-hoc adapters)
decisions.gist: Pick the escape hatch for using any repo, release tarball, or binary as a normal package: adapter recipes over fetched bytes, a new provider kind, or requiring upstream metadata.
decisions.explainer: Today jetpack has two clean paths: a source with pkg.jet realizes through the core provider; a source with Nix packaging realizes through the bridge. The missing path is the normal internet — a GitHub repo with only a Makefile, a release tarball with a binary, a Go/Cargo/npm project with no flake, a private tool that will never publish Jet metadata. The proposal: adapter packages — a typed recipe that turns already-fetched bytes into a normal Pkg. Providers answer "where do the bytes come from"; adapters answer "how do these bytes become a package output". U9 provider inference stays intact; no via: marker. Curated recipe families (prebuilt, copy, cargo, go, node, cmake/make) are sugar over one expert Recipe.build(fn(BuildContext)); autodetect drafts recipes from read-only probes and never executes upstream code; lock identity = source hash + recipe text hash + helper version + platform + declared tool deps + output hash.
decisions.story: Walter wants the codex CLI in his dev env. There is no pkg.jet upstream, the community flake is three versions stale, and nixpkgs lags the vendor by weeks. Nix's answer is "fork the repo and write a derivation." Walter types jet add github@openai/codex --adapt, reviews the drafted three-line recipe, and has the vendor's release from two days ago on PATH — locked, reproducible, no fork.
decisions.detail: Full proposal folded into docs/plans/epoch-5/README.md (§ Open / Proposed) from ad-hoc-adapters.md (2026-07-02). Safety contract regardless of option: probe is read-only (file names, manifests, release metadata — no upstream script runs); network during build denied except locked fetch(url, sha256:); ambient commands only through BuildContext with effect provenance in .jet/lock; outputs install only under the package output root; build tools are Pkg deps, never host /usr/bin. First build passes the U19 trust gate. Exact constructor names (Pkg.adapt, Recipe.*) are follow-up ballot surface; this ballot decides the model. New E12xx diagnostics: no usable metadata, ambiguous autodetect, missing declared bin, unpinned binary URL, undeclared build tool, ambient network/exec denied — each fix names the next command or field.

options.name: Adapter packages as Pkg values (recommended)
options.detail: One package mechanism; adapters are recipes, not providers; inline in env.* or named in pkg.jet, same IR and lock path. jet add <ref> --adapt drafts a recipe from a read-only probe.
options.code:
$ jet run github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d
Error [E1240]: `github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d` has no Jet package or Nix flake
 Why: jetpack needs package metadata or an adapter recipe before it can run a repo
 Fix: run `jet add github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d --adapt` to draft one

$ jet add github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d --adapt
  detected: CMake project, binary candidate `weirdctl`
  recipe:   cmake + ninja, install `build/weirdctl`
  save to:  module env.dev in toolchain.jet? [Y/n] y
✓ locked (source hash + recipe hash + output hash)

options.name: New provider kind (adapter@ / via: adapter)
options.detail: A provider that owns both fetching and realizing. Leaks policy back into refs — the exact thing U9 dissolved; every ref grows a second axis and inference weakens.

options.name: Require upstream metadata
options.detail: Every repo must add pkg.jet or a flake before jetpack can touch it. Kills "use anything now"; users fork repos to add metadata — the Nix wall, restated.
options.code:
$ jet add github@acme/weirdctl
Error: no pkg.jet in source
 Fix: ask upstream to adopt Jet, or fork and add pkg.jet   // <- the wall

comparisons.note: Writing a derivation + often forking the repo; the exact wall this removes.
Formula DSL in a separate tap repo; adapters keep the recipe at the call site.
comparisons.code:
class Weirdctl < Formula
  url "https://..."
  def install; ...; end
end

comparisons.note: Plugin-per-tool shell scripts; unlocked, unhashed, curl|bash under the hood.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U21 — How does a dependency track a vendor's releases? (channel refs + jet update / jet outdated)
decisions.gist: Decide how "give me the latest from this vendor" is spelled and when it resolves: channel refs updated only by jet update, floating resolution, an update-only verb with no syntax, or a separate channels module.
decisions.explainer: Adapters and deps pin an exact rev — right for reproducibility, but nothing yet says how a ref FOLLOWS a vendor. Without a tracking story, "use the latest directly from any vendor" is a one-time snapshot: the codex adapter written today serves v0.48.2 forever until someone hand-edits the rev. The invariant every option must keep: the lockfile stays exact, so jet env / jet build never surprise-upgrade; the question is only where update INTENT lives and which verb moves the pin.
decisions.story: Doris added the codex CLI via an adapter last month at v0.48.2. The vendor ships weekly; v0.50.1 fixes the bug she reported. She should not have to visit the vendor's releases page, copy a tag, and edit a ref by hand — she types jet update codex, reviews the bump, commits the lock. Her teammates stay on v0.48.2 until that commit lands.
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (jetpack-vision walkthrough, gap 2). Applies to every source-ref position: adapters, deps on git sources, jet run <ref>, script-dep use lines (U11). Channel grammar if ratified: #latest (newest release/tag), #v0.x (semver mask over tags), #main (branch head — discouraged, allowed). Resolution happens ONLY in jet update (and first add); lock records the exact rev + channel that produced it. jet outdated is read-only: compares locked revs against channels and registries, prints available bumps, changes nothing. CI never resolves channels — a channel ref with no lock entry is an error, not a silent fetch of newest.

options.name: Channel refs, resolved only by jet update (recommended)
options.detail: Intent is declared where the dep is declared: #latest / #v0.x / #main on any source ref. jet update [pkg] re-resolves channels and moves the lock; jet outdated reports; realize verbs never resolve.
options.code:
source: github@openai/codex#latest

$ jet update codex
  codex  v0.48.2 → v0.50.1  (github@openai/codex, released 3h ago)
  lock updated · teammates get 0.50.1 on next `jet env` after commit

$ jet outdated
  codex     v0.50.1 → v0.51.0   github releases
  textkit   1.4.2   → 1.5.0     jet registry

options.name: Floating resolution at realize time
options.detail: jet env / jet run resolve #latest on every entry. Maximally fresh, but two machines realize different envs from the same commit — breaks the reproducibility promise that is the whole point.
options.code:
source: github@openai/codex#latest

$ jet env        # Monday: fetches v0.50.1
$ jet env        # Friday, teammate: fetches v0.51.0  ← same commit, different env

options.name: No channel syntax; jet update bumps exact pins
options.detail: Refs are always exact. jet update <pkg> finds the newest release/tag and rewrites the pinned rev in source. Smallest surface, but tracking intent lives nowhere: update cannot know "stay on v0.x" vs "jump majors", and the tool edits the user's .jet files.
options.code:
source: github@openai/codex#v0.48.2   // always exact

$ jet update codex
  codex v0.48.2 → v1.0.0   ← wanted to stay on v0.x; nowhere to say so
  rewrote toolchain.jet:6

options.name: Separate channels module
options.detail: Refs stay exact; a module channels { } block maps names to policies. Splits one fact across two places — the reader of the dep cannot see it tracks the vendor without hunting for the channels block (anti-repetition pressure says no).

comparisons.note: Ranges resolve at update time; Cargo.lock pins. The model users already trust — but only for registry deps, not arbitrary vendors.
Inputs float to branch head; nix flake update moves flake.lock. No release/semver awareness — you track main or a hand-pinned tag.
"latest" dist-tag plus package-lock; the two-file split confuses beginners but the resolve-at-update-only rule is right.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U22 — Hangar disk contract: GC policy, disk reporting, and the zero-/tmp guarantee
decisions.gist: Decide how hangar disk space is reclaimed (manual verb, safe auto-GC, or explicit roots) and make "no /tmp litter" a tested guarantee instead of a vision bullet.
decisions.explainer: Nix's disk story is a top-three complaint and the owner hits it daily: every nix develop -c litters a ~200 MB /tmp/nix-shell.* directory, hundreds of them fill a 31 GB tmpfs, and the store itself grows until a scary all-or-nothing nix-collect-garbage. The vision claims "no result symlink or /tmp litter" but no mechanism is specified. This ballot fixes three contracts: (1) reclaim policy — what jet gc keeps and when it runs; (2) reporting — jet hangar du showing live vs stale vs build-tmp; (3) hygiene — build scratch lives inside the hangar, is deleted on build exit, and orphans from crashes are swept by the next jetpack command. Retention floor for every option: anything reachable from a lockfile or a jetos generation is never collected.
decisions.story: Earl runs an overnight agent session: four hundred env entries and test runs. On Nix that morning greets him with a 94% full tmpfs and phantom "No space left on device" test failures that look like compiler bugs. On jetpack the same session writes nothing outside the hangar, and the hangar can tell him exactly what it holds and what is safe to drop.
decisions.inWild:
$ df -h /tmp        # after 400 nix develop invocations today
tmpfs  31G  29G  2.1G  94%  /tmp
$ ls /tmp | grep -c nix-shell
147
error: writing to file: No space left on device   # phantom test failure

# the jetpack contract under decision:
$ jet hangar du
hangar: ~/.jet/hangar
  live      (reachable from lockfiles/generations)   3.4 GB
  stale     (unreferenced > 14 days)                 1.1 GB
  build tmp (active builds)                          0 B     # always 0 when idle

$ jet gc
freed 1.1 GB · kept everything a lockfile or generation references
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (gap 3). Applies to jetpack now and jetos generations later (generations are GC roots; jet rollback must always find its target). Hygiene contract shared by all options, to be enforced by a golden test: a full env-enter/build/run cycle writes zero bytes outside the hangar and .jet/; build scratch is hangar-scoped (~/.jet/hangar/tmp/<build-hash>), removed on success AND failure; orphaned scratch from a killed process is swept opportunistically by the next jetpack invocation, no daemon. Reporting contract: du output is stable, machine-readable with --json (D-JPK-DISPATCH1 contract), and never lies about reclaimable space.

options.name: Manual jet gc only
options.detail: Reclaim happens only when the user types jet gc (retention: lockfile/generation-reachable is kept; the rest goes). Predictable, zero magic — but beginners never type it and rediscover the Nix disk balloon a year in.
options.code:
$ jet gc
freed 1.1 GB

$ jet gc --dry-run
would free 1.1 GB (38 objects, oldest referenced 2026-03-11)

options.name: Safe auto-GC by age + manual verb (recommended)
options.detail: Unreferenced objects age out automatically (default: untouched 14 days), swept opportunistically after jetpack commands — no daemon. jet gc still exists for "free it now". Beginners never think about disk; experts tune or disable per config. Only unreachable objects are eligible, so nothing reproducible is ever lost — worst case is a re-download/re-build.

options.name: Explicit GC roots, Nix-style
options.detail: Projects register roots (.jet/ links into the hangar); gc drops whatever no live project references. Precise, but imports Nix's hardest-to-teach concept — deleted-but-unregistered projects silently pin gigabytes, and users must learn what a root is to understand their own disk.
options.code:
$ jet gc
kept: 12 roots (9 projects, 3 generations)
^ user must now learn what a "root" is
$ jet roots list
/home/earl/old-experiment/.jet   4.1 GB   # deleted from mind, not from disk

comparisons.note: Manual, global, scary: gc deletes everything not rooted; roots are symlink trivia most users never learn; shell litter in /tmp is unmanaged entirely.
comparisons.code: $ nix-collect-garbage -d   # hope nothing you needed was unrooted

comparisons.note: prune verbs + system df — the reporting shape users like; but unreferenced != unwanted bites people constantly (yesterday's image, repulled today).
comparisons.code:
$ docker system df
$ docker system prune

comparisons.note: No GC at all; target/ grows until users delete it by hand. The absence this ballot avoids.
comparisons.code: $ rm -rf target   # the industry standard, sadly

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome). AMENDED by owner 2026-07-03: (1) the verb is `jet clean`, not `jet gc` — one command that both garbage-collects AND optimizes the hangar (hardlink/dedup, `nix store optimise` equivalent); (2) default stale_after is 30 days, not 14. Auto-sweep behavior (opportunistic, no daemon, reachable-never-collected) unchanged.

decisions.title: U23 — What happens on a machine without Nix? (bridge fallback + the no-Nix diagnostic)
decisions.gist: Define the exact experience when a ref needs the Nix bridge on a Nix-less machine: degrade gracefully with a precise diagnostic, offer to install Nix, or require Nix outright.
decisions.explainer: U16's bridge and the owner-approved native-deps stopgap (nixpkgs for C libs/BLAS) both assume Nix is installed. Nothing defines the other machine: a Windows-adjacent laptop, a fresh VM, a locked-down CI runner. What must be true regardless: jet-registry deps, core-provider builds, and adapters with prebuilt/copy recipes need no Nix — most of the vendor-tool story works on a bare machine. This ballot decides what the nixpkgs@-shaped hole says and does, and doubles as the exit-ramp marker: every adapter written is one fewer nixpkgs dependency, and this diagnostic is where users see the seam shrink.
decisions.story: Hank clones his team's repo onto a fresh Fedora laptop — no Nix, never heard of it. jet env realizes fourteen packages fine, then hits default.postgres_16, which today rides the nixpkgs stopgap. What Hank reads next decides whether his first jetpack hour feels like a product or like a stack of shims.
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (gap 4). Owner precedent: nixpkgs approved as native-deps stopgap IF the user has Nix, with an explicit requirement that non-Nix users get a clear message — this ballot writes that message. Whatever the option, the diagnostic must (a) name exactly which packages needed the bridge, (b) never block the packages that did not, (c) point at the narrowest fix. Partial realization semantics: env enters with realized packages on PATH and lists the holes, or refuses atomically — the option code blocks show the recommended shape; atomic-vs-partial can be sub-balloted if the owner wants it separate.

options.name: Graceful degrade + precise diagnostic (recommended)
options.detail: Everything Nix-free realizes; bridge-needing packages fail with one E12xx naming them, the why, and both fixes (install Nix, or switch to an adapter/core path). CI-friendly: --json lists the holes.
options.code:
$ jet env
✓ 14 of 16 packages realized
Error [E1252]: 2 packages need the Nix bridge, and Nix is not installed
 Why: `postgres_16`, `openblas` currently realize through nixpkgs on this platform
 Fix: install Nix (https://jet.dev/nix-bridge), or replace with an adapter:
      `jet add postgres --adapt` can draft a prebuilt recipe from postgresql.org

options.name: Offer to install Nix inline
options.detail: Same detection, plus jetpack offers a pinned, single-user Nix install on the spot. One keypress from working — but jetpack now owns a root-touching installer for a third-party system, its failure modes, and its corp-policy fights.
options.code:
$ jet env
2 packages need the Nix bridge. Install Nix now (single-user, ~/.nix)? [y/N] y
downloading nix 2.24.1 (pinned, checksum verified)...
✓ bridge ready · resuming realization

options.name: Require Nix for any bridge-era project
options.detail: jetpack refuses to realize an env containing any nixpkgs-path package until Nix exists. Honest about the dependency, but punishes the 14 packages that were fine and makes jetpack read as a Nix frontend — the opposite of the pitch.
options.code:
$ jet env
Error: this project requires Nix (2 packages realize via nixpkgs)
 Fix: install Nix, then re-run `jet env`
^ the 14 Nix-free packages are hostage

comparisons.note: The null case: no Nix, no anything. Install is a curl|bash that creates /nix and a daemon — famously heavy on corp machines.
Gold standard for a toolchain that self-bootstraps without a system package manager; jetpack's core provider should feel like this.
comparisons.code: $ rustup target add wasm32-wasi   # no apt, no brew, just works

comparisons.note: Formulae simply fail on Linux-without-brew; no graceful subset. The shape to avoid.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U24 — Binary cache / substitution: how do machines share built hangar objects?
decisions.gist: Pick the direction for a build-once-substitute-everywhere cache (the cache.nixos.org equivalent). Decided now because it constrains the hangar object format being built today; implementation can land later.
decisions.explainer:
The one Nix superpower the Epoch 5 plan never mentions. cache.nixos.org is why Nix is usable at all: without substitution, every machine compiles the world from source. Jetpack has the same exposure — every core-provider package and every Recipe.cargo/go/cmake adapter builds from source on every machine that lacks the output. The model that fits the hangar: objects are already content-addressed; a cache is any store that can answer "do you have output for platform

?" and hand back bytes whose hash is verified on arrival — hash verification means even an untrusted mirror cannot substitute wrong bytes; signatures answer provenance policy on top. What must be decided NOW regardless of ship date: the hangar object envelope (output hash + platform key + signature slot + provenance link into the lock schema), because retrofitting it after adapters and lockfiles ship means migrating every hangar and lockfile in existence.
decisions.story: Betty's team has nine engineers and a CI fleet. Their env has two adapter builds (a cargo tool, a cmake tool) totaling 40 minutes of compile. With substitution, CI builds each output once per bump; nine laptops fetch verified bytes in seconds. Without it, every laptop and every CI job pays the 40 minutes, every time the lock moves — the exact tax that makes teams abandon source-based tools.
decisions.detail: Raised from the 2026-07-02 vision review (gap 5). Scope of THIS ballot: pick the architecture direction and freeze the object-envelope fields into the hangar/lock schema now; protocol, hosting, and push tooling are Epoch 6 implementation cards. Interacts with: D-JPK-OCITOOL1 (registry push shares the TLS gate), U14 (OCI layouts are hangar objects and should be substitutable like any other), D-JPK-ADAPTER1 (adapter lock identity already includes output hash — the same hash a cache serves). Trust model note for the owner: content addressing makes substitution tamper-evident by construction; the signature layer decides WHOSE builds you accept, not WHETHER the bytes match the hash.

options.name: Output-hash-addressed cache protocol, signed objects (recommended)
options.detail: Any HTTP(S) store answering GET by output hash + platform; bytes verified by hash on arrival, accepted per the configured signing keys. Works for self-hosted, S3-style, and a future jet-hosted public cache. Envelope fields frozen into hangar/lock schema now; protocol ships Epoch 6 behind the same TLS gate as OCI push.
options.code:
# CI, after tests pass:
$ jet cache push https://cache.acme.dev --key ci.key
pushed 2 outputs (codex, weirdctl)

# any machine, any time:
$ jet env
  weirdctl  substituted (890 KB, hash verified, signed: acme_ci)

# miss is never an error — it just builds:
  newtool   no cache hit · building from source (2m10s)

options.name: Registry-coupled cache only
options.detail: The jet package registry serves prebuilt outputs for published packages; nothing else substitutes. Covers registry deps but abandons exactly the expensive cases — adapters and private/unpublished builds — and couples cache trust to registry identity.
options.code:
$ jet env
  textkit    substituted from registry ✓
  weirdctl   adapter — not publishable, no cache path · building (18m)  ← the expensive one

options.name: Dumb hangar mirror (rsync/object store, trust by transport)
options.detail: Sync hangar directories through any file store; whoever can write the bucket is trusted. No protocol to design, but no signatures, no provenance, and partial-sync corruption becomes the user's problem — a footgun dressed as simplicity.
options.code:
$ jet hangar sync s3://acme-hangar
^ anyone with bucket write access now feeds binaries to every laptop, unsigned

options.name: Defer entirely (source builds until Epoch 6)
options.detail: Decide nothing now. The trap is not the missing feature — it is that the hangar object format and lock schema ship without envelope fields, and adding them later migrates every hangar and lockfile in existence.
options.code:
$ jet env    # nine laptops, every lock bump
  weirdctl  building from source (18m)   × 9 engineers × every update

comparisons.note: Substituters + signed narinfo; cachix built a business on hosting it. Proof the shape works at world scale.
Remote cache keyed by action hash; same build-once economics, famously transformative for team CI times.
Registry layers are the degenerate case: content-addressed blobs everyone already substitutes without thinking about it.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U25 — Which platforms are first-class for jetpack? (Linux / macOS / Windows tiers)
decisions.gist: Decide jetpack's platform tiers: is Windows a native tier-1 target alongside Linux and macOS, a documented WSL2 path, or best-effort? (jetos stays Linux either way.)
decisions.explainer: Nix's platform story is a top adoption blocker: macOS is half-supported (nix-darwin, frequent breakage on OS updates), Windows is nothing — the standard answer is "use WSL2", which excludes most corporate and student machines as they actually exist. No env/package tool in this space works natively on all three desktop platforms. jetpack choosing Windows tier-1 would be a differentiator no competitor can answer — and it is a choice about the hangar, providers, services, and adapters, not about jetos: the OS tier is Linux regardless. Tier-1 means: hangar, core provider, adapters (prebuilt/copy/cargo/go/node), services supervision, secrets, and the trust gate all work natively; CI runs the suite per platform; a platform-specific failure is a P1 bug, not a shrug. The Nix bridge is Linux/macOS only by nature — Windows leans on core + adapters + D-JPK-CACHE1 substitution, which is also the exit ramp story.
decisions.story: Mabel teaches a 30-student class; twenty laptops run Windows. With Nix the first lab day dies in WSL2 installs, virtualization BIOS settings, and IT tickets. With tier-1 Windows she says "download jet, run jet dev" and the whole room is compiling in five minutes — same commands, same lockfile, all three OSes.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 1). Scope: jetpack tiers only; jetos parity bar stays the Linux HalcyonOmega baseline. Platform-conditional surface already exists in adapter design (platforms: [Platform.linux_x64], {target} asset substitution) — this ballot decides which values of Platform the product stands behind. Windows-specific facts for the record: services supervision maps to Win32 job objects; build sandboxing has no user-namespace equivalent (AppContainer is the nearest; honest-warning fallback per U28 applies); path/exec semantics differ (no shebangs, .exe suffix) and are jetpack's to absorb, never the user's. Per philosophy.md, implementation effort is not a factor in this ranking — only reach, beginner experience, and the master-of-ALL goal.

options.name: Linux + macOS + Windows, all tier-1 native (recommended)
options.detail: One product on the three desktop OSes; hangar/core/adapters/services/secrets native everywhere; per-platform CI; platform break = P1. Nix bridge stays Linux/macOS; Windows realizes via core + adapters + cache substitution, with the U23 diagnostic naming any bridge-only package.
options.code:
win> jet dev
First entry to this repo. env.dev wants: ...
Trust and continue? [y/N] y
✓ postgres  healthy on :5432 (native service supervision)
pulseops listening on http://localhost:8080

win> jet env
Error [E1252]: `openblas` needs the Nix bridge, unavailable on Windows
 Fix: `jet add openblas --adapt` can draft a prebuilt recipe

options.name: Linux + macOS tier-1; Windows via documented WSL2 path
options.detail: Native on Unix; Windows users install WSL2 and run the Linux build. Honest and shippable sooner, but inherits every WSL failure mode (IT policy, virtualization, file-system seams with editors on the Windows side) — the exact wall Nix users hit.
options.code:
win> jet dev
'jet' is not recognized...
# docs: install WSL2, then Ubuntu, then jet inside it;
# VS Code needs the Remote-WSL extension; repo must live in the WSL filesystem

options.name: Linux tier-1 only; macOS and Windows best-effort
options.detail: Smallest promise; matches where jetos lives. Concedes the entire differentiator and caps jet's audience at Nix's current audience — hard to reconcile with master-of-ALL.
options.code:
macos% jet dev
⚠ macOS is best-effort: services supervision untested on this platform
# every macOS user reads this and hears "not for you"

comparisons.note: Linux first, macOS strained, Windows never. The gap this ballot decides whether to own.
comparisons.code:
# Windows answer today:
> wsl --install   # + BIOS virtualization + IT approval

comparisons.note: All three tier-1 from day one; widely cited as why Rust onboarding feels effortless everywhere. The model.
comparisons.code: > rustup default stable   # identical on win/mac/linux

comparisons.note: Recent proof the bar moved: single binary, native Windows, no daemon — and adoption followed.
comparisons.code: > uv sync   # works on a locked-down corp Windows laptop

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U26 — Package & option discovery: jet search / jet info / LSP completions in env modules
decisions.gist: Decide the discovery surface: how users find package names, versions, and typed options — full CLI + in-editor completions, CLI only, or a web index.
decisions.explainer: Nix discovery is grep-shaped: `nix search` is slow and fuzzy, NixOS options live on a separate website, and the standard workflow is search.nixos.org in a browser tab next to the editor. Jet's env modules are typed — that already paid for a better answer: the checker knows every source, package, version set, and Service/option field, so discovery can live where the user is typing. This is the Blueprint north star cashed in for environments: completing default.postgres_16 from a typo, hovering a Service field for its docs and default, and a fast local jet search — no browser, no second language, no website lag behind reality.
decisions.story: Ruth needs Postgres and image tooling in her env. In Nix she has three browser tabs: search.nixos.org for the attr name, the options site for service flags, a blog post for the overlay incantation. In Jet she types default.post, the editor completes postgres_16 and postgres_17, hover shows versions and platforms, and Service.{ completes its typed fields with defaults inline. She never leaves the file.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 2). Feeds on existing machinery: E09xx nearest-name diagnostics already do fuzzy matching; the LSP is an existing epoch track; sources (default/unstable/registry) are typed values with enumerable members. Contract questions the option decides: search index is local and offline (synced with lock/provider metadata, so results match what would actually resolve — never a stale web index); `jet info <pkg>` shows versions, platforms, source, and typed options with defaults; completions and hover work in any .jet file inside module env/system/image blocks. Registry-side full-text search can ride the registry track later without changing this surface.

options.name: Full surface: jet search + jet info + LSP completions/hover (recommended)
options.detail: Fast local index for the CLI pair; LSP completes package names after source dots and typed option fields inside Service/module bodies, hover shows docs/defaults/platforms. One source of truth: the same provider metadata the resolver uses.
options.code:
$ jet search postgres
  default.postgres_16    16.4   linux, macos, windows
  default.postgres_17    17.2   linux, macos, windows
  unstable.postgres_18   18.0b  linux

$ jet info default.postgres_16
  versions: 16.0–16.4 · service options: version, port, init, ephemeral, data_dir

// in-editor: packages: [default.post▌] → completes postgres_16 / postgres_17
// hover Service.init → "SQL file run once on first service start"

options.name: CLI only (jet search / jet info)
options.detail: Terminal answers without the editor half. Solid floor, but leaves the typed-options payoff on the table — the user still context-switches to ask "what fields does Service take", which is the question they ask most.
options.code:
$ jet search postgres     # works
// editor: services: { postgres: Service.{ ▌ } }   ← still guessing fields

options.name: Web index (search.jet.dev), minimal CLI
options.detail: The Nix model with better paint. A hosted index lags providers, needs network, and keeps discovery outside both the terminal and the editor — two context switches where A has zero.
options.code:
$ jet search postgres
see https://search.jet.dev?q=postgres   ← the browser tab, again

comparisons.note: CLI search slow; options on a website; the browser-tab workflow this deletes.
comparisons.code:
$ nix search nixpkgs postgres   # …seconds pass
# then open search.nixos.org for the service options anyway

comparisons.note: cargo search + docs.rs is serviceable but out-of-editor; rust-analyzer completes code, not manifest deps.
The in-editor bar: typed config objects complete their own fields with docs on hover. Jet env modules are exactly this shape.
comparisons.code: const cfg: ServerOptions = { po| }   // completes port, with docs

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U27 — Failed-build debuggability: --shell-on-fail, jet explain, persisted build logs
decisions.gist: Decide the debugging contract when a package or adapter build fails: drop into the exact failing build env + explain resolution + persisted logs, logs only, or verbose-rerun.
decisions.explainer: When a Nix build fails, the human is locked out of the crime scene: the sandbox is gone, `nix log` shows a wall of text, and reproducing interactively means arcana (keep-failed, nix develop on the derivation) that even experts google. Jetpack builds — core packages and adapter recipes — will fail too; the question is whether the failure hands the user the exact environment and step that failed or just a log. Three parts under one ballot: (1) --shell-on-fail: on failure, open a shell inside the preserved build scratch dir with the build's exact PATH/env, positioned at the failing step; (2) jet explain <ref>: why this ref resolved to pkg.jet vs flake vs adapter, what was locked (source hash, recipe hash, platform), and which step failed; (3) jet logs <pkg>: full per-step logs persisted in .jet/, survive the failure, --json for CI.
decisions.story: Vernon's adapter build for a C tool dies at the ninja step on his machine only. In Nix he would rerun with --keep-failed, hunt /tmp for the half-built tree, and reconstruct the env by hand. Here he reruns with --shell-on-fail, lands in the preserved build dir with the build's exact toolchain on PATH, runs the failing command himself, and sees the missing header in thirty seconds.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet env
Error [E1246]: adapter `weirdctl` failed at step 2 of 3 (ninja -C build)
 Why: `ninja` exited 1 — full log: `jet logs weirdctl`
 Fix: rerun with `jet env --shell-on-fail` to debug inside the build environment

$ jet env --shell-on-fail
build failed at step 2 · shell in preserved build dir (tools on PATH: cmake, ninja)
[weirdctl-build]$ ninja -C build
build/src/net.c:14: fatal error: openssl/ssl.h: No such file or directory
[weirdctl-build]$ # ah — missing dep. exit, add default.openssl to deps, done.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 3). Interlocks: preserved-on-failure scratch dirs are the one exception to U22's always-cleaned rule — kept under the hangar tmp area, tagged, and swept by the next jet gc or auto-GC age-out, so the zero-/tmp guarantee holds; jet explain generalizes the adapter proposal's `jet adapter explain` to every ref kind; the shell-on-fail shell is inert (nothing auto-runs in it — it is the user's hands, consistent with U19's intent boundary). Diagnostics: build-failure E12xx always names the step, the log verb, and the shell-on-fail flag — the fix line is the debugging tutorial.

options.name: Full contract: --shell-on-fail + jet explain + persisted logs (recommended)
options.detail: Failure hands over the crime scene: preserved scratch + exact build env shell at the failing step; explain shows the resolution/lock story per ref; logs persist per step with --json. Every build-failure diagnostic names all three.
options.code:
$ jet explain weirdctl
  ref      github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d
  path     adapter (no pkg.jet, no flake upstream)
  locked   source 8a31c9d · recipe hash 4be2… · platform linux_x64
  deps     default.cmake, default.ninja
  status   FAILED step 2/3 (ninja) · scratch preserved · `jet logs weirdctl`

options.name: Persisted logs only
options.detail: jet logs <pkg> with per-step structure; no preserved scratch, no shell. Better than Nix's wall of text, but the user still reconstructs the environment by hand for anything a log line does not explain — which is most native-build failures.
options.code:
$ jet logs weirdctl
[step 2/3 ninja] build/src/net.c:14: fatal error: openssl/ssl.h...
$ # now what? recreate the env yourself to poke at it

options.name: Verbose rerun (Nix model)
options.detail: On failure, suggest rerunning with -v for more output. No preserved state, nothing interactive; debugging stays read-only archaeology. Listed for completeness — it is the status quo this ballot exists to beat.
options.code:
$ jet env -v
…4000 lines later, the same error, now with company

comparisons.note: keep-failed + manual env reconstruction; the interactive path is folklore, not product.
comparisons.code:
$ nix build --keep-failed
$ ls /tmp/nix-build-*   # now reconstruct PATH yourself

comparisons.note: The workflow everyone actually uses: run a shell from the last good layer. Proof that "shell at the failure" is the debugging primitive people want.
Structured logs + explain exist and are loved; interactive failing-env entry still missing — half the answer.

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U28 — Product constraint: no resident daemon, no root for jetpack operations
decisions.gist: Ratify (or reject) a standing constraint: jetpack never runs a daemon and never needs root; root appears only transiently at jetos activation; build sandboxing uses unprivileged mechanisms with an honest fallback warning.
decisions.explainer: Nix's daemon + root exist because /nix/store is system-global and shared: something privileged must write the shared store, dedupe across users, sandbox builds (pre-user-namespace 2006 design), and enforce machine-wide cache trust. Jetpack's hangar is per-user by design, so the daemon's reason evaporates — the cargo/rustup/uv model. This ballot makes that a ratified constraint rather than an accident, because constraints not written down accrete violations: a "small helper daemon" for service supervision, a root hook for a sandbox, a setuid shim for ports. What the constraint costs, eyes open: no cross-user store dedup on shared servers (mitigated by U24 substitution + in-hangar hardlink dedup); sandbox strength rides unprivileged user namespaces on Linux (disabled on some hardened distros) and weaker mechanisms on macOS/Windows; no admin-enforced machine-wide trust policy (org config layer later); concurrent builds coordinate by file locks, not a broker.
decisions.story: Gladys is on a locked-down corporate laptop: no admin rights, software installs need tickets. Nix is dead on arrival — the installer wants /nix and a root daemon. jetpack is one binary in her home directory; jet dev works the first minute. Her company's shared build server pays the flip side: forty users, forty hangars — substitution from the team cache is what keeps that cheap.
decisions.inWild:
# install, no ticket:
$ curl -LO https://jet.dev/dl/jet && chmod +x jet && ./jet env
✓ works — no /nix, no daemon socket, no sudo

# the day root is actually needed, it is explicit and momentary:
$ sudo jet switch --name "pre-gpu-driver"   # jetos activation only

# the honest edge (security-relevant, plainly stated):
$ jet env
⚠ build sandboxing unavailable: this kernel disables unprivileged user
  namespaces. Adapter builds will run unsandboxed — they execute with your
  user's full permissions. `jet config sandbox require` refuses instead.
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 5; tradeoffs walked with owner same day). Contract if ratified: (1) no resident process ever — supervision (U12) parents services from the jet dev session; auto-GC (U22) is opportunistic post-command work; (2) no operation requires root except jetos activation verbs, which use transient sudo and say so; (3) builds are sandboxed by unprivileged user namespaces on Linux, the best available native mechanism per platform elsewhere; where unavailable, jetpack states plainly that builds run unsandboxed and offers `sandbox require` policy to hard-fail instead — never a silent downgrade; (4) concurrent jetpack processes coordinate via hangar file locks. Enforced like an invariant: any future design that wants a daemon or root path comes back to the owner as a ballot.

options.name: Hard constraint, ratified and tested (recommended)
options.detail: No daemon, no root, transient sudo for jetos activation only, unprivileged sandboxing with honest fallback + `sandbox require` policy. CI asserts no-root operation; violations need a new ballot.
options.code:
$ jet env && jet dev && jet gc   # all as plain user, no daemon socket exists
$ sudo jet switch                # the one explicit root moment, jetos only

options.name: No daemon, but optional root helper for stronger sandboxing
options.detail: Default identical to A; hardened-distro users may install a small setuid/root helper that provides namespace-grade sandboxing where unprivileged userns is off. Closes A's weakest edge, but jetpack now ships and maintains a privileged component — the exact attack surface A exists to refuse.
options.code:
$ jet config sandbox helper install   # sudo once; setuid helper owns sandbox setup
⚠ jetpack now has a privileged binary to audit, patch, and trust

options.name: Leave open (no constraint; daemon allowed if a future design wants one)
options.detail: Decide nothing; each future feature picks. History says this drifts daemon-ward one convenience at a time (Docker), and the corp-laptop story silently dies the day the first helper lands.
options.code:
# year two, some feature ships:
$ jet services enable --system   # "requires the jetpack agent; sudo to install"
^ the constraint that was never written down

comparisons.note: Daemon + root default; single-user mode exists but is second-class. Corp-laptop DOA case is common.
comparisons.code: $ sh <(curl -L https://nixos.org/nix/install) --daemon   # wants root, /nix, launchd/systemd units

comparisons.note: The model: one user-owned binary, no daemon, no root, corp-safe. Adoption followed.
The cautionary tale: root daemon became its biggest security and ops liability; rootless mode retrofitted a decade later.
comparisons.code: $ sudo systemctl start docker   # and docker group ≈ root

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: U29 — Offline guarantee: once realized, envs work with zero network, forever
decisions.gist: Decide whether "realized once → works offline forever" is a tested product guarantee with an --offline enforcement flag, a best-effort behavior, or an explicit prefetch verb.
decisions.explainer: Lock + hangar already imply this: everything an env needs is content-addressed on disk after first realization. The ballot is whether jetpack promises it. The guarantee: any verb that succeeded against the current lock succeeds again with the network cable cut — jet env, jet dev, jet build, jet run, service startup, all of it. --offline makes the promise enforceable: any operation that would touch the network fails loudly with what it wanted and why, instead of hanging or silently fetching. Guarded by a golden test that realizes an env, severs network, and re-runs the full verb set. What it forbids, permanently: phone-home version checks, lazy metadata refreshes on realize verbs, telemetry in the realize path — the quiet network habits that make tools flaky on planes and in air-gapped CI.
decisions.story: Frank demos on conference wifi that died an hour ago. His repo's lock hasn't changed since yesterday; jet dev brings up postgres and the app from the hangar without noticing the network is gone. The person next to him watches npm install spin on a registry it can't reach.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev            # wifi dead, lock unchanged since yesterday
✓ env.dev realized from hangar (0.1s) · ✓ postgres healthy · app on :8080
# no timeout, no retry spinner — network was never consulted

$ jet update codex --offline
Error [E1258]: `jet update` needs the network (queries github@openai/codex releases)
 Why: --offline forbids all network access
 Fix: drop --offline, or pin the wanted rev explicitly

# air-gapped CI:
$ jet build --offline   # cache miss = loud failure naming the object, never a fetch
decisions.detail: Raised on owner go-ahead 2026-07-02 (vision follow-up list, item 6). Semantics: verbs classify as realize-class (env/dev/run/build/test/services — never touch network when lock is satisfied; with --offline, hard-fail instead of fetch on any miss) or network-class (update/outdated/add/publish/cache push — honestly network-bound, refuse under --offline with E1258 naming the need). Channel refs (U21) resolve only in network-class verbs, so they cannot break the guarantee. Interlocks: U22 auto-GC must never collect objects the current locks reference (already its retention floor) or GC could break the promise; U24 substitution is an optimization inside realize-class verbs — a cache miss falls back to local build, and under --offline to a loud failure. Golden test shape: realize → deny network at the process level → full verb sweep must pass.

options.name: Hard guarantee + --offline enforcement + golden test (recommended)
options.detail: Realized-once-works-forever is product contract: realize-class verbs never consult the network when the lock is satisfied; --offline turns any would-be fetch into a loud E1258; golden test enforces it in CI permanently.
options.code:
$ jet env --offline      # lock satisfied → identical to jet env
$ jet env --offline      # after a lock bump with an unfetched object:
Error [E1258]: `codex` v0.50.1 is not in the hangar and --offline forbids fetching
 Fix: run `jet env` once with network, or push the object to a reachable cache

options.name: Best-effort offline, no promise, no flag
options.detail: Architecture already mostly delivers it; ship without the contract or the test. Costs nothing today — and erodes silently the first time a feature adds a metadata ping to jet env, which nothing would catch.
options.code:
$ jet dev    # on a plane, some future version:
checking for updates… (30s timeout)   ← the ping nobody balloted

options.name: Explicit prefetch verb required (jet fetch)
options.detail: Offline use is opt-in preparation: jet fetch downloads everything the lock needs; realize verbs may otherwise fetch lazily. Honest, but makes offline a mode users must anticipate — Frank's demo dies because he didn't run the magic verb yesterday.
options.code:
$ jet fetch              # yesterday, with wifi — did you remember?
$ jet dev                # today, offline: works only if you did

comparisons.note: Mostly offline-capable in practice, never promised; eval can still surprise-fetch (flake inputs, tarballs), and failures hang on timeouts instead of failing fast.
comparisons.code: $ nix develop   # on a plane: …waiting on github.com…

comparisons.note: The precedent: --offline exists, fails loudly with the missing crate named, and vendoring is a supported workflow. Users trust it.
comparisons.code:
$ cargo build --offline
error: no matching package named `foo` found (offline mode)

comparisons.note: The anti-model: --offline exists but registry metadata habits make it unreliable; nobody trusts it, so nobody uses it.
comparisons.code: $ npm ci --offline   # works, sometimes, depending on cache weather

decisions.comment: Owner ratified 2026-07-02 (in-session, recommended outcome).

decisions.title: Contextual dot-member blocks inside marker scopes: how does a #Test block spell its vocabulary?
decisions.gist: Inside a block marker like #Test, should typing `.` offer scope-specific sub-blocks (`.expect_fail { … }`), and what is the one general rule for all scoped markers?
decisions.explainer: A block marker (#Test("name") { … }, #Bench, #Transact) creates a scope with its own vocabulary: a test can expect failure, run setup, set a timeout, skip on a condition. Today that vocabulary has no home — S82 gives markers arguments and bodies, but no way for a scope to offer named sub-blocks over a region of its body. This decision picks the spelling for scope vocabulary: the thing the editor suggests when you type inside a marker block, and the thing a reader sees marking a region. Whatever wins becomes the ONE spelling (I8) for every scoped marker, not a #Test special case.
decisions.story: Betty is writing parser tests. One case documents a known bug — the parser wrongly accepts an empty config file — and she wants just that region of the test marked expected-to-fail until the bug is fixed, without splitting the file into a second test or memorizing a new top-level marker. She types `.` on a fresh line inside the #Test block and wants the editor to show her exactly what a test scope can do.
decisions.detail: Interplay: the two-plane law (D-MARKER-FAMILY1) is untouched — scope members are per-scope vocabulary, not new global markers; S82 grammar shapes stay. If B is ratified, other block markers (#Bench, #Transact, #Unsafe) may later declare members under the same law, each addition being an API decision, not a syntax one. Whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test before shipping, and the unknown-member diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4). Recommendation rationale: B is the only option that gives region granularity AND a closed, teachable vocabulary with a great error, and it is the strongest LSP-discoverability move — rank on beginner experience and one-path.

options.name: Marker arguments only — no new syntax
options.detail: Whole-block flags via existing marker arguments. Region granularity means splitting into more tests. Zero new grammar; vocabulary lives in the marker's signature and LSP completes argument labels. The cost: Betty's one-region case forces a file reorganization, and scope words that wrap code (setup, expected-fail region) have no honest spelling.

options.name: Contextual dot-member blocks (recommended)
options.detail: General law: inside a #Marker { } block body, a statement-position `.name { … }` or `.name(args) { … }` resolves against that marker's declared scope members. Unknown member is a teaching error that lists the scope's whole vocabulary. Typing `.` in statement position inside the block pops the member menu — the Blueprint-style 'what can I do here' move. Per I8 this becomes the ONLY spelling for scope vocabulary (no parallel nested-marker spelling for the same job). Grammar is unambiguous: distinguished from a leading-dot enum value (`.Circle(2.0)`, D-ENUMDOT1) by the required trailing `{ … }` block; from dot-construction `.{` and inferred destructuring (S74) by the identifier after the dot; method calls need a receiver expression.

options.name: Nested scoped markers
options.detail: Reuse S82's existing `#Marker { }` statement grammar: #ExpectFail("bug #412") { … } is legal only inside #Test. Vocabulary = which markers are legal in which scopes; discoverability = marker completion filtered by context. No new grammar, but the global # plane grows a per-scope directive for every scope word, and the page reads heavier — a reader must know #ExpectFail is test-only, not a general directive.

options.name: Block-valued marker arguments
options.detail: Scope vocabulary stays in the marker head; arguments may take blocks. Everything is one mechanism (marker args), but the head gets heavy for real tests, ordering between the main body and argument blocks is invisible (does setup run before the body? where does the reader look?), and a region in the middle of a test can't be expressed at all.

comparisons.note: Implicit member expressions: `.red` resolves against the expected type. Same discoverability move, expression position only.
DSL receivers: test frameworks offer scope words as lambdas-with-receiver; powerful but any function can be a 'scope word' — no closed vocabulary, weak errors.
#[should_panic] is whole-function only; no region granularity, discovered by memorization.
test.failing — whole test, dot-discoverable off the test object.

decisions.title: U30 — Toolchain as a dependency: does pkg.jet pin the jet version, with any jet auto-fetching and re-executing it?
decisions.gist: Should a project's pkg.jet name which jet version builds it, so any installed jet automatically fetches that toolchain and delegates to it — making clone-and-run just work forever?
decisions.explainer: Today the jet that builds a project is whatever is on PATH. A project written on jet 0.4 may use spellings jet 0.6 removed (or not yet have spellings it needs), so an old project greets a new machine with a wall of errors that look like the project is broken. The proposal treats the toolchain itself as a dependency: pkg.jet names a jet version; any jet binary reading the manifest realizes that toolchain into the hangar like any other package and re-executes itself as that version (the same exec dispatch already ratified in D-JPK-DISPATCH1). One law makes this safe forever: the pkg.jet identity block (the payload: block and jet: line) stays parseable by every future jet — frozen-forward grammar — so an old jet can always read enough of a newer project to fetch the right toolchain.
decisions.story: Hank clones a teammate's simulation repo six months after it was written. His laptop has jet 0.6; the project was built on 0.4 and uses a spelling 0.6 removed. Without a pin, `jet run` prints forty syntax errors and Hank concludes the project is rotten. With the pin, it prints `project pins jet 0.4 — fetching 0.4.2 (12 MB)… done` and runs.
decisions.detail: Bootstrap law (ships with A): the pkg.jet identity block — the `payload:` block and `jet:` line — has frozen-forward grammar; every future jet parses at least that block of every past and future manifest, so version dispatch can never be wedged by manifest evolution (Go proved this contract works at ecosystem scale). Version-proliferation is bounded by hangar GC (D-JPK-GC1) and shared caches (D-JPK-CACHE1). Interplay with the minimal-surface rule (U7/U10): no new files, no new commands — one field in the one reserved manifest, verbs on the one command. Recommendation rationale: A is the only option where the beginner's first contact with an old project succeeds; rank on beginner experience and long-term correctness.

options.name: Pin + auto-realize + exec (recommended)
options.detail: pkg.jet gets a `jet:` field (channel semantics per D-JPK-CHANNEL1; the lock records the exact version). A jet whose version differs from the pin realizes the pinned toolchain into the hangar — prebuilt objects via the D-JPK-CACHE1 substitution path, offline thereafter per D-JPK-OFFLINE1, GC'd per D-JPK-GC1, no Nix required per D-JPK-NONIX1, no daemon/root per D-JPK-NODAEMON1 — and execs it (D-JPK-DISPATCH1 mechanism). Frozen-forward identity-block law ships with it. `jet toolchain` shows the pin; `jet update jet` moves it deliberately.
options.code:
// pkg.jet
payload: { name: "sim_dashboard", version: "0.3.0" }
jet: 0.4

$ jet run .
jet: project pins toolchain 0.4 (installed: 0.6.1)
jet: realizing jet 0.4.2 into hangar… done
building sim_dashboard… ok

$ jet toolchain
pinned: 0.4 (locked 0.4.2, hangar) — installed: 0.6.1

$ jet update jet
jet: 0.4 -> 0.6 updates 3 spellings; run `jet fix` after. Proceed? [y/N]

options.name: Warn only (engines-style)
options.detail: Mismatch prints a warning naming the pinned version, then proceeds with the installed jet. No fetch machinery, but the warning scrolls past and Hank still gets the forty errors — Node's engines shows exactly how this decays into a convention nobody trusts.
options.code:
$ jet run .
warning: project pins jet 0.4, installed is 0.6.1 — output may not build
error[E0xxx]: unknown spelling `…` (x40)

options.name: Dev-shell only — toolchain is an env.jet package
options.detail: The toolchain pins only inside the dev shell: env.jet lists jet@0.4 in packages; `jet dev` / `jetpack enter` use it; a bare `jet run` outside the shell uses whatever is installed. Consistent with 'env.jet is dev shell only', but the beginner path — clone, `jet run` — is exactly the path left unprotected.

options.name: No pin — editions carry compatibility
options.detail: pkg.jet declares `edition: 2027`; one jet binary keeps every edition's grammar alive, so new compilers always build old code. This is the Rust editions bet — but editions cover surface grammar, not stdlib behavior, codegen differences, or pre-1.0 breakage, and they obligate the compiler to carry every historical grammar forever. Editions remain a good complementary idea after 1.0; they are not a substitute for a pin while the language moves fast.

comparisons.note: The gold standard: go.mod's toolchain directive; any Go ≥1.21 auto-downloads and re-executes the pinned toolchain. Clone-and-run just works.
rust-toolchain.toml; works, but only because a separate manager (rustup) intercepts every invocation — a resident middleman jetpack's no-daemon law avoids.
engines is warn-only and widely ignored; teams bolt on nvm/.nvmrc by convention. The cautionary tale for option B.
Flake pin: exact and hermetic, but the pin lives outside the language's own manifest and costs the whole Nix mental model.

decisions.title: Next-generation FFI: what one structure makes every foreign language near-trivial to wrap, replace in situ, and tap immediately?
decisions.gist: Pick the architecture every foreign language shares: per-language namespaces with pluggable binders, uniform extern blocks, typed projection importers, or runtime-broker sidecars.
decisions.explainer: Jet already speaks two foreign languages, each with its own shape: Rust via extern rust "crate@version" { … } (S50) and C via generated bindings mounted at c.<lib> with a user overlay (S59). JS is sequenced next, Swift later (D-JSWIFTFFI1). The owner's bar: using a library from almost any language should feel almost as easy as using a Jet package — every ecosystem's work immediately usable, and any foreign dependency replaceable later by a native Jet implementation without touching call sites (in-situ replacement). This ballot picks the one structure all languages share. How deep each language's binding goes (shallow declaration binding, full typed projection, or a runtime broker) is a per-language follow-up ballot on top of the winning frame — the frame is what must never vary.
decisions.story: Doris is building a lab-data tool in Jet. The only mature reader for her instrument's file format is a Python package; the best plotting library is on npm; a checksum routine she needs ships as a C header. She wants all three working this afternoon, each behind an ordinary typed Jet API with honest effects — and when a native Jet plotting package appears next year, she wants to swap it in by changing one dependency line, not rewriting call sites.
decisions.inWild:
use py.h5instrument as h5     // Python package, typed surface
use js.plotly as plot          // npm package (D-NPMTYPE1 stubs)
use "xxhash.h" as xx           // C header, script tier (S59)

fn main() #(Fs, Proc) {
    run := h5.read("run-0142.h5")
    print(xx.hash64(run.raw))
    plot.line(run.times, run.values)
}
decisions.detail: A, C, and D compose rather than exclude: A is the surface law (namespaces, three tiers, overlay, in-situ shadowing, lockfile provenance); C and D are per-language binder strategies BEHIND that surface — projection importers for static languages (C, Swift, Rust), a broker likely right for Python/JS dynamic tails, shallow declaration binding where that's enough. Ratifying A means: the surface ships now; follow-up ballots (D-FFI-PY1, D-FFI-JS1 folding in D-NPMTYPE1, D-FFI-SWIFT1 honoring D-JSWIFTFFI1 sequencing) pick each language's strategy on the common frame. Existing ratifications are preserved, not reopened: S59 is already the C instance of A; S50's extern rust block becomes the rust binder's declaration format inside rust.*; D-DEP1's vendoring/hash-pinning law extends to every language's refs. I8: one FFI structure for all languages is the point — shipping B alongside A would be two spellings for one job. I1/I2 hold in every option: user code is safe unless #Unsafe; no foreign toolchain's errors ever reach the user unlaundered — binder diagnostics are Jet diagnostics with codes and snapshots (I4). Recommendation rationale: A is the only option that is uniform (one structure to learn), immediate (a new language needs only a binder, at whatever depth exists first), deep where it counts (projection strategy per language later), and structurally in-situ-replaceable — rank on beginner experience, one-path, and long-term correctness.

options.name: Language namespaces + pluggable binders (recommended)
options.detail: Generalize S59's proven C structure into the law for every language. Each foreign world mounts as a namespace <lang>.<lib> with the same three tiers everywhere: script tier (use "xxhash.h" as xx — bind on first compile), project tier (use py.h5instrument as h5 with the dep pinned in pkg.jet), overlay tier (#Extern module py.h5instrument { … } to refine generated types; overlay wins). `jet bind <lang>` is a per-language binder producing inspectable, committable bindings in .jet/bindings/<lang>/<lib>.jet. Safety: generated bindings are safe wrappers by construction (marshaling internals compiler-vetted like std internals — I1); calling a foreign symbol outside a binding requires #Unsafe("reason"). In-situ replacement is structural: any <lang>.<lib> can be shadowed by a Jet package exporting the same surface — call sites never change. Per-language depth (projection vs broker vs shallow) is chosen behind this surface, one follow-up ballot per language.

options.name: Uniform extern blocks (generalize S50)
options.detail: Every language uses S50's declaration-first shape: extern <lang> "ref@version" { fn … = "path" }. Maximal explicitness — every crossing is written in the file — and one grammar for all languages. The cost is the wall: wrapping a real library means hundreds of declaration lines per library (generated or not, they live in your project), there is no namespace to shadow so in-situ replacement means hand-built wrapper modules, and 'almost trivial' is exactly what it isn't.

options.name: Typed projection importers only
options.detail: Every language gets a full compiler importer (Swift-Clang-importer style): use py.h5instrument elaborates the package's surface — from type stubs and introspection — directly into checked Jet types with effects and ownership mapped; overlays refine (raw pointer -> checked handle). The deepest 'feels native' ceiling, and the right end-state for static languages. As the only mechanism, it makes every new language wait for a full importer before ANY access exists — the opposite of tapping ecosystems immediately.

options.name: Runtime broker sidecars only
options.detail: Foreign runtimes run as supervised sidecar processes with a typed message boundary; py.* calls marshal to a Python worker (Mojo's play). Any language with a runtime works day one and effects are honest (#(Proc) on every call) — but values are serialized at every crossing (no zero-copy, no shared memory), C headers and Rust crates don't fit the model at all, and production binaries grow a process tree. Right as a per-language strategy for dynamic tails; wrong as the only structure.

comparisons.note: @cImport makes C trivial — but only C. The lesson: binder-in-the-compiler is magic; the miss: no structure for a second language.
Clang importer: full typed projection of C/ObjC — foreign APIs feel native. The depth ceiling to aim per-language binders at.
comparisons.code: import Accelerate   // C library, arrives as typed Swift

comparisons.note: Imports any Python module day one via a runtime broker — instant ecosystem reach, marshaled boundary. The play for dynamic-language tails.
comparisons.code:
from python import Python
let np = Python.import_module("numpy")

comparisons.note: P/Invoke plus WinRT projections: two tiers under one runtime — proof that shallow decls and deep projections coexist behind one surface.
Polyglot: many languages, one VM — reach bought with total runtime lock-in; the anti-goal for an AOT language.

decisions.title: Nested variant groups in `enum`: can a variant hold sub-variants so a group name matches its whole subtree?
decisions.gist: Can enum variants nest into groups, so testing `.Fire` also matches `.Fire.Burn` and `.Fire.Scald`?
decisions.explainer: Cross-system code constantly needs a name-tree: damage kinds, permission scopes, diagnostic categories, feature flags. UE ships this as stringly GameplayTags (Damage.Fire.Burn) matched by ancestry, which composes beautifully but renames break silently and there is no counting (two stuns applied, one removed, still stunned). Jet already has closed enums, leading-dot values (D-ENUMDOT1), and the ==-pattern law (S31). This decision adds one axis to `enum`: a variant may group sub-variants, and a group name matches its subtree in == and match arms. No new keyword — the `tag` spelling was killed for colliding with the ratified D-QUAL2 tag qualifier and minting a second closed-name mechanism beside enum (I8). Also on the table: a core `Bag<T>` counted multiset (sibling of Set) so `add`/`remove` counts correctly, and whether `Bag.has(.Fire)` accepts a subtree pattern as sugar for the `any` closure.
decisions.story: Hank is building the damage system for a roguelike. He has two physical damage kinds, two fire kinds, and cold, and armor should soak any physical hit. Today he lists every physical leaf by hand in the armor check; the day he adds a pierce variant he forgets to update it and armor silently stops working against it. He also tracks active damage-over-time in a Set, so a second fire tick and one cure leaves the target un-burning when it should still burn.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: it is the one path that makes the tree a compile-time fact (exhaustiveness, rename-safe, LSP-completable) using machinery beginners already know, with counting handled by a plain core container; the `has` sugar (D) can follow as a library call once A ships. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Nested variant groups, leaf-only payloads (recommended)
options.detail: A variant may enclose sub-variants in `{ }`; a group name matches its whole subtree in == and match arms; exhaustiveness is checked at the group level; payloads live on leaves only. Ships alongside a core `Bag<T>` counted multiset so add/remove counts correctly. `Bag.has` stays an explicit `any` closure for subtree queries. Renames become refactors, the LSP completes every `.` level, and a value is always a leaf.

options.name: Enum-of-enums (Rust-style nesting, no new syntax)
options.detail: No grammar change: model the tree as separate enums carried as payloads. Ancestor tests become `d is .Physical(_)`; you carry a second type name per group and there is no subtree-level exhaustiveness or dot-path value. Cheapest surface, but the group name is not a value and the compiler cannot see the tree.

options.name: Flat enum + naming convention (status quo, reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Keep `PhysicalBlunt`, `FireBurn` and match ancestry by hand with an else arm. Honest baseline: no new mechanism, but every subtree check is hand-maintained and silently rots when a leaf is added, and there is no counted container so multiset bugs stay.

options.name: Grouping plus subtree-pattern sugar on `Bag.has` (A, extended)
options.detail: Everything in A, and additionally `Bag.has(.Fire)` accepts a subtree pattern as sugar for the `any` closure, so counted-multiset ancestor queries read as one call. More reach, one more thing to learn on the container; the sugar must be exactly equivalent to the closure to avoid a second meaning (I8).
options.code:
active.add(.Fire.Burn)
active.has(.Fire)        // sugar for active.any((t) => t == .Fire)  -> true
active.has(.Fire.Scald) // false

comparisons.note: Swift nests enums inside enums; ancestor matching is by hand (`if case .physical = d`), no subtree exhaustiveness.
GameplayTags are stringly dot-paths matched by ancestry (`.HasTag("Damage.Fire")` catches `Damage.Fire.Burn`). Renames break silently; no compile check.
No grouping axis; nest enum-in-enum and match with a wildcard arm. No subtree name, no counting container in std.
comparisons.code:
enum Damage { Physical(Physical), Fire(Fire), Cold }
match d { Damage::Physical(_) => armor(), _ => {} }

comparisons.note: Discriminated unions with a shared prefix or a nested `kind` field; ancestry is a manual string `startsWith` or a switch group.

decisions.title: `@[Patchable]` derive: generate a typed `T.Patch` change-value you can hold, diff, merge and serialize?
decisions.gist: Should a derive generate a typed `T.Patch` — an all-optional twin of a struct — that you can hold, apply later, diff, merge and log?
decisions.explainer: Jet's ratified `.{ }` copy-update (D-COPYUPDATE1) applies a change now. But a change you hold for later — an undo stack, an audit log, an API PATCH body, optimistic-UI predict-then-reconcile — is hand-rolled per type today: an optional-field struct plus a merge function, written again for every record. UE's insight (GameplayEffect) is that a change should be a data value: previewable, loggable, revertible, sendable. This decision picks a derive on the `@` contract plane (like `@Codable`) that generates a nested `T.Patch` struct whose fields are all optional, plus `apply`/`diff`/`merge`, Codable by construction. No new expression syntax — you build a Patch with ordinary `.{ }`. Killed already: relative magnitudes (`level: +1`), which are literal semantics found nowhere else; `invert(base)`, a footgun valid only against its exact base; duration/stacking policy, which is library speculation.
decisions.story: Doris maintains the employee directory for a mid-size firm. It has an undo button and an audit log. For every kind of record she writes an optional-field struct and a merge function by hand, once per type, forever; and the audit log stores freeform JSON that slowly drifts out of sync with the real field names. She wants one canonical 'here is the change' value she can apply, reverse, and log without writing the plumbing again.
decisions.inWild:
@[Patchable]
struct Employee {
    level: Int
    title: String
    team: String
}

promote :: Employee.Patch.{ level: 4, title: "Senior" }   // ordinary .{ } — set fields = the change
emp2    :: emp.apply(promote)
undo    :: Employee.diff(emp2, emp)      // the patch that gets you back
both    :: promote.merge(relocate)       // right side wins on overlap
audit.log(promote)                       // Patch is Codable by construction
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: one canonical, typed, serializable change value (I8) that reuses `.{ }`, pattern-matching and Codable, and kills the hand-rolled-patch bug class outright; the full apply/diff/merge surface is what the driving use cases (undo, audit, optimistic UI, DB partials) actually require. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: `@[Patchable]` derive → `T.Patch` struct + apply/diff/merge, Codable (recommended)
options.detail: A derive on the `@` plane generates a nested all-optional `T.Patch` struct plus `apply(base)`, `Type.diff(new, old)`, and `merge(other)`; the Patch is Codable by construction. You construct and read it with skills you already have (`.{ }`, field access, patterns). `apply` is defined in terms of `.{ }` semantics, so there is one meaning of "edited copy" (I8 seam: `.{ }` is change-applied-now, Patch is change-as-a-value).

options.name: Generic library `Patch<T>` type (no per-struct codegen)
options.detail: A single std generic instead of a derive: one type for all structs, no generated code. But field access becomes dynamic/stringly — you lose field-name completion, compile-checked field names, and exhaustiveness. The value is opaque to the type system, which is exactly what a typed patch was meant to fix.
options.code:
p: Patch<Employee> := Patch.new()
p.set("title", "Staff")         // field name is a string; typo compiles
emp2 :: p.apply(emp)

options.name: Manual optional-field structs (status quo, reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Keep hand-writing an optional-field struct and an apply/merge function per record type. No new mechanism, but the plumbing, the diff code, and the audit-log drift all stay, re-implemented everywhere.

options.name: `@[Patchable]` derive, apply-only (defer diff/merge)
options.detail: Generate `T.Patch` and `apply` only; leave `diff` and `merge` to a later library decision. Smallest surface that still gives one canonical change value and Codable serialization. The cost: undo (diff) and combining changes (merge) — two of the four driving use cases — have no answer yet.

comparisons.note: TypeScript `Partial<T>` gives the all-optional twin type for free, and JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7386) standardizes apply. But there is no diff, no field-wise merge helper, and null-vs-absent is ambiguous.
comparisons.code:
type EmployeePatch = Partial<Employee>;
