const next = { ...emp, ...promote };   // apply; no diff, no typed merge

comparisons.note: No built-in. A derive crate or a hand-written struct of `Option<T>` fields plus an apply fn; diff/merge are bespoke each time.
comparisons.code:
struct EmployeePatch { level: Option<i32>, title: Option<String> }
fn apply(e: Employee, p: EmployeePatch) -> Employee { /* per-field ?? */ }

comparisons.note: No built-in partial type. Teams hand-roll an optional-field struct or use key-path writes; no standard diff or merge.
comparisons.code: struct EmployeePatch { var level: Int?; var title: String? }

comparisons.note: A GameplayEffect is data: a modifier list applied to attributes, previewable and reversible — but game-specific, not a general record patch.

decisions.title: Computed struct fields: can a field be a formula over its siblings — `attack: Int => strength*2+gear_mod`?
decisions.gist: Can a struct field be defined by a formula over its sibling fields, recomputed on every read instead of stored?
decisions.explainer: UE's attribute sets bake clamping and derivation into the field so no caller can produce a -3 health. Jet already has the clamping half: `type Health :: Int(0..1000)` (D-RANGETYPE1) and `#Invariant` (D-REFINE1). The missing half is a field defined by its siblings. Today that is a zero-arg method — which works, but is invisible to `@Codable` output and, the moment someone stores the value for speed or serialization, goes stale. This decision adds a computed field: `name: T => expr` where the expression reads sibling fields. It recomputes under `.{ }` and patches, appears in Codable encode, is unsettable (assigning it is an error with a fix-it), and takes no parens. The spelling uses `=>` (already 'computes to', from lambdas); `=` is left free for the eventual field-default decision, which every mainstream language spells with `=`. Cycles are a compile error; derived-from-derived is allowed, dependency-ordered.
decisions.story: Earl is writing the character sheet for a tabletop companion app. Attack power is strength times two plus gear bonus. He stores attack as a plain Int field and computes it in the constructor. A week later a teammate edits strength through a copy-update on the saved character; attack keeps its old value, the sheet shows the wrong number, and the bug hides because everything type-checks.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A: the standard cross-language spelling for derived state, it kills the stale-denormalized-field bug class at the source, composes with patches (base/current for free), and keeps one authoring story per job by staying the non-reactive twin of `Computed<T>`. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Computed field `name: T => expr` (recommended)
options.detail: A field whose value is an expression over sibling fields, evaluated on read. Recomputes under `.{ }` and patches, appears in `@Codable` encode, is unsettable (assignment is a teaching error with a fix-it), takes no parens. `=>` already means 'computes to'; `=` stays reserved for the future field-default slot. Cycles are a compile error; derived-from-derived is allowed, dependency-ordered.

options.name: Keep zero-arg methods (status quo, honest reject)
options.detail: Do nothing. Derived values stay methods. Semantically the same result, but the value is absent from `@Codable` output, does not recompute inside a copy-update automatically (the method is fine but a stored cache is not), and reads as `s.attack()` with parens. No new spelling — and the stale-cache bug class stays whenever anyone denormalizes for speed or serialization.

options.name: Computed field, excluded from Codable output
options.detail: Same `name: T => expr` spelling and recompute-in-copy behavior, but treated as transient: never encoded, always recomputed on decode. Simpler contract (no encode ambiguity), but loses the base/current-in-the-wire-format win — a client that only has the JSON cannot read the derived value without the schema.

options.name: `#[Computed]` marker on a method (no new field grammar)
options.detail: Reuse method syntax with a marker that opts the method into Codable output and parens-free access, instead of a new field form. Avoids adding grammar to the struct body, but still reads as a method declaration and introduces a marker to learn; the `=>` field form is the more direct spelling of "this field is derived".

comparisons.note: Swift computed properties are the standard spelling: a stored-free property with a getter body, no parens at the call site.
A `val` with a custom getter — same idea, computed on read, no backing field.
comparisons.code: val attack: Int get() = strength * 2 + gearMod

comparisons.note: Expression-bodied property; recomputes on every access.
No computed fields; you write a method and call `s.attack()`. It is invisible to serde `derive(Serialize)` unless you add attributes by hand.
comparisons.code: impl Stats { fn attack(&self) -> i32 { self.strength * 2 + self.gear_mod } }

decisions.title: Reopen D-EFF4/5: make the effect vocabulary a tree with ancestor subsumption (`#(Fs.Read)` under `#(Fs)`)?
decisions.gist: Reopen the flat effect list: let effects nest so `#(Fs)` accepts any `Fs.*`, and `#(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` callee?
decisions.explainer: D-EFF4/5 deliberately ratified a flat, closed set of ten effects — Net, Fs, Io, Db, Time, Rand, Env, Exec, Log, Gpu — with NO subsumption (calling a `Net` effect under `#(Io)` is E0740). It was chosen for teachability: ten names, no taxonomy arguments. This is the one gameplay-dna transplant that reopens a decided question, and it carries that burden explicitly. The proposal: re-base the ten names as tree roots so `Fs.Read`, `Fs.Write`, `Net.Http.Get` are leaves, and ancestor matching IS subsumption — the exact same rule as the tag trees in D-TAG1, learned once. `#(Fs)` in a signature would accept any `Fs.*` callee; a `#(Fs.Read)` caller would reject an `Fs.Write` callee; `#Grant` (D-SCAP1) gains subtree precision. Existing flat names stay valid as roots, so there is no migration break. It also settles the acknowledged D-EFF2 subsumption documentation gap structurally. Sequence this last, behind D-TAG1/PATCH1/FIELDPOL1.
decisions.story: Walter is hardening a backend service. He has a config loader that should only ever read the filesystem, and he wants the compiler to prove it can never delete a file. Today `#(Fs)` is one indivisible capability: read and write are the same grant, so the loader is trusted with deletes and a stray `remove()` slipped past review would type-check clean. Read/write precision on Fs, Db and Net is the refinement his team asks for most.
decisions.detail: Recommendation — Option A: Recommend A on the merits: it delivers the most-requested read/write capability precision, unifies subtree matching with D-TAG1 into one rule learned once, and settles the D-EFF2 gap structurally with zero migration break — but it reopens ratified D-EFF4/5, so sequence it last behind the other three. · This ballot was minted from docs/proposals/gameplay-dna.md (card cauegas). Interplay: never propose syntax contradicting a ratified decision; whichever option wins needs formatter emission + a fmt STABILITY test and any new diagnostic gets a code + tests/ui snapshot (I4).

options.name: Effect tree with ancestor subsumption (recommended)
options.detail: The ten ratified names become roots; `Fs.Read`, `Fs.Write`, `Net.Http.Get` are leaves. `#(Fs)` accepts any `Fs.*` callee; `#(Fs.Read)` rejects an `Fs.Write` callee; `#Grant` gains subtree precision. Flat names remain valid as roots, so no existing code breaks. Reverses E0740. Ancestor matching is the same rule as D-TAG1, so a user learns subtree matching once and applies it to enums, tags and effects alike.

options.name: Keep flat, no subsumption (status quo, defer)
options.detail: Do nothing. Ten names, no taxonomy, E0740 stays; the model stays maximally teachable but there is no read/write precision, and the acknowledged D-EFF2 subsumption gap stays a documentation note rather than a structural answer. Walter cannot prove his loader is read-only.
options.code:
fn load(p: String) -> Config #(Fs)   // read and write are one grant
fn read_only(p: String) #(Fs) { remove(p) }  // type-checks — no way to forbid write

options.name: Fixed two-level split on a few effects only
options.detail: Add a curated, closed second level to just the effects that need it — `Fs.Read`/`Fs.Write`, `Net.In`/`Net.Out`, `Db.Read`/`Db.Write` — with no general nesting. Less taxonomy debate than open trees, but the second level is picked arbitrarily by the language and the rule is a special case rather than the general ancestor law shared with D-TAG1.

options.name: Precision via prohibition, not a tree
options.detail: Express read-only by combining the flat name with a D-PROP1 prohibition instead of nesting: `#(Fs) #(!Fs.Write)`. Keeps the ten flat names and adds no hierarchy, but the spelling is compound, `Fs.Write` still has to be a nameable sub-capability (so you half-need the tree anyway), and it does not compose with `#Grant` subtree precision.
options.code: fn read_only(p: String) #(Fs) #(!Fs.Write) { load(p) }  // remove(p) here -> prohibition error

comparisons.note: Deno's permission model splits filesystem into --allow-read and --allow-write, and read/write accept path prefixes — hierarchical capability, granted outside the type system.
GameplayTag subsumption again: a system requiring `Ability.Fire` is satisfied by `Ability.Fire.Fireball`. Same ancestor rule proposed here for effects.
Effects are rows of labels with no hierarchy; you get precise per-effect tracking but express read-vs-write as two unrelated labels, not parent/child.
No effect system; capability is by module privacy and the type of the handle you hold (e.g. `&File` vs write methods). No signature-level effect at all.

decisions.gist: Which app is Jet's flagship CLI slice — the command-line program we ship, benchmark, and point people at.
decisions.story: Hank, a sysadmin who lives in a terminal, hears Jet is 'great for CLI tools.' He wants proof: one real tool he can build from source, run on his own files, and time against what he already uses. Whatever we ship here is that proof — it gets compared, benchmarked, and quoted.
decisions.detail: [Owner 2026-07-03: flagship slices deferred to END of Epoch 4 — jetpack development takes priority. Web-app slice candidate when resumed: recreate Tower itself in Jet (owner suggestion, recorded on card #9).]

options.name: jetgrep — recursive regex search (recommended)
options.detail: Grow the E2 GA jetgrep into a ripgrep-class searcher: globs, ignore rules, --count/--files/--context, colored TTY output, parallel directory scan. Invites the single highest-signal CLI benchmark that exists (vs grep/ripgrep) and exercises regex, fs walk, streaming stdin, args, color, exit codes.
options.code:
$ jetgrep "fn \\w+_test" src/ --count
src/lexer.jet: 14
src/parser.jet: 22

$ time jetgrep TODO ~/big-repo   # the benchmark people will actually run
real 0m0.41s

$ jetgrep "(unclosed" src/
error: invalid pattern: unclosed group
  fix: escape the parenthesis: \\(

options.name: jetstat — typed CSV/JSON data cruncher
options.detail: Reads CSV with a header row into typed rows, filters, aggregates, emits JSON. Showcases serde derives, iterator adapters, and typed-pipeline safety — the 'awk but typed' pitch. Weaker on raw-speed comparison; stronger on type-safety story.
options.code:
$ jetstat sales.csv --filter "amount > 100" --group region --out json
{"west": {"count": 1204, "total": 981223.50}, "east": ...}

$ jetstat sales.csv --filter "amont > 100"
error: no column `amont` in sales.csv
  fix: did you mean `amount`?

options.name: jetship — static site generator
options.detail: Markdown tree in, HTML site out: templates, front-matter, live rebuild via jet dev. Credible (Hugo/Zola class), touches text/fs/templating, and its output can host Jet's own docs. Benchmarks less crisply than search; templating surface is a bigger bite.
options.code:
$ jetship build site/
  42 pages -> public/ in 180ms
$ jetship dev site/
  serving http://localhost:8080  (rebuild on save)

options.name: jetwatch — parallel task runner / file watcher
options.detail: make-meets-watchexec: declares tasks in a typed manifest, runs them in parallel on file change. Shows tasks/channels and process control in a tool devs run all day. Overlaps `jet dev` conceptually — risks a second way to mean 'watch and rerun' (I8 adjacency).
options.code:
$ jetwatch test lint
[test] 132 passed  [lint] clean   (parallel, 2.1s)
[watch] src/parser.jet changed -> rerunning test

options.name: jetdu — parallel disk-usage analyzer
options.detail: ncdu-class: walks a tree in parallel, ranks by size, TUI summary table. Simple mental model, good parallel-fs and TUI-table showcase. Narrower feature spread than A-C (no regex/serde/templates).
options.code:
$ jetdu ~/Projects
  3.2G  jet/target
  1.1G  jet/.jet/store
  212M  photos/raw
scanned 148,201 files in 0.6s

decisions.comparisons: Rust's domain proof is ripgrep — one tool did more for Rust's CLI reputation than any doc. Go's is the gh/docker generation of CLIs. Zig points at its own build system. The pattern: one polished, benchmarkable tool per language.
decisions.rec: A — the grep head-to-head is the strongest single proof a language is fast and pleasant for CLI work, and the heritage jetgrep already GA'd once, so the slice measures polish, not feasibility.
decisions.recommendation: A — the grep head-to-head is the strongest single proof a language is fast and pleasant for CLI work, and the heritage jetgrep already GA'd once, so the slice measures polish, not feasibility.

decisions.gist: Which service is Jet's flagship server slice — the HTTP program that proves the backend story.
decisions.story: Doris runs a small team's internal tools on one VM. She'll adopt Jet for services the day she can read one real service — routes, database, logging, shutdown — deploy it as a single binary, and curl it. This slice is that service.
decisions.detail: [Owner 2026-07-03: flagship slices deferred to END of Epoch 4 — jetpack development takes priority. Web-app slice candidate when resumed: recreate Tower itself in Jet (owner suggestion, recorded on card #9).]

options.name: jetpaste — pastebin with TTL expiry (recommended)
options.detail: POST a paste, get a short id; GET raw or HTML; expiry via TTL sweep; /stats and /health. CRUD + persistence + time + concurrent clients is the minimum honest service, and every behavior goldens through curl. Exercises routes, SQLite, serde JSON, structured logs, per-request deadlines, graceful shutdown.
options.code:

$ curl -d "hello world" localhost:8080/paste
{"id": "k3xq", "expires": "2026-07-03T12:00:00Z"}
$ curl localhost:8080/p/k3xq
hello world
$ curl localhost:8080/p/gone4
{"error": "not found or expired"}   # 404

options.name: jetlink — URL shortener with click stats

{"short": "http://localhost:8080/r/a7Kq"}
$ curl -i localhost:8080/r/a7Kq
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: https://jet.dev/docs

options.name: jetfeed — feed aggregator with background fetchers
options.detail: Background tasks poll RSS/JSON feeds via the HTTP client; the server serves a merged digest. Uniquely shows client+server+taskgroup in one program. Depends on outside networks for real runs, so its golden path needs local fixture feeds.

[fetch] lobste.rs ok (12 items)  [fetch] hn ok (30 items)
$ curl localhost:8080/digest | head -3
{"items": [{"title": "Jet 1.0 released", ...}

options.name: jetboard — kanban/task JSON API (pairs with the web slice)
options.detail: Boards/cards CRUD API. If the web slice is jettasks (D-FLAGSHIP3=A), this becomes its persistence backend — the two slices then demo a full-stack Jet story. Cost: the two pillars' fates couple; a change in one ripples into the other's goldens.

options.name: jetrelay — webhook receiver and fan-out
options.detail: Receives webhooks, verifies signatures (core.crypto), fans out to configured targets with retry. Ops-flavored and shows crypto + retry + concurrency; but its interesting behavior (retries, downstream failures) is the hardest to demo convincingly in a golden test.

decisions.comparisons: Go's proof was 'a static binary serving HTTP' (Docker, Caddy). Rust points at axum examples; TS at Express/Next starters. The convincing form is always a small, complete, deployable service — not a framework tour.
decisions.rec: A — CRUD + persistence + expiry covers the widest honest surface (db, serde, time, routes, logs, shutdown) while every proof stays curl-observable and golden-testable.
decisions.recommendation: A — CRUD + persistence + expiry covers the widest honest surface (db, serde, time, routes, logs, shutdown) while every proof stays curl-observable and golden-testable.

decisions.title: Style length spelling: unit literals vs Length wrappers vs bare numbers
decisions.gist: How a user writes a length like 320 pixels in a UI style.
decisions.story: Betty is laying out the settings page of her recipe app: a card 320 wide, 180 tall, 12 of padding. She wants to type those three numbers once, have the compiler catch a unit typo, and not wonder later whether 320 meant pixels or something else.

options.name: Unit-family literal: width: 320px (recommended)
options.detail: core.ui.style declares a #UnitFamily(length) { px } (D-QUAL3), so the ratified unit-literal syntax (D-UNITLIT1) applies: 320px is a compile-checked Px value. One canonical unit mechanism in the whole language (I8) — style lengths use the same machinery as 500ms and 12.50usd. Unit typos are compile errors (E0134); if a second unit ever ships, cross-unit math is a compile error too (E0127). Reads like the CSS every beginner has already seen.

options.name: Enum with per-unit variants: width: .Px.{value: 320.0}
options.detail: Length is an enum whose variants carry the value: Length { Px(value: Float) }. Fully typed and pattern-matchable, and the field type stays a single Length even if more units are added. But it duplicates what unit families already do with a second, style-only mechanism (I8), and every length costs a variant-construction spelling.

options.name: Flat pair record: width: Length.{value: 320.0, unit: .Px}
options.detail: Length is a two-field struct (value + LengthUnit enum) — the shape Phase 3's example shipped. Plain user-space types, nothing new to learn beyond structs. But it's the most ceremony per length, the unit and value can be read independently without matching (a backend can use .value and forget .unit), and it's a second unit mechanism next to unit families (I8).

options.name: Bare Float logical pixels: width: 320.0
options.detail: No Length type at all — style dimensions are Float, pixels by convention, like SwiftUI/Flutter. Least typing and no unit concept for beginners to learn. But the unit lives in documentation instead of the type: 320.0 could be anything, a duration mixed into a width compiles fine, and adding real units later changes every Style field's type.

options.name: CSS string: width: "320px"
options.detail: Lengths are strings parsed at render time, exactly like inline CSS. Familiar to web developers and trivially copy-pasteable from CSS. But every typo becomes a runtime failure in the user's running app, the compiler can't help with math on lengths, and stringly-typed values are the opposite of the typed-styles goal this phase exists for.

decisions.comparisons:
CSS:            width: 320px;              — unit-suffix literal, the shape every web tutorial teaches
Jetpack Compose: Modifier.width(320.dp)     — typed Dp via extension property; 320 alone is a type error
SwiftUI:        .frame(width: 320)         — unitless CGFloat points, unit is implicit convention
Flutter:        SizedBox(width: 320)       — unitless logical pixels, same implicit convention
React inline:   {{ width: 320 }}           — bare number silently means px; {{ width: '320px' }} string also accepted
Typst:          width: 320pt               — unit-suffix literal, checked at compile time
decisions.rec: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — reuses the one ratified unit mechanism (D-QUAL3 + D-UNITLIT1), so `320px` is compile-checked with zero ceremony and no second style-only unit system (I8).

// e3: web target stays the only real renderer

bundles its own engine — zero system deps, huge binary.
