decisions.title: How does ungated code get "the impl for this OS"?
decisions.gist: #Target(Os.*) now gates impls, but plain main has no ratified way to construct/dispatch to whichever gated impl survived the build.
decisions.story: Doris writes a desktop app. She gates LinuxBackend and MacosBackend impls per D-OSTARGET1. Now her ungated main needs a backend value. Constructing LinuxBackend directly in main is (correctly) E-OSTARGET-UNMATCHED-CALL — main is not Linux-only. There is no blessed way to say "give me the one that matched this build."

options.name: fn-level #Target(Os.*) + one-survivor rule (recommended)
options.detail: Extend gating to fns: several fns share one name/signature, each gated to a different OS, exactly one survives per build; ungated code calls it like any fn. Missing an OS the build targets = compile error listing covered OSes. Mirrors Rust cfg/Go build tags; no new expression syntax.

options.name: Comptime OS switch expression
options.detail: A compiler-known comptime value (e.g. build.os) usable in a match whose non-matching arms are discarded before OS-gating checks run. More general (any per-OS choice), but new comptime surface + a second way to express what A does (I8 pressure).

options.name: Status quo — gated modules own the choice
options.detail: Ungated code never touches gated types; each app ships a per-OS gated module exporting a common fn. Works today only if fn-level gating exists somewhere, which it does not — effectively forces apps to gate their whole main, hollowing the check.
options.code: // every call chain from main must itself be OS-gated — main per OS.

comparisons.note: #[cfg(target_os)] fns — one survives per build.
build tags: one file per OS defines the same fn.
comparisons.code:
//go:build linux
func newBackend() Backend { return gtk{} }

comparisons.note: comptime switch on builtin.os.
comparisons.code: const b = switch (builtin.os.tag) { .linux => Gtk{}, .macos => AppKit{}, else => unreachable };

decisions.rec: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).
decisions.recommendation: A — smallest ratified-shape extension (same marker, fns instead of impls), proven pattern in Rust/Go, keeps one dispatch idiom (I8).

decisions.gist: How you ask the compiler to show the facts it proved (inline decisions, resolved ref owners) — the command's exact shape and what it does with no lens named.
decisions.story: Doris maintains a telemetry indexer. A teammate's PR adds `@InlineAlways` to a hot dot-product and a new `&Incident` field whose owner the compiler inferred. Before approving, Doris wants to SEE what the compiler decided — which calls actually inlined, which arena owns that field — without reading generated Rust. Three ratified decisions promised her `jet expand --facts`; this ballot fixes the command's final shape.

options.name: jet expand --facts <lens>; bare expand shows everything (recommended)
options.detail: Exactly the surface the three ratified decisions name. `--facts <lens>` narrows to one lens; bare `jet expand <file>` runs every lens, grouped — the magic default is 'show me all of it'. `--json` (existing global flag) emits the stable semindex-schema document. Unknown lens lists the valid ones.
options.code:
$ jet expand src/index.jet
inline — call-site decisions (2 facts)
  src/render.jet:41:15  Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)
  src/hot.jet:88:9      Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)

refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  src/index.jet:12:5  Index.hot      owner: pool       (labeled @Ref(pool))
  src/index.jet:13:5  Index.cold     owner: arena      (labeled @Ref(arena))

$ jet expand --facts refs src/index.jet
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  ...

$ jet expand --facts spam src/index.jet
error: no lens named `spam`
 Fix: pick one — inline (call-site inline decisions), refs (resolved ref/view owners)

options.name: jet expand --facts <lens>; bare expand is a lens directory, name reserved
options.detail: Same ratified `--facts <lens>` spelling, but bare `jet expand <file>` prints the lens menu and exits nonzero instead of dumping everything. Keeps the bare name free for Epoch-4 derive/macro expansion audit (D-METHODMACRO1 routed DSL power there), so `jet expand` can later mean 'show generated code' without a meaning change breaking scripts.
options.code:
$ jet expand src/index.jet
error: `jet expand` needs a lens
 What: available lenses —
   inline  call-site inline decisions
   refs    resolved ref/view owners
 Fix: jet expand --facts refs src/index.jet

$ jet expand --facts inline src/index.jet
inline — call-site decisions (2 facts)
  src/render.jet:41:15  Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)
  src/hot.jet:88:9      Vec3.dot  inlined (@InlineAlways)

options.name: positional lens: jet expand <lens> <file>
options.detail: Drop the flag; the lens is the first word, like `jet schema status`. Reads faster and matches subcommand-verb muscle memory. REQUIRES AMENDING the transparency wording of D-METHODMACRO1, D-REF-SHORTHAND1, and D-DYNARRAY1, which all ratified the literal spelling `jet expand --facts <lens>`.
options.code:
$ jet expand refs src/index.jet
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

$ jet expand src/index.jet        // lens word missing
error: `jet expand` needs a lens: inline | refs
 Fix: jet expand refs src/index.jet

options.name: dedicated subcommand: jet facts <lens> <file>
options.detail: The command is about facts, so name it that; `expand` stays unclaimed until Epoch-4 code expansion actually exists. Clean noun, discoverable in `jet help`. REQUIRES AMENDING the three ratified decisions' `jet expand --facts` wording.
options.code:
$ jet facts refs src/index.jet
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

$ jet facts src/index.jet          // no lens: run them all
inline — call-site decisions (2 facts)
  ...
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  ...

options.name: fold into semindex: jet semindex <file> --facts <lens>
options.detail: The facts already live in the semantic index (D-SEMINDEX1); expose the lens there instead of minting a command. One tool for 'ask the index'. Costs beginners the discoverable verb — `semindex` is tooling vocabulary, not a word Doris would guess. REQUIRES AMENDING the three ratified decisions' wording.
options.code:
$ jet semindex src/index.jet --facts refs
refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

$ jet semindex src/index.jet       // unchanged: index summary
semantic index (schema v2)
  definitions: 14
  ...

options.name: check-mode flag: jet check <file> --facts <lens>
options.detail: Facts fall out of checking, so hang them on `jet check` — one compile, diagnostics plus facts in a single run, nothing new in `jet help`'s top level. Muddles check's contract (exit status = did it compile) with a reporting surface, and buries the transparency story the ballots sold as its own command. REQUIRES AMENDING the three ratified decisions' wording.
options.code:
$ jet check src/index.jet --facts refs
ok: src/index.jet checks clean

refs — resolved owners (3 facts)
  src/index.jet:8:5   Owner.primary  owner: incidents  (inferred — sole candidate)
  ...

decisions.comparisons: Rust: `cargo expand` (nightly, macro output only) and `rustc --emit=mir` — dumps of transformed code, not curated facts; inlining is invisible. C: `gcc -E` preprocessed soup. Jai: metaprogram message loop can print build facts, but there's no standard lens command. Swift: `-emit-sil` expert dump. Nobody ships a beginner-readable 'what did the compiler decide' surface; Jet's is per-fact lines with file:line, plus `--json` for tools.
decisions.rec: A — the only shape that honors all three ratified decisions verbatim (no amendment churn), and bare `jet expand` showing every lens is the right magic default: the beginner who doesn't know lens names still gets the answer, the expert narrows with --facts.
decisions.recommendation: A — the only shape that honors all three ratified decisions verbatim (no amendment churn), and bare `jet expand` showing every lens is the right magic default: the beginner who doesn't know lens names still gets the answer, the expert narrows with --facts.

decisions.title: Should decode apply migration{} blocks to old stored data at runtime?
decisions.gist: Old stored data currently fails to decode; should the compiler generate the code that upgrades it in place during decode?
decisions.story: Betty (from D-MIGRATE3) ships schema v3 of UserRecord. Her nightly import reads three-year-old v1 JSON. Today that decode simply errors — the migration blocks she wrote only prove a migration EXISTS at compile time. She expected the old records to load and upgrade; decode_traced exists to tell her it happened, but nothing can happen yet.

options.name: Generate the migration chain into decode (recommended)
options.detail: Codegen lowers each migration{} block to a step function; decode of a @PublishedSchema type first tries the current shape, on mismatch walks stored version tags/shape detection oldest to current, applying steps. decode_traced records from+steps; plain decode applies silently. Zero cost for types without migrations (nothing generated).

options.name: Explicit opt-in call: decode_migrating only
options.detail: Plain decode keeps failing on old shapes; a third method decode_migrating<T> applies the chain. Callers must choose migration explicitly; surface grows to three decode verbs (I8 pressure).
options.code:
user :: json.decode_migrating<UserRecord>(raw)?   // applies chain
old  :: json.decode<UserRecord>(raw)               // still errors on v1

options.name: Defer past Epoch 3 (status quo)
options.detail: Keep compile-time-only checks; decode_traced stays always-false until a later epoch. Stored-data users must hand-write upgraders.
options.code:
// no change; v1 JSON keeps failing:
user :: json.decode<UserRecord>(raw) ?? panic("DecodeError")

comparisons.note: serde has no built-in versioning; versioning crates bolt it on manually.
comparisons.code:
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct UserRecord { /* one shape only; old JSON = error */ }

comparisons.note: wire-level field ids + defaults make old data readable by construction.
comparisons.code: message UserRecord { int64 id = 1; string display_name = 2; bool verified = 3; }

comparisons.note: Codable: manual init(from:) branching on version keys.
comparisons.code: init(from d: Decoder) throws { /* if v1 { … } else { … } */ }

decisions.rec: A — the authoring surface (migration verbs) and the transparency surface (decode_traced) are both ratified and shipped; A is the semantics both were designed around, keeps one decode verb (I8), and costs nothing for unversioned types.
decisions.recommendation: A — the authoring surface (migration verbs) and the transparency surface (decode_traced) are both ratified and shipped; A is the semantics both were designed around, keeps one decode verb (I8), and costs nothing for unversioned types.

decisions.title: How do the first-party core.* ring libraries reach a build — baked into the compiler, or realized like any package?
decisions.gist: Decide whether core.http, core.regex and the rest ship embedded in every jet binary, get built from source on first use, or ride the pinned toolchain as prebuilt objects.
decisions.explainer: Today the ring libraries (core.http/regex/crypto/db/archive/log/reactive) are compiled into the jet binary via bridge templates; the hangar-realization seam (is_ring_module_staged) exists but always returns false. The card's second facet — 'ships ring packages' — is the question of whether that changes. It interacts hard with U30 toolchain pinning: if ring libs travel with the pinned toolchain object, the stdlib version equals the compiler version by construction, and there is never a Rust build or a network hit on a user's machine to use core.http.
decisions.story: Marion, a data analyst on a locked-down laptop with no internet and no Rust toolchain, clones a teammate's repo that uses core.http and core.encoding.json. She types `jet run .`. Whatever we pick decides whether that just works, downloads something first, or tries to compile a Rust crate she can't build.
decisions.detail: The four models differ on: (1) does a beginner's first offline run of a repo using a ring lib succeed with no toolchain; (2) is the stdlib version coherent with the pinned compiler or a separate matrix; (3) binary size; (4) whether there is one realization path or two. Ranking is on beginner offline experience, version coherence, one-path, and long-term correctness.

options.name: Embedded in the compiler only (status quo)
options.detail: Ring libs stay baked into every jet binary via bridge templates. Always offline, no realization, but the stdlib version is rigidly the compiler version, the binary grows with every ring lib, and 'ship ring packages' — the card's second facet — is declared out of scope.
options.code:
$ jet run .          # offline, fresh laptop
reportgen: running (core.http, core.encoding.json linked from compiler)
# works — but core.http can only ever be the version baked into this jet binary,
# and the binary carries every ring lib whether the project uses it or not.

options.name: Realized source packages, built on first use
options.detail: Ring libs live as core.* source packages in a first-party channel and realize from source into the hangar on first use, like any dependency — including a Rust build for their FFI bridges. Independently versioned. Trades the offline-first-run magic for decoupling.
options.code:
$ jet run .          # offline, fresh laptop, no Rust toolchain
error[E1239]: core.http needs a build toolchain that isn't available
  why: ring libraries realize from source on first use; this machine has no
       realized Rust toolchain and no Nix
  fix: run online once to cache the prebuilt object, or install the toolchain

options.name: Hybrid — prebuilt ring objects ride the toolchain, embedded fallback (recommended)
options.detail: The pinned jet toolchain object (D-JPK-TOOLCHAIN1) carries prebuilt per-platform ring artifacts; realizing the toolchain stages them into the hangar, offline forever (D-JPK-OFFLINE1). is_ring_module_staged flips true when present; the compiler-embedded templates remain the zero-config fallback for a freshly-built dev compiler. Ring version equals toolchain version by construction. One resolution path, two sources, no user-visible difference.
options.code:
$ jet run .          # offline, fresh laptop
reportgen: pins toolchain 0.4 -> realizing jet 0.4.2 (+ core.* prebuilt) ... done
reportgen: running
# core.http is exactly the 0.4 stdlib, staged beside the toolchain, no Rust build,
# no network after the toolchain is realized; a dev-built jet with no toolchain
# object silently uses the embedded template instead.

options.name: Independently-versioned realized packages
options.detail: Ring libs are realized packages with their own version line, decoupled from the compiler (deps: { core.http: "2.1" }). Maximum flexibility, but reintroduces a compiler/stdlib version matrix and a skew failure mode Jet has otherwise avoided.

comparisons.note: The standard library ships inside the toolchain SDK — pin the Go version, get exactly that stdlib, offline. Model C mirrors this.
comparisons.code:
// go.mod
go 1.22   // net/http is whatever 1.22 shipped, no separate version

comparisons.note: std ships with the rustc toolchain (channel-locked); crates.io libs are separate and independently versioned — a blend of C (for std) and D (for the ecosystem).
comparisons.code:
[toolchain]
channel = "1.78"   // std is 1.78's; serde is its own version

comparisons.note: The cautionary tale for A/D: the stdlib is bundled (like C) but pip packages drift, producing the exact compiler/library skew D risks.
comparisons.code: python3.12   # stdlib bundled; `pip install requests` is a separate, driftable version

decisions.rec: C — a beginner's first offline run of any repo using the stdlib succeeds with no toolchain and no network; stdlib version is coherent with the pinned compiler by construction; one realization path; the embedded fallback keeps dev builds friction-free.
decisions.recommendation: C — a beginner's first offline run of any repo using the stdlib succeeds with no toolchain and no network; stdlib version is coherent with the pinned compiler by construction; one realization path; the embedded fallback keeps dev builds friction-free.

decisions.title: When jetpack builds a dependency that wraps a Rust/C crate from source, what toolchain compiles it — and is it pinned?
decisions.gist: Pick whether an extern-rust bridge dependency is compiled by a pinned, realized build toolchain (reproducible) or by whatever cargo/rustc happens to be on the host.
decisions.explainer: D-BFS1 says crate-backed capabilities ship as Jet packages wrapping a vendored, hash-pinned crate via `extern rust`. Building one requires a Rust compiler (and sometimes a C toolchain). The shipped code (build_rlib_from_cargo) shells out to host `cargo` — which means the output hash varies with whatever Rust the machine has, and the build simply fails on a machine with no Rust. That directly undermines D-JPK-CACHE1: content-addressed cache substitution only works if the same source produces the same output hash on every machine, which requires a pinned build toolchain.
decisions.story: Dale, a backend engineer, adds a dependency that wraps a fast Rust checksum crate. It builds on his machine. His teammate on a fresh laptop pulls the lock and expects a cache hit — but her host rustc is a different version, so the output hash differs and she rebuilds the world, or has no Rust at all and it fails.
decisions.detail: This is distinct from U30 (which pins the jet compiler) and from the native-deps stopgap (which covers C system libraries via nixpkgs). Here the question is the Rust compiler used for bridge crates. Rank on reproducibility (cache correctness depends on it), no-Nix/offline coherence, and no host-toolchain leakage.

options.name: Pinned, realized build toolchain (recommended)
options.detail: The Rust toolchain that compiles a bridge crate is itself a hash-pinned hangar object — prebuilt/substituted via D-JPK-CACHE1, or via the standing nixpkgs native-deps stopgap on Nix machines, with the D-JPK-NONIX1 honest error when neither is present. Same source + same pinned toolchain -> same output hash -> cache hits across machines. The toolchain id enters the output provenance.
options.code:
$ jet build     # any machine
  fastsum  building from source (rust 1.79.0 [pinned], hash verified)
$ jet build     # teammate
  fastsum  substituted (hash matches — same pinned toolchain built it)

options.name: Host toolchain (status quo)
options.detail: Keep shelling out to whatever cargo/rustc is on PATH. Non-reproducible: output hash varies by host toolchain, so cache substitution silently misses or mis-serves; fails outright on machines with no Rust. A warn-only lint flags the unpinned build.
options.code:
$ jet build
warning[L02xx]: fastsum built with an unpinned host toolchain (cargo 1.74)
  output hash is not portable; other machines may rebuild
# on a machine with no Rust:
error[E12xx]: fastsum needs a Rust toolchain and none is on PATH

options.name: Prebuilt-only — no local from-source Rust builds
options.detail: No machine ever compiles a bridge crate. Every crate-backed dependency must be published as a prebuilt per-platform object; a machine lacking the object gets an honest error naming the publisher path. Maximally reproducible and zero-toolchain for consumers, but blocks building your own bridge locally.
options.code:
$ jet build
error[E12xx]: no prebuilt object for fastsum on aarch64-linux
  why: this project builds bridge crates ahead of time; nothing compiles locally
  fix: `jet publish fastsum --platform aarch64-linux` from a build host

comparisons.note: Pins the whole toolchain in the derivation so a build is bit-reproducible and substitutable from cache.nixos.org — exactly A's contract.
The status-quo trap of B: `cargo build` uses whatever rustc is installed; nothing guarantees two machines produce the same artifact.
comparisons.code: $ cargo build   # output depends on the host rustc version

comparisons.note: Pins toolchains as explicit build dependencies for hermetic, cache-shareable builds — A at scale.

decisions.rec: A — cache correctness (D-JPK-CACHE1) is meaningless without a reproducible output hash, and that requires a pinned build toolchain; it also removes host-toolchain leakage and gives a clean D-JPK-NONIX1 error path.
decisions.recommendation: A — cache correctness (D-JPK-CACHE1) is meaningless without a reproducible output hash, and that requires a pinned build toolchain; it also removes host-toolchain leakage and gives a clean D-JPK-NONIX1 error path.

decisions.title: What are the exact spellings for adapter packages and build recipes? (the naming ballot D-JPK-ADAPTER1 deferred)
decisions.gist: Name the adapter constructor and the recipe builders that turn fetched bytes into a package — the surface a user types to package any repo, tarball, or binary.
decisions.explainer: D-JPK-ADAPTER1=A ratified the mechanism (adapters are Pkg values; recipes over fetched bytes; read-only probe; sandboxed build) but explicitly left the constructor and recipe spellings as a follow-up ballot. The vision doc uses Pkg.adapt(...) and Recipe.build/prebuilt/copy; nothing binds those names yet. This is the user-facing surface for the escape hatch, so it should read naturally and stay consistent with dot-construction (D-DOTCTOR1: T.{ } / .{ } are the only struct-literal spellings).
decisions.story: Ruth, a platform engineer, needs a niche CLI (`weirdctl`) that has no pkg.jet, no flake, and isn't in nixpkgs. She reaches for the adapter. Whatever we name it is the first thing she types and the thing she'll search the docs for — it has to be obvious and hard to misspell.
decisions.detail: Two names to fix: the adapter constructor and the recipe family (curated: prebuilt, copy, cargo, go, node, cmake, make; expert: the fn(BuildContext) form). Rank on consistency with the one ratified construction mechanism (D-DOTCTOR1 dot-construction), one-path (I8), beginner learnability, and how naturally it reads at a call site.

options.name: Pkg.adapt(...) + Recipe.* (recommended — the shipped-vision spelling)
options.detail: Adapter is a named constructor on Pkg; recipes are a Recipe family. Verb-shaped (adapt, build, copy) reads as an action; consistent with core.* dot paths and dot-construction. `jet add <ref> --adapt` drafts one.
options.code:
packages: [ Pkg.adapt(name: "weirdctl", source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, recipe: Recipe.cargo) ]

// typo:
packages: [ Pkg.adap(name: ...) ]
error[E12xx]: no constructor `Pkg.adap`
  fix: did you mean `Pkg.adapt`? (packages an external source with a recipe)

options.name: Adapter.{ ... } record + Recipe.*
options.detail: Adapter is a dot-construction record literal (maximally consistent with D-DOTCTOR1 — it looks exactly like every other Jet value). Recipe family unchanged. Reads as data rather than an action.
options.code:
packages: [ Adapter.{ name: "weirdctl", source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, recipe: Recipe.cargo } ]

// typo:
packages: [ Adaptor.{ ... } ]
error[E12xx]: unknown type `Adaptor`
  fix: did you mean `Adapter`? (a package built from an external source)

options.name: Bare adapt(...) function + recipe.*
options.detail: A free function, no namespace prefix — shortest to type. Costs the discoverability that a Pkg./Recipe. prefix gives (no completion anchor) and reads less clearly next to typed package values.
options.code: packages: [ adapt(name: "weirdctl", source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, recipe: recipe.cargo) ]

options.name: Pkg.from(...) + Build.*
options.detail: Frames it as 'a package from a source' with a Build.* recipe family. 'from' is gentle but vague (from what? already implied by source:); 'Build' collides conceptually with fn build / D-BUILDSCOPE1.
options.code: packages: [ Pkg.from(source: github@acme/weirdctl#8a31c9d, build: Build.cmake) ]

comparisons.note: The adapter equivalents are named by builder function — stdenv.mkDerivation, buildRustPackage, buildGoModule. Verb-ish builder names, like Recipe.cargo/go.
A formula is a class with a declarative body and a verb-y `install do ... end` block — mirrors Pkg.adapt + Recipe.build(fn).
comparisons.code:
class Weirdctl < Formula
  def install; system "cmake", "."; end
end

comparisons.note: Rules are verb-shaped functions (rust_binary, cc_library) — reinforces that the recipe family reads best as named actions.

decisions.rec: A — Pkg.adapt reads as the action a user takes, anchors editor completion under Pkg./Recipe., stays consistent with core.* dot paths, and matches the ratified vision so no fixtures need re-spelling; the Recipe.* family names each build strategy as a verb the way Nix/Bazel builders do.
decisions.recommendation: A — Pkg.adapt reads as the action a user takes, anchors editor completion under Pkg./Recipe., stays consistent with core.* dot paths, and matches the ratified vision so no fixtures need re-spelling; the Recipe.* family names each build strategy as a verb the way Nix/Bazel builders do.

decisions.title: Python binder depth: how deep does `use py.<lib>` reach into CPython?
decisions.gist: The D-FFI-UNIFY1 frame is law; this picks Python's binder strategy behind it. Python's ecosystem is C-extension-heavy (numpy, torch), so the binder must reach real CPython. Choose the host model: crash-isolated sidecar broker, in-process libpython embed, Python-on-WASM, or a shallow script shim.
decisions.explainer: The owner's bar (card #180) is tapping any ecosystem immediately. Python is the biggest prize and the hardest: its value lives in native C-extension packages, so a pure reimplementation or a WASM-only path forfeits most of the ecosystem. Two real hosts remain: an in-process libpython embed (zero-copy on buffer-protocol arrays, but a buggy native extension can take the whole process down and the GIL must be managed) and a supervised sidecar worker (a crashing extension dies with the worker, honest #(Proc)-style effect, but values marshal across a process boundary — no zero-copy of large tensors). Under I1, crash containment argues for the broker as the safe default; the embed is the expert performance tier for hot numeric paths, mirroring how D-PLUGIN1 made the WASM sandbox the default and native the opt-in. One `use py.X` surface either way; the host tier never moves call sites. Adds a `#(Py)` effect to the D-EFF4 set (owner-visible).
decisions.story: Doris is building a lab-data tool. The only mature reader for her instrument's file format is a Python package, and numpy is her numeric stack. She wants both working this afternoon behind an ordinary typed Jet API with honest effects — and she does not want a segfault in someone's C extension to take down her whole program.
decisions.detail: All options honor D-FFI-UNIFY1: `<lang>.<lib>` namespace, three tiers, `jet bind py` emitting inspectable `.jet/bindings/py/<lib>.jet`, safe wrappers by construction, `#Unsafe` only to reach a raw symbol outside a binding. The choice is only the host/depth. Marshalling law (all options): scalars<->Int/Float/Bool, str<->String, bytes/buffer-protocol arrays<->[T] or zero-copy View<T> in embed / copied in broker, dict<->struct or Map, list/tuple<->[T], None<->optional, Python exception->Jet Result + E-code (never a raw traceback). Async: asyncio coroutine -> Jet async task. Distribution: PyPI ref pinned in pkg.jet, wheel fetched + vendored + hash-pinned (D-DEP1); the CPython interpreter/libpython is a native runtime dep provisioned by jetpack/nixpkgs (ballot D-DEP-PY1). I1/I2/I4 hold in every option.

options.name: Sidecar-broker default + opt-in embed tier (recommended)
options.detail: The default host is a supervised CPython worker process (reuse the jetpack `services` supervision seam) with a typed message boundary — a crashing native extension takes down the worker, not your program, and the compiler restarts it. `#(Py)` effect on every call. An opt-in `py@embed` (dep flag or `#Embed` marker on the import) switches to in-process libpython for zero-copy on buffer-protocol arrays, for hot numeric paths. One `use py.X` surface; the tier is a distribution/perf choice, never a call-site change. Mirrors D-PLUGIN1's sandbox-default / native-opt-in shape.

options.name: Sidecar broker only
options.detail: Every py.* call marshals to a supervised worker; no in-process path ever. Maximum crash isolation and the simplest safety story; large arrays always copy across the process boundary, so a tensor-heavy inner loop pays a serialization cost with no escape hatch.

options.name: In-process libpython embed only
options.detail: Every py.* call runs in-process against linked libpython, GIL-scoped, zero-copy on buffer-protocol types. Fastest and simplest to reason about for numeric code; a faulty native extension segfaults the host process (weaker isolation), which sits uneasily with I1's crash-containment posture as an unconditional default.

options.name: Python-on-WASM sandbox
options.detail: Run CPython compiled to WASM (Pyodide/CPython-wasi) on the already-approved wasmtime runtime. Fully sandboxed and I1-clean by construction, and reuses the #5 runtime — but the C-extension long tail (arbitrary wheels, native torch) does not run under it, so it forfeits the exact packages that make Python worth calling. Right as a niche isolation tier, wrong as the reach story.
options.code: use py.pure_python_lib as p        // sandboxed; native wheels unavailable

options.name: Subprocess script shim (shallow)
options.detail: `jet bind py` emits thin declarations that shell out to `python -c`/script invocations per call. Trivial to stand up; no persistent interpreter, so state does not carry between calls, everything re-imports each time, and rich values degrade to stringly-typed exchange. Below the frame's typed-surface bar.
options.code: use py.h5instrument as h5          // each call = a fresh python process

comparisons.note: Imports any Python module day one via an in-process CPython embed — the reach bar to match. Mojo accepts the embed's coupling; Jet's I1 posture pushes the safe default toward isolation with embed as the opt-in.
comparisons.code:
from python import Python
let np = Python.import_module("numpy")

comparisons.note: In-process libpython with GIL tokens and typed conversions — the mechanism the embed tier wraps. Shows zero-copy buffer-protocol bridging is a solved shape.
Out-of-process typed boundary with supervision — the broker model. Proven isolation; the cost is marshaling, which is why large-array paths want the embed escape hatch.

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: JS/npm binder depth: two hosts (browser + native), one `use js.<lib>` surface
decisions.gist: JS is unique: the web target already has a JS engine (the browser), but a native Jet CLI/server has none. Pick how npm is mounted on each host, and reconcile the `jet bind js` binder with D-NPMTYPE1's hand-authored-stub floor.
decisions.explainer: On the web target (D-WEBBACKEND1=A) the browser is the JS engine, boundary types are fixed by D-JSBIND1=A, the WASM triple by D-WEBKIND1=A, the partition by D-WASM1=A — so `use js.plotly` there is a solved binding into the browser JS host. The open question is native targets: to let a native binary call an npm package there is no ambient JS engine, so JS must be mounted as a WASM component on the already-approved wasmtime runtime (D-DEP-WASM1=A, the #5 substrate) via a QuickJS/componentize-js interpreter — sandboxed, I1-clean, and zero new runtime dependency. Recommended is one `use js.X` surface whose host is chosen by the compile target. Second, the depth ballot must reconcile D-NPMTYPE1=A (typed npm surfaces are first-party hand-authored Jet stubs, no .d.ts parsing) with the frame's `jet bind js` binder: the recommendation is that `jet bind js` generates a committable, Jet-checked stub from the package's .d.ts (inspectable binder output, not runtime .d.ts semantics), which supersedes D-NPMTYPE1's hand-authored-only floor — this is what tapping all npm immediately requires. Long-tail packages with no .d.ts fall back to a #Unsafe-gated dynamic Any surface.
decisions.story: Priya writes a dashboard. In the browser her chart view calls plotly.js; on the server her CLI wants lodash and a markdown npm package. She wants the same `use js.<lib>` line to work in both places, typed, without hand-writing a stub for every package she touches.
decisions.detail: Honors D-FFI-UNIFY1 (namespace, three tiers, `jet bind js` -> `.jet/bindings/js/<lib>.jet`, safe wrappers, `#Unsafe` for raw). Marshalling is governed by D-JSBIND1=A on BOTH hosts: number<->Int/Float, string<->String, array<->[T], object<->Codable struct or Map; JS throw -> Jet Result + E-code; JS Promise <-> Jet async (`await js.fn(...)`); a Jet closure crosses as a JS callback only via the explicit wrap D-JSBIND1 requires. Distribution: npm ref in pkg.jet, fetched from the npm registry, vendored + hash-pinned (D-DEP1); the JS-on-wasm runtime is the already-approved wasmtime (no new I6 dep); registry-provider policy rides D-JPK-EXTPROV1. Sequencing honors D-JSWIFTFFI1=A (JS first). The D-NPMTYPE1 reconciliation is the one place this ballot amends a prior ratification and must be stated in the outcome.

options.name: Target-dispatched host (browser + JS-on-wasm) with generated stubs (recommended)
options.detail: `use js.X` binds on both hosts: on the web target it wires into the browser JS engine (D-WEBBACKEND1); on native targets it runs the package inside a QuickJS/componentize-js WASM component on the existing wasmtime runtime — sandboxed, no new runtime dep. `jet bind js` generates a committable typed stub from the package's .d.ts (superseding D-NPMTYPE1's hand-authored floor); no-.d.ts packages get a #Unsafe-gated dynamic Any fallback. A Node-subprocess broker is an opt-in tier for packages needing full Node APIs or native addons.
options.code:
$ jet bind js: plotly.js@2
  -> .jet/bindings/js/plotly.jet (from plotly.d.ts, 118 typed fns)

use js.plotly as plot      // browser on web target
use js.lodash as _          // JS-on-wasm on native target, same line

// long-tail, no .d.ts:
use js.obscure_pkg as ob    // error unless wrapped:
#Unsafe("untyped npm package") { ob.frobnicate(x) }

options.name: Web-target-only binding
options.detail: `use js.X` is valid only inside web-target modules; the browser is the sole JS host. Smallest surface and rides D-WEBBACKEND1 directly. A native CLI or server can never call an npm package, so the entire server-side npm ecosystem stays out of reach.

options.name: In-process V8/Node embed for native
options.detail: Native targets embed a full V8/Node engine in-process. Fastest native JS and full Node API coverage; pulls a large in-process engine as a new runtime dependency separate from the approved wasmtime, and an in-process engine is a weaker isolation boundary than the sandbox for untrusted npm code.
options.code: use js.lodash as _         // in-process V8 in the native binary

options.name: Node subprocess broker for native
options.detail: Native targets spawn a supervised `node` worker and marshal JSON; the browser still hosts the web target. Full Node ecosystem including native addons, process-isolated; requires a node install present, marshals every value (no zero-copy), and grows a process tree in production binaries. Best kept as the opt-in tier under A rather than the default.
options.code: use js.sharp as sharp      // supervised node worker, marshaled

comparisons.note: Compiles logic to WASM and generates JS bindings for the browser host — the web-host half of A, and the pattern D-WEBBACKEND1 already adopted.
Runs JS as a WASM component on wasmtime — the native-host half of A, reusing the #5 runtime with no new dependency and full sandbox isolation.
comparisons.code: // npm package -> wasm component -> loaded by the same PluginHost

comparisons.note: Embed V8 in-process (option C) for a full Node-compatible runtime — great API coverage, but a heavy in-process engine and a weaker boundary for untrusted code.
comparisons.code: // V8 embedded in the host process

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: Swift binder depth over the fixed C-ABI seam
decisions.gist: D-JSWIFTFFI1=A already fixed the transport (Swift via the stable C-ABI, since Swift's own ABI is unstable). This picks how much typed projection sits on top: shallow hand-exported C-ABI, a swift-bridge-style generated bridge, or a full Clang-importer projection.
decisions.explainer: The Swift use case (card #122) is calling platform framework libraries — Foundation, AppKit, networking — from a native macOS/iOS Jet app, so the real Swift runtime and its frameworks are required; a WASM path forfeits the frameworks and is out. D-JSWIFTFFI1=A fixed the transport at the C-ABI (@_cdecl is Swift's only stable cross-language seam). The remaining choice is projection depth. Shallow means the user (or a hand-written shim) marks each Swift function @_cdecl and Jet binds the resulting C ABI via the existing S59 C binder — real but low-level, no classes/generics/String ergonomics. A swift-bridge-style generated bridge runs swiftc from a bridge description to auto-emit the @_cdecl shims and generate typed Jet wrappers: classes/actors become opaque ref-counted handles, String/Array/Optional/throws/async marshal, and it feels native while the C-ABI stays the stable transport underneath. Full Clang-importer projection of .swiftinterface is the aspirational ceiling but a moving target against Swift's evolving module format. Recommended is the generated bridge: it delivers the frame's 'feels native for static languages' depth without reopening D-JSWIFTFFI1's C-ABI transport.
decisions.story: Marco is writing a macOS menubar app in Jet. He wants to call Alamofire for networking and a Foundation date formatter without hand-writing a C shim for every function, and without a NSObject handle leaking or a Swift `throws` turning into a crash.
decisions.detail: Honors D-FFI-UNIFY1 (swift.<lib> namespace, three tiers, `jet bind swift` -> `.jet/bindings/swift/<lib>.jet`, safe wrappers, `#Unsafe` for raw pointers) and D-JSWIFTFFI1=A (C-ABI transport, sequenced after JS + the native backend). Marshalling: Swift String<->String (UTF-8), Array<T><->[T], Optional<->optional, structs by-value, classes/actors as opaque ref-counted handles (retain/release compiler-vetted, I1), throws->Result, async->Jet async via @_cdecl continuation shims; no raw pointer crosses outside #Unsafe. Distribution: SwiftPM/git ref pinned in pkg.jet, vendored + hash-pinned (D-DEP1); swiftc is a build-time native toolchain (like cc for S59), provisioned via jetpack/nixpkgs/Xcode, not an I6 compiler dep; registry fetch rides D-JPK-EXTPROV1. Platform-gated: macOS/iOS + Linux-Swift only; elsewhere `use swift.X` is an honest gated E-code. swiftc/linker errors laundered to Jet E-codes (I2/I4).

options.name: swift-bridge-style generated projection over the C-ABI (recommended)
options.detail: `jet bind swift` runs swiftc to emit @_cdecl shims for the declared surface, compiles them to a static lib, and generates typed Jet wrappers reusing the S59 C-binding lowering. Classes/actors become opaque ref-counted handles, String/Array/Optional/throws/async all marshal. The C-ABI stays the stable transport underneath (honoring D-JSWIFTFFI1); the projection is the depth. Feels native without hand-written shims.
options.code:
$ jet bind swift: Alamofire@5.8
  -> generates @_cdecl shims + .jet/bindings/swift/Alamofire.jet

use swift.Alamofire as af
let r = af.request(url).await   // handle, async, error all projected

options.name: Hand-exported C-ABI only (shallow)
options.detail: The user marks Swift functions @_cdecl themselves (or wraps a library in a hand-written C-compatible shim) and Jet binds the resulting C header via the existing S59 C binder. No new binder machinery. But every function needs a hand-written export, classes/generics/String ergonomics do not come across, and wrapping a real framework is a wall of manual shims — the opposite of the frame's near-trivial bar.

options.name: Full Clang-importer projection of .swiftinterface
options.detail: Parse .swiftinterface/.swiftmodule and project whole Swift modules into typed Jet, the way Swift's own Clang importer projects C — the deepest 'feels native' ceiling and the right static-language end-state. Swift's module format and ABI instability make it a moving target that would chase every toolchain release; better as an aspirational upgrade on top of A than the first landing.
options.code: use swift.Alamofire as af   // whole module projected, no bridge description

options.name: Swift-to-WASM component
options.detail: Compile Swift with the swiftwasm toolchain to a WASM component on wasmtime (reuse #5). Sandboxed and I1-clean — but swiftwasm loses the platform frameworks (AppKit/Foundation/UIKit), which are the entire reason for Swift interop. Wrong for the native-app use case.
options.code: use swift.PureSwiftLib as p  // frameworks unavailable

comparisons.note: Generates @_cdecl shims + typed Rust wrappers from a bridge description over the C-ABI — exactly option A's mechanism, proven in production.
Full typed projection of C/ObjC modules so foreign APIs feel native — the ceiling option C aims at, and why A keeps C as the transport it can later deepen onto.
comparisons.code: import Accelerate   // C library arrives as typed Swift

comparisons.note: Generates typed bindings from a def file over the C-ABI for Apple frameworks — the same generated-bridge-over-C-ABI shape as A, for the same platform-framework reason.

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: Approve a CPython runtime dependency for the Python binder
decisions.gist: The Python binder needs a real CPython interpreter — libpython linked in-process (embed tier) and/or a CPython executable for the sidecar worker. That is a new runtime-side external dependency, an I6 owner decision, exactly parallel to D-DEP-WASM1 for wasmtime.
decisions.explainer: I6 keeps the compiler (Source/) zero-external-crate forever and requires owner approval for any new stdlib/runtime external dependency. D-FFI-PY1's reach depends on real CPython: the sidecar broker needs a CPython executable present, and the embed tier links libpython. This is runtime-side only — never in Source/ — mirroring how D-DEP-WASM1=A approved wasmtime for plugins. The dependency is provisioned per the ratified native-deps policy (nixpkgs interim, jetpack core provider long-term), carries a native-ize obligation (the frozen end-state), and is hash-pinned in .jet/lock. Without this approval the Python binder cannot ship at any depth except the WASM-sandbox tier (which forfeits the C-extension ecosystem).
decisions.story: The build needs numpy to actually run. That means a CPython the compiler can drive — linked or spawned. Before any code assumes libpython is on the link line, the owner decides whether Jet takes that runtime dependency and how it is provisioned.
decisions.detail: Runtime-side only (I6 holds — never in Source/). Provisioning follows the ratified native-deps policy: nixpkgs where the user has Nix, jetpack core provider long-term, with a clear message on machines lacking both. Native-ize obligation recorded (parallel to D-DEP-WASM1's frozen own-runtime end-state). Hash-pinned in .jet/lock (D-DEP1). Only pulled in when a project actually uses py.* — a pure-Jet project never acquires it.

options.name: Approve CPython runtime dep (libpython embed + broker interpreter), provisioned via nixpkgs/jetpack (recommended)
options.detail: Sanction CPython as a runtime-side dependency for the Python binder: libpython on the link line for the embed tier, a CPython executable for the sidecar worker. Never in Source/ (I6 holds). Provisioned by nixpkgs (interim) / jetpack core provider (long-term); hash-pinned; native-ize obligation recorded; acquired only when a project uses py.*. This is the D-DEP-WASM1 precedent applied to Python and unblocks D-FFI-PY1 at full depth.
options.code:
deps: { numpy: py@">=1.26" }   // pulls the approved CPython runtime
// pure-Jet projects never acquire it

options.name: Broker interpreter only (no libpython linkage)
options.detail: Approve only a CPython executable for the sidecar worker; never link libpython. Keeps the dependency at arm's length (out-of-process only) and avoids in-process linkage entirely; forecloses the zero-copy embed tier of D-FFI-PY1, so large-array numeric paths always marshal.
options.code: deps: { numpy: py@">=1.26" }   // worker process only; no embed tier

options.name: No CPython dep — WASM-sandbox Python only
options.detail: Decline the CPython runtime dependency; the Python binder is limited to the Python-on-WASM tier on the existing wasmtime. No new dep at all, fully sandboxed — but the native C-extension ecosystem (numpy/scipy/torch) does not run, gutting the reason to call Python.
options.code: use py.pure_python_lib as p    // native wheels unavailable

comparisons.note: The exact precedent: a runtime-side external dep approved for a capability (plugins), never in Source/, hash-pinned, native-ize obligation. Option A is the same shape for Python.
comparisons.code: // wasmtime approved runtime-side for target: plugin

comparisons.note: Both bundle or link a CPython to reach the ecosystem — the accepted cost of real Python interop.
comparisons.code: // libpython embedded in the distributed binary

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: npm / PyPI / SwiftPM as jetpack registry providers
decisions.gist: `use js.lodash` / `use py.numpy` / `use swift.Alamofire` must fetch from foreign registries. This decides whether jetpack gains npm/PyPI/SwiftPM providers (like the Nix bridge U16), and the network/trust/vendoring policy for them.
decisions.explainer: The FFI binders are only 'trivial' if the dependency is fetched as easily as a Jet package. That means jetpack reaching npm, PyPI, and SwiftPM registries. D-DEP1 already fixes the mechanics (fetch -> vendor -> hash-pin -> lock), and U16 already set the precedent of jetpack consuming a foreign ecosystem (Nix). What is an owner call is the policy: do foreign registries become first-class providers resolved by `<lib>: <lang>@"ref"` in pkg.jet, and how do they obey the ratified jetpack laws — U29 offline guarantee (no network when the lock is satisfied, `--offline` makes any fetch a loud error), U21 channels (a floating `@latest` npm ref resolves only during update, never in CI), U28 no-daemon, and trust/provenance on fetched artifacts. Recommended: first-class providers under the existing provider seam, every foreign artifact vendored + hash-pinned into the hangar exactly like a Jet package, subject to the same offline/lock/trust laws. This is one gate shared by all three per-language ballots' distribution stories.
decisions.story: Doris types `use js.plotly`, `use py.h5instrument`, `use swift.Alamofire` and expects `jet build` to fetch each from its home registry, lock it exactly, and rebuild offline forever after — the same contract she gets from a Jet package.
decisions.detail: Extends D-DEP1 (vendor + hash-pin every language's refs) and the U16 foreign-ecosystem-provider precedent. Must obey the ratified jetpack laws: U29 (offline/lock), U21 (channel refs resolve only on update, exact in lock, unlocked ref in CI = error), U28 (no daemon), U24 (provenance envelope on fetched objects), U23 (honest message on machines that cannot reach a registry). Foreign artifacts land in the hangar like Jet objects and GC per U22. Trust: fetched artifacts are hash-verified on arrival; a registry compromise cannot alter a locked build.

options.name: First-class npm/PyPI/SwiftPM providers under the jetpack provider seam (recommended)
options.detail: Each foreign registry is a provider resolved by `<lib>: <lang>@"ref"`, fetching into the hangar, vendored + hash-pinned to .jet/lock, obeying every ratified jetpack law (U29 offline, U21 channels, U28 no-daemon, U24 provenance, U23 honest fallback). Foreign artifacts are hash-verified on arrival so a registry compromise cannot alter a locked build. One uniform distribution story across all three binders.
options.code:
deps: { lodash: js@"lodash@4", numpy: py@">=1.26" }
// resolved by the npm / pypi providers; locked exactly; offline-safe after

options.name: Manifest-declared registry endpoints only (no built-in providers)
options.detail: No first-party providers; the user declares each foreign registry endpoint and credentials in pkg.jet and jetpack fetches generically. Maximum control for private registries; every project re-specifies boilerplate and there is no curated default, so `use js.lodash` does not just work out of the box.
options.code:
registries: { npm: "https://registry.npmjs.org", pypi: "https://pypi.org/simple" }
deps: { lodash: js@"lodash@4" }

options.name: Vendor-only, no live registry fetch
options.detail: jetpack never contacts a foreign registry; users vendor foreign packages into the repo by hand (or via an external tool) and jetpack only hash-pins what is already present. Strongest supply-chain posture and zero network policy to design; but it forfeits the 'trivial to use any library' bar — adding a package is a manual vendoring chore.
options.code: // user vendors node_modules / wheels by hand; jetpack only locks them

comparisons.note: Already-ratified precedent: jetpack consumes a foreign ecosystem as a provider with honest gating. Option A applies the same model to npm/PyPI/SwiftPM.
comparisons.code: jet run nixpkgs@tool   // foreign provider, gated, locked

comparisons.note: Fetch npm/PyPI into a hermetic, hash-locked store obeying an offline/repro contract — the shape of option A under Jet's U29/U21 laws.

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: How a `plugin` target declares its exported surface
decisions.gist: D-PLUGIN1=B + D-DEP-WASM1=A settled the substrate (sandboxed WASM Component Model). This picks how a plugin package declares which entry points the host may call — the .wit surface generation. Deferred at ratification as Owner Q1.
decisions.explainer: A plugin builds a typed Component Model .wit contract; the open question is what in the plugin's source or manifest declares that contract. A new in-source #Plugin marker joins the #Test/#Bench family and lets each export tag its role explicitly, at the cost of a new keyword (I7 entry). A manifest-level declaration reuses the existing target `entry:`/`export:` fields (D-TGT3/4) with no new syntax. A pure-convention rule takes all `pub` items in the entry module as the ABI, frozen like `api: stable` (D-CAP4) — no new surface at all, reusing the capability-freeze machinery Jet already has. Recommended: the convention path (pub surface = the contract, frozen via the existing api: freeze), optionally named by a manifest `export:` field, which avoids a new keyword while giving the host a stable, inspectable .wit. Whichever wins needs a decision ID + Syntax.rs I7 entry.
decisions.story: Sam ships a plugin package. He wants to say 'these functions are the plugin API' once, have the host see a typed contract, and get a clean error if he accidentally breaks it — without learning a new keyword if he does not have to.
decisions.inWild:
// a plugin package today: target: plugin, but no way to name its exports
// this decides the spelling that generates the .wit the host binds
decisions.detail: Substrate is fixed (D-PLUGIN1=B sandboxed WASM, D-DEP-WASM1=A wasmtime + Component Model, safe by default, no #Unsafe gate). This ballot is surface-only; it generates the typed .wit the PluginHost loads. Needs a decision ID + I7 entry in Syntax.rs and a formatter round-trip + fmt STABILITY test if it adds syntax. Pairs with D-PLUGIN-VERSION1 (the version handshake on the resulting contract).

options.name: Convention: `pub` entry-module surface, frozen via `api: stable`, named by a manifest `export:` (recommended)
options.detail: All `pub` items in the plugin's entry module are the exported ABI; the manifest `export:` field names the entry module; the surface is frozen with the existing D-CAP4 `api: stable` machinery so a breaking change is a diagnostic, not a silent ABI break. No new in-source keyword. The .wit is generated from the pub signatures. Reuses machinery Jet already has (I8).

options.name: New in-source `#Plugin { … }` marker
options.detail: A `#Plugin { export fn transform(...) ... }` block (joining #Test/#Bench) lists exports explicitly and can tag each export's role. Most explicit and self-documenting in-source; adds a new keyword and I7 entry, and a second place (besides `pub`) that means 'public', which brushes against I8.

options.name: Manifest-only `entry:`/`export:` list
options.detail: The plugin target block in pkg.jet names the exported functions/module directly, reusing D-TGT3/4 target fields; source stays unannotated. No new in-source syntax; the export list lives away from the code it describes, so drift between manifest and source is possible and the freeze/versioning must be manifest-driven.
options.code: target: plugin { entry: src/api.jet, export: [transform, reset] }

comparisons.note: The export set is exactly a .wit `world` — every option here is a spelling that generates that world; A derives it from pub signatures.
comparisons.code: world plugin { export transform: func(input: frame) -> frame; }

comparisons.note: Native plugins mark each export explicitly (option B's spirit). Component Model lets Jet derive the surface instead, which is why the convention path (A) is viable.

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: Plugin load-time version / ABI compatibility handshake
decisions.gist: How the host detects an incompatible plugin at load and rejects it with a clean diagnostic (I2) instead of a crash. Deferred at D-PLUGIN1 ratification alongside the export surface.
decisions.explainer: A host loading a plugin built against a different contract must fail cleanly, never crash (I2 — the loader never speaks raw to users). Three shapes: a per-build ABI hash (exact-match, simplest, but any rebuild of either side breaks compatibility even when the interface is unchanged); a declared semver compatibility range on the plugin interface (flexible, familiar, but relies on authors versioning honestly); or reuse of the D-CAP4 `api: stable` capability-signature freeze as the frozen .wit interface contract, so compatibility is structural — the host checks the plugin's interface signature against what it expects. Recommended: the D-CAP4 freeze reused as the .wit contract signature (structural compatibility), because it makes 'compatible' mean 'same typed interface' rather than 'same build', and it reuses machinery Jet already ships. Mismatch is an E-code with the expected-vs-found interface, snapshot-tested.
decisions.story: A host app ships v2 and loads a plugin built for v1's interface. Instead of a segfault deep in wasmtime, the user sees a Jet error naming the interface that changed and how to rebuild the plugin.
decisions.inWild:
$ myapp --load ./plugins/old.wasm
error[E12xx]: plugin `old` was built for interface `plugin_api@1`,
  host expects `plugin_api@2`
  fix: rebuild the plugin against this host, or install a v2 build
decisions.detail: The handshake runs against the typed Component Model .wit contract from D-PLUGIN-EXPORT1. Mismatch must be a Jet diagnostic with an E-code + tests/ui snapshot (I2/I4), never a loader crash. Substrate fixed by D-PLUGIN1=B/D-DEP-WASM1=A.

options.name: Reuse D-CAP4 `api: stable` freeze as the frozen .wit interface signature — structural compatibility (recommended)
options.detail: The plugin's exported interface carries the D-CAP4 capability-signature freeze; the host checks the plugin's interface signature against the one it was built to expect. 'Compatible' means 'same typed interface', not 'same build' — a plugin rebuilt with an unchanged interface still loads. Reuses machinery Jet already ships (I8); mismatch is a clean E-code naming the interface delta.
options.code:
target: plugin { export: plugin_api, api: stable }
// host records the frozen signature of plugin_api; load checks it structurally

options.name: Declared semver compatibility range
options.detail: The plugin declares an interface version; the host declares the range it accepts; load checks the range. Familiar and flexible across many plugin builds. Correctness rests on authors bumping the version honestly — a silent breaking change under an unchanged version still crashes.
options.code:
target: plugin { interface_version: "1.2" }
// host: accepts plugins matching ^1.0

options.name: Per-build ABI hash (exact match)
options.detail: Hash the full interface + toolchain into an ABI tag; load requires an exact match. Zero ambiguity — any incompatibility is caught. But it is maximally brittle: any rebuild of host or plugin, even with an identical interface, invalidates every existing plugin, forcing lockstep redistribution.
options.code:
// plugin embeds abi_hash = sha256(interface + toolchain)
// host loads only if the hash matches its own

comparisons.note: A component's typed .wit world IS a structural contract — the host can check interface compatibility by shape, which is exactly option A's basis.
Native dylibs have no stable ABI across compiler versions, forcing exact-build matching (option C's brittleness) — the pain the Component Model + structural check (A) avoids.
comparisons.code: // rustc version mismatch -> UB on load

decisions.recommendation: A

decisions.title: Memory model v5 — the borrow checker, humanized
decisions.gist: Owner reset (2026-07-03): keep Rust borrow-checker semantics (read-only default, exclusive writers, moves, RAII, zero-cost); fix the experience. Three sigils: bare=read (default, signatures cannot lie), &=write, ^=take — both mirrored at call sites so mutation and moves are always visible. Borrows are second-class (never stored in structs, never returned raw) so lifetime syntax cannot exist; view-shaped APIs use view VALUES (counted Str/List slices, invisible); walls get named escape hatches (Shared<T>, Pool<T>) suggested by teaching diagnostics. ~ deleted; no word spellings.
decisions.explainer: Semantics = Rust verbatim: ownership, shared-xor-mutable, move analysis, deterministic RAII, no GC, no runtime ownership machinery. The five documented Rust pains each get a targeted surface fix: (1) lifetimes — second-class borrows flow only down the stack, so every extent is compiler-obvious; nothing to annotate, nothing to learn; struct fields hold owned values / Shared / Id, never borrows (kills the struct<'a> infection); returns are owned values or library view-values that share storage internally (one Str, one List; no String/&str dualism). Precedent: Hylo second-class references; Graydon's stated preference. (2) invisible moves — every transfer is written ^ at the call site; use-after-move errors point at the ^ the user typed, with a fix menu (copy / reorder / Pool). (3) checker-voiced errors — every borrow error is a what/why/fix teaching diagnostic, I4-pinned. (4) wrapper-assembly escape hatches — Shared<T> (Arc+lock class) and Pool<T>+Id<T> (generational arena; parent pointers/graphs/observers) are named language-level types that diagnostics suggest by name. (5) call-site opacity — & required at mutating calls, so reviewers see effects (Rust's map.insert mutates markerless). Beginner rule set is one sentence: unmarked = looking, & = changing, ^ = giving away, one writer at a time. Deletes from ratified state: ~ glyph, D-CAP8 elevation/freeze + api:explicit, L0201 (heap copies are explicit `copy`), D-REF-SHORTHAND1/2 (no stored borrows to infer owners for), &-as-share (sharing is Shared<T> by name). Keeps: ^ semantics, call-site mirroring where it informs (&/^), D-MUTSELF1 receiver-on-self (&self/^self), copy verb, S63 RAII, #SingleUse resources, arenas/uninit/*T/#Unsafe, S53 posture (borrows cannot cross spawn — unrepresentable, races impossible). Experts lose exactly one Rust feature: storable/returnable raw borrows — replaced by views/Shared/Pool/arenas/raw tier; philosophy C1 already reserves first-class borrows as optional post-v1 tier 2. Implementation reality: closest of all five proposals to the existing AccessConvention Read/Mutate/Move machinery — largely a rename + feature deletion, not a rebuild. On approval, next deliverable is the staged migration path. Full write-up: docs/proposals/memory-greenfield.md.
decisions.story: A beginner reads any signature and knows the whole truth: unmarked can only be looked at, & gets changed, ^ is given away. Their first move error points at the ^ they typed themselves and offers copy/reorder/Pool by name. They never meet a lifetime because the language cannot express one.
decisions.inWild:
fn enroll(party: &Party, player: ^Player)
enroll(&party, ^kai)            // both effects visible at the call

error[E—]: kai was given away on line 1 (`^kai`)
fix: keep a copy:      party.members.push(copy kai)
     or one player referenced everywhere: Pool<Player> (jet explain pools)

fn domain(email: String) -> String { return email.split("@")[1] }   // view; no lifetimes
decisions.detail: Owner directive trail (all 2026-07-03): v1 One-Home rejected; v2 completed-sigils rejected (from-clauses, ~ frequency); v3 progressive-ceremony rejected (copies unclear, read-only-args felt wrong at first); v4 identity-model interrupted; final reset — "use the rust borrow checker system but make it much more ergonomic & beginner friendly… read-only by default… sigils not words… no ~, prefer & or ^". v5 delivers exactly that. Glyph assignment is the live sub-question (options A/B/C). After ratification: follow-on ballots for Shared<T>/Pool<T> APIs, view-value semantics in stdlib, diagnostic voice, then the migration-path plan (owner-gated deliverable #2).

decisions.title: core.fs/core.files merge: the `append` name collides
decisions.gist: Two different stdlib modules both want the method name `append`, with different meanings — merging them under `core.files` (D-FILES-WRITE1) needs one renamed.
decisions.explainer: D-FILES-WRITE1 (ratified) says `core.files` becomes the one file module and folds `core.fs` into it — but a single Rust match arm can't dispatch `(module="files", method="append")` two different ways by argument count without a form of overloading the language doesn't otherwise use (I8 risk). Both spellings already exist in the compiler today in two separate modules: `core.fs.append(path, text)` is a 2-arg whole-file convenience; `core.files`'s handle type (after `.open`/`.create`) has a 1-arg `.append(text)` streaming method. Recommendation: rename the whole-file one-shot function to `append_all`; keep `append` as the streaming-handle method (unchanged). Zero ambiguity, smallest migration, no collision with D-FILES-WRITE1's own decree that `.write` is the handle's overwrite method.
decisions.story: Walter Higgins is porting a log-rotation script to Jet. He already has whole-file code using `core.fs.append(path, "line\n")` to tack one line onto a file, and now wants to switch a long-running job to `core.files.open(path)` streaming handles for a hot loop — he expects both to live under the same module name once D-FILES-WRITE1 lands (`core.files` is decreed as THE file module).
decisions.inWild:
use core.files as fs

// Whole-file convenience — one call, opens+writes+closes:
fs.append("audit.log", "user logged in\n")

// Streaming handle — many writes, one open/close:
h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.append("user logged in\n")   // same method name, different receiver/arity
h.close()
decisions.detail: Found 2026-07-04 while implementing card cv5syntaxdecrees's decree 5 (D-FILES-WRITE1). Decrees 1-4 and 6 of that card shipped independently; this is decree 5's only blocker.

options.name: Rename whole-file convenience to `append_all` (recommended)
options.detail: `append` is always the handle method; `append_all` is always whole-file. Clean under I8, low migration cost (one stdlib fn + any examples/tests using `core.fs.append(path, text)`), reads unambiguously at a glance.
options.code:
use core.files as fs

fs.append_all("audit.log", "user logged in\n")   // one-shot, opens+writes+closes

h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.append("more\n")                                // streaming handle, unchanged
h.close()

options.name: Rename handle method, keep whole-file `append`
options.detail: Collides with D-FILES-WRITE1's own text, which already says the handle's overwrite method is `.write` — renaming the handle's append method risks a second collision, and `.write` for append reads as ambiguous (does it append or overwrite?).
options.code:
use core.files as fs

fs.append("audit.log", "user logged in\n")        // whole-file, unchanged name

h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.write("more\n")                                  // but .write already means overwrite
h.close()

options.name: Keep one name, dispatch by argument count (rejected)
options.detail: Silent overloading by arity — no precedent elsewhere in Jet, violates I8 (one way to mean it). Same name, silently different job depending on receiver/arity.
options.code:
use core.files as fs

fs.append("audit.log", "user logged in\n")   // 2-arg: whole file
h :: fs.open("audit.log")
h.append("more\n")                            // 1-arg: handle — same name, different job

comparisons.note: Whole-file convenience doesn't exist as a free function; it's OpenOptions::append(true).open(path). No collision because there's no free-function form to begin with.
Whole-file convenience is a different verb (appendFile); handle-based writes use write(). No collision because the names differ.
No whole-file one-shot append built in; open(path, "a") then write(). No collision to resolve.

decisions.title: Shared<T> construction + access API surface (S6 blocker)
decisions.gist: D-MEM1 names `Shared<T>` as the v5 escape hatch for state shared across tasks, but only the TYPE NAME is ratified — its constructor and read/write methods only exist as gallery worked examples, never balloted.
decisions.explainer: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md's D-MEM1 row lists `Shared<T>` by name as a named escape hatch. docs/proposals/memory-v5-gallery.md section 8 ("Web dev — handlers, state, tasks", explicitly marked *(Shared: proposed)* in its own header) shows a consistent worked example: `Shared.new(x)` to construct, `.read(closure)` for a read-locked closure callback, and (per an S6 investigation of D-MEM1's parent proposal doc) `.edit(closure)` for a write-locked closure callback. None of this — constructor spelling, method names, closure-callback shape vs. an alternative (e.g. a guard object with RAII unlock) — has its own ratified decision row. S6 of the memory-v5 migration (Tower card cmemgreenfield) is blocked on this.
decisions.story: Priya is porting a small web server to Jet. Every handler needs read access to shared session state, and one background task needs to mutate it. In Rust this is `Arc<Mutex<App>>` plus `.lock().unwrap()` everywhere; Jet's whole pitch is that `Shared<T>` collapses that ritual into one named concept — but the compiler can't build it until the exact method names are decided.
decisions.detail: Blocks Tower card cmemgreenfield stage S6. The type collapses Rust's `Arc<Mutex<T>>`/`Arc<RwLock<T>>` + explicit lock/unwrap/clone ritual into one CoreLib type; the read/write split matters for allowing concurrent readers.

options.name: Closure-callback API — `.read(f)` / `.edit(f)` (gallery spelling, recommended)
options.detail: Matches the gallery's own consistent worked example across its Shared section. The lock is scoped to the closure's body — impossible to forget to release it, impossible to hold it across a `spawn`/`await` boundary by accident (closures can't smuggle a guard out). `.read` takes a read-lock, allows concurrent readers; `.edit` takes a write-lock, exclusive. `Shared.new(x)` constructs (bare type-name call, no turbofish needed — inferred from `x`).

options.name: RAII guard object — `.read()` / `.write()` return a guard
options.detail: Mirrors Rust's `RwLock::read()`/`write()` directly: returns a guard value that derefs to `&T`/`&mut T` and releases the lock on scope-end (Drop). More flexible (can hold the guard across several statements) but reintroduces the exact footgun class v5's whole `&`/`^` model exists to prevent: a guard can be squirreled away, held too long, or accidentally crossed into another task, deadlocking or violating the borrow that spawned it.
options.code:
state :: Shared.new(App.new())

g :: state.read()
user :: g.sessions.get(req.token)
// g drops here, unlocking

w :: state.write()
w.sessions.insert(token, user)
// w drops here, unlocking

options.name: Single unified method, mutability inferred from body (rejected — ambiguous)
options.detail: One `.access(f)` method whose lock kind (read vs write) is inferred from whether the closure mutates — would require whole-closure-body analysis to decide locking strategy before the closure even runs, and silently changes locking behavior based on incidental code shape. No prior art does this; rejected as a design direction, shown for completeness.
options.code:
state :: Shared.new(App.new())
state.access(s => s.sessions.get(req.token))       // inferred read?
state.access(s => { s.sessions.insert(token, user) }) // inferred write?

comparisons.note: Arc<RwLock<T>> requires explicit lock()/read()/write(), .unwrap() on poison, and Arc::clone at every task-spawn boundary.
sync.RWMutex is a separate value from the data it guards — no compiler-enforced pairing, easy to forget the lock/unlock or lock the wrong mutex for a given field.
Swift's actor model serializes all access through async methods — closest existing-language analogue to a closure-scoped access API, though actors reach further (isolation domains, not just locking).
comparisons.code:
actor App { func getUser(_ token: Token) -> User? { sessions[token] } }
let user = await app.getUser(token)

decisions.title: Pool<T>/Id<T> construction + insert + access + stale-id API surface (S6 blocker)
decisions.gist: D-MEM1 names `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>` as the v5 generational-arena escape hatch, but only the TYPE NAMES are ratified — construction, insert, indexed access, iteration, and stale-id error behavior only exist as gallery worked examples, never balloted.
decisions.explainer: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md's D-MEM1 row lists `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>` by name. docs/proposals/memory-v5-gallery.md sections 6 ("one world, many entities") and 10 ("Graphs & back-references") — both explicitly marked *(Pool/Id: proposed)* in their own headers — show a consistent worked example: `Pool<T>.new()` to construct, `.add(val)` to insert (returns `Id<T>`), `pool[id]` index operator for read+write field access, `.ids()` to iterate live entries, and `Id<T>?` for optional back-references using Jet's EXISTING option syntax (no new syntax needed there). What's completely unspecified anywhere, in gallery or proposal: what happens on a STALE `Id` access (the entity was removed, the generation counter no longer matches) — panic, a checked error return, an effect-tracked fallible op? This is the actual safety mechanism a generational arena exists to provide, and it has zero spec text. S6 of the memory-v5 migration (Tower card cmemgreenfield) is blocked on this.
decisions.story: Marcus is writing a small game in Jet. Entities reference each other (a `target` field on `Player`, a `parent` field on `Node`) — the classic case Rust developers solve with `Rc<RefCell<T>>` graphs or reach for a crate like `slotmap`/`hecs` for. Jet's pitch is that `Pool<T>`/`Id<T>` is first-class and built in, no crate hunt — but the compiler can't build it until insert/access/iteration spellings are decided, and nothing has ever specified what happens when an `Id` outlives the entity it names (the whole safety point of a generational arena).
decisions.detail: Blocks Tower card cmemgreenfield stage S6. Pool<T> owns a collection of T; Id<T> is a lightweight (index + generation counter) handle into it that safely detects use of a removed/replaced slot instead of silently reading garbage or a reused slot's new occupant (the classic ABA bug plain indices have).

options.name: Gallery spelling as-is: `.new()`/`.add()`/`pool[id]`/`.ids()`, stale access is a runtime error (recommended)
options.detail: Matches all 3 gallery worked examples verbatim (sections 6, 10, plus the parent-pointer-tree section). `pool[id]` reads AND writes through the existing index-assignment machinery (already shipped, used throughout the compiler's own examples). Stale-`Id` access (generation mismatch) is a runtime panic with a clear message naming the stale-access class — matches how an out-of-bounds array index already panics in Jet today (consistent with existing runtime-bounds-check precedent, not a new error class). `.remove(id)` (not shown in gallery but necessary for a working Pool — an insert-only Pool isn't really a Pool) needs its own spelling decided here too since nothing shows it.
options.code:
world := Pool<Player>.new()
kai :: world.add(Player.{ name: "Kai", hp: 100 })
world.remove(kai)
world[kai].hp     // panics: stale Id — this entity was removed

options.name: Stale access is a checked/fallible op instead of a panic
options.detail: `world[id]` returns something checkable (`?`-chainable or an effect-tracked fallible call) instead of panicking outright, letting a long-running game loop or server recover from a stale reference instead of crashing. Diverges from existing array-index panic precedent, which is exactly why the plain index operator (`world[id]`) may not be the right spelling for this if fallibility is wanted — might need a distinct method (`.get(id)`) alongside the panicking index.

options.name: Turbofish-explicit construction: `Pool::<T>::new()` (rejected — inconsistent with rest of Jet)
options.detail: Rust-style explicit turbofish construction. Rejected for consistency: every other generic CoreLib type constructed this session (Sender<T>/Receiver<T> via tasks.channel<T>()) already uses the bare `Type<T>.new()`/`Type<T>()` dot-call convention, not Rust's `::<T>::` path syntax — a second construction convention would violate I8.
options.code: world := Pool::<Player>::new()   // inconsistent with Type<T>.new() used elsewhere

comparisons.note: SlotMap<DefaultKey, T> + world.insert(x) -> DefaultKey + world[key] indexing (panics on stale) + world.keys() iteration — the closest prior art, and the gallery's own comparison target.
Arena<T> + arena.insert(x) -> Index + arena[index] (panics on stale) + arena.remove(index) -> Option<T> — remove returns the removed value, a pattern worth considering for Pool::remove.

comparisons.lang: C# (List + generation-tagged struct, common game-dev pattern)
comparisons.note: No language-level generational handle; games hand-roll a (index, generation) struct and check generation on access, panicking or returning null on mismatch — same design space, no built-in precedent either way on panic-vs-checked.
comparisons.code:
struct EntityId { int index; int generation; }
var player = world.Get(id); // null if generation mismatch

decisions.title: policy no_alloc enforcement semantics — what counts as an allocation, local-only or interprocedural? (S7 blocker)
decisions.gist: D-MEM1 ratifies the `policy no_alloc` mechanism and names it the first policy floor, but never specifies what operations trip it or whether the check follows calls out of the module.
decisions.explainer: docs/spec/syntax-decisions.md's D-MEM1 row ratifies module `policy` floors with `no_alloc` first, and the surface syntax (`policy no_alloc` as a bare module-top item) is unambiguous and safe to parse — that part isn't in question. What's unspecified: (1) which operations count as "allocation" — String concatenation/interpolation, `[T]`/List `.push`, `Map` insert, a closure capturing by value, `copy` of a heap-owning type, a struct/enum literal with a heap-owning field — none of these are named anywhere as in-scope or out-of-scope; (2) whether the check is LOCAL (only flags allocation-shaped expressions written directly in the module's own function bodies) or INTERPROCEDURAL (walks the call graph — same pattern already used by `@Pure fn`'s effect-purity check, Sema/Effects.rs's `solve()` — and flags a call if ANY reachable callee, in this module, another module, or the stdlib, allocates). The gallery's own framing ("the module claiming embedded-grade guarantees") reads like it wants interprocedural, but that needs its own ruling on opaque/FFI/extern-rust callees (can the compiler even see whether an `extern rust` function allocates?).
decisions.story: Marcus's game has a hot per-frame `integrate` function he wants embedded-grade guarantees on — no surprise heap traffic from an innocent-looking helper call three functions deep. He writes `policy no_alloc` at the top of that module expecting the compiler to catch it. Today nothing defines what "it" catches.
decisions.detail: Blocks Tower card cmemgreenfield stage S7. Once ruled, the actual build is small: one parser item, one sema pass (reusing Effects.rs's existing call-graph/fixpoint machinery if interprocedural is chosen — proven buildable in this codebase already, just needs the ruling on whether to use it here), one diagnostic code, one example + golden.

options.name: Local-only, explicit denylist (recommended for S7's first cut)
options.detail: Flags only allocation-shaped expressions written directly in the policy'd module's own function bodies: String concat/interpolation producing a new String, List/Map insert-that-grows-capacity, a struct/enum literal for any type with a heap-owning field, an explicit `copy` of a heap type. Does NOT follow calls to other functions/modules — calling a helper that itself allocates is the CALLEE's module's problem, not flagged here. Simpler, no interprocedural-analysis edge cases (FFI/extern-rust opacity, recursive call cycles), ships faster, matches how most systems-language "no alloc in this scope" checks actually work in practice (Rust's `#[no_std]`-adjacent tooling, embedded C static-analysis checkers) — they're almost universally local/lexical, not whole-program, because whole-program alloc-freedom for arbitrary stdlib calls is a much bigger claim to make honestly.

options.name: Interprocedural, reuses Effects.rs's existing solve()
options.detail: Walks the call graph the same way `@Pure fn` already does (Sema/Effects.rs), flagging a call under `policy no_alloc` if ANY reachable callee allocates — including callees in other modules and the stdlib. Matches the gallery's "embedded-grade guarantees" framing more literally — a truly alloc-free hot loop can't call an allocating helper and not know it. Needs its own answer for opaque boundaries: does an `extern rust`/FFI call count as "unknown, assume allocates" (conservative, breaks legitimate zero-alloc FFI) or "unknown, assume doesn't" (permissive, could silently violate the claim)? Bigger build: needs the whole stdlib's alloc-shape annotated or inferred once, not per-check.

options.name: No denylist — treat ANY heap-owning type construction as the sole rule (rejected, too broad without a ruling on which types count)
