options.detail: Offer the NixOS-style baseline: build a generation, switch, and rollback. Good core, but risky classes are discovered after activation.
options.code:
$ jetos switch laptop
$ jetos rollback

options.name: Risk-aware proof pipeline (recommended)
options.detail: Plan/diff always; VM proof and rollback proof required for boot/kernel/filesystem/service-risk classes and CI policy. Weakness fixed: small edits stay light, dangerous edits get proof.
options.code:
$ jetos switch laptop
Plan: boot/kernel risk detected
Fix: run jetos test laptop --vm, or policy override with #Unsafe("reason")

options.name: GUI preview only
options.detail: Show plan and risk in Studio. Friendly, but headless CI and server admins lose the same gate.
options.code:
jetos Studio: preview boot risk
# no CLI proof artifact

comparisons.note: `test`, `build-vm`, and rollback are loved primitives.
Rollout health and rollback are expected for services.
Already models generations/hangar; jetos can add risk-aware activation.

decisions.title: Typed data Core
decisions.gist: Whether data analysis becomes a first-party Core domain.
decisions.explainer: Native typed floor plus foreign accelerators gives reach now and conquest path later.
decisions.story: June reads CSV, joins telemetry, computes stats, calls a Python model for one step, and ships a native dashboard. Jet should not require Python for the whole workflow, but should borrow Python reach while Core grows.
decisions.inWild:
use core.data
use core.stats
use py.numpy as np

fn run() -> Unit ? {
    rows :: data.csv<Row>("events.csv")?
    daily :: rows.group_by(.day).summarize(count: count(), p95: p95(.latency))
    print(daily)
}

options.name: Interop-only data
options.detail: Use Python/R/JS packages for data work. Reach is immediate, but Jet has no native data identity.
options.code:
use py.pandas as pd
fn run() { df :: pd.read_csv("events.csv") }

options.name: Core data floor plus accelerators (recommended)
options.detail: Ship typed tables/series/stats/plot basics in Core; Python/R/GPU bridges accelerate gaps. Weakness fixed: every bridge-heavy workflow exposes native replacement status.
options.code:
rows :: data.csv<Row>("events.csv")?
model :: py.sklearn.load("model.pkl")
jet migrate native --domain data

options.name: SQL-only data
options.detail: Make databases/query blocks the main data story. Strong for DBs, weak for notebooks, files, arrays, and local analysis.
options.code: #Sql<Row> { select * from events }

comparisons.note: Wins data through batteries and ecosystem, but packaging/native deps leak friction.
Strong numeric syntax/perf, smaller ecosystem than Python.
Excellent statistics workflow, less general systems/app story.

decisions.title: Game development lane
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets a blessed game-dev substrate.
decisions.explainer: Substrate plus replaceable backends gives beginner workflow and expert control.
decisions.story: Imani builds a 2D game, then an editor, then a 3D prototype. She needs assets, hot reload, ECS, fixed-step simulation, input, audio, GPU, deterministic replay, and editor hooks without giving up low-level control.

options.name: Graphics bridge only
options.detail: Bless `core.raylib`/graphics wrappers and let game architecture grow in packages. Good for samples, not a world-class game workflow.
options.code:
use core.raylib
fn run() { raylib.draw_circle(...) }

options.name: Stable game substrate (recommended)
options.detail: Core owns assets, ECS, input, fixed-step timing, replay, editor hooks, and budgets; renderer/audio/editor backends are packages. Weakness fixed: engine sprawl is avoided by making Core the substrate, not one monolithic engine.

options.name: Third-party engines only
options.detail: Let Godot/Unity/custom engines bind to Jet. Interop works, but Jet does not become the best language for game code itself.
options.code:
use c.godot
# Jet scripts foreign engine APIs

comparisons.note: Great workflow and editors; language/runtime control is not Jet-shaped.
Powerful but fragmented game ecosystem.
Attract game devs through control and simple builds; Jet can add batteries and safety.

decisions.title: Embedded and freestanding profiles
decisions.gist: How Jet scales down to microcontrollers, kernels, and no-OS targets.
decisions.explainer: One language, invisible defaults for beginners, complete target control for experts.
decisions.story: Tessa writes firmware for a sensor board. She wants no allocator, fixed memory, volatile/MMIO gates, linker script control, panic policy, and the same Jet diagnostics. Her web teammates should never see any of it.

options.name: Freestanding build flags
options.detail: Expose `jet build --freestanding --target ...` and rely on low-level code when needed. Expert path exists; product guidance is thin.
options.code: $ jet build firmware.jet --freestanding --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf

options.name: Typed target profiles (recommended)
options.detail: Board/target profiles make hidden defaults explicit only when embedded/kernels are selected. Expert controls memory, linker, allocator, panic, volatile, and audit output. Weakness fixed: normal Jet never sees target jargon.

options.name: Separate Jet dialect
options.detail: Make embedded Jet a different surface with its own defaults. It can be lean, but violates one-language identity.
options.code:
firmware.jet uses embedded-only syntax
app.jet uses normal Jet syntax

comparisons.note: Excellent target/control story.
Safe and powerful, but many crates/tool concepts surface early.
Ubiquitous control with weak safety/default tooling.

decisions.title: Proof and replay mode
decisions.gist: How Jet turns contracts, tests, budgets, and replay into a correctness product.
decisions.explainer: Progressive proof preserves beginner ergonomics and gives experts real evidence.
decisions.story: Omar ships payment code and a distributed job runner. He wants contract checks, property tests, budget enforcement, deterministic replay, and proof reports before deploy, without raw solver errors becoming the user interface.

options.name: Tests and contracts only
options.detail: Keep today's practical path: tests, contracts, and diagnostics. Useful, but proof/replay are not unified product surfaces.
options.code:
jet test
jet bench
# replay/proof separate or absent

options.name: Progressive proof and replay (recommended)
options.detail: `jet prove` layers contracts, refinements, effects, budgets, property tests, and replay facts. Weakness fixed: beginner face is tests/contracts/replay; deeper solvers are opt-in lenses with Jet diagnostics.
options.code:
$ jet prove src/payments.jet
proved: @Pre/@Post for 12 funcs
checked: 4 budgets
needs test: network timeout path

$ jet prove --lens bounds --json

options.name: Formal verification first
options.detail: Make proof obligations central before code ships. Strong guarantees, but daily Jet becomes proof-tool-shaped.
options.code:
fn charge(...) -> Receipt
proof { forall amount: Money where amount > 0 ... }

comparisons.note: Compile-time memory safety proof is a major adoption driver.
Strong verification, high ceremony.
Practical confidence with shrinking; Jet can integrate it with contracts.

decisions.title: Performance budget profiles
decisions.gist: Whether performance expectations are declared and enforced as product facts.
decisions.explainer: Budgets make performance visible without hiding expert policy knobs.
decisions.story: Mei owns a latency-sensitive HTTP service. She wants startup, allocation, binary size, p99 latency, and generated-unsafe budgets in CI, with local runs that explain what changed.

options.name: Benchmarks only
options.detail: Use `jet bench` and human review. Flexible, but regressions are easy to miss or debate.
options.code:
$ jet bench
p99_latency: 7ms

options.name: Typed budgets (recommended)
options.detail: Budgets attach to packages/envs/services and feed build, bench, dev, dossier, and CI. Weakness fixed: deterministic budgets are hard gates; statistical budgets use pinned baselines and trend policy.
options.code:
$ jet build --release
Error [E14xx]: binary_size budget exceeded: 3.4MiB > 3MiB
Fix: inspect jet dossier --lens size, raise budget, or use profile small

options.name: Optimizer promises
options.detail: Rely on compiler/runtime to optimize without user budgets. Nice default story, but no explicit contract for teams.
options.code:
$ jet build --release
# no declared perf contract

comparisons.note: Simple deployment and predictable operational profile are valued.
Peak performance is excellent, but tuning often spreads across flags/crates/profilers.
Bundle-size budgets are common because teams need explicit gates.

decisions.title: Native replacement overlays
decisions.gist: How Jet replaces foreign packages with native Jet without changing call sites.
decisions.explainer: This turns interop into conquest: same surface, native implementation, proven fit.
decisions.story: A team starts with `js.plotly` and `py.numpy`. Later `core.plot` and `core.linalg` mature. They need to swap implementations without rewriting every import and call.

options.name: Manual rewrites
options.detail: Teams edit imports and call sites when native packages mature. Clear, but migration cost delays replacement.
options.code:
use js.plotly as plotly
# later:
use core.plot as plotly
# fix call mismatches by hand

options.name: Compatibility-proved overlays (recommended)
options.detail: A Jet package declares it replaces a foreign surface only after compatibility proof over public types, effects, errors, examples, and golden fixtures. Weakness fixed: semantic mismatch is visible before the overlay is allowed.
options.code:
core.plot replaces js.plotly {
    surface: generated(js.plotly)
    examples: inherit
}

$ jet replace js.plotly with core.plot
proved: 94% surface compatible
blocked: dynamic plugin API needs adapter

options.name: Permanent interop
options.detail: Keep foreign packages as normal forever. Reach stays high, but native Jet never absorbs the ecosystem.
options.code:
deps: { plotly: js@"plotly.js@2" }
# no native replacement contract

comparisons.note: Preserved JavaScript surfaces while strengthening types.
Can replace package definitions, but not API compatibility.
API compatibility matters; Jet can prove more with examples/effects.

decisions.title: Optional run return and failure annotations
decisions.gist: Whether beginners may keep bare `fn run()` while experts can type an explicit fallible entrypoint.
decisions.explainer: `Unit` is Jet's "nothing meaningful is returned" type, like `void` in C/Java or `()` in Rust. A bare `fn run() { ... }` means `fn run() -> Unit { ... }` by default. The ballot is not asking whether beginners must write `Unit`; they do not. It asks whether experts may opt into the explicit fallible form `fn run() -> Unit ?`.
decisions.story: Priya writes a tiny deploy tool. A beginner should type `fn run() { ... }` and never learn return-type ceremony. Later, Priya wants startup failure to flow with `?`, so she writes the expert form `fn run() -> Unit ?`. Both spell the same entrypoint name; the annotation only states what the function returns and whether failure can escape.

options.name: Bare run by default, explicit fallible run for experts
options.detail: Beginners write `fn run() { ... }`. The compiler treats that as returning `Unit` and infallible. Experts may write `fn run() -> Unit ?` when startup can fail and they want `?` to propagate from the entrypoint. `run` remains the only entrypoint name.

options.name: Bare run only for now
options.detail: Only `fn run() { ... }` is accepted today. Fallible startup must be handled inside the body. This keeps the entrypoint rule tiny, but makes normal CLI/file setup noisier once users need `?`.

options.name: Require explicit return annotations on run
options.detail: Every entrypoint writes its return type: `fn run() -> Unit`. This is explicit, but spends ceremony on every beginner program and conflicts with the magic-out-of-the-box entrypoint goal.

comparisons.note: `main` can omit the return type for the simple path or return `Result` for fallible startup.
comparisons.code:
fn main() { println!("hi"); }
fn main() -> Result<(), Error> { run()?; Ok(()) }

comparisons.note: `main` cannot return an error; startup failures are handled manually.
comparisons.code: func main() { if err := run(); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) } }

decisions.comment: But instead of "Unit" use Void

decisions.title: Web backend TIR boundary
decisions.gist: Whether browser builds must use the same executable TIR as every other target.
decisions.story: Mara ports a Jet UI from native dev mode to the browser. A branch works in one target and not the other because the web emitter read older AST shapes instead of the checked TIR. That breaks the promise that rustc and target backends never become alternate semantic judges.

options.name: TIR-only web execution
options.detail: All executable web bodies lower through sema/TIR first. Unsupported web features produce Jet diagnostics before emission. This keeps one semantic pipeline and one source of truth across dev, JIT, AOT, and web.
options.code:
$ jet build --target web app.jet
Error [E-WEB001]: this effect is not available in the browser target
Fix: move file IO behind a server boundary or choose a native target.

options.name: Explicit web carve-out
options.detail: Allow the web backend to keep a separate AST emitter for a documented subset. The docs must say web is a distinct semantic path with its own conformance suite. This is a real exception to R7/R12.

options.name: Freeze web target until TIR-ready
options.detail: Stop growing the web backend until all executable emission can come from TIR. This avoids split semantics, but browser examples remain frozen while the backend catches up.
options.code:
$ jet build --target web app.jet
Error: web target is frozen until TIR lowering is complete.

comparisons.note: One typed core feeds JavaScript output; JS is not a second checker.
The compiler can emit JS even with type errors unless configured; Jet should not copy that split.

decisions.title: External regex dependency in compile-time path
decisions.gist: Whether a compile-time semantic path may keep an external regex dependency.
decisions.story: Nora adds a compile-time helper and expects the compiler surface to stay std-only. The dependency graph shows regex in `jet-comptime`; if that crate participates in compiler semantics, it weakens I6 and makes future bootstrapping less honest.

options.name: Remove the dependency
options.detail: Replace regex use with a small std-only scanner or parser in the compile-time path. If regex-like power is needed for user code, it belongs in stdlib/runtime code, not the compiler semantic core.
options.code:
// compiler-side scanner: std-only
fn scan_ident(src: &str) -> Token { ... }

options.name: Approve a narrow I6 carve-out
options.detail: Keep regex in `jet-comptime` and document that this crate is allowed an external dependency until a named removal date. The carve-out is explicit and owner-owned.
options.code: // I6 exception: jet-comptime may depend on regex until <date/card>.

options.name: Move regex behind a tool boundary
options.detail: Keep compiler semantics std-only, but let a separate generated-data/tooling step use regex outside the compiler trust boundary. The generated artifact is checked into the repo and audited.
options.code:
$ jet devtools generate-comptime-tables
# tool may use regex; compiler reads generated tables only.

comparisons.note: The compiler has strict dependency policy; procedural tools and libraries have different rules.
The standard toolchain favors small self-contained compiler machinery.

decisions.title: jetos syntax freeze boundary
decisions.gist: Whether jetos-only surface is live syntax law or research-only until the OS lane reopens.
decisions.story: Ari reads the syntax decisions and sees OS configuration examples. Another agent reads the roadmap and sees jetos frozen for research. One starts implementing commands; the other deletes examples. The board needs one boundary.

options.name: Research-only jetos surface
options.detail: Move OS-only spellings to a research appendix and keep only Jetpack-active env/image/generation pieces live. Syntax law stops implying jetos commands/modules are buildable today.

options.name: Frozen but ratified
options.detail: Keep the current jetos surface in syntax law, but mark it frozen and not implementation-ready. Agents may align docs around it, but must not implement new jetos behavior until the freeze lifts.
options.code:
// syntax decision note:
// jetos module syntax is ratified/frozen; implementation work blocked until OS lane opens.

options.name: Make jetos surface live now
options.detail: Treat current jetos examples as active language/product law and unblock implementation cards that use them. This makes the roadmap freeze obsolete and requires immediate cleanup of roadmap wording.
options.code:
$ jetos switch laptop
# live product surface; docs/tests must track it.

comparisons.note: OS module syntax is product law, not research prose.
Accepted proposals distinguish implemented, accepted, and deferred states.

decisions.title: Unsafe gate reason requirement
decisions.gist: Whether every user-written Unsafe gate must include a non-empty audit reason.
decisions.story: Sol reviews generated unsafe blocks before a release. A region labeled only `#Unsafe` says nothing about why the escape hatch exists. A region labeled with a reason can be audited, searched, and challenged.

options.name: Require non-empty reasons everywhere
options.detail: Both block and function Unsafe forms require a non-empty string. The compiler stores the reason for audit output and rejects empty or missing reasons with a Jet diagnostic.

options.name: Allow bare Unsafe with lint
options.detail: Bare `#Unsafe` compiles, but strict profiles and CI can reject it. Beginner code still never sees Unsafe by default; expert experiments are quick, but audit quality depends on policy.
options.code:
#Unsafe { c_call() }
// lint: add an audit reason before release.

options.name: Require reasons for blocks only
options.detail: Unsafe blocks require reasons; `#Unsafe fn` may be bare because the function name is considered the audit anchor. This is less consistent and makes function-level gates easier to under-document.
options.code:
#Unsafe("manual aliasing proof") { ... }
#Unsafe fn fast_copy(...) { ... }

comparisons.note: `unsafe` has no required reason; many teams add comments by convention.
Some Rust teams require SAFETY comments by lint/review.
comparisons.code:
// SAFETY: pointer came from slice bounds check
unsafe { ... }

decisions.title: Collection shorthand and named collection canon
decisions.gist: Whether Jet uses short bracket forms for default list/map and named generic types for specialized collections.
decisions.explainer: The useful split is common-shape shorthand versus specific data-structure name. Lists and default maps are semantic defaults, so shorthand can reduce noise. Specialized collections encode performance/order/hash policy, so their names should stay visible: `HashMap<K, V>`, `Deque<T>`, `Set<T>`. The sharp edge is map shorthand: comma form `[K, V]` is compact but can read like pair/tuple/list; colon form `[K: V]` makes key-to-value meaning clearer and matches map literals/field association.
decisions.story: Bea learns Jet from examples. Lists and maps are everywhere, so short notation helps. But when she reaches `HashMap`, `BTreeMap`, `Deque`, or `SmallVec`, she needs a consistent named-type rule that scales without inventing a new shorthand for every container.

options.name: Hybrid: `[T]`, `[K: V]`, named specific collections
options.detail: Default list and default map get short forms. Specific collection types use Rust-style named generics: `HashMap<K, V>`, `BTreeMap<K, V>`, `Deque<T>`, `Set<T>`. This gives beginners compact common cases and experts visible data-structure policy.

options.name: Rust-style named generics for everything
options.detail: Use `List<T>`, `Map<K, V>`, `HashMap<K, V>` everywhere. Very consistent and searchable; common types are noisier and Jet loses the lightweight feel of list/map shorthand.

options.name: Comma map shorthand: `[T]`, `[K, V]`, named specific collections
options.detail: Matches the proposed `[Map, MapVal]` shape most directly: list has one bracket argument, map has two. Compact and symmetric with generic argument lists, but `[K, V]` can be mistaken for a pair/tuple/list-of-two-types rather than key-to-value mapping.

options.name: No collection shorthand
options.detail: Every collection is a named type. This is maximally explicit, but spends the most ceremony on the two containers users write constantly.
options.code:
let names: List<Text> = List.of("Ada")
let ages: Map<Text, Int> = Map.of("Ada", 36)

comparisons.note: Named collection types make data-structure policy visible.
Short forms for common list/map, named types when policy matters.
Both shorthand and named forms exist for arrays; too many equivalents can fragment style.

decisions.title: Bench marker spelling
decisions.gist: Whether benchmark markers use parenthesized arguments like other marker calls.
decisions.story: Theo writes tests and benchmarks in the same file. `#Test("fast path")` and `#Bench "fast path"` look like two marker grammars even though both attach metadata to a function.
decisions.inWild:
#Test("parses dates") fn parses_dates() { ... }
#Bench "parse throughput" fn bench_parse() { ... }

options.name: Use `#Bench("name")`
options.detail: Bench follows the same parenthesized marker-call shape as Test and other metadata markers. This gives one parser/documentation rule for marker arguments.
options.code: #Bench("parse throughput") fn bench_parse() { ... }

options.name: Bless `#Bench "name"` as an exception
options.detail: Keep the space-string form specifically for benchmarks. It reads nicely, but creates a special marker grammar users must learn.
options.code: #Bench "parse throughput" fn bench_parse() { ... }

options.name: Accept both spellings
options.detail: Both forms compile and the formatter normalizes one. This is a transition path only; as permanent law it is two spellings for one semantic job.
options.code:
#Bench "parse throughput" fn a() { ... }
#Bench("parse throughput") fn b() { ... }

comparisons.note: Attributes use one bracketed argument form.
Attributes with arguments use parentheses.

decisions.title: Runtime profile name canon
decisions.gist: What Jet calls the target environment a program expects.
decisions.explainer: `Runtime profile` means the environment contract for a build target. Examples: `bare` = no OS services, `alloc` = heap but no hosted OS, `hosted` = normal OS process with files/network/time. The audit issue is naming: current prose/examples used `std`, but Jet docs also say user-facing library naming is `Core`, never `std`/`stdlib`. The decision is whether the public profile name should avoid `std` too.
decisions.story: Lena configures a package for normal desktop/server use. Another package targets a tiny embedded board. They need a word for "what runtime services exist here": no OS, heap only, or full OS/filesystem/network. The old ballot called that a ring layer; clearer wording is runtime profile.

options.name: Use `runtime: hosted` for the normal OS profile
options.detail: `hosted` means the program runs with normal OS services. `bare`/`alloc` can name smaller targets later. Core remains the library brand; `std` disappears from user-facing runtime config.

options.name: Keep `layer: std` as a runtime exception
options.detail: `std` remains the public name for the normal runtime layer, with a written exception saying the no-std rule applies only to library names. Existing examples stay familiar to Rust users, but the naming law has a special case.

options.name: Use `runtime: core`
options.detail: The normal profile uses the Core brand. This avoids `std`, but overloads Core-the-library with runtime availability and can make embedded/no-OS profiles harder to explain.

comparisons.note: `std`, `core`, and `alloc` are library tiers; the names are powerful but easy to confuse with target/runtime policy.
Target/environment choices are separate from the standard-library import name.
Hosted versus freestanding is a long-standing environment distinction.

decisions.title: Grant command surface
decisions.gist: Choose the command family users use to list, explain, grant, and revoke Jet trust grants.
decisions.story: Mira clones a service. Jet asks for package fetches, a local database, a secret, and a build wrapper. Later she needs one place to inspect and revoke those choices.
decisions.inWild:
jet dev
jet trust list
jet trust explain postgres.service
jet trust revoke postgres.service

options.name: `jet trust` command family
options.detail: Names the product concept directly. Beginner prompts, expert JSON, revoke, explain, and one-shot grants all sit under the same authority graph.
options.code:
jet trust list
jet trust explain --json
jet trust revoke github@acme/web:postgres.service

options.name: `jet grant` command family
options.detail: Names the internal object. Precise for experts, weaker for a beginner seeing a risk prompt for the first time.
options.code:
jet grant list
jet grant explain --json

options.name: `jet config trust` command family
options.detail: Keeps older config-shaped wording, but frames trust as settings instead of authority produced by code, packages, services, envs, images, and builds.
options.code:
jet config trust list
jet config trust revoke postgres.service

comparisons.note: Substituter and sandbox trust are separate knobs; Jet needs one user-facing trust graph.

decisions.title: Grant policy fields
decisions.gist: Choose whether projects may write reviewed trust policy in Jet source.
decisions.story: Noah maintains CI for a service. Local developers can be prompted, but CI must fail instead of prompting unless a reviewed policy permits the exact cache, registry, service, and wrapper facts.
decisions.inWild: policy: { trust: { default: prompt, ci: { prompt: deny } } }

options.name: `policy.trust` field
options.detail: One manifest policy namespace feeds the same grant graph used by prompts, CLI, locks, and audit.
options.code: policy: { trust: { default: prompt, ci: { prompt: deny }, services: { postgres: prompt } } }

options.name: No source policy fields
options.detail: All grants live in trust store, lock, and CLI. Source stays smaller, but teams cannot review repo policy beside package/env/build declarations.
options.code: jet trust grant cache@ci --scope repo

options.name: Role-local trust fields
options.detail: Each package, env, service, and build role writes local trust hints. Local when reading one role, fragmented when auditing one authority graph.
options.code:
module env dev
trust: { services: prompt, secrets: deny }

comparisons.note: Source-reviewed permissions are part of the workflow contract.

decisions.title: Workspace catalog surface
decisions.gist: Choose where shared dependency versions live and how packages opt in.
decisions.story: Priya owns a monorepo with thirty services. Most services share one HTTP version; one audited service pins another. Missing-dependency fixes must name either direct add or catalog opt-in.

options.name: `catalog:` in `workspace.jet`
options.detail: Catalogs live at the workspace authority point. Packages still opt into visible direct deps, so strict visibility remains intact.

options.name: `deps.catalog` inside each package
options.detail: Clear locally, but central version policy scatters across package manifests.
options.code: deps: { catalog: { http: npm@"undici#6.19.2" } }

options.name: CLI-only catalog edits
options.detail: Easy command path, less reviewable canonical source.
options.code: jet add npm@undici#6.19.2 --catalog http

comparisons.note: Workspace dependencies centralize versions while members opt in.

decisions.title: Strict visibility diagnostics
decisions.gist: Choose the diagnostic contract for hidden transitive package use.
decisions.story: Leo imports a package because another dependency already brought it in. Jet must explain transitive deps are hidden, name the asking package, and offer the smallest valid fix.
decisions.inWild:
use leftpad.pad

error[E12xx]: `leftpad` is not visible to package `acme.web`

options.name: Dedicated strict-visibility diagnostics
options.detail: New E12xx diagnostics name requester, hidden package, reason, and direct-dep or catalog fix.
options.code:
error[E12xx]: `leftpad` is not visible to package `acme.web`
fix: run `jet add npm@leftpad --package acme.web`

options.name: Reuse module-not-found diagnostics
options.detail: No new family; hidden packages look missing with extra help text.
options.code: error[E0606]: module `leftpad` not found

options.name: Warning plus resolution failure
options.detail: Splits one user problem into two messages.
options.code:
warning[W12xx]: transitive dependency hidden
error[E0606]: module not found

comparisons.note: Strict deps errors name the missing direct dependency.

decisions.title: Importer command
decisions.gist: Choose how users import foreign project metadata into Jet source.
decisions.story: Sam has a Nix flake and a Cargo workspace. He wants Jet to generate editable package, role, dep, adapter, and TODO files, then safely rerun the importer.
decisions.inWild:
jet import nix ./flake.nix
jet import cargo ./Cargo.toml --update

options.name: `jet import <ecosystem> <path>`
options.detail: Direct migration command. Generated Jet source is canonical; update, dry-run, and conflict rules define repeat behavior.
options.code:
jet import nix ./flake.nix
jet import cargo ./Cargo.toml --update

options.name: `jet migrate <ecosystem> <path>`
options.detail: Names the larger user intent, but migration also includes replacement progress beyond this file-emission job.
options.code: jet migrate nix ./flake.nix

options.name: `jet add --from <file>`
options.detail: Familiar for deps, too narrow for role modules, services, wrappers, FFI stubs, and TODO diagnostics.
options.code: jet add --from ./package.json

comparisons.note: Module commands ingest existing dependency state into canonical files.

decisions.title: Importer TODO diagnostics
decisions.gist: Choose how importer gaps appear in generated Jet projects.
decisions.story: Ari imports a Python package with dynamic metadata and a Node project with lifecycle scripts. Jet should not hide assumptions; it should leave precise review items tied to source spans.
decisions.inWild: warning[W12xx]: importer TODO: dynamic Python metadata

options.name: Dedicated importer TODO diagnostics
options.detail: Stable E/W12xx diagnostics carry what/why/fix, source path, generated target, and migration status.
options.code:
warning[W12xx]: importer TODO: npm lifecycle script needs review
fix: keep generated build recipe or replace with native Jet build code

options.name: Inline generated comments only
options.detail: Readable in files, weak for CI and audit.
options.code: // TODO(importer): postinstall needs review

options.name: Lock/explain TODO facts only
options.detail: Good audit trail, easy to miss while editing generated source.
options.code: jet dossier import

comparisons.note: Plan output surfaces review facts before apply.

decisions.title: Provider trust roots
decisions.gist: Choose how users control registries, mirrors, keys, and allowed providers.
decisions.story: Inez works at a company that allows crates.io and an internal npm mirror, denies public PyPI, and pins registry signing keys. Provider refs already have a spelling; this decides trust-root policy.
decisions.inWild: policy: { providers: { npm: { registry: "https://npm.acme.test" }, pypi: deny } }

options.name: `policy.providers` in source
options.detail: Provider trust roots are reviewable source policy feeding fetch grants, cache, signatures, and lock rationale.
options.code: policy: { providers: { npm: { registry: "https://npm.acme.test" }, pypi: deny, cargo: allow } }

options.name: User/global config only
options.detail: Good for personal machines, weaker for repo-reviewed CI.
options.code: jet trust provider allow npm --registry https://npm.acme.test

options.name: Lockfile-pinned trust only
options.detail: Reproducible after lock, less explicit before first resolution.
options.code: jet lock explain provider npm

comparisons.note: Registry scope config controls fetch source but not a unified trust graph.

decisions.title: Native replacement policy
decisions.gist: Choose how users allow, deny, or prefer proved native replacements.
decisions.story: Gwen depends on an npm HTTP client. Jet finds a proved native replacement. Her team wants replacements active in CI after review, never silent on developer machines.
decisions.inWild: policy: { replacements: { default: prompt } }

options.name: `policy.replacements` field
options.detail: Source policy names allow, deny, or prefer. Compatibility proof remains mandatory; policy only decides activation.
options.code: policy: { replacements: { default: prompt, npm@"undici#6.19.2": prefer core.http.undici } }

options.name: CLI-only replacement grants
options.detail: Useful for local experiments, less reviewable for repo policy.
options.code: jet trust replacement prefer npm@undici#6.19.2 core.http.undici

options.name: Always prompt
options.detail: Beginner-safe but teams cannot encode reviewed choices as project policy.
options.code: Jet can replace npm@undici#6.19.2 with core.http.undici.

comparisons.note: Patch redirects sources but does not prove compatibility.

decisions.title: Replacement proof metadata
decisions.gist: Choose how packages publish compatibility proof for native replacements.
decisions.story: Omar writes a native replacement for a Python CSV library. Users should see which public symbols, effects, errors, examples, and goldens were proved before Jet routes calls to it.
decisions.inWild: replacementProof: { replaces: pypi@"csvkit#2.0.1", public: all }

options.name: `replacementProof:` metadata
options.detail: User-authored proof metadata lives beside the native package and feeds proof runner, lock rationale, and audit.
options.code: replacementProof: { replaces: pypi@"csvkit#2.0.1", public: all, examples: find("./compat/examples") }

options.name: Generated index facts only
options.detail: Keeps source smaller, but package authors cannot publish intent directly in Jet source.
options.code: jet prove replacement core.csv.compat pypi@csvkit#2.0.1

options.name: External proof manifest
options.detail: Clear boundary for large fixture sets, but creates another canonical metadata surface.
options.code: replacement.jetproof

comparisons.note: Publishes compatibility intent for JS types, not runtime behavior proof.

decisions.title: Fidelity signal API
decisions.gist: Choose the API apps use to read and pin runtime fidelity.
decisions.story: Mira tunes a Jet game across laptops and handhelds. Effects can scale down, but no user function may disappear because the machine is hot, and tests need deterministic pins.
decisions.inWild:
use core.perf.{Perf}
fidelity :: Perf.fidelity()

options.name: `core.perf.Perf` static API
options.detail: One runtime-global signal: read, override, reset. App code decides behavior; runtime never silently changes semantics.

options.name: Scoped override block
options.detail: Cleaner test isolation, but adds a second control shape beyond read/override/reset.
options.code: Perf.with_fidelity(0.2) { render_frame() }

options.name: Task-local fidelity
options.detail: Expert isolation, but less direct and conflicts with runtime-wide signal wording.
options.code: task.spawn(() => { Perf.override_fidelity(0.2)? })

comparisons.note: Global quality knobs are read by app code.

decisions.title: Platform signal provider surface
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet exposes battery, thermal, network, load, or carbon facts in Epoch 3.
decisions.story: Noor ships a tablet field app. Battery and network facts could tune sync, but Jet must not silently change scheduling, storage, or cleanup policy.
decisions.inWild: Signals.current() // if accepted

options.name: No platform providers in Epoch 3
options.detail: Keep only the ratified fidelity signal. Other facts remain platform packages or research notes.
options.code:
use core.perf.{Perf}
if Perf.fidelity() < 0.5 { draw_low_detail() }

options.name: Read-only `Signals.current()`
options.detail: Expose facts as one read-only value. Apps choose behavior explicitly.
options.code: signals :: Signals.current()

options.name: Injectable provider interface
options.detail: Deterministic and expert-controlled, but becomes a real platform abstraction layer.
options.code: Signals.use_provider(SignalProvider.fixed(...))

comparisons.note: Battery/network facts are readable; apps decide policy.

decisions.title: Explicit solver library
decisions.gist: Choose whether Core gets a finite constraint solver API in Epoch 3.
decisions.story: Iris writes a level generator with keys, doors, and enemies under constraints. She wants deterministic search with normal Jet ownership, not hidden backtracking.
decisions.inWild:
use core.solve.{Solver}
solver.require(path_exists(start_room(), key))

options.name: Core finite solver library
options.detail: Add `core.solve` with explicit solver state, deterministic order, ordinary values, and iterator output. No syntax.
options.code:
solver :: Solver.new(42)
solver.require(x + y == 10)

options.name: Experimental package first
options.detail: Explore API evidence without making Core law.
options.code: use core.experimental.solve.{Solver}

options.name: Defer solver API
options.detail: Keep logic work out of Epoch 3 Core. Use normal iterator adapters and keep examples research-only.
options.code: rooms().filter((r) => path_exists(start, r))

comparisons.note: Explicit solver objects keep search visible to host code.

decisions.title: Structural merge command surface
decisions.gist: Choose how users invoke Jet structural diff and merge.
decisions.story: Sam renames a type while Priya moves methods into a new module. Text merge conflicts, but Jet can see program entities and should expose one Jet-aware merge path.
decisions.inWild:
jet diff --structural main...feature
jet merge --structural base.jet ours.jet theirs.jet

options.name: `jet diff --structural` and `jet merge --structural`
options.detail: One command surface for read-only diff and three-way merge. Git/editor integration can call it later.
options.code:
jet diff --structural main...feature
jet merge --structural base.jet ours.jet theirs.jet --out merged.jet

options.name: Dedicated structural commands
options.detail: Plain feature name, but creates a parallel command family.
options.code: jet structural-diff main...feature

options.name: Git-only merge driver
options.detail: Convenient when installed, poor for learning, debugging, CI, and editor reuse.
options.code: git config merge.jetstruct.driver ...

comparisons.note: Text merge is default; drivers are opt-in per repo/path.

decisions.title: Public conflict identity model
decisions.gist: Choose what identity Jet shows in structural conflict reports.
decisions.story: Lena reviews a CI merge report. She needs to know whether a function changed, moved, or became a different definition without reading internal hashes first.
decisions.inWild: conflict: fn Parser.parse_expr(self, TokenStream) -> Expr

options.name: Human identity plus stable internal ID
options.detail: Reports show module/type/function/signature first and include stable IDs for tools and rename tracking.
options.code:
conflict: fn Parser.parse_expr(self, TokenStream) -> Expr
stable id: def:7YDK4Q6V

options.name: Name/path identity only
options.detail: Readable, but rename/move cases lose the proof structural merge exists to preserve.
options.code: conflict: Source/Parser.jet Parser.parse_expr changed

options.name: Content IDs first
options.detail: Precise for machines, weak beginner report.
options.code: conflict: def:7YDK4Q6V changed

comparisons.note: Structured identity internally, human names in UI.

decisions.title: Structural conflict report shape
decisions.gist: Choose how structural merge conflicts are shown to humans and tools.
decisions.story: Owen hits CI after two refactors. Terminal output must be readable; editor and review bots need structured facts from the same model.
decisions.inWild: jet merge --structural base.jet ours.jet theirs.jet --report json

options.name: Human text only
options.detail: Best direct CLI, but tools must scrape text.
options.code: conflict: fn Parser.parse_expr changed on both sides

options.name: JSON only
options.detail: Machine-stable, weak direct CLI experience.
options.code: {"kind":"signature_conflict","identity":"fn Parser.parse_expr"}

options.name: One schema, text/JSON/editor renderers
options.detail: One typed conflict model. CLI renders Jet-style text, JSON writes same facts, editor consumes same schema.
options.code:
jet merge --structural base ours theirs
jet merge --structural base ours theirs --report json

comparisons.note: Human diagnostics plus JSON output for tools.

decisions.title: Git and VCS integration policy
decisions.gist: Choose how structural merge plugs into Git and other VCS tools.
decisions.story: A team adopts Jet in a monorepo. Beginners keep normal Git; release engineers enable structural merge for `.jet` files in CI and protected branches.
decisions.inWild: jet merge install-driver --repo .

options.name: Opt-in Git driver generated by Jet
options.detail: Jet configures `.jet` paths for this repo. Other VCS tools call the same structural merge command.
options.code: jet merge install-driver --repo .

options.name: Always-on Git replacement
options.detail: Strong stance, but adds source-control ceremony before identity safety has proven out.
options.code: git merge feature

options.name: Standalone only
options.detail: Simple boundary, but misses where conflicts happen.
options.code: jet merge --structural base ours theirs --out file.jet

comparisons.note: Syntax-aware diff is opt-in around Git.

decisions.title: Core data surface
decisions.gist: Choose the public Core API for tables, series, stats, and plots.
decisions.story: Mira analyzes support tickets from CSV in one file. She wants typed rows, grouped summaries, and a small plot without first learning Python, SQL, or package manifests.
decisions.inWild:
use core.data
summary.plot.bar(x: .team, y: .p95_minutes).save("ticket-p95.svg")?

options.name: One `core.data` facade
options.detail: Tables, series, stats, CSV, and plot builders live behind one beginner import; expert modules remain below with same operation names.
options.code:
use core.data
rows :: data.csv<Ticket>("tickets.csv")?

options.name: Split by domain modules
options.detail: Ownership explicit, but first tutorial spreads across several namespaces.
options.code:
use core.table
use core.stats
use core.plot

options.name: Method-only table API
options.detail: Compact call sites, but reusable stats/plot vocabulary hides inside table values.
options.code: Table.csv<Ticket>("tickets.csv")?.group_by(.team)

comparisons.note: Composable pipelines are strong; Jet should keep column misses as Jet diagnostics.

decisions.title: Data bridge providers
decisions.gist: Choose how Python, R, and accelerator bridges are named and imported.
decisions.story: Ishan has a mostly native analytics job, with one Python clustering step and one accelerator kernel. He needs bridges visible, typed, and replaceable.
decisions.inWild:
use py.sklearn as sklearn
model :: sklearn.KMeans(k: 8).fit(customers)?

options.name: Use provider roots directly
options.detail: `py.*` and other accepted bridge roots stay visible under the FFI structure law; data APIs accept typed bridge results and report status.
options.code:
use py.sklearn as sklearn
use r.forecast as forecast
use gpu.cuda as cuda

options.name: Nest bridges under `core.data.bridge`
options.detail: Discoverable from data, but creates a second spelling for foreign providers.
options.code: use core.data.bridge.py.sklearn as sklearn

options.name: Manifest-named accelerators
options.detail: Policy control, but hides bridge authority from single-file readers.
options.code: deps: { sklearn: py@sklearn#"1.6.0" }

comparisons.note: Provider identity is obvious, but native replacement status is absent.

decisions.title: Native replacement status
decisions.gist: Choose how users see which data steps are native, bridged, or missing.
decisions.story: Rae moves notebook work into Jet for a regulated report. She must prove which steps are native, which bridge into Python or R, and which replacements exist.
decisions.inWild:
data.status().write("data-status.json")?
jet dossier data analysis.jet

options.name: `jet dossier data` lens plus API
options.detail: Machine status via Core API; canonical human view through the D-WD dossier umbrella.
options.code:
data.status().write("data-status.json")?
jet dossier data analysis.jet

options.name: Standalone `jet data status`
options.detail: Discoverable for analysts, but adds another explain surface beside dossier.
options.code: jet data status analysis.jet --json

options.name: Build warning summary only
options.detail: Visible during run, weak for audits unless another artifact appears.
options.code:
jet run analysis.jet
Data status: native, bridged

comparisons.note: Stable scriptable graph/report views work well.

decisions.title: Deterministic plotting policy
decisions.gist: Choose the first plotting backend and deterministic output rule.
decisions.story: Noor checks a generated report into CI. Charts must be readable and golden-test stable across host fonts, timestamps, and graphics libraries.
decisions.inWild: summary.plot.bar(x: .region, y: .revenue).save("revenue.svg")?

options.name: First-party deterministic SVG plus text fallback
options.detail: Core emits stable SVG with pinned layout and a text backend for terminal/CI. Bitmap export can layer on the same model later.
options.code:
plot.save("revenue.svg")?
plot.save("revenue.txt")?

options.name: Text plots only in Core
options.detail: Maximally stable, weaker beginner report story.
options.code: plot.save("revenue.txt")?

options.name: Backend package required
options.detail: Maximal backend control, too much setup for first chart.
options.code: plot.render(svg.backend()).save("revenue.svg")?

comparisons.note: Portable declarative specs are useful; Jet can own a smaller typed model first.

decisions.title: Game asset handles
decisions.gist: Choose how game assets are declared, loaded, and diagnosed.
decisions.story: Lena makes a platformer. She wants a typed `player_sprite` handle everywhere and a Jet diagnostic if a PNG is missing or used as a sound.
decisions.inWild: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Scene asset registry with typed handles
options.detail: Assets load through `scene.assets`, returning typed handles tied to scene identity.
options.code:
player :: scene.assets.image("assets/player.png")?
jump :: scene.assets.sound("assets/jump.wav")?

options.name: Top-level loaders
options.detail: Flexible, but weakens scene-owned diagnostics and editor identity.
options.code: player :: game.asset.image("assets/player.png")?

options.name: Manifest asset catalog
options.detail: Strong packaging provenance, more ceremony for one-file games.
options.code: targets: { game: { assets: { player: "assets/player.png" } } }

comparisons.note: Resource handles are editor-friendly; Jet should keep them typed and source-owned.

decisions.title: ECS over Scene
decisions.gist: Choose the component and query API that layers over `Scene`.
decisions.story: Omar starts with a simple scene, then adds hundreds of enemies. Components and queries should be another view over the same scene data, not a second engine.
decisions.inWild:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.query(Position, Velocity)

options.name: `component` declarations plus `scene.query`
options.detail: Components are typed declarations; queries are scene methods, preserving one scene identity.
options.code:
component Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
loop item in scene.query(Position, Velocity) { }

options.name: Struct marker components
options.detail: No new declaration form, but component intent is less visible.
options.code:
struct Velocity { dx: Float, dy: Float }
scene.component<Velocity>()

options.name: System functions over query parameters
options.detail: Concise for experts, but puts scheduler vocabulary before the beginner scene story.
options.code: system move(pos: Position mut, vel: Velocity, frame: Frame) { }

comparisons.note: Typed queries are strong; Jet should hide scheduler complexity until needed.

decisions.title: Game input bindings
decisions.gist: Choose how input bindings and per-frame snapshots are named.
decisions.story: Aya wants keyboard today and gamepad later. Replay files should store actions, not raw device quirks, so logic is deterministic across dev, CI, and builds.
decisions.inWild:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Scene bindings plus frame snapshot
options.detail: Bindings live on `scene.input`; frame logic reads deterministic `frame.input` snapshots.
options.code:
scene.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])
frame.input.pressed(.jump)

options.name: Global input map
options.detail: Short, but weak multi-scene/editor isolation.
options.code: game.input.bind(.jump, keys: [.space])

options.name: Typed action enum
options.detail: Explicit and replay-friendly, more ceremony for tiny games.
options.code:
enum Action { jump }
frame.input<Action>().pressed(Action.jump)

comparisons.note: Action maps are beginner-friendly and replayable.

decisions.comment: Both A & C

decisions.title: Game replay contract
decisions.gist: Choose the replay API, file format, and determinism contract.
decisions.story: Ben gets a physics bug report. The player sends one replay file; Ben runs it under `jet dev` and compiled mode and gets the same frame transcript.
decisions.inWild: game.Replay.record("runs/bug-142.jreplay")

options.name: `game.Replay` API plus `.jreplay` artifact
options.detail: First-party typed artifact contains input actions, seeds, fixed-step timing, backend identity, and budget events.
options.code:
game.run(scene, replay: game.Replay.record("run.jreplay"))
game.Replay.play("run.jreplay", scene)?

options.name: CLI-only replay
options.detail: Keeps source clean, weakens tests that need replay facts.
options.code: jet game record game.jet --out run.jreplay

options.name: User serialization hooks
options.detail: Expert control, but no shared deterministic contract.
options.code: scene.on_snapshot((frame) => writer.write(frame.input))

comparisons.note: Input-stream replay is proven; Jet should type and version the artifact.

decisions.title: Game backend selection
decisions.gist: Choose how renderer, audio, and editor backends are selected.
decisions.story: Sana starts with a no-op CI backend, develops on raylib, and later targets wgpu. Gameplay code should not change when backend changes.
decisions.inWild: game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Typed `game.Backend` value
options.detail: Backends are explicit typed values passed to `game.run`; beginners can omit for the default headless/no-op path.
options.code:
game.run(scene)
game.run(scene, backend: game.Backend { renderer: raylib.renderer() })

options.name: Manifest target backend
options.detail: Fits packages, but single-file games need hidden defaults or a second path.
options.code: targets: { game: { backend: { renderer: core.raylib } } }

options.name: CLI-selected backend
options.detail: Useful for CI, harder to audit from source.
options.code: jet run game.jet --game-renderer=core.raylib

comparisons.note: Plugins are flexible; Jet should keep one stable Core scene API above replaceable backend packages.

decisions.title: Game budgets
decisions.gist: Choose how frame, memory, asset, and draw-call budgets attach and report diagnostics.
decisions.story: Nico ships a handheld build with strict frame, memory, and draw-call ceilings. Violations should be Jet diagnostics with replay context.
decisions.inWild: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Scene/package budgets, same model
options.detail: Budgets attach to scenes for one-file games and package targets for projects; sema/runtime treat both as one fact model.
options.code: scene.budgets.set(game.Budgets { frame: 16.ms, memory: 96.mb })

options.name: Package-only budgets
options.detail: Clean for CI, but one-file games lose budget diagnostics unless packaged.
options.code: targets: { game: { budgets: { frame: 16.ms } } }

options.name: Runtime watcher API
options.detail: Dynamic control, weaker build/dossier/CI facts.
options.code: budget_watch.attach(scene)

comparisons.note: Budgets work best when CI can fail deterministically.

decisions.comment: Both A & C

decisions.title: Target profile surface
decisions.gist: Choose where embedded and freestanding target profiles are declared and selected.
decisions.story: Tess writes hosted CLIs most days, then firmware for a sensor board. Hosted hello-world stays zero ceremony; board builds expose every target assumption.
decisions.inWild: module board.sensor_v1 { target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4 }

options.name: Typed profile module selected by `targets:`
options.detail: Profiles are Jet modules with typed fields; packages select them through existing targets. Hosted single-file programs never mention profiles.
options.code:
module board.sensor_v1 { target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4 }
targets: { firmware: { profile: board.sensor_v1 } }

options.name: All profile data in `pkg.jet`
options.detail: Centralizes build data, harder to reuse and review large board profiles as source modules.
options.code: targets: { firmware: { target: embedded.arm.cortex_m4 } }

options.name: CLI-selected board files
options.detail: Good for vendor imports, less visible source provenance.
options.code: jet build src/main.jet --target-profile boards/sensor_v1.jet

comparisons.note: Target JSON plus linker scripts work, but Jet should validate before codegen.

decisions.title: Target memory regions
decisions.gist: Choose how memory regions and units are written and validated.
decisions.story: Jules has flash, SRAM, and MMIO windows. Jet should catch overflow or MMIO outside declared regions before generated Rust exists.
decisions.inWild: memory: board.memory({ flash: { origin: 0x0800_0000, size: 512.kib } })

options.name: Named regions with typed units
options.detail: Profiles use named regions with origin, size, access, and kind; sizes use distinct units and addresses stay numeric.
options.code: memory: board.memory({ flash: { origin: 0x0800_0000, size: 512.kib, access: .rx } })

options.name: Linker-section-first memory
options.detail: Matches linker thinking, hides hardware layout from MMIO and audit checks.
options.code: memory: board.sections({ text: { at: 0x0800_0000, max: 384.kib } })

options.name: Imported vendor memory map
options.detail: Useful for large boards, should not be the only authoring path.
options.code: memory: board.import("vendor/stm32f4.svd")

comparisons.note: MEMORY blocks name origin and length; Jet should type-check earlier.

decisions.title: Linker provenance
decisions.gist: Choose how linker scripts are sourced, generated, and overridden.
decisions.story: Priya builds two boards. One can use Jet-generated linker input; one must consume a vendor script. Audit must show exactly which path happened.
decisions.inWild: linker: board.linker.generated

options.name: Generated by default, hashed file override
options.detail: Jet generates linker input from typed profile facts; expert override uses explicit hashed file and appears in audit.
options.code:
linker: board.linker.generated
linker: board.linker.file("vendor/memory.x", hash: "sha256:abc123")

options.name: User linker file required
options.detail: Exposes provenance but duplicates typed memory facts.
options.code: linker: board.linker.file("memory.x", hash: "sha256:abc123")

options.name: Toolchain-provided linker policy
options.detail: Convenient, but hides board assumptions from source review.
options.code: linker: board.linker.toolchain_default

comparisons.note: Build scripts can own linker args; Jet should make source visible to dossier/audit.

decisions.title: Allocator and panic policy
decisions.gist: Choose how freestanding allocator and panic behavior are declared.
decisions.story: Mateo writes boot firmware with no heap while another board uses a fixed arena. Jet should reject accidental heap use and make panic behavior explicit.
decisions.inWild: allocator: board.allocator.fixed(region: .ram, size: 32.kib)

options.name: Typed profile fields
options.detail: `allocator` and `panic` are required freestanding profile facts; hosted defaults stay hidden. Sema rejects unavailable Core APIs from these facts.
options.code:
allocator: board.allocator.none
panic: board.panic.abort

options.name: Package target policy only
options.detail: Compact, less reusable across board modules.
options.code: targets: { firmware: { allocator: none, panic: abort } }

options.name: Source markers on entry functions
options.detail: Localizes policy but mixes build target facts into ordinary code.

comparisons.note: Panic handlers are special items; Jet should expose typed target facts.

decisions.title: Target audit report
decisions.gist: Choose the shape of the target-profile audit report.
decisions.story: Hana sends firmware to a lab. They need memory layout, linker source, allocator, panic policy, unavailable Core APIs, and unsafe/MMIO regions in one stable artifact.
decisions.inWild: jet dossier target firmware --json > target-audit.json

options.name: `jet dossier target` plus build artifact
options.detail: Canonical human/machine view is a dossier lens, and builds also write the same JSON into `.jet/` for CI archives.
options.code:
jet dossier target firmware
jet dossier target firmware --json > target-audit.json

options.name: Build artifact only
options.detail: Stable for CI, less discoverable during planning/debugging.
options.code: cat .jet/audit/firmware.target.json

options.name: Command output only
options.detail: Visible, weak for archives and tooling.
options.code: jet build firmware --audit

comparisons.note: Machine-readable build facts are useful; Jet target safety facts should be first-class.
NixOS declares options separately from module values.

decisions.title: jetos option declaration and privacy
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos options are declared and marked private.
decisions.story: Doris writes a laptop module and needs net.hostname to be typed, documented, defaulted, and discoverable. Later she marks a hardware serial option private so imported modules and lift reports cannot read it. The spelling decides whether options feel like documentation or like ordinary values.

options.name: Option declaration keyword (recommended)
options.detail: Declares once; modules only set values. private is a declaration modifier. Clear LSP anchor, beginner-readable docs, and no confusion between declaring and setting.
options.code:
option net.hostname: Text = "jet-box" doc "The machine hostname."
option hardware.serial: Text private doc "Host-only."

options.name: Option record value
options.detail: Use ordinary role-record syntax like Option.{}; fewer keywords, but declaration vs setting is less visible and private/docs become fields.
options.code: net.hostname: Option.{ type: Text, default: "jet-box", doc: "The machine hostname" }

options.name: Type-only declaration
options.detail: Declare type/privacy only; defaults are ordinary module sets. Minimal law, but default docs live in two places.
options.code:
option net.hostname: Text doc "The machine hostname."
module system.defaults { net.hostname: "jet-box" }

comparisons.note: Git keeps one entrypoint with subcommands.
comparisons.code: git switch; git restore; git worktree

comparisons.note: NixOS uses a separate OS command.

decisions.title: jetos command verb surface
decisions.gist: Choose the user command shape for jetos verbs.
decisions.story: Hank wants to check a config, build it, switch, list generations, and roll back. The commands must be beginner-obvious while still crossing the engine process boundary required by Jetpack and jetos architecture.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os check laptop
$ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu
$ jet os generations
$ jet os rollback

options.name: jet os subcommand (recommended)
options.detail: Users keep one jet entrypoint; os names the expert tier and dispatches to the jetos engine process. Verbs: check, init, build, switch, rollback, generations, lift, image.
options.code:
$ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu
$ jet os rollback

options.name: Top-level jet verbs
options.detail: Shortest for daily use, but crowds the base jet command and revives older vision-doc drift.
options.code:
$ jet switch laptop
$ jet rollback

options.name: Separate jetos binary
options.detail: Clean engine boundary for experts, but beginners learn a second command name for the same family.
options.code:
$ jetos switch laptop
$ jetos rollback

comparisons.note: Flakes allow local defaults and explicit host attrs.

decisions.title: jetos host selection and search root
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos finds the target machine module.
decisions.story: Betty has module system.laptop and module system.server in one repo. On her laptop she wants the short command. In CI she wants an exact path and host so no ambient config leaks in.

options.name: Only path@host
options.detail: Explicit and scriptable, but keeps the older config-file mental model and adds ceremony to the common repo case.
options.code: $ jet os switch ~/.jet/config.jet@laptop

options.name: Only bare module name
options.detail: Simple repo discovery, but weaker for CI, remote configs, and exact-file automation.
options.code: $ jet os switch laptop

options.name: Bare name plus path@host (recommended)
options.detail: Discover module system.<name> in the current repo for the common case; keep path@host for exact external roots. One host-selection mechanism with two entrypoints.
options.code:
$ jet os switch laptop
$ jet os switch ./systems/halcyon.jet@laptop

comparisons.note: NixOS generations are numbered; users often add profile comments externally.

decisions.title: jetos generation naming UX
decisions.gist: Choose how OS generations get human names.
decisions.story: Earl is about to install a GPU driver. He wants the previous generation to be clearly named before he switches, and rollback should show something more useful than an opaque hash.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu-driver
$ jet os generations
48  current  post-gpu-driver
47           pre-gpu-driver

options.name: Name at switch
options.detail: One moment to name the artifact while creating it. Clear and scriptable, but unnamed generations still need a default display.
options.code: $ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu-driver

options.name: Separate rename verb
options.detail: Lets users name after inspection, but creates a second mutation path for generation metadata.
options.code: $ jet os rename 47 pre-gpu-driver

options.name: Auto-name plus override (recommended)
options.detail: Every generation gets a stable auto name; --name overrides during switch. generations sorts newest-first and shows chosen or auto name. No separate rename path.
options.code:
$ jet os switch laptop
generation 48 "2026-07-06-1842"
$ jet os switch laptop --name pre-gpu-driver

comparisons.note: NixOS favors long nested names.

decisions.title: jetos standard option namespaces
decisions.gist: Choose top-level option namespace and enum names for the standard OS tree.
decisions.story: Mabel writes her first system module. The names she sees for boot, disks, network, users, services, desktop, and packages become the jetos teaching surface and Studio sidebar.

options.name: Plain OS nouns (recommended)
options.detail: boot, fs, net, users, services, desktop, pkgs; enums like .SystemdBoot and .Ext4. Boring, searchable, beginner-first.
options.code:
boot.loader: .SystemdBoot

decisions.title: Browser event and storage API for jettasks
decisions.gist: How Jet web apps bind DOM events and persist browser state.
decisions.story: Betty is replacing a React TodoMVC with Jet. She wants the add box, checkbox toggles, filters, and reload-persistent tasks to live in Jet code, not handwritten JavaScript glue. This choice decides whether the browser slice proves Jet as an app framework or only as a compute/render island.
decisions.detail: Current friction: `jettasks` can render through exported #Js functions, but Jet code cannot bind DOM events or browser storage itself. Host-page JS can call exports, yet that leaves app ownership outside Jet. If A is ratified, implementation touches `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/Web.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/DomRuntime.js`, `examples/apps/jettasks/*`, `tests/web_build.rs`, and `tests/slices.rs`; proof is fake-DOM event/storage harness plus static web build and TodoMVC reducer/output goldens.

options.name: Typed core.web events plus storage (recommended)
options.detail: Add a first-party browser Core surface: typed selectors, event objects, input values, and localStorage/sessionStorage wrappers. Beginner path stays direct, expert path can still drop to #Js exports when needed. One canonical browser-side mechanism.
options.code:
use core.web as web
web.on("#toggle-3", "click", (_) => toggle(3))
web.storage.local.set("tasks", json)
json :: web.storage.local.get("tasks") ?? "[]"

options.name: Host-page JavaScript drives exported #Js functions
options.detail: Keep Jet web output as exported functions called by handwritten JS in index.html. Avoids new Core API, but the flagship app would not prove Jet owns browser interaction or persistence.
options.code:
<script type="module">
  import { addTask, toggle } from "./app.js";
  input.addEventListener("keydown", e => addTask(input.value));
</script>

options.name: Component callbacks inside core.ui nodes
options.detail: Events are attached as properties on UI nodes. Strong long-term component ergonomics, but requires the view tree to become the source of event wiring and storage still needs a separate answer.
options.code: ui.input(value: title, on_key: (ev) => { if ev.key == "Enter" { add(title) } })

options.name: Do not persist browser state yet
options.detail: Events land, storage stays out. This cannot satisfy TodoMVC persistence and would weaken the web flagship proof.
options.code:
web.on("#new-task", "keydown", add_from_input)
// reload loses tasks

comparisons.note: Events are declared in component code and state persistence usually uses localStorage through typed wrappers or hooks.
Events are typed messages; ports are used for browser APIs like storage.
Event handlers live in markup and storage is ordinary browser API.

decisions.comment: Components also should have events, like react and typescript

decisions.title: MMIO write API for metal
decisions.gist: How low-level Jet writes to memory-mapped hardware registers.
decisions.story: Earl is bringing up a tiny board. Reading a status register is not enough; he must write a byte to UART data and stream the Life transcript. Jet needs this power, but only inside an audited unsafe region so beginners never see the footgun.
decisions.detail: Current friction: `core.mem` has `volatile_read` and target-profile MMIO validation, but no write operation and no pointer-deref assignment lvalue. Without a write, `metal` cannot emit UART serial bytes. If A is ratified, implementation touches `crates/jet-foundation/src/Syntax.rs`, `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/{subset,lower,emit}.rs`, diagnostics/tests for unsafe gating, `examples/apps/metal/*`, and `tests/slices.rs`; proof is gated `mem.volatile_write` plus freestanding/QEMU-oriented serial transcript path.

options.name: mem.volatile_write(ptr, value) (recommended)
options.detail: Pair the existing volatile_read with an audited write helper. It is gated by use core.mem plus #Unsafe, validates against target-profile MMIO ranges, and reads naturally in UART code.

options.name: Pointer assignment p.* = value
options.detail: Looks like ordinary assignment through a pointer. Compact, but expands lvalue grammar and makes volatile semantics less visible at the call site.

options.name: mem.mmio(region).write(offset, value)
options.detail: More structured and profile-aware. Strong for experts, more ceremony for first bring-up, and a second API alongside raw Ptr unless it replaces Ptr use entirely for MMIO.

options.name: Keep read-only volatile for now
options.detail: Cannot ship the metal UART proof because the app cannot write serial bytes.
options.code:
mem.volatile_read(status)
// no write path

comparisons.note: Volatile writes are explicit unsafe operations.
Volatile pointer writes are explicit in the pointer type/access.

decisions.title: core.raylib bridge completion boundary
decisions.gist: How the game slice proves real raylib without making CI depend on a display.
decisions.story: Earl runs the game at a club and wants a window, sprites, sound, input, and replay. CI still needs to verify the same rules without opening a display server. This choice sets the first real raylib bridge boundary.
decisions.detail: Current friction: `core.raylib` is a typed no-op skeleton: `window_open` returns a struct, `should_close` returns true, and no texture/audio/input bridge exists. If A is ratified, implementation touches `crates/jet-sema/src/Sema/CheckerCoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Prelude/CoreLib.rs`, `crates/jet-codegen/src/Codegen/TIR/{subset,lower,emit}.rs`, `Source/CmdCompile.rs`/link handling as needed, `examples/apps/jetfighter/*`, `tests/corelib.rs`, and `tests/slices.rs`; proof is real display bridge when available plus headless replay transcript in CI.

options.name: Real bridge plus headless replay verifier (recommended)
options.detail: Window/audio/input are real when display and raylib are present; CI runs the same game logic through a headless replay backend with frame transcript and budget checks. Strong proof without flaky display dependency.
options.code:
$ jet run examples/apps/jetfighter/main.jet
# opens window when raylib/display available
$ jet run examples/apps/jetfighter/main.jet -- --headless --replay fixtures/demo.moves
frames=900 score=1250 checksum=...

options.detail: CI-friendly, already works, but does not prove raylib/window/audio. This is the current smoke slice, not the full flagship.
options.code: game.run(scene, replay: replay)

options.name: Display-required native test only
options.detail: Proves raylib but makes CI fragile and excludes headless machines.
options.code: JET_RAYLIB_DISPLAY=1 cargo test --test slices

options.name: External C FFI example instead of core.raylib
options.detail: Uses existing C link plumbing but bypasses the ratified first-party core.raylib surface, weakening the standard-library story.
options.code: use c.raylib as rl

comparisons.note: Examples open windows directly; CI usually compiles or runs under xvfb/headless.
Separates app logic from render backend so headless tests can verify gameplay.

decisions.comment: I don’t want flagship slices to be included in CI. They should be checked and functional but not run every time we push

decisions.title: jetos bootloader and kernel defaults
decisions.gist: Choose the first real boot path for jetos systems.
decisions.story: Doris is replacing a NixOS laptop with jetos. She wants one config to build a bootable machine, while her admin teammate needs to see and override the kernel, initrd, and bootloader facts before switch.

options.name: systemd-boot + Linux LTS (recommended)
options.detail: Default UEFI path is systemd-boot, kernel is Linux LTS, initrd is generated from declared filesystems/secrets/services. Expert options can select a kernel package and boot entry fields, but the semantic model stays one boot graph.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.loader: .SystemdBoot,
    boot.kernel: .LinuxLts,
    boot.initrd.modules: ["virtio_blk", "ext4"],
]

options.name: GRUB-first Linux
options.detail: Default boot path is GRUB for broad firmware compatibility. UEFI/systemd-boot remains an override. This prioritizes one mature multi-firmware bootloader as the first target.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.loader: .Grub,
    boot.kernel: .LinuxLts,
]

options.name: Kernel-install abstraction
options.detail: jetos records a boot graph and lets a backend choose systemd-boot or GRUB from firmware facts. Users see boot intent, experts can pin the backend.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.backend: .Auto,
    boot.kernel: .LinuxLts,
]

comparisons.note: NixOS exposes boot.loader.* and boot.kernelPackages as ordinary module options.
Kernel and bootloader are managed by system packages plus grubby/kernel-install.

decisions.comment: I want to use the limine boot loader and cachyos kernel

decisions.title: jetos plan proof provenance API
decisions.gist: Choose how tools read exact jetos plan, proof, and provenance facts.
decisions.story: Hank runs jetos Studio in CI review mode. The GUI and pipeline must read the same plan, diff, provenance, proof, health, and rollback facts that `jet os switch` enforces, with no private GUI state.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os plan halcyon --json > plan.json
$ jet os proof halcyon --json > proof.json
$ jetos studio
# Studio shows the same plan/proof/provenance artifacts and exact source diff

options.name: Artifacts only
options.detail: Build writes stable JSON files under each generation; users inspect files directly. Lowest surface area, but no canonical command for Studio/CI to refresh proof.
options.code:
.jet/systems/generations/<name>/plan.json
proof.json
provenance.json

options.name: jet os plan/proof (recommended)
options.detail: Add read-only `jet os plan` and `jet os proof` verbs that emit the same stable JSON artifacts build/switch uses. Studio and CI call the verbs; switch still enforces the artifacts.
options.code:
$ jet os plan halcyon --json
$ jet os proof halcyon --json
$ jet os build halcyon

options.name: jet dossier os lens
options.detail: Use the broader D-WD dossier umbrella: `jet dossier os` exposes human and JSON plan/proof sections. Nice consolidation, but less direct for OS workflows.
options.code: $ jet dossier os halcyon --json --section proof

comparisons.note: nixos-rebuild shows a derivation path and switch result, but plan/provenance are scattered across store paths and logs.
kubectl diff/apply separates plan from apply and exposes machine-readable objects.
comparisons.code:
kubectl diff -f system.yaml
kubectl apply -f system.yaml -o json

decisions.title: jetos installer user flow
decisions.gist: Choose how the installer asks for disk and host choices.
decisions.story: Betty boots a jetos USB on a new laptop. She wants a guided install that does not mention package graphs, while Earl installing servers needs a scripted path that writes the same transaction and proof.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os image installer halcyon
$ jet os vm install halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
# guided default: ext4 root, host halcyon, rollback generation recorded

options.name: Guided plus scripted (recommended)
options.detail: One installer transaction model. Beginner guided path asks host and disk; expert CLI feeds the same transaction non-interactively. Both produce the same proof.
options.code:
Install mode: Guided | Scripted
$ jet os install halcyon --disk /dev/vda --mode guided

options.name: Scripted first
options.detail: Only a CLI installer is shipped first; graphical/guided UI layers later. Good for CI, weak for beginner drop-in replacement.
options.code: $ jet os install halcyon --disk /dev/vda --yes

options.name: Studio installer first
options.detail: The installer is a Studio flow from the start. Best visual continuity, but couples boot media readiness to GUI stack maturity.
options.code: $ jetos studio --installer

comparisons.note: Graphical installers are separate from declarative rebuild; manual install is script-heavy.
Guided install first, advanced storage path available.

decisions.title: jetos installer media format
decisions.gist: Choose the bootable installer artifact format.
decisions.story: Walter wants to download one file, boot it in QEMU, and later write it to a USB stick. CI also needs the same artifact to install onto a virtual disk and reboot.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os image installer halcyon
# writes jetos-installer-x64.iso plus SHA/provenance
$ qemu-system-x86_64 -cdrom jetos-installer-x64.iso -drive file=disk.qcow2,format=qcow2

options.name: Hybrid ISO first (recommended)
options.detail: Primary artifact is a bootable ISO named by D-JPK-OSBRAND1. It boots QEMU and physical USB paths; installed disk remains qcow2/raw as target output.
options.code:
jetos-installer-x64.iso
install-target: halcyon.qcow2

options.name: Raw disk image first
options.detail: Installer media is a raw disk image. Simple to dd and boot, but less standard for virtual CD installer workflows.
options.code: jetos-installer-x64.raw

options.name: QCOW2 appliance first
options.detail: Ship a prebuilt VM appliance as the first artifact. Useful for demos; not an installer replacement for physical machines.
options.code: jetos-halcyon.qcow2

comparisons.note: NixOS publishes ISO install media and can also build VM images.
ISO is the universal live/install artifact; VM disk images are separate.

decisions.title: jetos VM install proof command
decisions.gist: Choose the command that runs QEMU install and reboot proof.
decisions.story: Mara changes filesystem and service options. Before switch, CI must boot an installer, install to a blank virtual disk, reboot from that disk, and verify the guest with one command.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
# boots installer ISO, installs, reboots from disk, runs guest checks, writes vm-proof.json

options.name: jet os vm prove (recommended)
options.detail: Dedicated OS sub-verb makes VM proof discoverable and keeps install/reboot semantics under jetos. It writes the artifact switch and Studio consume.
options.code: $ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2 --reboot

options.name: jet os image --prove-vm
options.detail: Attach proof to image build. Good when every proof starts from media, but hides the fact that proof is a separate install/reboot run.
options.code: $ jet os image installer halcyon --prove-vm

options.name: jet prove os
options.detail: Use the broader proof product namespace. Good long-term umbrella, less direct for installer acceptance.
options.code: $ jet prove os halcyon --vm-install

comparisons.note: NixOS has VM tests, but usually through Nix expressions and Python driver code.
Packer drives QEMU installs through a declarative template.

decisions.title: jetos VM and installer external tools
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos may depend on QEMU and image-building tools.
decisions.story: Olive runs CI on a clean Linux runner. jetos needs QEMU, firmware, and ISO/disk image utilities, but the compiler must not grow linked external dependencies or silently use random host tools.
decisions.inWild:
devShell: qemu, OVMF, xorriso, dosfstools, e2fsprogs
$ jet os vm prove halcyon --offline
