# tool provenance appears in proof.json

options.name: Pinned tool packages (recommended)
options.detail: QEMU, firmware, ISO, and filesystem tools are Jetpack-realized tool packages with versions and hashes in provenance. Dev shell may provide them, but proof records exact tools.
options.code:
tools: [core.qemu, core.ovmf, core.xorriso, core.e2fsprogs]
proof.toolchain.tools[].sha256

options.name: Host tools with diagnostics
options.detail: Use PATH tools when present and fail with Jet diagnostics when missing. Simple for local dev, weaker provenance.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove halcyon
Error: qemu-system-x86_64 not found

options.name: Nix-only test harness
options.detail: VM proof runs only through `nix develop`/nixpkgs tools. Good immediate reproducibility, conflicts with no-Nix jetos direction.
options.code: $ nix develop -c jet os vm prove halcyon

comparisons.note: Image and VM tests use build inputs from nixpkgs, captured in derivations.
Packer shells out to QEMU and expects the executable/plugins installed.

decisions.title: jetos standard system tree surface
decisions.gist: Choose the full standard OS option tree for users, groups, secrets, boot, and health.
decisions.story: Earl is moving a workstation from NixOS. Packages and networking are not enough: he needs users, groups, filesystems, services, secrets, boot facts, and health checks in one source-backed tree Studio can edit.

options.name: Full-word option namespaces (recommended)
options.detail: Extend D-JPK-OSNS with clear full-word namespaces: users, groups, secrets, boot, kernel, init, health, plus existing filesystem, network, packages, services. One option declaration/setting mechanism; generated Linux files are projections.
options.code:
options: [
    users.nate.normal: true,
    groups.wheel.members: [users.nate],
    secrets.wifi.source: "secrets/wifi.age",
    boot.loader: .SystemdBoot,
    health.openssh.command: "systemctl is-active sshd",
]

options.name: Dedicated top-level System records
options.detail: Add top-level System fields such as users:, groups:, filesystems:, networking:, secrets:, boot:, health:. More structured at the top level, but it creates a second setting mechanism beside option declarations.

options.name: Keep three namespaces only
options.detail: Keep filesystem/network/packages and encode other facts through services or generated files. This preserves current narrow law but cannot honestly replace NixOS-class systems.

comparisons.note: NixOS has a broad option tree with users, services, boot, fileSystems, networking, and systemd.
Linux splits users/groups/files into separate declarative files; jetos can project one canonical tree into those files.

decisions.title: jetos CachyOS kernel source
decisions.gist: Choose where jetos gets the CachyOS kernel it boots.
decisions.story: Doris chose Limine and the CachyOS kernel for her jetos laptop. The generation proof must name the exact kernel, initrd inputs, patches, and hashes, so the installer can boot the same kernel in QEMU and on hardware.

options.name: First-party kernel package
options.detail: Jet carries or vendors a first-party CachyOS kernel package recipe with exact source, config, patches, initrd inputs, and hashes. Beginners still type `.CachyOS`; experts can audit and override the package path.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.kernel: .CachyOS,
]

proof.kernel.source = "jetos:cachyos-kernel"
proof.kernel.hash = "sha256:..."

options.name: External CachyOS binary repo
options.detail: Jet trusts a pinned CachyOS binary kernel artifact source. Fast to verify and boot when signatures are available, but provenance depends on the external release channel and signature policy.
options.code:
options: [
    boot.kernel: .CachyOS,
]

proof.kernel.source = "cachyos:<version>"
proof.kernel.signature = "..."

options.name: Policy-selected kernel package
options.detail: `.CachyOS` is an alias resolved by project policy to a pinned kernel package. Beginners get the default; expert teams can point the alias at a reviewed package without changing system modules.
options.code:
kernelPolicy.default.CachyOS: packages.cachyos-kernel

options: [
    boot.kernel: .CachyOS,
]

proof.kernel.policy = "kernelPolicy.default.CachyOS"

comparisons.note: NixOS selects a kernel package from nixpkgs or overlays; proofs are derivation/store-path based.
CachyOS distributes kernel packages through package repositories signed by repo keys.

decisions.title: How should Canvas persist manual layout and comment regions while staying source-backed?
decisions.gist: Blueprint users expect draggable nodes and comment boxes. Canvas law forbids a hidden graph asset or semantic sidecar. We need one shared mechanism for durable layout/comment intent that preserves Jet source as truth.
decisions.explainer: Deterministic layout alone is reproducible but feels less like Blueprint. A binary or JSON sidecar gives perfect visual freedom but violates Canvas acceptance. Source-anchored metadata comments can carry shared visual intent while remaining ordinary source, formatter-visible, reviewable, and removable.
decisions.story: I drag a group of nodes into a readable cluster, draw a comment box named "damage path", commit the file, and another developer opens Canvas. They should see the intent without needing a hidden Canvas asset.
decisions.inWild:
// canvas:region title="damage path" color="#2f80ed" anchors=[span-120-260]
// regular Jet source below remains the only semantic truth
decisions.detail: Devil pass: comments are the hardest source-backed feature. Free-floating geometry cannot round-trip through code naturally. The shared artifact must be text-reviewable and non-semantic; per-user viewport state must stay local.

options.name: Source-anchored hints plus local view cache (recommended)
options.detail: Persist shared layout/comment intent as ordinary Jet comments anchored to source spans. Keep per-user pan/zoom/selection/MRU local. Formatter preserves comments; Canvas ignores hints if stale and falls back to deterministic layout.
options.code:
// canvas:node span=120..180 pos=(420,160)
// canvas:comment span=120..260 title="damage path" color="#2f80ed"

options.name: Deterministic layout only
options.detail: No shared manual positions or regions. Safest source model, but misses expected Blueprint UX for organizing large graphs.
options.code: // no layout hints; graph always auto-layouts from source

options.name: External layout sidecar
options.detail: Store exact geometry in a Canvas file/cache. Best visual fidelity, but conflicts with no hidden source of truth and creates drift/review problems.
options.code: main.jet + main.jet.canvas.json

comparisons.note: Blueprint stores graph layout in the Blueprint asset, which Jet Canvas explicitly cannot copy as hidden semantic storage.

decisions.title: What should Canvas do when a user connects compatible but different pin types?
decisions.gist: Blueprint inserts auto-cast nodes for compatible mismatched pins. Jet must avoid invisible second semantics while preserving the authoring speed of drag-to-connect.
decisions.explainer: Canvas can make conversion authoring fast without making conversion implicit. The graph may suggest and insert a visible conversion node/call that writes ordinary Jet source, or use a compiler-ratified canonical coercion if one exists.
decisions.story: I drag an Int pin into a Float input. Canvas should help me finish the graph, but source review must show the conversion rather than hiding it in graph metadata.
decisions.inWild:
let speed_f = Float.from(speed_i)
move(speed: speed_f)
decisions.detail: Devil pass: Blueprint comfort comes from magic casts, but invisible conversions are exactly where source-backed trust fails. Wrong connections must be impossible; helpful conversions must be explicit.

options.name: Visible conversion nodes only (recommended)
options.detail: Drag-to-connect opens a compatible conversion menu. Selecting one inserts a visible conversion node/call and writes source. Compiler-ratified canonical coercions may render as a small inline conversion badge.
options.code: Float.from(count)

options.name: Allow limited implicit Canvas-only autocasts
options.detail: Canvas creates graph-only cast edges for friendly cases. Fast, but creates behavior source readers cannot see.
options.code: count -> Float input // graph-only cast

options.name: No conversion help
options.detail: Reject every mismatched pin. Safest, but worse than Blueprint and slower than text editing.
options.code: error: expected Float, got Int

comparisons.note: Compatible mismatched pin links create an autocast node.
comparisons.code: Int pin -> Float pin creates conversion node

decisions.title: What is Canvas parity for Blueprint collapsed graphs and macros?
decisions.gist: Blueprint has collapsed graphs and macros. Jet already has functions/blocks and has not ratified user macro semantics for Canvas. We need Blueprint organization power without a duplicate semantic mechanism.
decisions.explainer: Collapse should be an editor organization and refactor workflow over source spans. Reusable behavior should become ordinary Jet functions. Visual-only collapse can exist only when it expands back to the same source block without hidden semantics.
decisions.story: I select a validation chain, collapse it to one node while sketching, then either expand it again or extract it into a helper function before committing.
decisions.inWild: fn validate_order(order: Order) -> Result<Order, Problem> { ... }
decisions.detail: Devil pass: macros duplicate functions and become a second language. Canvas should use extract/inline and source blocks first; a separate macro surface belongs behind a later owner decision.

options.name: Collapse as source block; reuse as extract-to-fn (recommended)
options.detail: Collapsed node is a view over a source span. Reusable collapse extracts an ordinary helper function. Tunnel pins are projected params/returns/captures.
options.code: fn helper(a: A) -> B { ... }

options.name: Add visual macro surface now
options.detail: Implement macro nodes with arbitrary tunnels and reuse. Powerful, but creates unratified semantics and risks I8 duplication.
options.code: macro ValidateOrder(...) { ... }

options.name: No collapse until macro design exists
options.detail: Avoids semantic risk, but loses essential Blueprint organization.
options.code: // large graph only

comparisons.note: Macros are reusable collapsed node networks with tunnel nodes and multiple exec outputs.

decisions.title: How should Canvas represent Blueprint-style event graphs in Jet?
decisions.gist: Choose the temporary Canvas projection policy while first-party Event/Hook semantics are decided in D-EVENT1.
decisions.explainer: Canvas does not own event semantics. The core event system is tracked by #286 / D-EVENT1. Canvas can only project ordinary callback functions now, then project the ratified Event/Hook model later.
decisions.story: I add a BeginPlay-like callback in Canvas. In source, I should see the ordinary Jet function that the framework calls, with no hidden asset-owned event body.
decisions.detail: Superseded by owner steer 2026-07-07: event system is a major first-party core language/runtime feature, not a Canvas subset. Canvas #281 is blocked by #286 / D-EVENT1. This Canvas ballot should not decide event semantics; it only decides projection behavior while the core model is pending.

options.name: Event views over ordinary callback functions
options.detail: Canvas groups framework-recognized functions into Event Graph views. Adding an event writes the ordinary function signature from the framework API. This is source-backed and safe today, but only covers callback-style events until the Event/Hook library exists.
options.code: fn on_tick(dt: Duration) { ... }

options.name: New event declaration syntax
options.detail: Add user-typeable event declarations. Ergonomic, but a syntax/API gate and premature before the runtime event model is ratified.
options.code: event Tick(dt: Duration) { ... }

options.name: No event graph concept
options.detail: Canvas only shows functions. Source-pure but fails Blueprint parity.
options.code: fn main() { ... }

options.name: Hybrid: callback views now, first-class Event/Hook model next (recommended)
options.detail: Canvas ships event graphs as views over ordinary callback functions now. In parallel, a separate Event/Hook runtime design defines typed payloads, subscription handles, lifecycle ownership, sync/async dispatch, hook phases, cancellation, backpressure, failure policy, debugger traces, and Canvas projection. Once ratified, Canvas event nodes project the same Event/Hook semantics instead of inventing a UI-only event system.

comparisons.note: Event Graphs expose engine events such as BeginPlay and Tick as nodes.

decisions.title: Where should Canvas store breakpoints and watches?
decisions.gist: Blueprint persists breakpoints and watches in editor state. Canvas must support debugger parity while preserving source truth and avoiding accidental committed debug noise.
decisions.explainer: Breakpoints and watches are not program semantics. They should be local dev state anchored to source spans by default, with optional explicit source annotations only if the user wants team-shared debugging probes.
decisions.story: I set a breakpoint on a Canvas node, reload, and it still lands on the same source span. It should not silently edit my program unless I explicitly choose a shared probe.
decisions.inWild:
~/.jet/canvas/debug-state/... anchors source hash + span
// optional later: #[debug_probe] if ratified separately
decisions.detail: Devil pass: source-span drift will destroy trust. Local state must validate source hashes and degrade to invalid breakpoint/warning state when stale.

options.name: Local source-span debug state with explicit shared probes later (recommended)
options.detail: Store breakpoints/watches locally, anchored by file hash and source span. Stale anchors become invalid. Team-shared probes require explicit source annotations in a later decision.

options.name: Always write debug annotations to source
options.detail: Reviewable and portable, but pollutes source with personal debug state.
options.code: #[breakpoint] call()

options.name: Session-only debug state
options.detail: No persistence risk, but misses basic debugger UX.
options.code: // lost after reload

comparisons.note: Blueprint breakpoints persist in editor ini files and can become invalid until compile.

decisions.title: What source-control model should Canvas expose?
decisions.gist: Blueprint integrates asset checkout/diff workflows. Jet source is text-first and Git-first. Canvas needs conflict safety without adopting asset-lock semantics as truth.
decisions.explainer: Canvas should surface Git text state, transaction diffs, stale revisions, and conflict reloads first. Lock/check-out UI can be an optional adapter over enterprise VCS, not a Canvas storage model.
decisions.story: Before applying a graph edit, I want to preview the exact Jet source diff and know whether my graph projection is stale relative to disk or Git.
decisions.inWild:
Canvas transaction preview:
- let x = old()
+ let x = new()
decisions.detail: Devil pass: asset-style checkout encourages thinking the graph is the artifact. The artifact is the Jet file; Canvas diff must make that obvious.

options.name: Git text diff plus stale transaction guard (recommended)
options.detail: Show exact source diffs, dirty markers, history hooks, and stale edit rejection. Optional lock/check-out adapters may wrap external VCS later.
options.code: git diff -- Source/main.jet

options.name: Blueprint-style checkout abstraction
options.detail: Expose check-out/check-in/lock as the primary workflow. Familiar to Unreal users, but wrong default for Jet source.
options.code: Check Out Canvas Graph

options.name: No source-control UI
options.detail: Keep scope narrow, but misses required stale/conflict UX.
options.code: // rely on terminal git only

comparisons.note: Editor source control supports checkout, status icons, history, and depot diff for assets.

decisions.title: What Canvas extension API is allowed for third-party nodes?
decisions.gist: Blueprint exposes C++ functions and libraries as node palette entries. Jet needs package/function projection and plugin extensibility without creating an unsafe second compiler or hidden behavior layer.
decisions.explainer: The first extension boundary should be facts and metadata: palette entries, docs, schemas, examples, and links to ordinary Jet functions. Providers that execute code, rewrite source, or define new semantics need a separate safety/protocol decision.
decisions.story: A package should make its Jet functions appear as Canvas nodes with docs and pin types, but the call still writes an ordinary Jet function call.
decisions.inWild:
package math exposes fn clamp(x: Float, lo: Float, hi: Float) -> Float
Canvas palette shows clamp node from semindex facts
decisions.detail: Devil pass: plugin nodes can become a second language. Start read-only and source-producing only through ratified edit transactions.

options.name: Read-only palette/schema providers first (recommended)
options.detail: Packages expose ordinary Jet functions/types/docs. Canvas projects them into palette nodes and writes normal calls. No provider-defined behavior or side effects.
options.code: clamp(x, lo, hi)

options.name: Behavior-producing node providers
options.detail: Plugins can define custom node behavior and edit actions. Powerful, but needs safety, protocol, capability, and diagnostics design.
options.code: plugin node emits custom source transform

options.name: No extensibility API
options.detail: Safest short term, but prevents function-library parity.
options.code: // built-in nodes only

comparisons.note: BlueprintCallable/Pure functions and function libraries expose C++ APIs as nodes.

decisions.title: What is Jet's first-party event system semantic model?
decisions.gist: Choose the core event model Jet should standardize for games, web UI, servers, plugins, hooks, Canvas, and debugging.
decisions.explainer: Events touch too many domains to be a Canvas-only affordance. Jet needs one source-visible, type-safe, lifetime-safe event model that beginners can use with one line and experts can tune for dispatch, ordering, cancellation, async, backpressure, and failure policy.
decisions.story: Doris is building a game HUD and a server dashboard in the same Jet codebase. A button click, a collision, a save hook, and a hot-reload notification should all use the same typed event model, so Canvas, source, debugger, and tests agree on what happened.
decisions.detail: Audit pass: C# gives typed delegates/events but weak lifetime/async policy; DOM gives phases, once/passive, and AbortSignal cleanup but stringly/weak typing; Node EventEmitter is tiny but stringly and has special error/async traps; Godot signals fit games/editor UX but can stay dynamically loose; UnityEvent gives designer-persistent callbacks but ties truth to scene/editor data; Unreal dispatchers feel right visually but live in Blueprint assets. Jet should take typed delegates, signal/editor projection, AbortSignal-style lifetime cleanup, explicit phases/options, and structured-concurrency integration while rejecting stringly names, hidden graph assets, untyped payloads, and unhandled async failures.

options.name: Library-only Event and Hook values
options.detail: Ship Event<T>, Hook<T,R>, Subscription, EventScope, and EventPolicy as ordinary Core/runtime types. No special syntax, no compiler-known event diagnostics beyond normal typing. Smallest language surface, but tools/debugger may not get enough semantic facts unless we later make the library magical.

options.name: Language-level event declarations
options.detail: Add first-class user syntax for declaring events and hooks. Excellent readability and toolability, but risks a new mechanism before the semantic model is proven and creates syntax churn across domains.
options.code:
event clicked(Click)
hook before_save(SaveRequest) -> SaveDecision

options.name: Actor/mailbox/channel-first events
options.detail: Treat events as typed messages delivered to actors/tasks. Strong for concurrency and servers, but awkward for UI/game editor workflows where direct owner lifetimes, inspector wiring, and hooks matter.

options.name: Hybrid Event/Hook family: typed values, compiler-known facts, syntax reserved (recommended)
options.detail: Build Event<T>, Hook<T,R>, Subscription, EventScope, and EventPolicy as ordinary source-visible values, but make the family compiler/tooling-known for diagnostics, debugger traces, Canvas projection, ownership cleanup, async/failure checks, and docs. Reserve user syntax only after real examples prove library spelling is too noisy. One semantic model serves beginner clicks, game collisions, web lifecycle, server hooks, plugin interception, and expert async/backpressure policies.

comparisons.note: Typed delegates/events, many subscribers, sync invocation by default; lifetime leaks and async policy are not solved by the event type.
EventTarget has phases, once/passive options, and AbortSignal cleanup, but event names are strings and handlers receive generic Event objects.
Signals are editor-friendly and first-class enough for games, but payload/arity checking can remain a runtime/user responsibility.
Event Dispatchers feel right in visual scripting but are tied to Blueprint assets; Jet needs source-owned semantics.
comparisons.code: Bind Event to StartFire; Call StartFire

decisions.title: jetos Studio GUI host runtime
decisions.gist: Choose what runs the jetos Studio window.
decisions.story: Betty opens jetos Studio on a fresh laptop to enable OpenSSH and add her user. She expects a real visual control center, while Earl needs the same screen to be scriptable in CI review mode and auditable as exact Jet source, diff, plan, proof, and provenance.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon
# opens Studio: guided controls + source + diff + provenance

$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon --serve 127.0.0.1:7417
# same projection service available to browser, CI screenshots, and future native shell
decisions.detail: Two-facet pass: beginners need one command that opens a usable GUI with no package-manager ceremony. Experts need an inspectable local protocol, stable JSON facts, deterministic screenshots, and no GUI-owned semantics. The host choice must not create a second configuration language or hide state outside Jet source/proof artifacts.

options.name: Local projection service plus bundled browser shell (recommended)
options.detail: Studio starts a local Jet-owned projection/edit service and opens a first-party web UI in the system browser by default; a bundled native webview shell may wrap the same local protocol when available. One semantic backend powers GUI, browser, CI screenshots, and future native packaging. No hidden GUI state; all edits still write source transactions.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon
opened http://127.0.0.1:7417/studio/halcyon

$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon --headless --screenshot proof.png
# same service, deterministic UI artifact for review

options.name: Native Canvas shell only
options.detail: Studio is implemented as a native Canvas app from the start. Strong visual continuity with Canvas, but Studio readiness becomes coupled to the native Canvas runtime and cannot fall back to a simple browser review surface.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon
# opens native Canvas-backed Studio window
# no browser/local web protocol is part of the contract

options.name: Browser-only local server
options.detail: Studio is always a local web app served by jetos. Simple, source-visible, and CI-friendly, but users do not get a desktop-app window or OS integration unless another layer is designed later.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon
Studio listening at http://127.0.0.1:7417
# user opens browser manually or via auto-open

options.name: External desktop shell dependency
options.detail: Studio ships through an Electron/Tauri-style shell as the primary host. Rich desktop packaging, but the host adds external runtime/tooling authority that must be pinned and audited separately from the jetos projection service.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon
# launches packaged desktop shell
proof.host.runtime = "external-shell:<version/hash>"

comparisons.note: NixOS has CLI and module files as the canonical path; GUI configuration tools are not the source of truth.
A browser UI projects API objects and sends ordinary API edits; the API object remains truth.
A local service/webview style can power desktop UI and browser/remoting from one protocol.

decisions.title: jetos CachyOS kernel bootstrap source
decisions.gist: Choose how the first-party CachyOS kernel package gets real bootable bits for VM/install proof.
decisions.explainer: D-JOS-KERNELSRC1=A says .CachyOS resolves to a first-party package. #263 now needs that package to contain real kernel/initrd artifacts, not fixture text, so QEMU can boot and reboot installed jetos.
decisions.story: Doris selected Limine plus CachyOS. She expects jet os vm prove to boot the same kernel the installed machine will boot. Earl needs the proof to show exact source, config, patches, hashes, and whether any binary artifact was trusted.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
# proof.kernel.source, proof.kernel.config, proof.kernel.hash, proof.initrd.hash
# guest boots the same payload recorded in generation boot/facts.json
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: users still write boot.kernel: .CachyOS or use the default; no package-source ceremony. Expert pass: the package exposes source/config/patch/provenance and can be replaced by policy later. Hybrid pass: one first-party package mechanism feeds build, ISO, VM proof, and installed boot; no separate test kernel.

options.name: Source-built first-party package (recommended)
options.detail: Jet vendors/declares the CachyOS kernel recipe, config, patches, and initrd inputs, then builds boot artifacts into the first-party cachyos-kernel package. Proof records source hashes and build inputs.

options.name: Pinned signed binary bootstrap
options.detail: Jet pins CachyOS kernel/initrd binary packages plus signatures as the first boot source, with source-built recipe still tracked as the replacement target. Fastest honest VM proof, weaker than source-built provenance.
options.code:
proof.kernel.source = "cachyos-binary:<version>"
proof.kernel.signature = "valid"
proof.native_replacement = "source recipe"

options.name: Temporary generic Linux kernel
options.detail: Use a pinned generic Linux kernel only for installer/VM proof until CachyOS packaging lands. This proves the installer path but violates the selected default users will boot.
options.code:
boot.kernel: .CachyOS
vm.kernel = linuxPackages.kernel  # proof-only override

comparisons.note: NixOS kernels are derivation-built from source or overlays; VM tests boot those store paths.
CachyOS distributes signed binary kernel packages; users trust repository signatures unless rebuilding locally.

decisions.title: What authority boundary should behavior-producing Canvas actions use?
decisions.gist: Choose how package-supplied Canvas actions may run, edit source, and request authority. Read-only palette entries are just projected Jet functions/types. Behavior-producing actions need an explicit boundary.
decisions.explainer: Rename the extension pieces: a palette entry is metadata projected from ordinary Jet code; a Canvas action is package-supplied behavior that can propose edits or run a preview; an external adapter is a native/tool bridge and must be opt-in. The best hybrid is sandboxed Jet Canvas actions that reuse Jet's existing front end, executable TIR, and JIT for immediate run/preview. Canvas never gets a second compiler or runtime: actions return source transactions or preview requests, Canvas validates through formatter/sema, and AOT remains the build/export path.
decisions.story: Doris installs a physics package. Canvas shows `simulate_step` as a normal node from Jet function facts. If she asks Canvas to set up the simulation graph, the package's Canvas action runs immediately in the Jet JIT sandbox, returns an ordinary source diff, and Canvas rechecks it before writing. Earl can audit the action id, package version, authority list, touched files, generated diff, JIT run result, and whether any external adapter was requested.
decisions.inWild:
package physics exposes:
- palette entry: fn simulate_step(world: &World, dt: Float) -> World
- Canvas action: create_simulation_setup(ctx) -> CanvasEdit ? String
- execution: Jet front end -> executable TIR -> JIT sandbox for preview/run
- write: returned source transaction only, then formatter + sema recheck
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: installing a package makes useful nodes appear; simple actions just work, and prompts appear only when an action asks for extra authority. Expert pass: every action has package id/version/hash, authority manifest, source diff, touched files, diagnostics, JIT/AOT parity evidence, cache key, and audit log. Hybrid pass: one semantic mechanism covers both surfaces: Jet source remains truth, the existing compiler/JIT executes previews, and Canvas accepts only validated Jet diffs. No separate Canvas VM, graph asset, broad editor extension host, or hidden proc-macro-like code execution.

options.name: Static palette entries and edit templates
options.detail: Packages publish metadata and declarative edit templates only. No package code runs inside Canvas. Excellent for audit and simple function-library parity, but cannot perform package-specific analysis, dynamic setup, preview computation, or smart source rewrites.

options.name: Sandboxed Jet Canvas actions using existing JIT (recommended)
options.detail: A package declares ordinary Jet action functions with explicit `canvas.action` authority. Canvas invokes them through the existing checked TIR/JIT path for immediate preview/run. The action cannot write files directly; it returns a CanvasEdit, source diff, diagnostics, or preview value. Canvas then formats, sema-checks, records audit metadata, and rejects undeclared file/tool/network/unsafe authority.

options.name: External adapters for native tools
options.detail: Packages may ship out-of-process adapters for heavyweight native/tool integrations. They run only after an explicit capability prompt naming files, tools, network, cache, and unsafe needs. Canvas still accepts only returned source transactions. Useful as an expert tier, too much authority for the default path.
options.code:
canvas.adapter = "physics-nodegen"
capabilities = ["tool:physicsc", "read:assets/physics", "canvas.source_edit:project"]

Canvas prompt: physics-nodegen wants tool + project edit authority.

comparisons.note: BlueprintCallable exposes compiled engine/module C++ as nodes. Powerful and fast, but authority is bundled with the native module. Jet should copy the palette power, not the broad native trust model.
comparisons.code:
UFUNCTION(BlueprintCallable)
void SimulateStep(UWorld* World, float Dt);

comparisons.note: Extensions run arbitrary extension-host code with broad workspace/process reach, then rely on marketplace trust and workspace trust. Canvas actions should be narrower: declared authority, source-diff output, Jet validation.
Proc macros execute compiler-plugin code and emit tokens during compilation. Canvas must avoid that hidden execution model; actions run as audited Jet code and produce explicit diffs/previews.
Plugins/scripts can mutate documents directly after user trust. Canvas should not grant direct graph mutation; action output is proposed Jet source, then checked.

decisions.title: jetos interactive VM launch command
decisions.gist: Choose how a user opens an installed jetos VM.
decisions.story: Betty has just built a jetos ISO and wants to try the system like a normal OS: boot it, log in, open a terminal, and later start the desktop. Earl needs the same path in CI with exact QEMU args and proof artifacts, without inventing a second runtime separate from `jet os vm prove`.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os image installer halcyon
$ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
$ jet os vm run halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
# opens QEMU on the installed disk; serial/TTY login uses the same generation proof

options.name: prove plus run (recommended)
options.detail: `jet os vm prove` remains the non-interactive install/reboot proof. `jet os vm run` opens the same installed disk for human use, defaulting to terminal/serial first and later desktop when declared. One harness model feeds proof, CI, and manual use.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
proved jetos VM install/reboot ...

$ jet os vm run halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
booting halcyon generation known-good
login: nate
$ jet --version

options.name: prove with interactive flag
options.detail: Keep one verb and add `--interactive`. This avoids a second command, but mixes proof mode and human launch mode in one spelling; CI and users must remember a mode flag.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2 --interactive
# install/prove first if needed, then leave QEMU open

options.name: studio launches VMs
options.detail: Make Studio the primary human launch path and keep CLI proof-only. Good GUI continuity, but terminal-first users and CI lose a simple command-line launch surface.
options.code:
$ jetos studio ./machines --host halcyon
# click Run VM
# CLI still has only `jet os vm prove`

options.name: emit QEMU script only
options.detail: Proof writes `run-vm.sh` and users execute it themselves. Fully auditable, but beginners do not get a first-class `jetos` launch command.
options.code:
$ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
wrote systems/vm-proofs/halcyon/run-vm.sh
$ ./systems/vm-proofs/halcyon/run-vm.sh

comparisons.note: NixOS can build runnable VM scripts beside test drivers; the script and test share system config.
Packer proves and builds images, while users often run QEMU directly afterward.

decisions.title: jetos default desktop session
decisions.gist: Choose what desktop/window manager a jetos VM boots into.
decisions.story: Betty boots the jetos VM after proving install/reboot. She wants a real graphical session with a terminal and jetos Studio available from the system, not a proof-only shell. Earl needs the same session to be declarative, auditable, and replaceable by policy for workstation images.
decisions.inWild:
system.halcyon: {
    services.desktop.enable: true,
    services.desktop.profile: .Default,
}

$ jet os vm prove halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
$ jet os vm run halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
# graphical login/session starts; terminal + jetos Studio are installed apps

options.name: Wayland-first JetOS session (recommended)
options.detail: Default desktop is one JetOS-owned Wayland session profile: display manager, seat/session service, wlroots-class compositor, terminal, browser fallback, and jetos Studio app. Beginners get a graphical system by enabling one desktop profile; experts can replace compositor, terminal, display manager, and session services through the same `services.*` tree and proof artifacts.
options.code:
services.desktop.profile: .Default
proof.desktop.session = "jetos-wayland"
proof.desktop.apps = ["terminal", "jetos-studio", "browser-fallback"]

options.name: KDE/GNOME profile first
options.detail: Default desktop is a mainstream full DE profile. Familiar for users and good hardware coverage, but JetOS proof becomes centered on a large external desktop policy stack instead of a small canonical JetOS session.
options.code:
services.desktop.profile: .Plasma
proof.desktop.session = "kde-plasma"
proof.desktop.external_policy = "desktop-upstream"

options.name: Terminal-first, desktop deferred
options.detail: The VM stays text-login only for now. This keeps the current terminal proof as the whole acceptance surface, but it does not meet the owner goal of opening a desktop/window-manager JetOS VM.
options.code:
services.desktop.enable: false
$ jet os vm run halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
login: nate
$

options.name: X11-first session
options.detail: Default desktop starts with Xorg plus a lightweight window manager. It supports older software paths, but makes the first JetOS desktop center on the compatibility display server instead of the modern default graphics path.
options.code:
services.desktop.profile: .X11
proof.desktop.session = "xorg+wm"
proof.desktop.compat = true

comparisons.note: NixOS exposes desktop choices declaratively and can enable a display manager plus desktop manager/window manager in the same system config.
Fedora chooses a mainstream Wayland-first GNOME desktop as the default workstation experience.
comparisons.code: default graphical target + GNOME Wayland session

comparisons.note: Small Wayland compositors give a complete desktop session while keeping policy surface compact and inspectable.

decisions.comment: We should prefer wayland, but we will have gnome de by default, with terminal version as the secondary option/fallback. This way beginners get something easy & experts can get exactly what they want

decisions.title: Typed URL and mime modules: core.url + core.mime
decisions.gist: Whether Jet gets typed URL/mime values as new core modules, and under which names.
decisions.explainer: A keeps URL values first-class and discoverable for every consumer (http, web, files, config), and mime is a genuinely separate small domain. Typed values over strings is the owner-preferred direction.
decisions.story: Priya builds a webhook relay in Jet. She concatenates a base URL with a user-supplied path and query params by hand; a space in a param silently produces a bad request that only fails in production. Every serious language gives her a URL type that makes this impossible; today core.http takes raw strings.

options.name: Two modules: core.url + core.mime
options.detail: WHATWG-class typed Url value (parse/build/join/normalize, typed query pairs, per-component percent-encoding, IDNA) plus a small core.mime (extension↔type table, type/subtype+params parsing). core.http/core.web accept Url and mime types.
options.code:
use core.url as url

u := url.parse("https://api.example.com/notify")?
u.query.add("user", "ada lovelace")   // encoded correctly, by construction
http.get(u)?

use core.mime as mime
print(mime.from_extension("png") ?? "application/octet-stream")   // image/png

options.name: core.url only; mime lives inside core.http
options.detail: Same typed Url module; the mime table ships as http.mime helpers since HTTP is its main consumer. One fewer module name; files/static-serving reach through http for mime lookups.
options.code:
use core.url as url
use core.http as http

u := url.parse("https://api.example.com")?
print(http.mime.from_extension("png") ?? "?")

options.name: Fold both into core.http
options.detail: http.url.parse(...) and http.mime.*. No new top-level modules, but URL values are useful far beyond HTTP (file://, data:, config values, core.web) and burying them hurts discovery.
options.code:
use core.http as http

u := http.url.parse("https://api.example.com")?

options.name: Decline — keep strings
options.detail: URLs stay strings with documented escaping helpers in core.encoding. Cheapest surface, but every consumer re-solves encoding and the beginner footgun stays the default, against I1/philosophy.
options.code: raw :: "{base}/notify?user={encoding.percent(user)}"   // remembering to call percent() is on you

comparisons.note: The URL/URLSearchParams pair is the modern reference; browsers ship it built-in.
comparisons.code:
const u = new URL('https://api.example.com/notify');
u.searchParams.set('user', 'ada lovelace');

comparisons.note: net/url is stdlib and universally used; mime is its own stdlib package.
comparisons.code:
u, _ := url.Parse("https://api.example.com")
q := u.Query(); q.Set("user", "ada lovelace"); u.RawQuery = q.Encode()

comparisons.note: urllib.parse is stdlib but string-tuple based and widely considered clunky — the anti-example.

decisions.title: Canonical binary interchange format for core.encoding
decisions.gist: Which single binary serialization format Jet ships beside json/toml/yaml/csv.
decisions.explainer: A: standardization plus a specified deterministic form (hashing/signing/content-addressing all want stable bytes) outweighs MessagePack’s ecosystem edge; one format keeps I8.
decisions.story: Marco's game syncs replay state between a Jet server and clients 60 times a second. JSON is the only interchange format Jet has, so he pays text encode/parse on every tick and his packets are 3x larger than needed. He needs one blessed binary format that works through the same @[Codable] derive — not a menu of five.

options.name: CBOR (RFC 8949)
options.detail: IETF standard with a deterministic-encoding profile (stable bytes for hashing/signing — pairs with crypto.seal and content-addressed stores), native binary strings, and a clean extension model. Same parse/to_string/decode<T> verbs as every other codec.
options.code:
use core.encoding.cbor as cbor

bytes :: cbor.to_bytes(tick)              // [U8], ~1/3 the JSON size
back :: cbor.decode<Tick>(bytes)?

// deterministic profile: same value → same bytes, always
hash :: crypto.sha256(cbor.to_bytes_canonical(tick))

options.name: MessagePack
options.detail: The most popular binary format by ecosystem (Redis, Fluentd, many game stacks). Slightly tighter encoding than CBOR in common cases; no IETF standard, no canonical-form spec — deterministic bytes for hashing would be Jet-invented.
options.code:
use core.encoding.msgpack as msgpack

bytes :: msgpack.to_bytes(tick)
back :: msgpack.decode<Tick>(bytes)?

options.name: Ship both
options.detail: Maximum interop, but two mechanisms for one semantic job — exactly what I8 rejects. Every API that accepts one must document why not the other, forever.
options.code:
use core.encoding.cbor as cbor
use core.encoding.msgpack as msgpack   // which one does your team use? both, eventually

options.name: Decline binary interchange for now
options.detail: JSON stays the only interchange. Games, caches, and IPC keep paying text overhead or hand-rolling formats — the gap every systems language fills in year one.
options.code: // status quo: json.to_string(tick) on a 60Hz loop

comparisons.note: stdlib ships encoding/gob (Go-only) — everyone actually uses CBOR or msgpack third-party; shipping neither pushed the ecosystem off-stdlib.
Codable has JSON + plist only; binary interchange is a long-standing community complaint.
comparisons.code: JSONEncoder() // or a third-party CBOR encoder

comparisons.note: CBOR is the substrate for COSE signing/encryption and WebAuthn — standards momentum is behind it.

decisions.title: Filesystem watch surface and home
decisions.gist: Where filesystem change notifications live and what the beginner surface looks like.
decisions.explainer: A: discovery beats taxonomy — the person with a path in hand is already in core.files; normalize per-OS quirks and debounce by default.
decisions.story: Lena writes a static-site tool in Jet and wants rebuild-on-save. Today she loops fs.list_dir + mtimes on a timer — wasteful, laggy, and subtly wrong on renames. jet dev itself watches files internally; users deserve the same primitive.

options.name: files.watch in core.files
options.detail: One more capability on the module that owns paths: watch(path) returns a WatchHandle whose events() iterate typed changes (Created/Modified/Removed/Renamed). Debounced by default (beginner-safe); raw stream behind an option.

options.name: New core.watch module
options.detail: Separate module name for the whole watching domain (files now; maybe processes/ports later). Cleaner if watching grows beyond files, but today it is one function and a new top-level name to learn.

options.name: Decline — polling helper only
options.detail: Ship files.poll_changes(path, interval) sugar over mtime polling. No OS notification backends to maintain, but it bakes the laggy/wasteful pattern in as the blessed answer.
options.code: loop ev in files.poll_changes("site/", time.ms(500)) { rebuild() }

comparisons.note: fsnotify is the de-facto standard everyone pulls in — Go not shipping it in stdlib is a known gap.
fs.watch is stdlib but semantics vary per-OS; chokidar exists to paper over it — the lesson is to normalize events in the library.

decisions.comment: also include processes and ports now, not later

decisions.title: WebSocket module home
decisions.gist: Where WebSocket client/server support lives.
decisions.explainer: A: upgrade-from-a-route is the dominant real-world shape; keeping it inside core.http gives one import and shared types. Every mainstream stdlib that declined WebSockets regretted it.
decisions.story: Tomás builds a collaborative editor backend in Jet. HTTP endpoints come from core.http; for the live channel he needs WebSockets and finds nothing — he would have to hand-roll the upgrade handshake and frame protocol over raw sockets.

options.name: core.http.ws submodule
options.detail: WebSocket is an HTTP upgrade; it lives where the connection starts. Server: a route handler upgrades; client: ws.connect(url). Shares http types (headers, Url, TLS).

options.name: Standalone core.ws module
options.detail: Own top-level name, imports http types underneath. Slightly more discoverable in a module listing; splits the connection story across two imports for the common server case.

options.name: Decline for this epoch
options.detail: Server-sent events (already in the #301 audit scope) cover server→client push; bidirectional realtime waits. Collaborative/game use cases stay unserved or hand-rolled.
options.code:
// SSE only:
router.get("/live", (req) => http.sse(req, events))

comparisons.note: stdlib has no WebSocket — gorilla/websocket then nhooyr filled it; a decade of "why is this not stdlib".
stdlib has none; websockets/aiohttp fill it. Same story.
WebSocket is just there, next to fetch — the modern expectation Jet should match.

decisions.title: Home for system facts and signal handling
decisions.gist: Which module owns hostname/os/arch/cpu-count and interrupt handling.
decisions.explainer: A: one obvious module name for "facts about this machine/process" plus the safe interrupt hook; keeps core.env honest. Exact signal breadth beyond interrupt stays expert opt-in inside the same module.
decisions.story: Sam writes a build tool in Jet. It wants parallelism = cpu count, a cache dir under the right OS convention, the hostname for log stamps, and a clean ctrl-c that flushes the cache index before exit. None of those are environment variables, but core.env is the only place that sounds close.

options.name: New core.os module
options.detail: os.name()/arch()/hostname()/cpu_count()/temp_dir()/username()/pid(), plus the beginner-safe interrupt hook os.on_interrupt(handler). core.env keeps only environment variables + cwd/home. Matches Go/Python naming instincts.
options.code:
use core.os as os

workers :: os.cpu_count()
print("[{os.hostname()}] building with {workers} workers")
os.on_interrupt(() => { flush_cache(); process.exit(130) })

options.name: Extend core.env
options.detail: Everything lands on the module people already import: env.cpu_count(), env.hostname(), env.on_interrupt(...). No new name to learn, but "env" stops meaning environment variables and the module becomes a junk drawer.
options.code:
use core.env as env

workers :: env.cpu_count()
env.on_interrupt(() => flush_cache())

options.name: Split: facts in core.env, signals in core.process
options.detail: Read-only facts join env; interrupt/signal handling joins core.process (which already owns exit). Each piece lands near a neighbor, but the "where do I look" answer becomes two modules.
options.code:
use core.env as env
use core.process as process

workers :: env.cpu_count()
process.on_interrupt(() => flush_cache())

comparisons.note: os + runtime own this; env vars are one corner of os, not the container.
os/platform/signal split — three modules for one question is the anti-pattern to avoid.
std::env has vars, std::thread::available_parallelism has cpus, hostname needs a crate — famously scattered.

decisions.title: Human formatting: core.fmt module vs interpolation format-specs
decisions.gist: How Jet spells number/bytes/duration formatting — library functions or string-interpolation syntax.
decisions.explainer: C: A’s functions deliver the daily wins (bytes/duration/thousands) with zero syntax risk now, and the spec-sugar question stays a clean future reopen instead of a silent never.
decisions.story: Ana prints a report: file sizes, elapsed times, row counts with thousands separators, floats to 2 decimals. Today interpolation gives her the raw value only, so she writes arithmetic and string surgery by hand for each cell — the tenth time she has done it.

options.name: core.fmt module, functions only
options.detail: fmt.bytes(n), fmt.duration(ms), fmt.number(n, thousands: true, precision: 2), fmt.ordinal(n), fmt.pad/align helpers. No syntax change; composes in interpolation like any call. Locale-aware variants can join later behind the same names.

options.name: Interpolation format-specs
options.detail: Python/Rust-style mini-language inside braces: {x:.2f}, {n:,}, {s:>10}. Terse at the call site, but it is new user-facing syntax (lexer/parser/formatter/S8 interplay), a second sub-language to learn, and covers only what the spec grammar anticipates (no bytes/duration).
options.code:
print("{name}: {size:.1G}B in {elapsed:dur} ({rows:,} rows)")
// every marker is spec grammar to ratify, document, and format-stabilize

options.name: Both: functions now, spec sugar later
options.detail: Ship A; reopen a spec-syntax ballot only if call-site verbosity proves painful in real code. Keeps today’s decision small without closing the door.
options.code:
print("{fmt.number(rows, thousands: true)}")   // today
print("{rows:,}")                              // possible future reopen

options.name: Decline
options.detail: Raw interpolation only. Every report/CLI author keeps hand-rolling the same helpers — a daily papercut in exactly the beginner path Jet optimizes for.
options.code: print("{(size / 1073741824.0)} GB")   // and now round it yourself

comparisons.note: format-spec mini-language is powerful and famously unmemorizable; humanize is a separate library anyway for bytes/durations.
no format-specs in strings; helpers/libraries do it — humanize is one of the most-imported Go packages.
{:>10.2} exists in format! and still no bytes/duration answer without crates.

decisions.comment: full go-style humanize support in the fmt module/lib.

decisions.title: Password hashing surface: crypto.password_hash / password_verify
decisions.gist: Whether Jet ships a misuse-resistant password hashing pair, and what it exposes.
decisions.explainer: A: PHC-string self-description makes upgrades free and misuse hard; matches the ratified misuse-resistant envelope direction (D-CRYPTOENV1) and I1 safe-by-default.
decisions.story: Deb builds her first Jet web app with signup/login. The seal/open envelope (D-CRYPTOENV1) encrypts data but is wrong for passwords; without a blessed surface she will do what beginners do — sha256(password) — which is exactly the breach headline. The stdlib either hands her Argon2id correctly-parameterized, or the footgun is the default.

options.name: Misuse-resistant pair, Argon2id inside
options.detail: crypto.password_hash(pw) -> String encodes algorithm+params+salt in one PHC string (safe defaults, no knobs required); crypto.password_verify(pw, stored) -> Bool re-derives from the stored params — old hashes keep verifying after defaults change. Expert cost overrides via optional args. Backend follows the ratified D-DEP-CRYPTO1 bridge path.

options.name: Expose raw KDF primitives
options.detail: crypto.argon2id(pw, salt, cost…) and friends; users assemble salting/encoding/verification themselves. Full control, but the beginner path is back to holding sharp edges — the opposite of the libsodium lesson.

options.name: Decline — document seal + external services
options.detail: Point auth at hosted identity providers; stdlib ships nothing. Every self-hosted Jet app (the jetos story!) still needs it and will hand-roll worse.
options.code:
// docs: "use an identity provider" — meanwhile:
db.execute("…", [user, crypto.sha256(password)])   // what actually happens

comparisons.note: password_hash/password_verify with self-describing output is the acknowledged best-in-class API shape here — rare praise for PHP.
crypto_pwhash_str/_str_verify — same shape, same reasoning.
both push users to external packages (bcrypt/argon2 crates) — stdlib silence is the common gap, not the standard to copy.

decisions.title: Core filesystem depth surface
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical shape for deep file and path operations.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A keeps one semantic path model: typed Path is the backbone for composition and audit, while core.files keeps beginner-friendly string entrypoints that immediately coerce into Path. This reconciles D-PATHFS1 with today's core.files docs without creating two mechanisms.
decisions.story: Marta writes a static-site publisher. She needs to create nested folders, copy an asset tree, atomically write output, inspect mtimes, skip symlink cycles, and clean a temp directory when the build exits. If Jet gives her only read/write/list_dir, she falls back to brittle string paths and shell commands.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: Path-only purity makes beginner scripts noisy; string-only helpers make expert audit and cycle-safe walking weak. The hybrid is one mechanism because every string entrypoint lowers to Path before sema/codegen effects, docs, and audit facts see it. No aliases: names are stable once ratified.

options.name: Path backbone plus string entrypoints (recommended)
options.detail: Ratify typed Path as the internal and expert surface, and keep core.files string helpers as the beginner facade. Add Stat, FileKind, WalkEntry, TempDir, FileLock, and one canonical operation set: stat, create_dir_all, remove_dir, remove_all, glob, walk, symlink/read_link, hard_link, temp_dir/temp_file, lock, canonicalize, absolute, copy_dir, read_at/write_at/seek, fsync, write_atomic.
options.code:
use core.files as files

p :: Path.from("site").join("posts")
files.create_dir_all(p)?              // Path accepted
files.create_dir_all("site/posts")? // String accepted by same coercion

stat :: files.stat(p)?
if stat.kind == .Dir {
    loop ent in files.walk(p)? { print(ent.path.to_string()) }
}

tmp :: files.temp_dir()?              // RAII cleanup
lock :: files.lock("build.lock")?   // advisory, scoped
files.write_atomic(p.join("index.html"), bytes)?

options.name: String-only core.files
options.detail: All operations are module functions over String paths. Very easy to type, but path composition, relative roots, symlink-cycle handling, and audit output stay stringly typed.

options.name: Path-only methods
options.detail: Every deep operation hangs off Path methods. Strong audit and discoverability from a Path value, but beginner one-file scripts must learn Path before simple tasks like mkdir -p or remove_all.
options.code:
root :: Path.from("site")
root.join("posts").create_dir_all()?
root.walk().filter((e) => e.stat.kind == .File)

options.name: Decline depth for now
options.detail: Keep read/write/list_dir/open and document shell/core.process workarounds. This leaves Jet worse than Python pathlib, Go os, and Rust fs for everyday scripting and build tools.
options.code:
process.run(["mkdir", "-p", out])?
process.run(["cp", "-R", src, out])?

comparisons.note: pathlib gives a pleasant Path object, but many APIs still accept strings. Jet can keep that ergonomics while making audit facts typed.
os and filepath are robust but split path values into strings. Jet can be more discoverable with typed Path plus module helpers.
std::path and std::fs have strong types and broad coverage, but error copy is not beginner-facing. Jet keeps the front-end diagnostic contract.

decisions.title: Unified watch surface for files, processes, and ports
decisions.gist: Choose how watch-style change notifications cover files, processes, and ports.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A honors the owner's D-FSWATCH1 comment now: one Watch/Event model, with constructors in the domain where the thing lives. Beginners find files.watch(path); experts compose typed watchers across files, process exit, and port readiness without polling.
decisions.story: Earl builds a dev runner in Jet. It rebuilds when source files change, restarts a child server, waits until port 3000 is accepting connections, and exits cleanly if the child dies. Today he needs three different polling loops and timing guesses.
decisions.inWild:
use core.files as files
use core.process as process
use core.net as net

watch :: WatchSet.new()
watch.add(files.watch("src")?)
child :: process.spawn(["jet", "run", "server.jet"])?
watch.add(process.watch(child))
watch.add(net.watch_port(3000))

loop ev in watch.events() { handle(ev) }
decisions.detail: Devil pass: a single core.watch module looks clean, but it becomes a taxonomy drawer and steals discovery from the domain APIs. Domain constructors plus one shared WatchSet/Event type preserve one mechanism while keeping entrypoints where users already are.

options.name: Domain constructors plus shared WatchSet (recommended)
options.detail: files.watch(path), process.watch(child_or_pid), and net.watch_port(port_or_addr) return typed Watch handles with one shared WatchEvent enum and WatchSet multiplexer. Debounced file events are the default; raw event streams are explicit options.

options.name: One core.watch module
options.detail: watch.files, watch.process, and watch.port live under one top-level module. Easy to enumerate, but the common beginner case imports a taxonomy module instead of the file/process/net module already in use.
options.code:
use core.watch as watch

w :: watch.set([
    watch.files("src")?,
    watch.process(child),
    watch.port(3000),
])

options.name: Only files in Epoch 3
options.detail: Implement D-FSWATCH1 literally and defer process/port watching. This ignores the owner ratification comment and leaves dev-runner tooling polling process/port state.

options.name: Callback watchers
options.detail: Each watch call takes a lambda callback. Good for tiny examples, but harder to compose, cancel, test, and replay than event values.
options.code:
files.watch("src", (ev) => rebuild())?
process.watch(child, (ev) => stop())?
net.watch_port(3000, (ev) => ready())?

comparisons.note: Node has fs.watch and child process events, but port readiness is hand-rolled. Jet can unify these as typed event values.
comparisons.code: fs.watch('src', cb); child.on('exit', cb); net.createConnection(port).on('connect', cb)

comparisons.note: Go pushes file watching to fsnotify and process/port readiness to ad hoc goroutines/channels. Jet can ship the channel-like composition in Core.
notify plus tokio process/net can compose, but through external crates and async runtime choices. Jet keeps a blocking beginner surface and explicit expert control.

decisions.comment: a & b - instead of putting file watcher in file module/lib, put all watcher methods in a core.watcher lib. ALSO, support callback/event triggers with our new event system

decisions.title: Core process spawning and pipeline surface
decisions.gist: Choose the canonical subprocess API beyond one-shot process.run.
decisions.explainer: Recommendation A gives beginners the safe argv-only one-shot they already have, and gives experts a typed ProcessSpec/Child handle for streaming, timeouts, env/cwd, signals, pipelines, and output limits. One semantic mechanism: process.run is sugar over ProcessSpec.run.
decisions.story: Nora writes a Jet build tool. It must run a compiler, stream logs live, kill it after 30 seconds, pass a clean environment, pipe generated code into a formatter, and preserve the child's exact exit status. A capture-everything process.run either hangs, hides progress, or forces her into shell strings.
decisions.detail: Devil pass: a fluent builder can become opaque magic; raw spawn knobs can become a shell footgun. Patch: argv lists only by default, no shell interpolation helper in Core, every knob is a typed field on ProcessSpec, and shell execution remains an explicit expert escape if ever approved separately.

options.name: ProcessSpec + Child handles (recommended)
options.detail: Keep process.run(argv) as beginner sugar. Add process.cmd(argv) -> ProcessSpec with cwd/env/stdin/stdout/stderr/timeout/output_limit methods, spawn() -> Child, wait()/kill()/terminate()/interrupt(), typed ExitStatus, streaming readers/writers, and process.pipeline([...]) for argv-only pipelines without a shell.
options.code:
use core.process as process
use core.time as time

spec :: process.cmd(["cargo", "test"])
    .cwd("crates/app")
    .env_clear()
    .env("RUST_BACKTRACE", "1")
    .stdout(.Stream)
    .stderr(.Inherit)
    .timeout(time.seconds(30))

child :: spec.spawn()?
loop line in child.stdout.lines() { print(line) }
status :: child.wait()?
if !status.success { process.exit(status.code ?? 1) }

pipe :: process.pipeline([
    process.cmd(["cat", "input.txt"]),
    process.cmd(["grep", "error"]),
])?

options.name: Many direct module functions
options.detail: Add process.run_stream, run_timeout, run_env, pipeline, kill, etc. Discoverable in autocomplete, but the surface becomes a pile of near-duplicates and option combinations explode.
options.code:
process.run_timeout(["cargo", "test"], time.seconds(30))?
process.run_env(["env"], ["A=1"])?
process.pipeline([["cat", "x"], ["grep", "y"]])?

options.name: Shell string convenience
options.detail: Expose process.shell("cargo test 2>&1 | tee log") as the powerful path. Familiar for experts, but it makes injection and quoting footguns the blessed default unless gated separately.
options.code: process.shell("cd crates/app && cargo test 2>&1 | tee log")?

options.name: Keep one-shot run only
options.detail: Document that serious process orchestration should use external tools. This keeps Jet worse than Python subprocess, Go os/exec, and Rust std::process for build tools and agent operations.
options.code:
r :: process.run(["cargo", "test"])?
print(r.output)

comparisons.note: subprocess.run/Popen is flexible but easy to misuse with shell=True and text/bytes confusion. Jet can keep argv-only defaults and typed streams.
exec.Command gives explicit argv/cwd/env/stdout fields; pipelines require manual pipe wiring. Jet can wrap that pattern in a typed ProcessSpec and pipeline helper.
std::process::Command is the right safety shape, but verbose for common streaming and timeout cases. Jet can keep the shape and improve ergonomics.

decisions.title: Retired syntax teaching layer after D-S14-PAUSE
decisions.gist: D-S14-PAUSE pauses old-spelling teaching until after Epoch 6, but the implementation still recognizes many retired spellings for teaching diagnostics. Pick the canonical behavior so agents know whether to delete, preserve, or gate that layer.
decisions.story: A new Jet learner types `def main()` after coming from Python, while an agent implementing parser cleanup reads the greenfield law. Today the learner may get a bespoke teaching error, but the spec says retired spellings should be ordinary syntax errors. Both experiences cannot be the default law at once.
decisions.detail: Evidence: Syntax.rs FOREIGN_* constants, lexer tokens for retired words, parser recovery paths, diagnostics entries marked retired by D-S14-PAUSE, and the audit report at docs/plans/epoch-3/language-codebase-syntax-audit-2026-07-07.md. Beginner pass: teaching is useful, but only if it is predictable and documented. Expert pass: parser law must be small, auditable, and not preserve ghost syntax accidentally. Hybrid pass: one semantic language can still offer an opt-in migration/teaching mode if that mode is explicit and tested.

options.name: Strict pause now
options.detail: Honor D-S14-PAUSE literally. Remove or disable retired-spelling recognizers and teaching diagnostics until post-Epoch 6; retired forms fail like ordinary syntax. Smallest default language and strongest greenfield signal.
options.code:
$ jet check old.jet
Error [E0001]: this does not start a Jet item
 Fix: write `fn run() { ... }`

options.name: Curated teaching always on
options.detail: Amend D-S14-PAUSE. Keep a small tested set of high-value teaching diagnostics for common migrations, delete stale/low-value ones, and document the list as first-class compiler behavior.
options.code:
$ jet check old.jet
Error [E00xx]: Jet uses `fn`, not `def`
 Fix: write `fn run() { ... }`

options.name: Opt-in teaching mode (recommended)
options.detail: Default remains greenfield and small; `jet check --teach` or editor teaching mode enables curated migration diagnostics. This keeps the canonical language clean while preserving beginner/migration help when requested.
options.code:
$ jet check old.jet
Error [E0001]: this does not start a Jet item

$ jet check --teach old.jet
Error [E00xx]: Jet uses `fn`, not `def`

comparisons.note: Rust keeps diagnostics helpful for common mistakes, but does not accept or tokenize whole alternate language spellings as a migration surface.
Elm favors small syntax and strong compiler guidance; the language surface stays narrow.
TS migration friendliness is high, but compatibility surface is large. Jet should avoid that default-size cost.

decisions.rec: C — greenfield Jet stays small by default, while migration/onboarding help becomes explicit, documented, and testable instead of half-paused ghost syntax.

decisions.title: jetos VM test scenario surface
decisions.gist: How jetos VM test scenarios are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: top-level vmtest remains obvious, while compiling to the same test-target/proof machinery gives CI and expert replay control without a second driver model.
decisions.story: Mara maintains a web service on three jetos hosts. She wants one checked test that boots the database, API, and worker VMs, proves their services, and leaves artifacts CI can replay without writing Python driver strings.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: top-level vmtest remains obvious, while compiling to the same test-target/proof machinery gives CI and expert replay control without a second driver model.

options.name: Hybrid: vmtest declarations as test targets (recommended)
options.detail: Top-level vmtest.<name> declarations are the canonical scenario surface, and the same object is also a normal test target for CI, filtering, artifacts, and package integration. Single-host smoke tests can be authored as shorthand that expands to vmtest; multi-host topology stays explicit. Beginners run one command; experts control host graph, network, replay, timeout, artifacts, and proof capture.

options.name: system.<host>.tests blocks
options.detail: Tests live under each system declaration. This is concise for single-host smoke tests, but multi-host scenarios become split across systems and harder to read as one topology.

options.name: Package-style test targets
options.detail: VM tests are ordinary package/build targets that depend on systems. Good for build graph reuse, but the OS topology is less obvious to beginners and host/service references need extra ceremony.

options.name: External driver file
options.detail: Keep Jet declarations for hosts and point to a separate driver script. This copies NixOS's weakest part: service names and assertions are mostly strings, so Jet cannot catch typos before boot.

comparisons.note: NixOS VM tests declare nodes in Nix and drive them with Python strings.
Scenario resources and probes are declared in one graph, but application assertions often live elsewhere.

decisions.title: jetos VM test assertion API
decisions.gist: How VM tests express checked guest assertions.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: assertion methods give beginner readability, while their underlying check records give expert audit, replay, Studio rendering, and CI artifacts.
decisions.story: Earl changes an SSH service name during a refactor. He wants the VM test to fail at check time if it references a missing service, not after QEMU spends minutes booting a machine and a stringly driver times out.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: assertion methods give beginner readability, while their underlying check records give expert audit, replay, Studio rendering, and CI artifacts.

options.name: Hybrid: typed host handles plus declarative check values (recommended)
options.detail: The test body uses typed host handles and assertion methods. Those methods also produce declarative check values/proof facts, so Studio/CI can render and replay them. Common checks stay one-line and type-checked; experts can write ordinary Jet control flow around them. String shell commands remain an explicit fallback assertion, never the default.
options.code:
run: test {
    halcyon.wait_for_boot()
    halcyon.assert_unit_active(.openssh)
    halcyon.assert_port_open(22)
    check :: halcyon.check_file_contains("/etc/ssh/sshd_config", "PasswordAuthentication no")
    assert(check.ok)
}

options.name: Declarative check list
options.detail: Assertions are data entries rather than code. Easy to render in Studio and CI, but weaker for loops, retries, derived values, and multi-step workflows unless it grows a second mini-language.
options.code:
checks: [
    .UnitActive(host: halcyon, unit: .openssh),
    .PortOpen(host: halcyon, port: 22),
    .FileContains(host: halcyon, path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config, text: "PasswordAuthentication no"),
]

options.name: General Jet test functions
options.detail: Use ordinary Jet tests with imported VM helpers. Good reuse, but host topology and artifact capture are less visible unless every project follows conventions manually.

options.name: String command driver
options.detail: Expose low-level machine.shell("...") style commands as the primary API. Flexible, but service/path/command mistakes become guest-time failures and rustc-like subprocess output leaks into user experience.

comparisons.note: Powerful but mostly string-driven from Python; typos often fail after boot.
Typed-ish fluent assertions make multi-step scenarios readable and produce useful traces.
Declarative checks are inspectable, but imperative workflows need another layer.

decisions.title: jetos per-user environment declarations
decisions.gist: How user-level environments are declared.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one reusable source truth for home config, with explicit host overlays and standalone activation using the same generation/proof model.
decisions.story: Betty wants her shell, editor, terminal, and dotfiles to follow her from a laptop to a server without learning home-manager. Earl wants the same user profile to compose into a full jetos host or apply standalone on macOS/Linux with proof and rollback.
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one reusable source truth for home config, with explicit host overlays and standalone activation using the same generation/proof model.

options.name: Hybrid: reusable user.<name> profiles with host overlays (recommended)
options.detail: A user.<name> declaration is the canonical per-user environment. It works standalone and can be attached to system.<host>. Host-specific overrides live where the host composes the profile, so one profile can follow a person across machines while experts still control per-host packages, services, secrets, and generated files.

options.name: Only system.<host>.users.<name>.environment
options.detail: User environments live only inside host configs. Simple for OS installs, but loses home-manager's adoption path: applying a user profile without switching the whole OS.

options.name: programs.* modules only
options.detail: Expose app modules but no first-class user profile. Useful for app breadth, but dotfiles, shell, services, and standalone activation lack one shared home environment object.
options.code:
programs.git.enable: true
programs.helix.enable: true
# no reusable user profile boundary

options.name: Separate home.jet files
options.detail: Each user has a separate file format/entrypoint. Familiar to home-manager users, but it creates a second source-of-truth shape beside system.<host> and weakens one-path discoverability.

comparisons.note: Home-manager profiles can be standalone or imported into NixOS, but use a separate module layer.
NixOS system users cover identity and some packages, but not full home environment breadth.

decisions.title: jetos user profile apply command
decisions.gist: How standalone user profiles are built and activated.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: standalone home-manager-class adoption and full OS composition share one user-generation engine.
decisions.story: Doris is not ready to replace her OS, but she wants JetOS to manage her shell, editor, terminal, and app configs today. CI also needs to build the same user generation, inspect the diff, and prove rollback before anything touches her home directory.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetos user plan nate
$ jetos user switch nate
# writes a user generation, links managed files atomically, starts user services, and records rollback

$ jetos user rollback nate
# restores prior user generation without rebuilding the OS
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: standalone home-manager-class adoption and full OS composition share one user-generation engine.

options.name: Hybrid: jetos user commands plus system composition (recommended)
options.detail: `jetos user plan/build/switch/rollback/prove` is the standalone path, and system switching invokes the same user-generation engine when a host imports user profiles. Beginners can manage home config before replacing the OS; experts get proof, rollback, CI, and composition through one mechanism.
options.code:
$ jetos user plan nate
$ jetos user switch nate

$ jet os switch halcyon
# runs the same user-generation proof for users.nate.environment

options.name: jetpack env apply
options.detail: Put standalone home environments under jetpack. Good for non-OS adoption, but splits user-generation semantics away from jetos even though rollback/proof are OS-shaped.
options.code:
$ jetpack env plan user.nate
$ jetpack env switch user.nate

options.name: Only through system switch
options.detail: User profiles activate only when the host system switches. Strong system coherence, but fails the home-manager adoption path for non-jetos machines.
options.code:
$ jet os switch halcyon
# updates user.nate only as part of host switch

options.name: Generated shell script
options.detail: Build writes an auditable apply script and users run it manually. Easy to inspect, but not a first-class rollback/proof workflow and weak for beginners.
options.code:
$ jetos user build nate
wrote apply-user-nate.sh
$ ./apply-user-nate.sh

comparisons.note: Home-manager has a standalone switch command and a NixOS module integration path.
System switch handles OS generations; user profile rollback is a separate ecosystem concern.

decisions.title: Terminal and raw IO surface
decisions.gist: Choose the shape of terminal stdout/stderr, TTY facts, colors, progress, raw mode, and key events.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: one import for beginner CLIs, but a clean stream/terminal split inside core.io for expert control and audit.
decisions.story: Betty writes a deployment CLI. It prints a progress line, colors warnings only on terminals, flushes before running a child process, and reads one key in raw mode for confirmation. She should not hand-roll ANSI or leak escape codes into logs.
decisions.inWild:
use core.io as io

io.write("Building...")
io.flush()
if io.stdout.is_tty() { io.style(.Yellow).write("warn") }
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: one import for beginner CLIs, but a clean stream/terminal split inside core.io for expert control and audit.

options.name: Hybrid: stream backbone plus terminal capability namespace (recommended)
options.detail: core.io owns stdout/stderr/stdin streams, flush, raw bytes, and TTY facts. Terminal capabilities live under `io.terminal`/stream methods, not a separate module: style/progress/raw mode/key events all honor TTY/NO_COLOR by default, with explicit expert overrides for forced color/raw behavior.
options.code:
use core.io as io

io.stdout.write("Building...")?
io.stdout.flush()?
if io.stdout.is_tty() { io.stdout.style(.Green).write("done")? }
key :: io.terminal.raw(() => io.terminal.read_key())?

options.name: Split core.io and core.term
options.detail: core.io stays byte streams; core.term owns TTY/color/raw/key/progress. Separation is clean, but beginners must learn two modules for one terminal program.
options.code:
use core.io as io
use core.term as term
term.style(.Green).write(io.stdout, "done")?

options.name: Decline terminal depth
options.detail: Keep print/eprint/input only. Serious CLIs shell out or hand-roll ANSI/raw mode, so pipes and Windows terminals become user footguns.
options.code: print("\x1b[32mdone\x1b[0m")

comparisons.note: term/console needs x/term or third-party packages; stdlib leaves gaps.
crossterm gives capability breadth as a crate; Jet needs a blessed Core path.

decisions.title: Declarative CLI parser depth
decisions.gist: Choose how core.args grows beyond the typed run(args) layer and simple builders.
decisions.explainer: Best hybrid: derive ergonomics and builder control feed one checked command-spec model.
decisions.story: Hank ships a CLI with subcommands, env fallbacks, defaults, completion text, and exact errors. Typed entry args cover the common case; library code and custom launchers need the same parser without inventing another command language.
decisions.inWild:
use core.args as args

spec :: args.command("serve").flag("port", default: 8080).subcommand("migrate")
parsed :: args.parse(spec)?
decisions.detail: Hybrid review 2026-07-07: recommended option combines the beginner/default path with expert control where that preserves one semantic mechanism. Best hybrid: derive ergonomics and builder control feed one checked command-spec model.

options.name: Hybrid: one ArgsSpec from structs or builders (recommended)
options.detail: ArgsSpec is the single semantic model. Typed `fn run(args: T)` derives an ArgsSpec for beginners; library/tooling code can build the same ArgsSpec dynamically for subcommands, env fallbacks, completions, and tests. No string mini-language.

options.name: Struct-only derive everywhere
options.detail: All parsing starts from structs/enums. Clean for ordinary apps, but generated tools and dynamic command sets cannot compose specs at runtime.
