options.code:
jetpack  add ripgrep fd
           ▸ resolving from nixpkgs
           ✓ ripgrep  14.1.0  built 6s
           ✓ fd       9.0.0   cached
  jetpack  2 packages ready  ✓

  jetpack  env
           ✓ node     22.3.0  cached
           ✓ postgres 16.3.0  cached

  ── myproj ─ dev shell · exit to leave ──────────────

  (build failure: diagnostic prints inline, verbatim,
   no spinner left hanging)

options.name: Live region — one place to watch
options.detail:
Core loop: watch one pinned bottom region (progress bar, counts, elapsed, size); finished items promote up into clean scrollback; the region collapses to a one-line summary. The uv/bun/pnpm model — best "where am I now" for long builds: one aggregate 31/42 beats 42 log lines. Cost: cursor-up region redraw (std ANSI, noted in NOTES), must erase cleanly before any diagnostic prints, and non-TTY degrades to appended lines (= option A).
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/cli/live.html
options.code:
jetpack  add ripgrep fd
           ✓ ripgrep  14.1.0  built 6s
  ── live region · redraws in place ──────────────────
  realizing 1/2 · fd            00:06 · 42 MB
  ████████████████░░░░░░░░  unpacking
  ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        │ finished items promote UP, region stays pinned
        ▼
  jetpack  2 packages ready in 6s  ✓   (region replaced)

options.name: Plan — decide first, apply quietly
options.detail:
Core loop: every mutation prints a full plan (add/change/remove, download size, closure and generation delta), asks once [y/N], then applies tersely with each done line tied to a plan line. The nh/terraform model — safest for consequential ops (switch, gc): you decide from the diff and nothing mutates unseen. Cost: an extra step on trivial adds — needs sensible --yes and CI behavior (non-TTY prints the plan and exits without applying, never hangs).
file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/cli/plan.html
options.code:
jetos  switch

  Plan  generation 42 → 43 · 1 add, 1 change, 1 remove

    + firefox       —      → 129.0
    ~ linux         6.9.7  → 6.10.1
    - obsolete-lib  1.2.0  → —

  Download 240 MB · closure +18 MB · rebuild boot + current

  Apply? [y/N] ▏
     y → quiet apply, one ✓ per planned line
     Enter/N → nothing touched

options.name: Hybrid — consequence-scaled output
options.detail:
Core loop: output scales with consequence — trivial ops print a quiet ledger, long builds pin a live region that promotes finished lines into that ledger, and mutations gate on a plan first; the scrollback is always the record. Takes: ledger as the spine under everything + live's region for genuinely long work (finished items promote up as permanent ledger lines, region collapses to a summary) + plan's gate for mutations only (jetos switch, gc), whose apply reuses the same region-into-ledger flow with each ✓ tied to a plan line. Left out: plan's gate on trivial adds (prompt fatigue; --yes still available) and a region for short ops. One progress experience at three depths, chosen by what the command does (I8). Non-TTY: no region, mutation prints plan and exits.

    ✓ postgres 16.3.0        jetpack  build ready ✓        y → region+ledger

decisions.title: jet dev server — pick the UX archetype
decisions.gist: Where the dev server's richness lives: in the browser, in the terminal, or mirrored identically in both.
decisions.explainer: Hybrid — parity keeps both surfaces honest for free (one poll, one vocabulary), and each side gets its native depth on demand: the full overlay in the browser, the request log in the terminal. No starved surface, no second source of truth.
decisions.story: Kai runs `jet dev app.jet --target=web` with the browser on one monitor and the terminal on the other. On a broken save the last good build keeps serving — but where does he learn what broke, and how much does each surface tell him? Three splits of the same information: rich browser + silent terminal, rich terminal + clean browser, or strict parity where both always show the same status and the same verbatim E0102 frame. Browse: file:///home/nate/Projects/Github/jet/docs/design/frontends/index.html#devserver (←/→ switches, c compares).
decisions.inWild:
$ jet dev app.jet --target=web
serving http://localhost:8080 — watching app.jet …
# save a typo → E0102. Last good build keeps serving;
# the archetype decides where the error reaches Kai.
decisions.detail: Owner modification (2026-07-08): ratify hybrid dev server, with the nicely formatted terminal dashboard header pinned. The header remains visible while request logs, rebuild output, verbose detail, and errors scroll below. Keep mirrored browser status/overlay and terminal depth, but the pinned dashboard header is required as the terminal anchor.

options.name: Quiet terminal, rich browser
options.detail:
Core loop: live in the browser; the terminal is a three-line daemon. Terminal prints URL, watch target, last rebuild — then goes silent. Everything rich is in the page: vite-class full error overlay with the verbatim diagnostic, dim-while-rebuilding, a rebuild toast with timing, reconnect states. Matches how web developers actually work — eyes on the rendered page. Risk: with no tab open an error is invisible until you look (the terminal still prints the diagnostic as fallback).

options.name: Terminal dashboard, clean browser
options.detail:
Core loop: the terminal is the primary view — a pinned header (status dot, port, client count, last build time) over a scrolling request/rebuild log with timings; the browser shows only a thin error banner pointing back. Best for terminal-centric developers and multi-client debugging: every request and rebuild visible with timing, client count comes free from the 400ms pollers. Risk: pinned header needs cursor-home redraw (std ANSI) and degrades to a plain status line off-TTY; the browser is deliberately information-poor.

options.name: Paired — same truth on both sides
options.detail:
Core loop: glance at the terminal or the browser corner — same status, same error. A one-line terminal status and a browser corner strip mirror each other exactly (building / ok / error / n clients), both driven by the same version poll; on error both expand the identical verbatim diagnostic frame (once in ANSI, once in CSS, same snapshot text). No "which surface is authoritative" question, lowest cognitive overhead. Risk: parity must be genuinely lockstep or it's a lie; the frame is the only detail level — no request log.

options.name: Hybrid — mirrored status with on-demand depth
options.detail:
Core loop: a one-line terminal status and a browser corner strip mirror the same poll; on error the browser strip expands to the full overlay and the terminal can expand to a request log, but the parity line is always the shared truth. Takes: paired's contract (identical state from one poll — they cannot drift) + quiet's full vite-class overlay as the strip's expanded state (room, not a second truth) + dashboard's request/rebuild log behind v/--verbose, printed under the same parity header. Left out: any deliberately starved surface — no mute-daemon terminal, no info-poor browser banner; depth is additive on both sides of one status mechanism (I8).

decisions.title: REPL inline docs surface
decisions.gist: How the REPL opens docs for a name.
decisions.explainer: D-FE-REPL1 ratified hybrid REPL depth, but the original ballot explicitly left ?name docs as a follow-up gate. This decides whether docs are a REPL expression-like shortcut, a colon command, or absent from v1 REPL. The goal is one clear docs path, not two rival help systems.
decisions.story: Betty is exploring a library in jet repl. She has a value named `server` and sees a completion for `listen`. She wants the shortest way to ask what `listen` expects without leaving the REPL or searching the website.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet repl
user> server.listen
# completion shows listen(port: Int) -> Result
user> ?server.listen
# docs open inline, then the prompt returns
user> _
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: docs should be discoverable from the place where the question appears. Expert pass: docs need exact symbol identity, signatures, and source/provenance where available. Hybrid pass: the REPL should call the same docs index as jet ? / LSP hover, not maintain separate prose.

options.name: No ?name docs; use jet ? and completion only
options.detail: The REPL keeps completion/signature help but no docs command. Users open jet ? or editor hover for deeper docs. Smallest REPL surface, but breaks the hybrid ballot promise that docs are one keystroke away in the REPL.
options.code:
user> nums.fil<Tab>
filter (f: Fn) -> List

user> :help
# points to jet ? filter

options.name: ?name inline docs over the shared docs index (recommended)
options.detail: ?name is a REPL-only query form, not Jet source syntax. It resolves names exactly like completion/LSP hover, renders signature, short docs, source/module, examples when present, and returns to the same prompt. It preserves one docs index across REPL, jet ?, and editor tooling.
options.code:
user> ?List.filter
List.filter(f: fn(T) -> Bool) -> List<T>
Keeps items where f(item) is true.
Source: core.collections

user> _

options.name: Colon command only: :doc name
options.detail: Docs are explicit commands, not punctuation. This avoids confusion with Jet source, but is slower than the ratified REPL mockup and creates a separate docs spelling from the ?name convention many REPL users know.
options.code:
user> :doc List.filter
List.filter(f: fn(T) -> Bool) -> List<T>

user> _

comparisons.note: Uses ?name and name? to inspect Python objects inline.
Help mode is entered with ?, then a name queries docs.
rustdoc/IDE hover are shared docs surfaces; REPL-like tools should not fork docs text.

decisions.title: REPL rerun semantics
decisions.gist: What rerunning an old REPL turn does to later state.
decisions.explainer: D-FE-REPL1 ratified notebook-style rerun controls, but rerun affects truth: later bindings may depend on the old value, and turns may have effects. This decision chooses the one rerun model so the REPL never shows stale values as current.
decisions.story: Hank defines `rate`, computes `invoice_total`, then notices `rate` was wrong. He hits rerun on turn 1. He needs to know whether `invoice_total` changed, stayed stale, or needs a manual rerun before he trusts the session.
decisions.inWild:
1 user> rate :: 0.07
  0.07 : Float
2 user> invoice_total :: subtotal * (1.0 + rate)
  107.0 : Float
# Hank edits turn 1 to rate :: 0.08 and presses rerun. What happens to turn 2?
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: never make stale state look current. Expert pass: side effects and expensive turns need explicit control. Hybrid pass: one replay model can handle both by replaying pure/dependent turns automatically and requiring confirmation for effectful replay.

options.name: Replay from the edited turn forward with effect confirmation (recommended)
options.detail: Rerun rebuilds session state from the selected turn forward, recomputing dependent later turns in order. Pure/binding turns replay automatically. Effectful turns pause with a replay plan and require confirmation or skip/stale-mark. This keeps current state truthful while protecting side effects.
options.code:
rerun turn 1
Replay plan:
  1 rate :: 0.08        auto
  2 invoice_total ...   auto
  3 write_file(...)     confirm effect
Apply? [y/N]

options.name: Rerun one turn only; stale-mark dependents
options.detail: Only the selected turn reruns. Later turns that read changed bindings are marked stale and excluded from current binding truth until manually rerun. Safer for effects, but beginners must understand stale state and manually repair the session.
options.code:
1 rate :: 0.08  ok
2 invoice_total  stale: depends on old rate
current bindings: rate only; invoice_total hidden until rerun

options.name: Scratch rerun; does not change session state
options.detail: Rerun evaluates the old input in a temporary scratch scope and prints the result, leaving every binding untouched. Safe, but the button is not a real notebook rerun and does not help fix a session.
options.code:
rerun turn 1 as scratch
0.08 : Float
# session still has rate = 0.07

comparisons.note: Cells can be rerun out of order, which often leaves hidden stale state. Jet should avoid that footgun.
comparisons.code: Run cell 1, skip cell 2 -> displayed outputs can disagree with kernel state.

comparisons.note: Reactive dependency graph recomputes downstream cells when an input changes.
Command blocks can be rerun, but shell side effects are real; Jet needs stronger state truth because bindings are typed session state.

decisions.title: jet env prompt status strip config
decisions.gist: How users opt into the always-on prompt status strip.
decisions.explainer: D-FE-PROMPT1 ratified hybrid prompt behavior and kept an optional status strip, but the exact user-facing config key is not ratified. Existing env config already has a simple prompt label. This chooses the one config surface for prompt depth without creating multiple prompt mechanisms.
decisions.story: Doris works in a monorepo where she wants every prompt to show build/test/git state. Walter wants the default quiet prompt with env name and path only. Both should use the same env.jet mechanism, not shell-specific dotfiles.
decisions.detail: Beginner pass: default prompt needs no config and already shows env name plus path. Expert pass: teams need a reviewed env.jet switch for always-on status. Hybrid pass: one prompt engine with a mode field is cleaner than shell-specific flags or a second prompt file.

options.name: No config; default prompt only for now
options.detail: Implement env name + path and adaptive receipts, but omit the optional always-on strip. This avoids new config surface, but drops a ratified hybrid depth and forces teams into shell-local customization.

options.name: Structured prompt config in env.jet (recommended)
options.detail: Keep `prompt: "name"` as the beginner shorthand. Add `prompt: Prompt.{ label: "web-api", strip: .On, path: .Short }` for expert control. One env.jet-owned prompt engine handles default, glance, and strip words across shells.

options.name: Shell environment variable opt-in
options.detail: Use JET_PROMPT_STRIP=1 or per-shell rc overrides. Easy to test locally, but not source-reviewed in env.jet and differs by shell/session.
options.code:
JET_PROMPT_STRIP=1 jet env web
# shell-local, not part of project env source

comparisons.note: Prompt behavior is configured in a dedicated file, outside project language semantics.
Project env behavior comes from reviewed project files, but shell prompt customization is usually external.
shellHook can customize PS1, but it is raw shell code and not a typed project setting.

decisions.gist: How JetOS imports an existing NixOS flake, flake-parts, and Home Manager system.

options.detail: Evaluate the NixOS/Home Manager module graph into typed JetOS source with exact omissions.

decisions.title: JetOS real installed-guest acceptance gate
decisions.gist: What proof is required before JetOS can be called installed and usable.
decisions.explainer: Recommend C: replacement claim needs actual installed-guest behavior, not host proof text.
decisions.story: Doris boots the installer in QEMU, installs to disk, reboots from that disk, logs in, opens Studio, checks services, and rolls back. Host-side proof files alone are not enough.

decisions.title: Canvas node states: how a disabled node and a debug-only node are spelled in source
decisions.gist: What Jet source looks like when a Canvas node is switched off temporarily, and how a node can be marked to exist only in debug builds.
decisions.explainer: One attribute family gives both Blueprint states with real syntax that survives fmt/refactors and stays type-checked (a comment marker silently rots when the code around it is renamed); #DebugOnly hides the comptime plumbing beginners should never need to see, while comptime if build.profile remains available to experts if C's value is also ratified later.
decisions.story: Priya is wiring a pricing function in Canvas. A logging call keeps cluttering her test output, so she wants to switch that node off for a while without deleting it — same as unplugging a cable, not cutting it. Separately, she has a sanity-check node that should run in dev builds but must never ship in the release binary. Canvas is source-backed: both states must be spelled in the .jet file somehow, and today Jet has no spelling for either (only build.os exists as a comptime value, no debug/release distinction).

options.name: Comment marker for off, no debug-only yet
options.detail: Disabled node = the statement commented out with a marker comment Canvas recognizes and can re-enable. Zero new language surface; code is genuinely inert because it is a comment. Debug-only nodes wait for a separate build-profile decision.

options.name: #Off attribute statement gate
options.detail: A real attribute the compiler parses and skips (still type-checked, like Rust's #[cfg] siblings or C#'s [Conditional]). Survives formatting and refactors as real syntax; Canvas toggles it. Debug-only becomes #Off("release") or a sibling attribute later.

options.name: build.profile comptime value + comptime if (debug-only), comment marker (off)
options.detail: Adds build.profile (.Debug | .Release) beside build.os; debug-only nodes project as a comptime if rail Canvas renders as a badge, folded at compile time exactly like build.os dispatch. Temporary off stays the A-style comment marker since 'off' is a workspace state, not a program state.

options.name: Both as attributes: #Off and #DebugOnly
options.detail: One attribute family for node states: #Off (skipped every build, still type-checked) and #DebugOnly (compiled only when the build profile is debug; requires the same build-profile machinery as C under the hood but the user never sees comptime if).

comparisons.note: Nodes have a Disabled state (greyed, skipped) and a Development Only mode (hazard-striped, compiled out of shipping builds) — the two states Priya expects.

comparisons.note: cfg attributes gate code by build profile; debug_assert! is the idiomatic debug-only check that vanishes in release.

decisions.title: jetos is a from-scratch standalone OS; NixOS module system is not a backend
decisions.gist: jetos must be its own Linux system — jet, jetpack, and the hangar all the way down — functionally equivalent to NixOS. Building it by generating a NixOS configuration under the hood produces a reskinned NixOS and is forbidden.
decisions.story: The first working graphical jetos VM was realized by compiling the jetos option tree into a generated NixOS flake. It booted GNOME, but the guest was visibly NixOS: NixOS wallpaper, release codename "Yarara", NixOS module semantics throughout. The owner rejected this outright: adapters may leverage the nixpkgs package ecosystem, but the operating system itself — module/option system, generations, activation, /etc rendering, service units, boot, desktop glue, identity — must be jetos-native.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os vm run halcyon --disk ./halcyon.qcow2
boots a system whose settings panel reads "jetos" because it IS jetos: hangar store, jetos-generated systemd units, jetos activation — with firefox/steam/plasma fetched from nixpkgs through the jetpack adapter.

options.label: Native jetos system, nixpkgs as package adapter only
options.detail: jetos owns every OS-assembly concern natively; nixpkgs is reached through jetpack providers purely to obtain packages. Functional equivalence to NixOS is proven by behavior, not by sharing its implementation.

options.label: Hidden NixOS realizer (rejected)
options.detail: Compile jetos config to a generated NixOS system, rebrand the output. Fast to ship, but the product is a NixOS fork/reskin.

decisions.comment: Decreed live 2026-07-09: no forked/reskinned NixOS; standalone jetos with nixpkgs adapters.

decisions.title: On-disk package store inside a jetos system: hangar-native, staged
decisions.gist: The jetpack hangar is THE store of a jetos system — its layout, GC, and generation roots. Stage 1 keeps nixpkgs-built closures under a hangar-managed compatibility root so unmodified binaries run; a later stage re-roots/rebuilds packages natively.
decisions.story: Nixpkgs binaries hardcode /nix/store paths internally (ELF interpreters, dlopen paths, wrappers). Running them unmodified requires that path shape to exist on disk. Rather than adopting /nix/store as jetos's permanent format, the hangar owns the store from day one and treats the nix-shaped subtree as the adapter's compatibility root, with native re-rooting as the planned end state.
decisions.inWild:
/hangar/…            ← jetos store: metadata, GC roots, generations
/hangar/compat/nix/store/…   ← stage-1 root for unmodified nixpkgs closures
Later: packages rebuilt against hangar paths; compat root shrinks to nothing.

options.label: Hangar-native, staged compat root
options.detail: Hangar owns everything; nix-shaped compat subtree is an adapter detail with a planned exit.

options.label: Keep /nix/store layout permanently
options.detail: Simplest compatibility, least ownership of the format.

options.label: Hangar-native from day one
options.detail: Rewrite/rebuild every package before anything ships; purest but gates all system work.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09.

decisions.title: No `nix` binary anywhere in the jetos product path — this epoch builds jetpack's own nixpkgs pipeline
decisions.gist: jetos and jetpack must not shell out to the nix binary. Leveraging the nixpkgs ecosystem requires jetpack to evaluate, fetch, and build nixpkgs packages itself: a Nix-language evaluator (or equivalent artifact protocol), derivation hashing, the binary-cache substituter protocol, and a sandboxed builder — in scope for this epoch, not deferred.
decisions.story: Today the jetpack nix provider runs `nix build nixpkgs#pkg`. That makes the nix binary a load-bearing dependency of every jetos system build. The owner chose the strongest form of independence: the adapter speaks nixpkgs' formats (Nix language, drv hashing, NAR/narinfo caches) through jetpack's own implementation, so no Nix-project executable is required to build or run a jetos system.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack fetch nixpkgs#firefox
  evaluates nixpkgs with jetpack's evaluator, resolves the store hash,
  substitutes the NAR from cache.nixos.org into the hangar compat root —
  no /run/current-system/sw/bin/nix involved.

options.label: Staged: nix CLI now, native later
options.detail: Ship on the CLI, replace it on a scoped later card.

options.label: nix CLI permanently acceptable
options.detail: Never build an evaluator.

options.label: No nix binary at all this epoch
options.detail: The epoch includes jetpack's own evaluation/fetch/build pipeline before jetos ships.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09: no nix binary at all this epoch.

decisions.title: Epoch-7 exit bar: NixOS-class architecture natively + prioritized breadth
decisions.gist: The epoch exits when jetos natively delivers the full NixOS capability architecture (typed module/option system, generations, atomic activation, rollback, fully declarative system) PLUS: a terminal baseline, a graphical baseline, one-line desktop swaps (GNOME/KDE/Hyprland/niri; wayland/x11), and the owner's entire ~/nixos config running natively. Module breadth beyond that grows by demand through a defined process.
decisions.story: NixOS has on the order of 20k options; literal total parity is a multi-year tail. Functional equivalence is an architecture property plus enough module breadth to cover real systems. Nothing is baked into jetos itself: the entire system is driven by the user's jet config files — defaults may exist (terminal and graphical baselines), but composition is wholly the user's, written by hand or through jetos Studio.
decisions.inWild:
desktop: .Gnome        →  desktop: .Kde        (one line)
session: .Wayland      →  session: .X11        (one line)
desktop: .Hyprland — same config file, nothing else changes.

options.label: Architecture + prioritized breadth
options.detail: Exit = architecture + baselines + one-line desktop swaps + owner config native; breadth by demand after.

options.label: Full module parity
options.detail: Every NixOS option has a jetos equivalent before exit.

options.label: Owner config only
options.detail: Exit = owner's machine runs; everything else later.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09.

decisions.title: Fate of the jet→NixOS realizer: demoted to a clearly-labeled migration tool
decisions.gist: The generated-NixOS build path (formerly the `--real` tier realizer, D-JOS-NIXBACKEND1) is never a product path. It survives only as an explicit, clearly-labeled migration/transition tool for A/B-ing a config during a NixOS→jetos migration. The nixos→jet importer remains central and unaffected.
decisions.story: The realizer exists and works — it built and booted a rebranded NixOS from a jet config. Under D-JOS-NATIVE1 that can never ship as jetos. Its remaining value is migration: while a user transitions, building their jet config both ways and comparing behavior gives confidence the conversion is faithful.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet os migrate compare halcyon
  builds the config natively (jetos) and via the NixOS oracle, boots both,
  diffs services/packages/session facts — labeled a migration aid, not jetos.

options.label: Internal test oracle only
options.detail: Kept only inside the test suite as a differential oracle for parity proofs.

options.label: Delete entirely
options.detail: Parity verified against a plain NixOS guest built from the user's real flake instead.

options.label: Keep as labeled migration tool
options.detail: Exposed as an explicit transition command, separate from the native build path.

decisions.comment: Chosen via session ballot 2026-07-09: keep as clearly-labeled migration tool.

decisions.title: Desktop option spellings — the one-line swap surface
decisions.gist: The exact user-typeable spellings for choosing a desktop. Everything else derives from these lines, so they are the most-typed jetos options after packages. Under D-JPK-OSNS1=B full-word namespaces.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: B contradicts ratified namespace law (D-JPK-OSNS1=B / D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1 place desktop under services) and spends an amendment on saved keystrokes; C's record value has undefined merge semantics — does setting the record reset unset fields? — vagueness that bites the option-priority engine; D's combinatorial enum explodes on every new session type and has no home for displayManager. A wins but leaves `.Auto` derivation and invalid-combo diagnostics unstated, which is where implementers diverge. One flag for the ratifier: the environment enum has no value for the D-JOS-DESKTOP1=A JetOS-owned Wayland session — reconcile when that frozen surface (D-JETOS-FREEZE1) ships natively.
decisions.story: One line must swap the whole desktop; a second may pin the session type; a third may override the display manager. Enum values are teaching surfaces: unknown values list the valid set.
decisions.inWild:
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.desktop.environment: .Kde        // entire desktop swapped
services.desktop.session: .X11             // wayland is the default
services.desktop.displayManager: .Greetd   // else auto-derived

options.label: services.desktop.{environment, session, displayManager}
options.detail: Nested under the existing services.desktop.* namespace next to autoLogin/profile; enums .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri, .Wayland/.X11, .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd.

options.label: top-level desktop.* namespace
options.detail: desktop.environment / desktop.session / desktop.displayManager as a new top-level namespace — shortest to type, needs a namespace-list amendment to D-JPK-OSNS1.

options.label: single record option
options.detail: services.desktop: Desktop.{ environment: .Kde, session: .Wayland } — one structured value, one line for the common case, record fields for the rest.

options.label: DE value carries session
options.detail: desktop: .KdeWayland / .KdeX11 / .Gnome / .Hyprland — one enum, zero second line; combinatorial values, no invalid combos possible by construction.

options.name: services.desktop.* with lawful .Auto derivation and typed assertions (hybrid)
options.detail: Spellings are Option A's under the ratified full-word tree (D-JPK-OSNS1=B, D-JOS-SYSTEMTREE1): `services.desktop.environment: .Gnome/.Kde/.Hyprland/.Niri`, `session: .Auto/.Wayland/.X11` defaulting `.Auto`, `displayManager: .Auto/.Gdm/.Sddm/.Greetd` defaulting `.Auto` — one line swaps the desktop; the other two exist only as overrides. `.Auto` derivation is law, not vibes: session resolves to the DE's preferred session, displayManager resolves Gnome->.Gdm, Kde->.Sddm, Hyprland/Niri->.Greetd, and `jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager` prints the derivation and winning priority. Invalid combos fail at eval as typed assertions naming both source lines (`.Niri` supports only `.Wayland`/`.Auto`), and an unknown enum value lists the full valid set with a nearest-match suggestion. Combinatorial DE-x-session values (Option D) are rejected forever: every fact keeps exactly one option home, so adding a session type or DM never renames existing configs.
options.code:
services.desktop.environment: .Kde     // one line, whole desktop swaps
services.desktop.session: .X11          // optional; default .Auto -> wayland
// error: .Niri supports only .Wayland — set at services.desktop.session (line 7)
jet os explain services.desktop.displayManager   # .Sddm, derived from .Kde

decisions.title: Baseline profiles — exact visible contents of terminal and graphical installs
decisions.gist: Choose how jetos ships a lean modern terminal and a complete no-command-line desktop while keeping every installed part visible in config.jet.
decisions.explainer: Recommended D treats baselines as source templates, not runtime imports. The installer materializes every package, service, option, policy, and low-level component into config.jet; the realized closure must trace every installed root back to one of those source entries. The terminal template stays small but modern. The graphical template adds one complete GNOME path and hardware support, with Studio handling settings, packages, updates, generations, proof, and rollback without requiring a terminal. No duplicate app for the same job, no second package system by default, and no unexplained background service. Experts may remove or replace any layer; jetos reports broken obligations and proof failures but never silently restores a baseline choice.
decisions.story: Maya installs jetos on a small server and wants a useful modern terminal without a desktop. Her father installs it on a laptop and expects Wi-Fi, headphones, printing, updates, files, documents, media, and system settings to work without opening a terminal. Later Maya replaces the kernel and network stack. Both need config.jet to show the whole system, with no hidden profile contents or defaults silently returning after an edit.

options.name: Named profile imports
options.detail: config.jet imports baseline.terminal or baseline.graphical. This keeps the file short, but the installed package and service graph is hidden behind the import until the user follows it elsewhere. Baseline updates can also change a machine without an obvious local source diff.

options.name: Fully materialized minimal profiles
options.detail: Both terminal and graphical installs write their complete contents into config.jet, but the graphical set adds only GNOME, a browser, audio, fonts, Bluetooth, and printing. Auditability is strong; the desktop still leaves common beginner jobs and system administration dependent on package discovery or the terminal.
options.code:
packages: [packages.fish, packages.helix, packages.git, packages.ripgrep]
services.desktop.environment: .Gnome
services.audio.pipewire.enable: true
// Files, updates, documents, archives, disks, and media need later setup.

options.name: One universal batteries-included profile
options.detail: Every install writes the complete graphical tool and service set into config.jet, including headless machines. This is maximally consistent and visible, but a server receives desktop packages and services with no baseline job to perform.

options.name: Two fully materialized, purpose-built baselines (recommended)
options.detail: Terminal and graphical are two source templates, expanded directly into config.jet by init/installer; there is no baseline import and no hidden installed default. Terminal contains the boot/kernel/init/filesystem/user/logging/time/locale/certificate/network/firewall/package-management substrate; standard compatibility utilities; fish, Helix, Git, OpenSSH client, curl, rsync; and the curated modern interactive set ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, fzf, zoxide, jq, and btop. No remote server is enabled by default. Graphical contains all terminal entries plus GNOME on Wayland/GDM; NetworkManager UI; PipeWire/WirePlumber; Bluetooth; printing/scanning; firmware and power management; portals, polkit, keyring, fonts, input, automount, and notifications; jetos Studio; Firefox; Nautilus; GNOME Console, Text Editor, Papers, Loupe, Showtime, File Roller, Calculator, Calendar, Clocks, Disks, Snapshot, Settings, and a Jetpack-backed Software view. One app per baseline job; Flatpak and alternate app stores remain explicit opt-ins. Studio exposes install/remove, settings, updates, generations, proof, and rollback through the same config.jet transactions. Baseline evolution arrives as a reviewable source diff and never applies silently. Removing or replacing a low-level entry is authoritative: jetos shows unmet typed obligations and failed proof, but does not heal or reinsert the old choice.

comparisons.note: NixOS offers deep declarative control, but imports and module defaults can make the effective system larger than configuration.nix shows. D keeps the declarative graph while materializing the chosen baseline into the user's source and requiring source provenance for every installed root.

Arch makes a minimal system and expert choice straightforward, but the user assembles desktop completeness by hand. D preserves a lean terminal target while giving graphical users a complete, maintained starting source.
comparisons.code:
pacstrap /mnt base linux networkmanager
# User chooses and wires every desktop component afterward.

comparisons.note: Fedora provides a cohesive GNOME experience and modern applications, but image manifests and package layering are not a single user-owned declarative system file. D adopts cohesive desktop curation while keeping the whole machine editable as source.
comparisons.code:
rpm-ostree status
# Strong image provenance; baseline contents are not materialized into one local config.

comparisons.note: Guix can describe a whole system in one program and supports generations, but users still commonly compose imported service sets and package lists. D shares the source-owned system model and adds a no-terminal graphical authoring path over the same source.

decisions.title: jetos release identity — versioning scheme + codename line
decisions.gist: The guest must never again say “Yarara”. jetos needs its own version scheme and codename family for os-release, boot menus, and the welcome screen.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A, B, and C all adopt semver, which encodes a compatibility promise a distro cannot keep — 'what makes an OS 2.0?' is permanent bikeshed debt; B's aircraft names are trademark landmines and C's winds collide head-on with Zephyr RTOS, Mistral AI, and Nokia's Harmattan release; D is honest but discards the codename personality the owner explicitly wants. The hybrid takes D's calver plus A's collision-safest theme, adds the Ubuntu/NixOS alphabetical-ordering trick and a vetting canon, and turns the ballot's own 'never Yarara again' requirement into a stated os-release law with a CI gate.
decisions.story: Owner wants rich original naming menus, aviation-themed product naming canon (jet/jetpack/jetos). Codenames are the visible personality of each release.
decisions.inWild:
NAME=jetos
VERSION="1.0 (Meridian)"
PRETTY_NAME="jetos 1.0 (Meridian)"

options.label: Aviation waypoints/navigation
options.detail: Codenames from flight navigation: Meridian, Vector, Zenith, Apex, Transom, Beacon, Corridor, Flare, Glidepath, Holding — semver-style versions (1.0, 1.1).

options.label: Aircraft families
options.detail: Codenames after iconic aircraft: Comet, Constellation, Caravelle, Concorde, Mustang, Spitfire, Vulcan, Dakota — semver versions.

options.label: Winds
options.detail: Codenames after named winds: Zephyr, Mistral, Sirocco, Chinook, Bora, Levante, Pampero, Harmattan — semver versions.

options.label: Calendar versioning, no codenames
options.detail: jetos 26.07 style (year.month), clean and NixOS-like but codename-free — least personality, zero naming debt.

options.name: Calver releases with alphabetical aviation-waypoint codenames (hybrid)
options.detail: Version is calver `YY.MM` (Option D's scheme) — an OS release carries no API-compat fact for semver's major/minor to encode, and NixOS/Ubuntu proved date versions stay honest and sortable for decades — while each release also carries an aviation-navigation codename from Option A's family, assigned in alphabetical order (26.10 "Apex", 27.04 "Beacon", 27.10 "Corridor", …) so the codename itself encodes release ordering. Navigation words are generic vocabulary with low trademark exposure, unlike aircraft names (Concorde, Mustang, Spitfire are live marks and products) or winds (Zephyr RTOS, Mistral AI, Nokia's Harmattan); each codename is still vetted against existing OS and software names before ratification and recorded in a committed canon file. os-release law: NAME=jetos, ID=jetos, VERSION_ID=26.10, VERSION_CODENAME=apex, PRETTY_NAME="jetos 26.10 (Apex)"; pre-releases append `-pre`. A CI proof asserts no upstream NixOS identity string — Yarara or any successor — ever reaches os-release, the boot menu, or the welcome screen.
options.code:
NAME=jetos
VERSION="26.10 (Apex)"
VERSION_ID=26.10
VERSION_CODENAME=apex
PRETTY_NAME="jetos 26.10 (Apex)"
# CI gate: os-release/boot/welcome contain no 'NixOS'/'Yarara' — must be empty

decisions.title: Native Nix compatibility engine implementation
decisions.gist: Choose what code Jetpack uses to evaluate Nix inputs without an installed Nix.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A is right on sovereignty, but "implement from official specs" is fiction — Nix behavior is defined by its C++ implementation, and A leaves field-divergence handling unspecified. B and C both need I6 waivers for Tvix, which itself diverges from reference Nix at nixpkgs scale and carries license/upstream-tracking burden. The hybrid keeps A's native ownership, makes oracle use dev/CI-only law consistent with ratified D-JOS-NIXEVAL1 (no nix binary on product paths), and adds drvPath/NarHash self-verification so divergence fails closed instead of silently corrupting cache identity.
decisions.story: Walter moves a production flake to Jetpack. He expects the same derivations and cache hits on a clean machine, while Jet remains the only package language his team must learn.
decisions.inWild:
$ PATH=/usr/bin jetpack fetch nixpkgs:postgresql_16
resolved with Jetpack Nix compatibility engine
no `nix` executable used
decisions.detail: Correctness comes from pinned differential corpora; native ownership best preserves I6 and long-run control.

options.name: Native Jetpack engine
options.detail: Implement from official formats/specs, differential-test against Nix/Tvix, and keep Jetpack sovereign. Amends D-JPK-NONIX1: compatible Nix refs resolve natively; E1272 remains only for explicitly unsupported compatibility cases.
options.code:
$ jetpack fetch nixpkgs:postgresql_16
+ evaluated natively
+ verified cache closure

options.name: Vendor audited Tvix modules
options.detail: Vendor selected evaluator/NAR/derivation code only in an isolated Jetpack runtime binary behind the existing process protocol. Requires a scoped I6 waiver, license approval, and pinned source audit; never enters compiler/driver dependency closure.
options.code:
$ jetpack doctor
Nix engine process: vendored tvix modules
compiler dependency: none

options.name: External Tvix runtime dependency
options.detail: Use Tvix crates only inside an isolated Jetpack runtime binary behind the process protocol. Requires a scoped I6 waiver and locked/audited dependency; never enters compiler/driver dependency closure.
options.code:
$ jetpack doctor
Nix engine process: external tvix, locked
compiler dependency: none

options.name: Native engine, dev-only oracles, self-verifying store paths (hybrid)
options.detail: Implement the engine natively from formats and observed reference behavior; Jetpack ships no Tvix code and needs no I6 waiver. Reference Nix and Tvix run only in a dev/CI differential harness against the D-JPK-NIXBASELINE1-pinned corpus — never on product paths (per D-JOS-NIXEVAL1) — and any divergence is a hard internal compatibility failure, never a silent field difference. Product paths self-verify: computed drvPath/outPath/NarHash must match substituted cache metadata, and mismatch fails closed with one E-code naming the construct plus a `jetpack compat report` bundle. No provider/product path enables an evaluator stage before it passes the pinned corpus bit-exact (JP9/JP10). Amends D-JPK-NONIX1 as in A: compatible refs resolve natively; E1272 covers only named unsupported cases.
options.code:
$ jetpack fetch nixpkgs:postgresql_16
+ evaluated natively (baseline: Nix 2.34)
+ drvPath/NarHash cross-checked against cache metadata
$ jetpack compat diff --oracle nix   # dev/CI harness only
corpus <nixpkgs-pin>: 0 divergences

comparisons.note: Reference evaluator and store formats; compatibility oracle, never user-facing canon.
Own functional package engine and store implementation.

decisions.title: Strong sandbox default and fallback law
decisions.gist: Choose what happens when a machine cannot enforce Jetpack's strong build sandbox.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A keeps ambient-authority execution as the default, an opt-out footgun that violates philosophy and plan Law 4. Option B is sound but leaves the degrade order (substitution/remote before override), non-executing exemption, CI behavior, and error UX unstated; option C denies experts and beginners any path on platforms without a backend. The hybrid keeps B's audited digest-bound grant, adds C's exemption logic inverted (copy/prebuilt always safe), and closes the gaps with substitute-first fallback, deny-by-default CI, and exact fix lines.
decisions.story: Doris opens an unfamiliar repository and runs `jet build`. A dependency's build script tries to read her SSH keys and call localhost. The safe default must decide before that process starts.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build
Error [E12xx]: this package needs executable build steps, but strong sandboxing is unavailable
Fix: enable the platform sandbox or approve an untrusted local-only build
decisions.detail: Safe beginner default; expert override stays explicit, audited, and barred from trusted publication.

options.name: Keep warning fallback
options.detail: Current law: warn, then run executable builds with ambient host authority unless `sandbox require` was configured.
options.code:
warning L0205: build runs unsandboxed
$ jet build   # continues

options.name: Require for third-party execution; audited local-only override
options.detail: Strong sandbox is mandatory for fetched/transitive executable steps. A local-source action may receive an exact trust grant bound to action/source/script digest, declared capabilities, reviewer, and expiry; outputs stay private/untrusted and can never promote. Amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1 fallback default.
options.code:
$ jet build
blocked: strong sandbox unavailable
$ jet trust grant build-action:<digest> --expires 1h
~ output: private/untrusted

options.name: Require universally
options.detail: Any executable build without a strong backend fails, including local first-party work. Copy/prebuilt verification remains allowed because it executes no upstream code.
options.code:
$ jet build
Error: strong sandbox required on this platform

options.name: Sandbox-or-substitute; audited local grant; non-executing steps exempt (hybrid)
options.detail: Non-executing actions (copy, prebuilt verification) always proceed. Fetched or transitive executable steps require the strong sandbox with no warning fallback; when the backend is unavailable, Jetpack first tries substitution from a trusted cache or an approved remote builder (D-BUILDREMOTE1), then fails with an E12xx naming both the backend fix and the override. A local first-party action may run under `jet trust grant build-action:<digest>` bound to action digest, script digest, declared capabilities, reviewer, and expiry (default 1h); its outputs are marked private/untrusted, never promote to shared cache or trusted publication, and every grant lands in `policy.trust` and the audit log. CI defaults to deny; `sandbox require` remains the one-line tightening to option-C behavior. This amends only the D-JPK-NODAEMON1 warning fallback; rootless operation is unchanged.
options.code:
$ jet build
blocked [E12xx]: strong sandbox unavailable for fetched step sharp@0.34
try substitute: trusted cache... miss
Fix 1: jet doctor sandbox
Fix 2: jet trust grant build-action:sha256:9f2a --expires 1h
~ granted: output private/untrusted, never publishable

comparisons.note: Sandbox configuration can be enabled/disabled; multi-user builds add privilege separation.
Sandboxing is an execution strategy and remote-cache correctness boundary.

decisions.title: Secure shared-store architecture
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jetpack supports cross-user store sharing and how privilege separation works.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A abandons the epoch parity claim and gives CI hosts nothing; option C forces a resident privileged daemon on every machine, gutting D-JPK-NODAEMON1 far beyond need. Option B is right in shape but vague where implementers will bleed: no admission law, no builder-identity isolation rule, no fallback semantics, and 'broker' quietly re-introduces a resident daemon. The hybrid states the admission proof, makes the broker transient/socket-activated to preserve NODAEMON1's spirit, defines transparent fallback, and wires status/audit surfaces.
decisions.story: Hank runs a CI host used by thirty developers. They should share identical gigabyte toolchains without letting one user inject bytes another user trusts.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker
root: /var/lib/jet/hangar
builders: isolated identities
user writes: private namespace
decisions.detail: Rootless beginner path stays intact; shared machines gain secure dedup and isolated trust.

options.name: Per-user stores only
options.detail: Preserve D-JPK-NODAEMON1 without exception. Users never share local objects; teams rely on remote caches. Selecting this explicitly drops secure cross-user local-store parity from the epoch claim.
options.code:
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: per-user
parity exception: multi-user local store

options.name: Per-user default plus optional broker
options.detail: Default remains rootless. Admins may install a narrowly-scoped broker that owns the shared store, verifies immutable objects, isolates builders, and never evaluates user package source. Explicit amendment to D-JPK-NODAEMON1 only for shared mode.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker

options.name: Always-installed system daemon
options.detail: All Jetpack operations use one privileged service and shared store, matching classic multi-user Nix architecture. Explicitly amends D-JPK-NODAEMON1.
options.code:
$ jetpack daemon start
all users share /var/lib/jet/hangar

options.name: Per-user default; verifying transient broker opt-in, scoped amendment (hybrid)
options.detail: Default stays rootless per-user per D-JPK-NODAEMON1; every command works identically with no broker present. Admins opt in via `jetpack shared-store install`, which installs a socket-activated transient broker (no resident daemon) owning the shared store; the broker admits objects only after re-verifying canonical output digest, signatures, and provenance inside its own privilege domain — user-supplied bytes are never trusted on assertion — and it never evaluates user package source. Builds it performs run as ephemeral isolated builder identities inside the strong sandbox; user writes land in private namespaces, and promotion to shared follows D-JPK-CACHEAUTH1 writer law. Clients fall back to per-user mode transparently when the broker is absent, and `jetpack hangar status` plus `jet audit` report mode, broker version, and admission policy. This is an explicit audited amendment to D-JPK-NODAEMON1 scoped solely to shared mode.
options.code:
$ jetpack shared-store install   # admin, once
$ jetpack hangar status
mode: shared-broker (socket-activated, non-resident)
admission: digest+signature+provenance verified
user writes: private namespace
$ jet audit broker
builders: ephemeral isolated identities

comparisons.note: Multi-user mode uses a privileged daemon and isolated build users.
A system daemon owns the store and performs builds.

decisions.title: Dynamic dependency graph law
decisions.gist: Choose whether build results may create later build graph.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A forfeits the plan's Nix-parity exit claim; C is the rejected recursive-resolution anti-pattern that destroys determinism and cache identity. B is directionally right but silent on stage bounds, on how fragments enter action keys and the lock (so staged builds could silently break offline replay per D-JPK-OFFLINE1), and on diagnostics. The hybrid keeps B's architecture and adds the missing law: declared bounded depth, lock-recorded fragment identity, structural impossibility of recursive resolution, and a named diagnostic.
decisions.story: Betty generates bindings from a schema whose imports determine a second set of packages. She needs generated planning without letting arbitrary builds recursively call the package manager.
decisions.detail: Generated graphs work through one typed mechanism; Jet avoids ambient recursive planning while compatibility remains faithful.

options.name: Static graphs only
options.detail: Jet-authored graphs must be complete before execution and imported Nix IFD is unsupported. Selecting this explicitly narrows the Nix parity claim.
options.code:
Error: imported Nix input uses IFD
parity exception: IFD

options.name: Finite typed staging; isolated Nix IFD compatibility
options.detail: Jet-authored builds get one finite typed planning stage. Imported Nix compatibility preserves repeated IFD evaluation/realization semantics only inside the isolated compatibility engine, with the same sandbox, trust, and resource limits; it never becomes Jet syntax.
options.code:
Jet plan: one checked stage
Nix compatibility: isolated IFD trace, every realization verified

options.name: Arbitrary recursive planning
options.detail: Any build/evaluator step may inspect the store and invoke resolution recursively, matching maximum Nix flexibility.
options.code: build step calls jetpack resolve dynamically

options.name: Finite staged planning, locked fragments, isolated Nix IFD (hybrid)
options.detail: Jet-authored builds get finite typed staging: a sandboxed plan action emits a BuildPlan fragment that passes canonical-hash, sema, authority, and acyclicity checks before merging, with stage depth statically declared (default 1) and raised only by an audited manifest field. Fragment digests and their exact inputs enter action identity and the semantic lock, so staged graphs replay deterministically offline; no API exists for a build step to read the store or invoke resolution. Imported Nix IFD replays only inside the isolated compatibility engine under the same sandbox, trust, and resource limits, every realization verified; it never becomes Jet syntax. Stage violations raise one E12xx naming the plan action, the exceeded bound, and the fix.
options.code:
$ jet build
plan stage 1/1: bindings -> fragment sha256:... (sema ok, acyclic, authority ok)
lock: fragment + inputs recorded; offline replay proven
Nix compatibility: isolated IFD trace, every realization verified

comparisons.note: Import-from-derivation interleaves evaluation and realization.
Analysis creates a finite action graph before execution.

decisions.title: Package profile ownership and surface
decisions.gist: Choose how users declare atomic package profiles without duplicating JetOS user environments.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A stands up a second generation engine beside the ratified JetOS one, violating the plan's one-graph law and JP14's no-second-mechanism rule; B drops non-JetOS parity, hostile to the tier-1 three-OS product (D-JPK-PLATFORM1). C picks the right engine but leaves the verb set, generation naming, view drift, and GC rooting unspecified. The hybrid keeps C's shared engine and states the surface as law: verbs mirror ratified `jetos user`, D-JPK-OSGEN1 naming, plan-before-apply, one history, generations as JP4 roots.
decisions.story: Earl wants separate daily, graphics, and incident-response toolsets with offline rollback. His JetOS user config and Jetpack package profiles must not become two generation engines.
decisions.detail: One semantic generation engine serves package-manager and OS views; ownership stays source-backed and explicit.

options.name: Jetpack-only profile namespace
options.detail: `profile.*` and `jet profile` own package generations; JetOS `user.*` remains separate and imports profiles explicitly.
options.code:
module profile.daily { packages: [...] }
$ jet profile switch daily

options.name: JetOS user profiles own everything
options.detail: Package generations exist only through `user.<name>` and `jetos user`; non-JetOS users keep project envs only. Selecting this drops non-JetOS profile parity.

options.name: One generic generation engine, product-specific views
options.detail: A shared source-backed profile engine owns identity, switching, rollback, collision, and GC. Jetpack exposes package profiles; JetOS user environments compose the same objects. Selecting this amends D-JOS-USERENV1, D-JOS-USERAPPLY1, and D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1 only to share the engine and `profile.*` references.

options.name: One shared generation engine, mirrored verbs, one history (hybrid)
options.detail: A single source-backed generation engine owns identity, atomic switch, history, collision policy, and GC rooting for every profile object; `profile.<name>` is the sole package-profile declaration and `user.<name>` composes profiles by reference, amending D-JOS-USERENV1, D-JOS-USERAPPLY1, and D-PRODUCT-SPLIT1 only to share the engine. `jet profile plan/build/switch/rollback/generations` mirrors the ratified `jetos user` verb set, with D-JPK-OSGEN1 auto-naming plus `--name` and the ratified plan-before-apply UX on every mutation. A profile composed into an active user environment has exactly one history: switching it records a new generation through the same engine, so the Jetpack and JetOS views can never drift. Non-JetOS platforms get full parity per D-JPK-PLATFORM1; generations are JP4 GC roots with retained-generation defaults experts may tune.

comparisons.note: Per-user profiles provide atomic generations and rollback.
comparisons.code:
nix profile install nixpkgs#ripgrep
nix profile rollback

comparisons.note: User environment composition is separate from low-level Nix profiles.

decisions.title: Registry, publisher, and cache trust root
decisions.gist: Choose the trust architecture for registry metadata, publishers, caches, and offline verification.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A's TOFU defends none of the story's attacks and is already listed as a production blocker in the plan. Option B forbids identity-based signing, hurting key-loss recovery; option C is strongest but leaves bootstrap distribution, transparency-log checkpoint pinning, recovery drills, and the beginner verdict surface unstated, and both B and C amend D-PKGSIGN1, which does not appear in the ratified digest — that reference needs reconciliation at ratification. The hybrid keeps C's architecture and closes bootstrap, agility (D-PQCRYPTO1), offline-grace (D-JPK-OFFLINE1), and audit-UX gaps.
decisions.story: Martha's registry timestamp key is stolen. Attackers must not replace packages, roll clients back, freeze updates, or make a new publisher key look legitimate on first use.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet audit trust
root: 3-of-5 offline threshold
registry snapshot: current
publisher: verified identity bundle
cache builder: approved provenance
result: trusted
decisions.detail: Automatic beginner verification plus exact expert roots, thresholds, privacy, offline, and recovery controls.

options.name: Author TOFU plus Git index
options.detail: Keep first-seen Ed25519 author keys and current Git history as the principal trust model.
options.code: trust: first seen key for acme/web

options.name: TUF thresholds plus long-lived author keys
options.detail: Offline threshold root, delegated targets, snapshot/timestamp freshness, rotation/revocation; public-registry releases require publisher Ed25519/KMS signatures, explicitly amending D-PKGSIGN1 there. Private registries may set an equally explicit signature policy.
options.code:
root: 3-of-5
publisher: ed25519/acme

options.name: TUF thresholds plus hybrid publisher identity
options.detail: TUF secures registry authority/freshness; trusted-root bootstrap, monotonic updates, bad clocks, expiry, and signature stripping fail closed. Public-registry releases require either Sigstore identity bundles or Ed25519/KMS/HSM publisher signatures, explicitly amending D-PKGSIGN1 there; private registries choose an explicit offline policy. SLSA provenance covers builders.
options.code:
root: 3-of-5, monotonic + unexpired
publisher: required sigstore bundle OR offline key
builder: signed provenance

options.name: TUF + hybrid publisher identity, pinned bootstrap, agile algorithms (hybrid)
options.detail: TUF secures registry authority: offline threshold root, delegated targets, snapshot/timestamp freshness, consistent snapshots, monotonic versions; expiry, rollback, bad clocks, and signature stripping fail closed with named E12xx, while already-realized environments keep working offline per D-JPK-OFFLINE1. The trusted root ships pinned inside the jet toolchain object, so bootstrap never trusts first network contact; rotation, revocation, and threshold-minus-one recovery are drilled surfaces, and all signature algorithms ride the D-PQCRYPTO1 agility seam over the D-DEP-CRYPTO1 backend. Public-registry releases require a Sigstore identity bundle verified against a pinned transparency-log checkpoint OR an offline Ed25519/KMS/HSM publisher signature — both feed one monitorable audit stream — explicitly amending D-PKGSIGN1 there; private registries set an equally explicit offline policy. Cache builders and remote executors hold distinct identities with SLSA provenance bound to action and output digests. `jet audit trust` gives beginners one verdict line; `--json` exposes every role, threshold, and expiry.
options.code:
$ jet audit trust
root: 3-of-5 offline, pinned via toolchain, unexpired, monotonic
publisher: sigstore bundle (log checkpoint verified)
builder: SLSA provenance, approved identity
result: trusted
$ jet audit trust --json   # full chain: roles, thresholds, expiry

comparisons.note: Separates offline root, delegated targets, snapshot, and timestamp roles.
Binds ephemeral keys to workload/user identity with transparency proof bundles.

decisions.title: Shared-cache writer authority
decisions.gist: Choose which builders may publish objects that others consume as trusted.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A is the poisoning hole the story describes — a signature proves who, not build integrity. Option B kills all developer sharing and never defines builder approval; option C is the right shape but leaves credential lifetime, the approval evidence set, read-path verification, and compromised-builder revocation unstated. The hybrid keeps C's namespace split and pre-execution approval, then adds verify-on-read, provenance field law, quarantine-on-revocation, and the explain surface implementers need.
decisions.story: Frank's laptop builds a package with a locally modified compiler. That result may be useful to him, but it must not silently become the organization's trusted cache hit.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet build
cache write: private/frank
$ jet release
cache write: shared/release (approved builder + provenance)
decisions.detail: Fast local sharing never weakens organization-wide trust.

options.name: Any authenticated developer writes shared
options.detail: A cache token grants read/write to the common namespace; consumers verify object signatures only.
options.code: cache: shared write accepted from frank

options.name: Hosted release builders only
options.detail: Only centrally configured builders may write shared cache; all developer outputs stay local.
options.code: cache: shared write denied; builder not allowlisted

options.name: Private and shared namespaces
options.detail: Developers write private namespaces. Shared namespaces accept only builders approved before execution with action/platform/sandbox/policy/reproducibility proofs. An unapproved result must rebuild on an approved builder; provenance cannot retroactively promote authority. Read/write credentials are separate.
options.code:
cache write private/frank: accepted
cache promote shared: rebuild on approved release builder

options.name: Namespaces plus provenance-bound writers, verify-on-read, revocation (hybrid)
options.detail: Developers write private namespaces with short-lived write-scoped credentials; read and write credentials are always separate. Shared/trusted namespaces accept only builders allowlisted in source policy before execution, and every upload carries signed provenance binding action digest, output digest, platform, sandbox class, and policy hash — provenance can never retroactively promote authority. Consumers re-verify digest and signature on every hit in every namespace (Law 3: no trust by location); an unapproved result is rebuilt on an approved builder, never copied across on assertion. Revoking a builder quarantines every object it signed until re-verified or rebuilt. `jet build` prints the namespace of each cache write, and `jet explain --lens cache` states why a hit was trusted or refused.
options.code:
$ jet build
cache write private/frank: accepted (write-scoped token, 1h)
$ jet release
cache promote shared: rebuild on approved release builder
$ jet explain --lens cache pkg:foo
hit shared/release: digest ok, sig ok, builder approved, sandbox=strong

comparisons.note: Common guidance separates cache consumers from trusted CI writers.
Remote cache authorization is separate from action correctness.

decisions.title: Multiple-version resolution law
decisions.gist: Choose when two versions of the same package may coexist.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A is the Go-style global straitjacket that turns every major-version ecosystem migration into a flag day; B reproduces npm/cargo one-process ABI splits. C is sound but under-specified: it never says who proves isolation, gives no diagnostic quality bar, and forces unification even where cargo-style major coexistence is provably safe. The hybrid keeps C's typed domains, adds compiler-proven major coexistence with version-qualified identity, PubGrub causal proofs on E1201, and an audited expert escape recorded in the lock.
decisions.story: Alice builds a server whose code generator needs protobuf 3 while the runtime needs protobuf 4. Global unification fails; unrestricted duplication can split one runtime ABI.
decisions.inWild:
tool protobuf@3   domain: build/x86_64-linux
lib  protobuf@4   domain: target/aarch64-linux
both locked; runtime link domain remains coherent
decisions.detail: Avoids global straitjacket and uncontrolled duplication through typed isolation.

options.name: One version globally
options.detail: Every package name resolves once across the whole workspace and every build/target role.
options.code: Error: protobuf 3 and 4 cannot coexist

options.name: Unrestricted duplicates
options.detail: Every dependency edge may select its own version, even inside one runtime/link domain.
options.code:
app -> protobuf 4
plugin -> protobuf 3
both enter same process

options.name: One version per typed domain
options.detail: Identity is provider + namespace + name. Unify inside a domain; duplicate only across a proven isolation boundary for build/host/target, platform, runtime, linkage, or ABI. Feature differences alone do not prove isolation. Amends E1201 to reject incompatible versions in one typed domain.
options.code:
build domain: protobuf 3
target domain: protobuf 4
shared runtime/link domain: unify or E1201

options.name: Typed domains plus proven-safe major coexistence and causal proofs (hybrid)
options.detail: Identity is provider + namespace + name; one version unifies inside each typed domain, and duplication is automatic only across proven build/host/target, platform, runtime, linkage, or ABI boundaries — feature differences never prove isolation. Distinct semver majors may additionally coexist inside one domain only when the compiler proves no type or value crosses versions (identities are version-qualified); any crossing is E1201 carrying a PubGrub causal proof naming both requirement chains and the smallest fix. Experts may force a named coexistence via policy.resolution.allow_duplicate(package, domain, reason), recorded in lock rationale and audit output. Every coexistence appears in `jet explain duplicates` with its proving boundary.
options.code:
$ jet build
E1201: protobuf 3 and 4 meet in one runtime/link domain
  proof: server -> grpc 2.1 -> protobuf 4; codegen -> protobuf 3
  smallest fix: update codegen to >=1.8 (uses protobuf 4)
$ jet explain duplicates
protobuf: 3 [build] / 4 [target] — boundary: build/target roles

comparisons.note: Can resolve multiple crate versions but feature/type identity surprises remain.
Package identity includes settings/options/dependency identities.

decisions.title: Package variant vocabulary
decisions.gist: Choose the axes used to match package producers and consumers.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A pushes linkage/ABI/role back into ad-hoc recipes and recreates the vcpkg triplet explosion; B is Gradle's open-attribute ambiguity, an explicitly rejected anti-pattern. C names the right axes but omits the matching/defaulting law where Gradle actually hurts (ambiguous candidates), never binds the selected variant into action keys and the lock (JP15), and gives the closed set no evolution path. The hybrid states total defaults, deterministic tie-break with a naming diagnostic, lock/key entry, and ballot-gated axis growth.
decisions.story: George needs a static musl library for an ARM target, a native code generator for macOS, and a shared debug library for local tests. Variant facts must be precise and finite.
decisions.inWild:
need: role .Target, os .Linux, arch .Aarch64, libc .Musl, linkage .Static
selected: exact compatible artifact
decisions.detail: Captures real compatibility without Gradle-style unbounded ambiguity.

options.name: Platform only
options.detail: Selection considers OS and architecture; recipes handle linkage, ABI, runtime, and role ad hoc.
options.code: variant: aarch64-linux

options.name: Open attribute maps
options.detail: Providers and packages invent arbitrary keys; a generic matcher picks compatible maps.
options.code: variant: { os: linux, fooMode: turbo, abiX: 7 }

options.name: Typed core axes plus namespaced provider facts
options.detail: Closed native axes: build/host/target role, OS, arch, runtime/libc, linkage, ABI, artifact kind, feature set. Providers may preserve extra facts, but native selection uses them only after explicit mapping.
options.code:
variant: Variant.{ role: .Target, os: .Linux, arch: .Aarch64, linkage: .Static }
providerFacts: { conan.compiler.runtime: "libstdc++11" }

options.name: Closed axes, total defaults, deterministic match, ballot-gated growth (hybrid)
options.detail: Native selection uses only the closed typed axes — build/host/target role, OS, arch, runtime/libc, linkage, ABI, artifact kind, feature set — and every axis has a defined default derived from the requesting context, so beginners never write variants. Matching is exact-then-compatible under one total documented order; an ambiguous tie is an E12xx listing the candidates and the first distinguishing axis, never a silent pick. The selected variant enters the action key and the semantic lock. Provider facts persist under namespaced keys and influence selection only through explicit variant_map declarations in source policy; adding a native axis requires a decision ballot.

comparisons.note: Variant-aware resolution matches producer/consumer attributes.
Triplets encode platform/linkage/runtime choices.

decisions.title: New-release maturity default
decisions.gist: Choose whether newly published third-party versions wait before fresh resolution.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A leaves the compromised-account story wide open, and option C makes safety opt-in — a direct philosophy violation. Option B is correct but hard-codes 24h for every source including your own registry, and never resolves the ugly case where the held release is itself the security fix. The hybrid keeps B's transparency-anchored clock and exact exceptions, zeroes the window for first-party sources, makes it policy-tunable per registry, and surfaces the advisory conflict with a guided audited override.
decisions.story: Doris runs `jet update` minutes after a popular package account is compromised. Existing exact locks should keep working, while new resolution gets time for yanks and trust evidence.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet update http
held: http 4.8.1 (published 37m ago)
selected: 4.8.0
Fix: audit and grant an exact exception
decisions.detail: Beginner protection is automatic; audited exact overrides preserve urgent expert control.

options.name: No maturity delay
options.detail: Any valid new release is immediately eligible under version and trust policy.
options.code: selected 4.8.1, published 37m ago

options.name: 24-hour default with exact exception
options.detail: New direct and transitive third-party versions wait 24 hours from first immutable inclusion in trusted, monotonic signed registry/transparency metadata—not publisher, mirror, or local timestamps. Existing exact locks are unaffected. Exceptions bind one package/version plus that inclusion/evidence identity.
options.code:
held 4.8.1 until maturity
policy exception may name exactly 4.8.1

options.name: Opt-in maturity policy
options.detail: Default stays immediate; projects enable a delay in workspace policy.
options.code: module workspace { policy: Policy.{ release_maturity_hours: 24 } }

options.name: 24h default, policy-tunable per source, advisory-aware exact exceptions (hybrid)
options.detail: New direct and transitive third-party versions wait 24 hours from first immutable inclusion in trusted monotonic signed registry/transparency metadata — never publisher, mirror, or local timestamps; existing exact locks and realized environments are untouched (D-JPK-OFFLINE1). Workspace policy may raise or lower the window per registry or source class; first-party and workspace-internal sources default to zero. When a held version fixes a published advisory affecting the currently selected version, `jet update` says so and offers the audited exception; every exception binds exactly one package#version plus its inclusion/evidence identity, reviewer, and expiry in `policy.trust`. CI evaluates the same policy deterministically, and held versions print with age and the one-line fix.
options.code:
$ jet update http
held: http 4.8.1 (published 37m ago; matures in 23h)
selected: 4.8.0
note: 4.8.1 fixes advisory JSA-2026-114 affecting 4.8.0
Fix: jet trust grant release-exception:http#4.8.1 --expires 7d

comparisons.note: Supports minimum release age and trust-policy exclusions.
Default resolution has no maturity delay.

decisions.comment: the version specifier is package#version, not package@version

decisions.title: Upstream build and install hook approval
decisions.gist: Choose when third-party package scripts may execute.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: Option A converts sandbox containment into authorization and auto-runs third-party code; option B's name-scoped approval that survives script changes is the classic worm vector and leaves CI undefined. Option C has the right binding law but a cold policy error on `jet add` is beginner-hostile, and it never states that approval keeps the sandbox, nor grant revocation or transitive review aids. The hybrid keeps C's exact digest+capability binding, adds a guided interactive path and diff-on-change, mandates sandbox-after-approval, and allows only digest-bound curated allowlists.
decisions.story: Hank adds an npm tool whose transitive package has a postinstall script. The metadata can be read safely, but executing code needs an authority decision bound to what will run.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet add npm:sharp
blocked hook: sharp#0.34 install
requests: exec, filesystem write
$ jet trust grant package-hook:sharp#0.34
grant binds script digest + capabilities
decisions.detail: One approval mechanism covers providers and keeps both beginners and CI safe.

options.name: Run sandboxed hooks automatically
options.detail: All provider-declared hooks run inside the strong sandbox with declared/default capabilities.
options.code: install hook: auto-approved sandbox

options.name: Prompt on first execution
options.detail: Interactive users approve the package name once; later hook changes inherit approval.
options.code: Run sharp install hook? [y/N]

options.name: Deny unreviewed; exact intent approval
options.detail: Hooks never run during metadata probing. Approval binds package identity, script/recipe digest, provider/source, and capability set in source policy. Any change re-prompts. CI fails with the exact source fix.
options.code:
Error: unreviewed hook
Fix: `jet trust grant package-hook:sharp#0.34` drafts policy.trust

options.name: Deny unreviewed; guided exact grants, always sandboxed, CI fix line (hybrid)
options.detail: Metadata probing never executes upstream code; unreviewed hooks are held, not run. Interactive `jet add` shows package identity, provider/source, script digest, and requested capabilities, and one confirmation drafts an exact `policy.trust` grant binding all four; any digest or capability change re-prompts with a diff of what changed. Approval authorizes execution but never removes containment — approved hooks still run inside the strong sandbox with only their granted capabilities, under D-BUILDPOLICY1 tier rules. CI never prompts: it fails with the exact `jet trust grant package-hook:...` source fix, and grants are listable and revocable via `jet trust`. A workspace may pin a signed curated allowlist feed as pre-review evidence; feed entries are digest-bound, never name wildcards.
options.code:
$ jet add npm:sharp
held hook: sharp#0.34 install (digest sha256:4c11)
requests: exec, write $out
approve and record in policy.trust? [y/N] y
~ runs sandboxed with granted caps only
CI: Error [E12xx] unreviewed hook — Fix: jet trust grant package-hook:sharp#0.34

comparisons.note: Explicitly approves dependencies allowed to run install scripts.
build.rs executes as part of builds; sandboxing is external.

decisions.title: Pinned Nix compatibility baseline
decisions.gist: Choose which Nix version and experimental features define the parity contract.
decisions.explainer: Fable hybrid review: A amputates flakes, contradicting the epoch exit claim and the dominant real-world nixpkgs entry point. C promises bit-parity with dynamic derivations and IFD — experimental moving targets — even though IFD's hidden store coupling is a plan-listed rejected anti-pattern, and C states no baseline-advancement law. The hybrid keeps C's full coverage claim and its good impure trust-grant law, delivers IFD/dynamic through the already-gated JP21 typed staging instead of Nix's mechanism, and adds the machine-readable matrix plus a corpus-gated re-pin procedure that A/B/C all lack.
decisions.story: Walter compares Jetpack against Nix after a Nix upgrade changes derivation behavior. A pinned baseline tells CI whether Jetpack diverged or the oracle changed.
decisions.inWild:
$ jetpack compatibility
Nix baseline: 2.34 stable
nixpkgs: <pinned commit>
flakes: yes
CA derivations: yes
dynamic derivations: staged compatibility
decisions.detail: Meets the requested full pinned parity while keeping unsafe/impure behavior isolated from Jet authoring.

options.name: Stable Nix surface only; narrow parity claim
options.detail: Pin latest stable Nix language/store protocol; exclude flakes and experiments. Selecting this explicitly amends the epoch exit claim and drops flake/experimental compatibility.
options.code:
baseline: Nix stable
parity exceptions: flakes, experimental features

options.name: Stable plus selected production experiments
options.detail: Pin Nix 2.34 stable plus flakes, new CLI lock/registry behavior, and CA derivations. Dynamic/recursive/IFD and impure derivations remain named compatibility exceptions, narrowing full Nix parity.
options.code:
baseline: Nix 2.34
features: flakes nix-command ca-derivations

options.name: Full pinned Nix compatibility
options.detail: Pin one Nix release and implement its stable plus experimental package-manager/evaluator/store features, including flakes, CA, dynamic/recursive derivations, IFD, and impure compatibility. Impure Nix is never enabled by import/default: an explicit trust grant binds host/network/env capabilities; results stay private, untrusted, and non-promotable unless rebuilt hermetically.
options.code:
baseline: Nix 2.34
features: full pinned set
impure: explicit capability grant -> private/untrusted output

options.name: Pinned full baseline: tiered core/staged features, granted impurity (hybrid)
options.detail: Pin Nix 2.34 plus a nixpkgs commit as the sole parity oracle. The core tier — stable language/store/protocol, flakes, nix-command, and CA derivations — carries full bit-parity by default; IFD and dynamic/recursive derivations form a staged tier that lowers to the D-JPK-DYNAMICPLAN1 finite typed-staging mechanism, never Nix's hidden store coupling, and until that ballot ratifies such refs fail with one E-code naming the construct, tier, and fix. Impure evaluation is never enabled by import or default: an explicit `jet trust` grant binds host/network/env capabilities, and outputs stay private, untrusted, and non-promotable unless rebuilt hermetically. `jetpack compatibility` emits a machine-readable feature matrix; a baseline re-pin requires the full differential corpus green under the new pin and is recorded as a decision amendment.
options.code:
baseline: Nix 2.34 + nixpkgs <pin>
core: stable flakes nix-command ca-derivations -> bit parity
