DurableAtLeastOnce is the only retry path: sema requires a typed idempotency key, a declared dedup/transaction contract, and a retention window, and the call returns a receipt distinguishing Enqueued from Executed. Retry-budget exhaustion routes the message to a typed dead-letter endpoint the tree must handle; drops exist only in the separately named lossy telemetry API. Exactly-once is never claimed: dedup guarantees at most one committed effect per key within retention only when the handler commits through the declared transaction.
options.code:
now :: orders.call(cmd, delivery: .AtMostOnce, on_full: .Wait(ctx.deadline))?  // timeout after send -> typed .Ambiguous
receipt :: orders.call(cmd, delivery: .DurableAtLeastOnce(
    key: cmd.id, dedup: order_store.transaction, retain: time.days(7)))?  // receipt: .Enqueued | .Executed
// durable endpoint missing key/dedup -> sema diagnostic; retry budget exhausted -> orders.dead_letters (must be handled)

comparisons.note: At-least-once delivery requires idempotent processing, offsets, and transactional boundaries. Jet should make those facts typed rather than imply exactly-once magic.
Per-sender ordering is clear, but unbounded mailboxes can turn overload into failure. Jet keeps channel backpressure structural.

decisions.title: Service state: ephemeral, snapshots, and event logs
decisions.gist: Choose the first-party persistence relationship for supervised services, excluding durable workflow execution semantics.
decisions.explainer:
This decision covers service state only. Durable workflows, replayed timers, and effectful activities are a separate D-SERVICE-WORKFLOW1 choice. State schemas, migration, consistency, recovery, and storage authority must remain explicit; an in-memory field never becomes durable by accident.

Fable hybrid review: A is directionally right but silent on commit points, corruption, rollback reading newer state, and reuses none of the ratified D-MIGRATE3/4 machinery; B abandons uniform snapshot/recovery tooling; C forces event-sourcing semantics on transactional domains. The hybrid keeps the ephemeral default, gives both adapters a single commit-point law plus the existing migration chain, and converts corruption and version skew into typed refusals instead of silent data loss.
decisions.story: Mei has a cache that should restart empty, an order projection that should restore from a snapshot, and an audit stream that should rebuild from events. She wants those modes visible in the service declaration and dossier.
decisions.inWild:
root.worker("catalog-cache", cache, state: .Ephemeral)
root.worker("orders", orders, state: .Snapshot(order_store, schema: OrderState.v3))
decisions.detail: The selected model defines state ownership, snapshot consistency, event ordering, schema/version identity, migrations, corruption, recovery point, backup, encryption, retention, compaction, transaction scope, and what happens when a rollback cannot read newer state.

options.name: Ephemeral default with typed snapshot or event-log opt-ins
options.detail: Services restart empty unless they explicitly select a typed state adapter. Snapshot and event-log adapters share schema/version/migration/recovery facts but preserve their different semantics. Storage authority is injected, never ambient.
options.code:
root.worker("cache", cache, state: .Ephemeral)
root.worker("orders", orders, state: .Snapshot(store, schema: OrderState.v3))
root.worker("audit", audit, state: .EventLog(log, event: AuditEvent.v2))

options.name: Services are stateless; databases own all durability
options.detail: Core services have no persistence contract. Handlers use typed database clients and rebuild in-memory state explicitly. This keeps runtime semantics small but loses uniform snapshot/migration/recovery tooling.
options.code:
root.worker("orders", (ctx) => orders_from_database(ctx, db))
// database schema and migration remain outside service topology

options.name: Event log is the only durable service state
options.detail: Any durable service records typed events and rebuilds by replay; snapshots are only event-log accelerators. This gives one audit model but imposes event-sourcing semantics on domains better served by transactional snapshots.
options.code:
root.worker("orders", orders, state: .EventLog(order_log, event: OrderEvent.v4))
// snapshots contain log position and are never independent truth

options.name: Ephemeral default; adapters share one commit and migration law (hybrid)
options.detail: Services restart empty unless they declare a typed .Snapshot or .EventLog adapter; both adapters share one schema/version contract that reuses ratified migration{} chains and decode_traced provenance (D-MIGRATE3/4). Durability has exactly one commit point — state.commit() for snapshots, event append for logs — with no ambient mid-handler persistence, and recovery restores the last committed point, reporting applied migrations. Corruption and newer-than-code state are typed refusals: the worker fails start naming the required migration or forward recovery, and quarantine-then-restart-empty exists only as an explicit supervisor policy, never a silent reset. Storage authority is an injected capability; plain database clients remain first-class for state the service does not own.

comparisons.note: Processes commonly keep ephemeral state while durable truth lives elsewhere. Jet can preserve that default and make optional recovery contracts explicit.
Integrated state persistence is ergonomic but can hide storage and consistency boundaries. Jet should expose adapters, schema, and authority in source.

decisions.title: Durable workflow execution, replay, timers, and effectful activities
decisions.gist: Choose whether Jet ships a first-party durable workflow layer and how it separates deterministic replay from real-world effects.
decisions.explainer:
A durable workflow is execution semantics, not merely service storage. Replayable code must be deterministic; time, randomness, I/O, and external calls occur through recorded activities. History and version markers must survive code upgrades without silently re-running effects.

Fable hybrid review: A claims deterministic replay but never states the enforcement mechanism despite Jet owning a ratified effect tree; B defers determinism to runtime checks so divergence surfaces in production replay, the exact Temporal failure mode; C outsources the hardest correctness problem to FFI. The hybrid enforces replay purity at sema, adds the lessons A omits — continue-as-new history bounds, per-activity idempotency keys, deploy-time history-compatibility refusal — and keeps workers on the single service substrate.
decisions.story: Ava runs a month-long fulfillment workflow with timers, human approval, payment, retries, and deployment during execution. A crash or upgrade must resume from history without charging twice or inventing a different branch.
decisions.detail: The selected model defines deterministic workflow code, recorded activities, durable timers, retry, cancellation, compensation, history identity, version markers, schema migration, long-lived code upgrades, worker loss, observability, test-time time travel, and effect diagnostics. Ordinary service handlers remain ordinary tasks; workflow restrictions apply only inside the explicit workflow API.

options.name: First-party deterministic workflows over service infrastructure
options.detail: Core provides explicit workflow and activity APIs. Workflow bodies replay deterministically; activities own recorded effects and idempotency. Version markers and compatibility checks protect in-flight histories. The same service deployment and observability substrate runs workers.

options.name: First-party package, not Core/runtime semantics
options.detail: A blessed package implements workflow history and workers over normal service endpoints, timers, and storage. The compiler enforces only ordinary effects; the package performs replay checks and versioning at runtime.
options.code:
use jet.workflow as workflow
flow :: workflow.define(fulfill).activity(charge).timer(wait).activity(ship)

options.name: No first-party durable workflow layer
options.detail: Services, queues, state adapters, and schedulers ship, but long-running durable workflows remain external systems accessed through typed FFI/provider bindings.
options.code:
use js.temporal as temporal
temporal.start("fulfill", order)?

options.name: Effect-checked deterministic workflows, versioned bounded histories (hybrid)
options.detail: Core ships workflow/activity APIs whose bodies sema checks as replay-deterministic through the ratified effect tree (D-EFFTREE1): ambient time, randomness, I/O, channels, and free task spawn are rejected with a deterministic-replay diagnostic naming the recorded equivalent (w.now, w.random, w.activity, w.sleep, w.all). Activities own effects, a typed idempotency key, and retry policy; history identity is workflow id plus run id, and unbounded histories are cut by an explicit w.continue_as law. Version markers gate every branch change, and deploying code incompatible with live histories is refused with the affected history set, feeding D-SERVICE-UPGRADE1 compatibility checks. Workers, durable timers, and observability run on the one service substrate, and the test runtime replays histories under a deterministic clock.

comparisons.note: Deterministic workflow replay plus recorded activities and durable timers is the production bar. Jet can integrate those rules with its effect system and source diagnostics.
Long-lived systems need explicit version compatibility. Workflow histories make the compatibility boundary even stricter than process restart.

decisions.title: Service identity, discovery, cluster authority, and partition semantics
decisions.gist: Choose how typed service endpoints acquire identity and reach local or remote instances without ambient global authority.
decisions.explainer:
A service reference is a typed capability, not a string URL. Local development and production use the same identity contract. Deployment may project placement and discovery facts, but callers cannot discover undeclared services or bypass authentication. Partitions and stale discovery are typed outcomes.

Fable hybrid review: A's own recommended sample panics on unavailability and leaves discovery staleness, rotation overlap, and non-projected endpoints undefined; B repeats operational wiring by hand with no rotation story; C's signed table is auditable but cannot follow dynamic placement. The hybrid delivers A's capabilities through C's signed generational directories with a max-staleness law, dual-generation rotation, typed partition outcomes, and B's explicit connect retained as the audited expert escape.
decisions.story: Tariq calls the same Orders endpoint in a local process and a three-region cluster. He needs mutual authentication, key rotation, explicit authority, and a clear partition result rather than a hidden retry or ambient DNS name.
decisions.detail: The selected model defines logical identity, instance identity, endpoint typing, trust-root ownership, certificate/key issuance and rotation, local-dev projection, discovery freshness, placement constraints, load balancing, authorization, encryption, revocation, partitions, split brain, topology privacy, and audit output.

options.name: Typed capability endpoints with deployment-projected discovery
options.detail: Callers receive only declared typed endpoint capabilities. Jetpack/JetOS deployment projects logical identities to authenticated instances; a project/organization trust module owns roots and rotation. Local dev injects loopback capabilities from the same graph. Partitions, revocation, and stale discovery return typed failures.

options.name: Explicit typed addresses and manual configuration
options.detail: Endpoint types are checked, but applications construct them from explicit addresses, certificates, and policies. There is no first-party discovery or placement projection. This is transparent but repeats operational wiring.

options.name: Injected static deployment name table
options.detail: Build/deploy generates a signed typed table of logical names to endpoints; the application receives that table explicitly at startup. There is no dynamic discovery. Updates require a new table generation and controlled reload.

options.name: Typed capability endpoints over signed generational directories (hybrid)
options.detail: Callers hold only declared typed endpoint capabilities; discovery material arrives as signed, generation-versioned directory snapshots projected by Jetpack/JetOS from source trust policy (D-JPK-PROVIDERAUTH1 roots), and local dev injects loopback capabilities from the same graph with zero configuration. Every resolution carries directory generation and a max-staleness bound; partitions, revocation, expired directories, and stale generations return typed results — never a hidden retry or ambient DNS fallback. Key rotation is dual-generation: old and new credentials overlap for a declared window so no correct caller observes an authentication gap. Explicit service.connect with address and trust root remains the audited expert escape for endpoints outside the projected graph, gated by an explicit trust grant.

comparisons.note: DNS names are convenient but ambient and weakly typed. Jet should project deployment topology into explicit typed capabilities.
Possession of an unforgeable typed reference carries authority. This matches Jet's explicit-grant direction better than global names.

decisions.title: Service generation upgrade, drain, state migration, and rollback
decisions.gist: Choose how running services move between code generations while exposing mixed-version and rollback truth.
decisions.explainer:
No distributed switch is globally atomic under partition. The contract must name its atomic scope and convergence behavior. State rollback is permitted only with reversible migration, dual-write compatibility, or a proven snapshot; otherwise Jet refuses rollback and reports the required forward recovery.

Fable hybrid review: A is the strongest option but is silent on work that outlives the drain deadline and on in-flight workflow histories; B's two-version hot code imports a second runtime and memory model for marginal gain over shard pinning; C accepts downtime and has no mixed-version story. The hybrid keeps A's shard-scoped handoff, adopts B's typed migrate function with plan-time reversibility classification, adds an explicit pin-or-cancel drain-overrun law, and reconciles partitions through the already-ratified staged fleet rollout.
decisions.story: Grace deploys Orders v3 while v2 requests are in flight across three regions. One region partitions after migrating state. She needs bounded mixed-generation behavior, compatible routing, exact health proof, and an honest rollback decision.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet deploy orders --generation v3
plan: validate endpoint/state compatibility -> start v3 -> drain v2 -> switch each routing shard -> retain rollback proof
decisions.detail: The selected model defines compatibility checks, protocol/schema versions, drain deadlines, long streams, health gates, routing-shard atomicity, convergence, partition isolation, mixed-generation visibility, state migration, reversible/forward-only classification, dual writes, rollback window, failure recovery, and audit receipts.

options.name: Generation handoff with scoped switches and proven rollback
options.detail: Jet starts the new generation, validates endpoint and state compatibility, drains old work, and switches traffic atomically per declared routing shard. Global convergence is observable, not claimed atomic. Partitions retain an allowed generation or isolate. Rollback requires reversible migration, dual-write compatibility, or snapshot proof; otherwise deployment exposes forward-recovery state and refuses rollback.
options.code:
use core.time
plan :: service.upgrade()
    .compatible(OrdersV2, OrdersV3)
    .switch_scope(.RoutingShard)
    .migration(service.dual_write(v2_store, v3_store))
    .rollback_window(time.minutes(30))
// dossier lists shards on v2/v3 and convergence deadline

options.name: In-place two-version hot code
options.detail: A runtime process may hold old and new code concurrently and migrate live state through an explicit code-change function. Calls select by generation until old frames drain. This minimizes restart but expands runtime and memory-model complexity.

options.name: Restart-only generations
options.detail: Services stop or drain, state migration runs offline, and the new generation starts. There is no mixed-version routing or hot handoff. Rollback restores only a proven compatible snapshot.
options.code:
$ jet deploy orders --strategy=restart
drain v2 -> stop -> migrate snapshot -> start v3 -> health -> route

options.name: Shard-scoped handoff; classified migrations, typed drain overrun (hybrid)
options.detail: Deployment starts the new generation, validates endpoint and state compatibility, drains, and switches atomically per declared routing shard; global convergence is observed, never claimed atomic. State moves through a typed migrate function classified .Reversible(inverse), .DualWrite, or .ForwardOnly at plan time; a ForwardOnly migration prints a zero rollback window before the switch, and rollback without reversible, dual-write, or snapshot proof is refused with the forward-recovery plan. Work exceeding the drain deadline — long streams and live workflow histories — follows a declared on_exceed policy (.PinShard keeps it on the old generation; .Cancel is explicit), never a silent kill, with pinned shards and mixed generations visible alongside a convergence deadline. Partitioned shards retain their last allowed generation and reconcile on rejoin through the same staged, proof-gated rollout object ratified for fleets (D-JOS-FLEETROLLOUT1).
options.code:
plan :: service.upgrade()
    .compatible(OrdersV2, OrdersV3)
    .migrate(v2_to_v3, class: .Reversible(v3_to_v2))
    .drain(time.seconds(30), on_exceed: .PinShard)
    .switch_scope(.RoutingShard)
    .rollback_window(time.minutes(30))
$ jet deploy orders --generation v3
// 2 shards pinned on v2 (live streams); rollback proven until 14:32; convergence deadline shown

comparisons.note: Two code versions and code_change support live upgrade, but require strict compatibility discipline. Option B imports that deeper runtime model explicitly.
Rolling replacement and health gates are common, but mixed versions and database rollback remain application concerns. Jet should type and audit those facts.

decisions.title: Project formatter invocation, scope, ignore, and check semantics
decisions.gist: Choose how the existing zero-config Jet formatter expands from one file to projects, CI, stdin, VCS changes, and editors.
decisions.explainer:
Every option uses the same parser/formatter engine as LSP, Canvas, and single-file `jet fmt`. The choice is scope and command behavior. No multi-file filesystem transaction is falsely claimed: Jet preflights all files, stages sibling temporary files, replaces per file, and keeps a crash-recovery journal.

Fable hybrid review: All three options leave the CI contract vague: none separates 'needs formatting' from 'could not parse' in exit codes, none names stdin for editor diagnostics, and none states idempotence — the exact ambiguities behind years of prettier/rustfmt CI flakes. B makes the common project action a usage error and C rejects explicit paths, each hostile to one audience; the hybrid keeps A's discovery-plus-exact-scopes law and adds the exit-code triple, --stdin-path, one-pass preflight reporting, edition refusal, and the fixpoint guarantee, all consistent with ratified D-FMTPARENS1 engine behavior.
decisions.story: Inez formats one pasted file, checks a monorepo in CI, formats only her staged changes before commit, and expects her editor to produce byte-identical output without touching generated or vendored code.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet fmt
formatted 18 files
$ jet fmt --check --diff
clean
$ git add src/parser.jet
$ jet fmt --changed
decisions.detail: Recommended semantics: explicit files/directories format exactly that scope; no arguments finds the nearest enclosing workspace, else package, else the cwd tree. Workspace graph and VCS ignores exclude build/generated/vendor content and symlinks are not followed; an explicit ignored file is an expert override. Parse/preflight failure causes zero writes. Each replacement is atomic for that file; the journal detects and repairs a crash during a multi-file commit. `--check` never writes, exits 1 when changes are needed, and lists paths; `--diff` is valid only with `--check` and adds unified diffs. `--changed` means worktree, index, and untracked Jet files; `--changed=BASE` adds files changed from BASE plus local changes. It conflicts with explicit paths and stdin. `-` is the sole input and writes formatted source to stdout.

options.name: Hybrid project default with exact expert scopes
options.detail: No-arg formatting discovers workspace/package/cwd automatically. Explicit paths, stdin, CI check/diff, and VCS-changed modes provide exact control. The project graph, ignore law, staging, journal, output order, and exit codes are identical across CLI/editor/CI.
options.code:
jet fmt                         # nearest workspace/package, else cwd
jet fmt src tests               # exact explicit paths
jet fmt --check --diff          # no writes, exit 1 + unified diff
jet fmt --changed=origin/main   # base diff + index/worktree/untracked
jet fmt - < input.jet > output.jet

options.name: Explicit files and directories only
options.detail: `jet fmt` without paths prints usage; users or build tools choose every scope. Check, diff, changed, and stdin remain available. This avoids discovery surprises but makes the common project action ceremonial.
options.code:
jet fmt src tests
jet fmt --check src tests
jet fmt --changed
# bare jet fmt -> usage: supply PATH or --changed

options.name: Workspace/package only
options.detail: `jet fmt` always formats the nearest workspace or package according to its graph. Single explicit files use `jet fmt -` or editor formatting; arbitrary directory/path scopes are rejected. This is simple but weak for partial migrations and scripts.
options.code:
jet fmt                  # whole nearest workspace/package
jet fmt --check          # whole scope, CI
jet fmt src/one.jet      # error: project formatter does not accept partial paths

options.name: Project default with hardened exit, stdin-path, and idempotence law (hybrid)
options.detail: Adopts A's scope law verbatim (workspace/package/cwd discovery, explicit paths, `--check --diff`, `--changed`, stdin) and hardens the machine contract: exit 0 clean or formatted, 1 only when `--check` finds differences, 2 for usage, parse, or I/O errors, so CI distinguishes 'needs formatting' from 'broken'. `--check` lists paths sorted and root-relative; the existing global `--json` flag emits the stable machine report. Preflight reports every failing file in one pass before the zero-write abort; `--changed` outside version control is a diagnostic naming the fix, and a file declaring a newer edition than the engine knows is refused, never reformatted lossily. `jet fmt - --stdin-path=src/a.jet` names piped input for diagnostics and editor parity; stdin always formats, so the ignore law never applies to it. Output is a byte-identical fixpoint across CLI, LSP, Canvas, and CI — formatting twice equals formatting once.
options.code:
$ jet fmt --check --diff            # exit 1: differences; exit 2: parse/IO error
src/parser.jet
tests/lexer.jet
$ jet fmt - --stdin-path=src/a.jet < a.jet > out.jet
$ jet fmt --changed                  # outside a repo -> diagnostic with fix
$ jet fmt --check --json             # stable machine report for CI

comparisons.note: A canonical formatter plus project-aware tooling produces ecosystem consistency. Jet additionally preserves its ratified author choices and supplies one discoverable command.
File/stdin and Cargo project modes are useful but split across rustfmt and cargo fmt. Option A keeps one Jet command and one engine.

decisions.title: Performance-session command and one canonical trace artifact
decisions.gist: Choose how users collect CPU, wall, allocation, task, lock, I/O, native, and browser performance facts without colliding with package profiles.
decisions.explainer:
The identifier deliberately avoids the existing D-JPK-PROFILE1 package-generation surface and build profiles. Every first-party option uses one versioned Jet trace artifact; terminal, HTML, and JSON are projections, not competing truths. Collection occurs only under an explicit command or flag and never exposes generated Rust frames by default.

Fable hybrid review: A quietly forks execution semantics — nothing binds `jet perf run` to `jet run`'s flags and driver, the drift that made cargo bench diverge from cargo test; B entangles observation flags with execution and admits it still needs a separate perf utility surface; C abandons beginners and the merged browser+server artifact. The hybrid keeps the dedicated intent family but law-binds it to the base intents' exact surface and code path, makes `.jtrace` portable and version-honest, turns capture policy into an auditable artifact fact, ties compare to ratified D-PERFBUDGET-BASELINE1/SURFACE1 law, and folds C in as export projections.
decisions.story: Bea sees a slow request, profiles the CLI locally, attaches to the same-user service, merges browser and server spans, compares before and after, and gives CI a stable machine report without recording customer values or secrets.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet perf run api.jet --lens=cpu,alloc,tasks
summary: p99 42 ms; 61% parse; 22 MiB allocated
trace: .jet/perf/20260709T190402Z-7f3a.jtrace
$ jet perf view .jet/perf/20260709T190402Z-7f3a.jtrace
decisions.detail: `.jtrace` v1 is the source of truth and contains Jet source identities, source maps, OTel-aligned spans/metrics, scheduler causality, samples, allocation sites, backend facts, and clock calibration. Files default to `.jet/perf/<UTC>-<id>.jtrace`, mode 0600, ignored build state, latest 20 retained; `--keep` pins and `--out` chooses a path. Values, arguments, environment, request/response bodies, URLs/query strings, SQL, credentials, and secret types are excluded by default. Expert capture requires explicit field/capability allowlists. Same-user attach must pass OS permission checks; otherwise a Jet diagnostic explains required authority. Web collection uses the selected real browser through an authenticated loopback dev session and merges clocks into the same artifact; remote targets require explicit authority.

options.name: Dedicated `jet perf` intent family
options.detail: `jet perf run/test/bench/attach` makes collection unmistakable and keeps package/build profile vocabulary separate. Safe defaults print a short summary and write one trace. Expert lenses, frequency, target, duration, subprocess scope, privacy fields, output, retention, and comparison are explicit.
options.code:
jet perf run app.jet --lens=cpu,alloc,tasks
jet perf test --filter parser --compare baseline.jtrace
jet perf attach 4281 --duration 30s
# different user/denied ptrace -> Jet permission diagnostic, no raw OS error

options.name: Performance mode on existing intents
options.detail: `jet run/test/bench --perf` collects the exact same event model and `.jtrace` artifact. This keeps fewer top-level commands but mixes execution and observation flags and makes attach/view less discoverable.
options.code:
jet run app.jet --perf=cpu,alloc
jet test --perf=tasks
jet perf attach 4281   # attach/view still need a small perf utility surface

options.name: External profilers with Jet source-map export
options.detail: Jet emits symbols/source maps and documented adapters for perf, Instruments, ETW, browser traces, and OTel, but owns no collection or trace UI. Experts keep platform power; beginners face several tools and cross-target reports do not share one artifact.
options.code:
jet build app.jet --emit-profile-map
perf record build/app
jet devtools symbolize perf.data

options.name: `jet perf` family, verbatim base-intent surface, exported projections (hybrid)
options.detail: `jet perf run/test/bench` are law-bound to accept the exact flag and argument surface of `jet run/test/bench` (program arguments after `--`) and execute through the same driver code path, so observation never forks execution semantics and flag drift is impossible; `perf attach/view/compare/export` complete the family. `.jtrace` v1 is self-contained — embedded schema version, toolchain identity, source identities, and source maps — so any artifact views on any machine without the repo, and a reader meeting a newer major version names the required toolchain instead of misparsing. Capture policy is part of the artifact: the ballot's default exclusions apply, and every expert `--capture` allowlist is written into the trace manifest so reviewers audit exactly what was recorded. `jet perf compare` applies the ratified pinned-baseline law: hardware/toolchain identity mismatch is a refusal with an explicit override, and reports evaluate declared perf.* budgets. `jet perf export --pprof/--otel/--chrome` plus `--emit-profile-map` keep expert platform tools (C) as projections of the one artifact, never competing truths; generated Rust frames stay hidden unless `--frames=all`.
options.code:
$ jet perf run api.jet --lens=cpu,alloc -- --port 8080   # full `jet run` surface after --
$ jet perf compare base.jtrace head.jtrace   # hardware identity mismatch -> refusal + override
$ jet perf export last --pprof | pprof -      # projection; .jtrace stays the truth
$ jet perf view head.jtrace --frames=all      # expert: generated Rust frames visible

comparisons.note: Counters, traces, dumps, and profiler APIs form a coherent operational toolbox. Jet should unify those facts around Jet source and structured tasks.
One profile format and strong built-in analysis make production diagnosis approachable. Jet adds async/task, browser, privacy, and performance-budget integration.

decisions.title: Notebook client and Jupyter interoperability surface
decisions.gist: Choose the user-facing notebook clients over the already-ratified REPL session, addressable-turn, and effect-confirmed rerun semantics.
decisions.explainer:
Every option uses the same REPL engine, typed state, rollback, interrupt, DAP, and D-FE-REPL-RERUN1 dependency replay. No option permits stale Jupyter-only state. This decision depends on D-NOTEBOOK-DOC1 and D-NOTEBOOK-TRUST1 for persistence and rich-output safety.

Fable hybrid review: A builds a third first-party UI stack when ratified law (D-FE-CANVAS1=E, D-STUDIO-CANVASBRIDGE1=C) already mandates shared renderer/trust/proof components — duplicated sanitizer and sandbox code is duplicated attack surface. B demotes stale-turn and effect-confirmation truth to 'may be less discoverable' protocol extensions, an enforcement hole in exactly the clients most people use; C amputates live Jupyter interop entirely. The hybrid keeps A's surface and token law, reuses the Canvas component stack, folds in C's view as a lens of the same session, and converts B's weakness into a stated enforcement floor (stdin_request confirmation, no stale display in any client).
decisions.story: Nia opens an analysis with one command, edits an upstream cell, sees exactly which downstream turns are stale, confirms effectful reruns, then sends the same document to a teammate who uses JupyterLab.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet notebook analysis.jetnb
serving http://127.0.0.1:43127/#token=...
session: typed; stale turns: none; environment: workspace lock 8c2f...
decisions.detail: Option A's exact surface is `jet notebook PATH`, which launches a loopback-only first-party browser client and one REPL session. A random bearer token is placed in the URL fragment, not logs. Non-loopback bind requires explicit `--bind` plus `--auth-file` authority. The Jupyter kernelspec command is `jet notebook kernel --connection {connection_file}` and uses the same session engine. All options define rich MIME, completion, inspect, stdin, interrupt rollback, debug, profile, package/workspace environment, side-effect receipts, disconnect/reconnect, and headless protocol tests.

options.name: First-party notebook client plus Jupyter adapter
options.detail: Jet owns an ergonomic, source-truthful client and also installs a Jupyter kernelspec. Both are projections of one session. The first-party client can surface typed values, stale dependency edges, effect receipts, diagnostics, debugger, profiler, and trusted output state without protocol compromise.
options.code:
jet notebook analysis.jetnb
jet notebook install-jupyter
# kernelspec argv: jet notebook kernel --connection {connection_file}
jet notebook analysis.jetnb --bind 0.0.0.0 --auth-file ./token  # explicit remote authority

options.name: Jupyter clients only
options.detail: Jet ships the kernelspec and protocol server over the same REPL engine but no first-party notebook UI. JupyterLab and compatible clients own rendering; Jet-specific stale/effect/debug facts use protocol extensions and may be less discoverable.
options.code:
jet notebook install-jupyter
jupyter lab analysis.ipynb
# kernel still enforces typed addressable-turn replay and effect confirmation

options.name: Canvas notebook view only
options.detail: Canvas becomes the only first-party client over the same REPL engine; Jet may export/import Jupyter documents but does not install a live Jupyter kernel. This unifies Jet UI but weakens existing notebook ecosystem reach.
options.code:
jet canvas analysis.jetnb --view=notebook
jet notebook export analysis.jetnb --ipynb

options.name: One shared first-party client plus enforcing Jupyter adapter (hybrid)
options.detail: `jet notebook PATH` keeps Option A's exact surface — loopback-only serve, bearer token in the URL fragment, non-loopback only via explicit `--bind` plus `--auth-file` — but the first-party client is assembled from the shared Canvas/Studio protocol components (rich renderer, D-NOTEBOOK-TRUST1 sandbox, receipt and proof widgets) under D-STUDIO-CANVASBRIDGE1's strict boundary, so Jet ships one renderer and one trust engine, and `jet canvas PATH --view=notebook` opens the same live session as a lens, never a second truth. The kernelspec `jet notebook kernel --connection {connection_file}` is an enforcing projection, not best-effort: in foreign clients stale turns are recomputed per D-FE-REPL-RERUN1 before display, effectful replays confirm through `stdin_request`, and an output that would be stale renders as an explicit staleness notice, never a cached value. Headless protocol tests cover both projections; a Jupyter client can never observe session state the first-party client would refuse to show.
options.code:
jet notebook analysis.jetnb                 # loopback + fragment token
jet canvas analysis.jetnb --view=notebook   # same session, Canvas lens
jet notebook install-jupyter
# foreign client: effect confirm via stdin_request; stale output never displays

comparisons.note: The kernel protocol and ecosystem are essential interoperability targets, but traditional notebooks allow hidden stale state. Jet's adapter must preserve addressable-turn truth.
Reactive dependency execution prevents stale cells. Jet can combine that truth with explicit side-effect confirmation and its typed REPL state.
comparisons.code: editing an upstream cell recomputes dependent cells

decisions.title: Canonical notebook document, output cache, merge, and ipynb round-trip
decisions.gist: Choose the source of truth for ordered Jet and Markdown cells and define exactly where outputs and foreign notebook facts live.
decisions.explainer:
Notebook code cells always contain ordinary Jet source; the container is data, not a second language. Stable cell identity drives dependency replay, merge, output cache, diagnostics, and Jupyter interop. Ambient packages or interpreter state are never embedded as invisible environment truth.

Fable hybrid review: A's per-cell `source+environment` cache key omits the upstream dependency closure, so editing cell 1 leaves cell 9's cached output presentable — directly contradicting its own 'no stale output displays' law and D-FE-REPL-RERUN1; its import 'generates stable IDs' non-deterministically, churning identity on every re-import, and says nothing about duplicated-cell ID collisions. B inherits ipynb's JSON merge pain and embedded-output staleness; C splits review truth across two files and cannot interleave Markdown freely. The hybrid keeps A's architecture and fixes all three holes with concrete key, ID, and round-trip law.
decisions.story: Leah reviews a notebook diff, reorders two cells without losing identity, resolves a branch conflict, opens it offline against the pinned workspace, and exports an ipynb whose losses are explicit rather than silent.
decisions.inWild:
format: 1
notebook_id: "sales-q3"
environment: { kind: "workspace", root: ".", lock: "sha256-8c2f..." }

cell: {
  id: "01J4Q7M6B8Y9P0K2D3F4G5H6J7"
  kind: "markdown"
  source: """
# Q3 sales
This report is source-reviewed.
"""
}

cell: {
  id: "01J4Q7P1M2N3R4S5T6V7W8X9Y0"
  kind: "jet"
  source: """
use core.data
use core.files
csv_text :: files.read("sales.csv") ?? panic("can't read sales.csv")
sales :: data.csv<Sale>(csv_text) ?? panic("bad csv")
sales.group_by(.region).sum(.revenue)
"""
}
decisions.detail: Option A defines `.jetnb` v1 as the bytes shown above: a versioned Jet-data envelope, not executable Jet. Strings use Jet triple-string escaping; a literal triple delimiter is written `\"\"\"` and backslash is escaped. New cells receive a 128-bit OS-CSPRNG ID stored in the file; reorder preserves it. A same-ID divergent edit is a merge conflict; `jet notebook merge` aligns by ID, emits both source spans, and refuses execution until resolved. The environment references a relative workspace/package root plus semantic lock digest; a standalone notebook receives an explicit notebook lock. Outputs never enter canonical source: `.jet/notebooks/<notebook-id>/<cell-id>/<source+environment-hash>.jnbout`, ignored by default. Cache miss says `not run for this source and environment`; no stale output displays. `jet notebook export PATH --ipynb [--with-outputs]` embeds only matching cache entries. Import preserves safe opaque metadata, quarantines outputs under D-NOTEBOOK-TRUST1, maps Markdown/code cells, generates stable IDs, and writes an exact loss report for unsupported widgets, attachments, magics, metadata, or MIME. Re-export reports any fact that cannot round-trip.

options.name: Mergeable `.jetnb` source plus detachable output cache
options.detail: The readable container above is canonical. It stores ordered ordinary-Jet/Markdown source, stable IDs, and exact environment identity. Outputs are reproducible ignored cache; committed publication is an explicit export artifact. Cell-aware merge and ipynb import/export always report losses.
options.code:
jet notebook analysis.jetnb
jet notebook merge base.jetnb ours.jetnb theirs.jetnb
jet notebook export analysis.jetnb --ipynb --with-outputs
# output cache: .jet/notebooks/analysis/<cell>/<hash>.jnbout

options.name: `.ipynb` is canonical
options.detail: Standard Jupyter JSON stores source, IDs, metadata, and outputs. Jet adds environment and dependency metadata under a namespaced key. Interoperability is maximal, but diffs/merges and active-output trust inherit ipynb complexity; first-party tooling must still reject stale outputs.

options.name: Ordinary `.jet` source plus notebook layout sidecar
options.detail: A `.jet` module is canonical executable code. Top-level semantic items/expressions become code cells; doc comments become attached Markdown. A `.jetnb.layout` sidecar stores stable cell IDs, order, free-standing Markdown, environment identity, and output-cache links. This preserves ordinary source but splits review truth and cannot represent arbitrary interleaving in one file.

options.name: Mergeable `.jetnb` with closure-keyed cache and ID-faithful ipynb (hybrid)
options.detail: The canonical `.jetnb` v1 container, environment identity, CSPRNG cell IDs, and merge-by-ID law are Option A's, with the output-cache key hardened to source + environment + transitive dependency-closure hash: an upstream cell edit invalidates every downstream entry, so no stale output can ever display or export and the cache is exactly D-FE-REPL-RERUN1's replay truth materialized. Paste or duplicate always mints a fresh ID; ipynb import derives cell IDs deterministically from nbformat 4.5+ cell ids and export writes Jet IDs back, so round-trips preserve identity instead of churning it, with exact loss reports in both directions. `jet notebook merge` registers as an opt-in Git merge/textconv driver per D-MERGE-VCS1, and `jet notebook export --jet` projects cells to an ordinary reviewable `.jet` module as a stated-loss export (C's virtue), never a second truth.
options.code:
jet notebook merge base.jetnb ours.jetnb theirs.jetnb
# cache: .jet/notebooks/analysis/<cell>/<source+env+deps-hash>.jnbout
jet notebook export analysis.jetnb --ipynb --with-outputs  # only closure-fresh entries embed
jet notebook import report.ipynb   # deterministic IDs from nbformat ids + loss report

comparisons.note: Universal support and rich outputs are valuable, but embedded outputs and JSON diffs invite stale state and merge pain. Option A treats ipynb as a loss-reported interchange format.
comparisons.code: nbformat 4 JSON with cells and outputs

comparisons.note: Text-first notebooks improve review and reactive identity. Jet adds an exact environment reference and separates reproducible output cache from source truth.
comparisons.code: text source paired with notebook metadata

decisions.title: Notebook rich-output trust and active-content authority
decisions.gist: Choose how HTML, SVG, Markdown, CSS, widgets, and JavaScript outputs render without turning an imported notebook into ambient code execution.
decisions.explainer:
Plain text is always available. Sanitized passive MIME is the default. Active content never inherits parent page, kernel, filesystem, storage, cookie, credential, or network authority. Trust is local authority, not source metadata, and cannot travel with a notebook.

Fable hybrid review: A's per-payload prompts are the right key with the wrong ergonomics: Jupyter's core lesson is trust fatigue, and A even blocks zero-capability widgets the user just executed locally — beginner-hostile for `display(widget)` — while its `jet notebook trust` forks a second grant surface against the ratified one-authority-graph law (D-JPK-GRANTCMD1=A, D-WD1=B). C institutionalizes fatigue into notebook-wide grants (Jupyter's `trust` mistake with better hashes); B amputates interactive notebooks. The hybrid makes empty-sandbox active content promptless, collapses remaining prompts by intent with a full-audit drawer, and homes grants in the ratified trust graph.
decisions.story: Chen opens a notebook from a pull request containing a plot, SVG, links, and a custom widget. The report should render safely; the widget should remain inert until Chen reviews and grants its exact capabilities.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet notebook report.jetnb
active output blocked: cell 01J... requests JavaScript and network
plain-text fallback shown
$ jet notebook trust report.jetnb --cell 01J... --allow-widget sales.chart --allow-origin https://data.example
decisions.detail: Recommended passive sanitization covers HTML, SVG, Markdown links, CSS, data/blob URLs, dimensions, recursion, decompression, and total output size. Active output runs only in an opaque-origin sandbox iframe with strict CSP; forms, navigation, workers, objects, parent access, kernel access, storage, cookies, credentials, and external URLs are blocked by default. The trust key is notebook source hash + active payload/renderer hash + locked environment identity + policy version. Trust state lives only in per-user local state and is never imported, exported, committed, or synced. Any source/payload/renderer/environment/policy edit or import revokes it. Expert widgets require an origin/capability allowlist and a typed message bridge; network defaults to none. When any renderer fails policy, Jet shows safe `text/plain`.

options.name: Sanitized passive output plus hash-bound capability trust
options.detail: Passive MIME renders after strict sanitization and size limits. Active widgets/JavaScript require a local grant bound to exact source, payload, renderer, environment, and policy hashes. They run in an opaque sandbox with only explicitly granted typed messages and origins. Changes revoke trust automatically.
options.code:
jet notebook trust report.jetnb --cell 01J... \
  --allow-widget sales.chart \
  --allow-message SelectionChanged \
  --allow-origin https://data.example
# no parent/kernel/storage/cookie authority; source or lock edit revokes

options.name: Passive rich output only
options.detail: HTML, SVG, Markdown, images, tables, and plots render through the sanitizer, but JavaScript, active widgets, forms, and network are never executed. This is simplest and safest but excludes interactive notebook applications.
options.code:
display(plot)       // sanitized SVG/PNG works
display(widget)     // blocked; text/plain fallback and export hint

options.name: Trust the whole local notebook environment
options.detail: A user may mark a notebook and locked environment trusted; all its active outputs run until source or lock changes. Sandboxing and CSP remain, but capability review is notebook-wide rather than payload-specific. This is more convenient and grants substantially broader authority.
options.code:
jet notebook trust report.jetnb --all-active
# local only; source/renderer/lock/policy change revokes the notebook-wide grant

options.name: Passive-equivalent sandbox default plus unified intent-card trust (hybrid)
options.detail: Passive sanitization, the opaque-origin empty-capability sandbox, hash-bound grant keys, local-only non-traveling trust, and revoke-on-any-change are Option A's, with one beginner fix: active content that requests no capability beyond the empty sandbox — first-party plots, tables, zero-capability widgets — renders without any prompt, because a sandbox with no messages, origins, storage, kernel, or parent reach is passive-equivalent by construction. Capability-requesting widgets keep the full key (source + payload + renderer + locked environment + policy version), but grants live in the unified `jet trust` authority graph (D-WD1, D-JPK-GRANTCMD1) and prompt as one per-notebook intent card with an expert drawer expanding exact per-cell hashes, origins, and typed messages (D-CANVAS-ACTIONAUTH1) — C's one-review convenience without notebook-wide authority. Imported ipynb outputs always quarantine; any source, payload, renderer, lock, or policy change revokes to safe `text/plain` fallback.
options.code:
display(sales.chart)   # zero-capability widget: sandboxed, renders, no prompt
jet trust notebook report.jetnb --cell 01J... \
  --allow-widget sales.chart --allow-origin https://data.example
# intent card: "sales.chart wants network: data.example" — drawer shows hashes/messages
# grants live locally in the jet trust graph; any edit or import revokes

comparisons.note: Notebook trust historically signs cells to permit active output. Jet tightens the key, isolates origin, strips ambient authority, and grants explicit capabilities.
Opaque-origin iframes plus CSP and typed postMessage-style bridges provide a strong containment base when default capabilities are empty.

decisions.title: How much of the test suite CI runs, and when
decisions.gist: Pick what a green CI checkmark actually proves.
decisions.explainer: Work here lands directly on master, so push and merge are the same event — B's fast lane would gate nothing by itself. A makes the checkmark mean exactly one thing, which is the whole point once no strong reviewer stands behind it.
decisions.story: Priya lands a small formatter tweak late in the evening. CI goes green, she moves on. The formatter stability tests never ran — CI only executes 6 of the ~90 test targets — so the tweak silently drops a token when reprinting code, and the corruption ships. This exact failure lived in the repo for months once before. When the strongest reviewer is gone, the checkmark is the only reviewer left; this ballot decides what it means.
decisions.inWild:
$ git push
# GitHub Actions: ✓ CI passed (6 of ~90 test targets ran)

$ nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh
test fmt_stability_serde_markers ... FAILED
  expected: `name: text #[key]`
  emitted:  `name: text`        <- marker dropped, file corrupted on save

# Both of the above are true at the same time today.

options.name: Full suite on every push
options.detail: One lane, one meaning: CI runs verify-full.sh (all ~90 targets) on every push, with JET_REQUIRE_RUSTC=1 so environment self-skips fail loudly. A nightly lane adds rotating-seed fuzzing (N>=1000) and the perf ratchet. Green means the same thing as a local full-suite pass. Runs take tens of minutes; pushes are not blocked, only flagged.
options.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
- name: Full suite
  run: nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh
  env: { JET_REQUIRE_RUSTC: 1 }

# nightly.yml (03:00)
- run: FUZZ_SEED=${{ github.run_id }} FUZZ_N=1000 nix develop -c cargo test --test fuzz_sema
- run: nix develop -c tools/perf/ci-perf-check.sh

$ git push   # ~25-40 min later:
✗ CI failed — fmt: fmt_stability_serde_markers

options.name: Fast push lane + full merge/nightly lane
options.detail: Every push runs a ~3-minute doc-sync tier (lib tests, truthfulness, decisions, diagnostics_coverage, snapshots). The full suite runs on master merges and nightly. Quick signal per push; the deep signal arrives within a day. Risk: with direct-to-master work, push and merge are the same event, so in practice the fast lane alone gates nothing.
options.code:
# push lane (~3 min)
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --lib --test truthfulness --test decisions \
        --test diagnostics_coverage --test diagnostic_snapshots
# master + nightly lane
- run: nix develop -c scripts/agent/verify-full.sh

$ git push        # ✓ fast lane green in 3 min
# 03:00 nightly:  ✗ fmt stability failed — found the next morning

options.name: Keep the cherry-pick, fix the rot only
options.detail: Keep today's 6-target selection; repair the stale Tower step, add JET_REQUIRE_RUSTC, wire the perf check. The ~80 uncovered targets (fmt, ownership, repl, lsp, jetpack, ...) stay covered only by agents remembering to run verify-full.sh locally — the discipline dependency this epoch is trying to retire.
options.code:
# ci.yml unchanged in shape:
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test truthfulness
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test diagnostic_snapshots
- run: nix develop -c cargo test --test golden
# fmt/ownership/repl/lsp/... : still never run in CI

$ git push   # ✓ green — proves 6/90 targets

comparisons.note: PR CI runs a subset; nothing merges except through bors, which runs the full battery — merge green is total green.
comparisons.code: @bors r+   # queues full-suite gate before merge

comparisons.note: Fast premerge checks plus deep buildbots after landing; breakage found post-land is reverted by policy.
comparisons.code:
premerge: check-clang (fast)
buildbot: full stage2 + sanitizers (hours later)

decisions.title: Where maintainer helper commands live
decisions.gist: Pick the home for repo-maintainer tools: reduce, ice-report, snapshot bless, fixture scaffolds, fixture-path check.
decisions.explainer: Follows the ratified precedent (`jet devtools grammars`), keeps discovery in one --help screen, and adds no second binary. Beginner surface unaffected — devtools is already the maintainer shelf.
decisions.story: Sam is a maintainer (human or mid-tier agent) whose 400-line test program just crashed the compiler with the internal-error banner. Today the next step is hand-deleting statements one at a time to shrink the crash, then hand-copying expected output out of panic text to update fixtures — the two jobs where a weaker maintainer burns hours or gives up. These helpers make both mechanical; the ballot picks where they live. Whatever the spelling, none of it appears in beginner-facing help.
decisions.inWild:
$ jet run inventory.jet
internal compiler error: generated Rust rejected (I2)
this is a bug in jet — please report it

# Sam, today: open a 400-line file and start deleting lines by hand.
# Sam, after this card: one command produces a 10-line repro + report bundle.

options.name: jet devtools subcommands
options.detail: Extend the existing maintainer namespace that already holds `jet devtools grammars`: reduce, ice-report, bless, new-example, new-ui, check-fixture-paths. Discoverable in one place, ships with the compiler an agent already built, hidden from top-level `jet help` just like grammars is today.
options.code:
$ jet devtools reduce inventory.jet
reduced: 412 lines -> 11 lines (ICE preserved)  -> inventory.min.jet

$ jet devtools ice-report inventory.min.jet
wrote ice-report/: source, generated.rs, rustc.stderr, versions.txt

$ jet devtools new-ui move_out_of_view
created tests/ui/move_out_of_view.jet + .stderr (blessed)
reminder: add E-code row to docs/spec/diagnostics.md

options.name: Env vars + repo scripts only
options.detail: No new CLI surface: blessing via env vars on cargo test (UPDATE_EXPECT / JET_UPDATE_GOLDEN), reducer and scaffolds as scripts under scripts/dev/. Compiler binary untouched; tools only work from a repo checkout and are found by reading docs rather than --help.
options.code:
$ JET_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 nix develop -c cargo test --test golden
$ nix develop -c scripts/dev/reduce.sh inventory.jet
$ nix develop -c scripts/dev/new-ui.sh move_out_of_view

# discovery: ls scripts/dev/ + a docs table (no --help integration)

options.name: Separate jet-dev binary
options.detail: A second binary (cargo run -p jet-devtools or an installed jet-dev) holding all maintainer commands. Hard wall between user CLI and maintainer CLI — `jet help` can never leak a maintainer command — at the cost of a second entry point to version, build, and document.
options.code:
$ nix develop -c jet-dev reduce inventory.jet
$ nix develop -c jet-dev bless --ui move_out_of_view
$ nix develop -c jet-dev ice-report inventory.min.jet

# jet --help: unchanged, no devtools entry at all

comparisons.note: Maintainer tooling lives behind one entry point (x.py / bootstrap) plus cargo-bisect-rustc for reduction-style triage.
Maintainer commands ship inside the main tool under a namespace users never touch.
Standalone reducer proves the mechanical-reduction pattern this adopts.

decisions.title: Does the board refuse rule-breaking writes, or only report them?
decisions.gist: Pick how hard Tower enforces the working rules (done-gates, ballot completeness, owner-only actions).
decisions.explainer: The repeat offenders are agents, not you. C binds them at write time — prose rules become mechanical — while your phone workflow stays one tap. A ties your hands; B is today with extra steps.
decisions.story: An agent finishes step 2 of 5 on a card, marks it done, and moves on — the remaining steps evaporate until someone notices weeks later. Another agent files your acceptance verdict as a log note where you never see it again. Today every one of these writes succeeds, because the rules live in prose the agent may never have loaded. You have had to repeat these rules angrily more than once; this ballot decides whether the board itself starts saying no.
decisions.inWild:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
updated card #412 -> done        # 3 of 5 checklist items still open

$ tower decision add --title 'Cache strategy' --by helper-agent
added decision D-CACHE1          # no gist, no story, no options — reaches your queue empty

$ tower card activate '#413' --by helper-agent
activated #413                   # an owner-only action, performed by an agent

options.name: Hard gates for everyone
options.detail: The store refuses rule-breaking writes no matter who writes: done requires a complete checklist, ballots must be ballot-ready to enter the queue, ratify/activate demand owner attribution, frozen cards are read-only. Maximum consistency — but it also stops you: closing a card from your phone means ticking every box first, and there is no override when you just want something gone.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by owner
E_GATE: 3 checklist items unchecked — no done until complete (no override)

options.name: Lint-only, never refuse
options.detail: All writes keep succeeding; a `tower lint` sweep (run by agents, shown on the board) reports violations: done-with-open-checklist, empty ballots, mis-attributed ratifies. Zero friction — and zero protection at the moment of the write. A weak model that never runs lint recreates today exactly.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
updated card #412 -> done
$ tower lint
WARN #412 done with 3 unchecked items (by helper-agent)
WARN D-CACHE1 not ballot-ready: gist/story/options empty

options.name: Agent-hard, owner-soft
options.detail: Writes with --by other than owner hit hard gates: done-gate on checklists, ballot-ready validation (a --draft flag keeps drafts out of your queue), owner-only ratify/activate unless the agent quotes you explicitly (recorded in the event log), no writes to frozen/owner-lane cards, release of a building card requires a handoff note. Your own writes bypass everything. The rules bind exactly the population that keeps breaking them.
options.code:
$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by helper-agent
E_GATE: 3 checklist items unchecked — complete them or --release --handoff "..."

$ tower decision ratify D-CACHE1 --outcome B --by helper-agent
E_OWNER: ratify is owner-only — use --on-behalf-of-owner "<owner's words>"

$ tower card update '#412' --phase done --by owner
updated card #412 -> done        # owner bypass, no ceremony

comparisons.note: Branch protection blocks contributors while admins may bypass — the standard shape for solo-owner + helpers.
comparisons.code:
Require status checks: on
Include administrators: off

comparisons.note: Hooks enforce by default with an explicit, visible escape.
The compiler refuses at the moment of the mistake instead of reporting it later — the reason the invariant holds in practice.

decisions.title: Where ratified decisions and done cards go to rest
decisions.gist: Whether finished board history stays inside tower.json or moves to a separate archive file, and what triggers the move.
decisions.explainer: A keeps you in control of when history moves (matching how you already close out epochs), keeps one mental model (tower.json = the board), and shrinks writes, backups, git churn, and phone payload all at once. B is the same end-state but moves things the instant they close — done cards vanish from the Board's Done lists into a second file mid-session. C treats the symptom (transport) and leaves the file growing forever.

decisions.title: How an agent gets its marching orders from Tower
decisions.gist: Whether starting work on a card takes one command that returns everything, a generated brief file, or native harness tools.
decisions.explainer: A collapses the error-prone five-step ritual into one call that cannot omit the ratification comment or an open question, and it works identically for Claude, codex, and bare scripts. B helps only harnesses with auto-load; C is a strong later layer on top of A (same packet, typed transport).
decisions.story: A fresh Claude session is told 'work the board'. Today it runs five commands (status, next, card show, decision list, question list), re-reads the skill doc to remember the phase rules, and only then starts. Every extra step is a place a sub-agent skips something — the cards that bounced usually bounced because the agent never saw a ratification comment or an open question sitting right on the card.

questions.text: How do other languages handle this? What are the tradeoffs for each approach?
questions.answer: Most modern toolchains use Option A — one binary, tool subcommands: Deno (deno fmt/lint/lsp), Gleam (gleam format/lsp), Ruff (ruff format/check/server), Bun. The recurring exception is the LSP, shipped as a separate artifact by Zig (ZLS), Go (gopls), and Rust (rust-analyzer) because editors spawn it long-lived on its own cadence. Rust's fmt/clippy are separate binaries (B) but hidden behind cargo subcommands and version-locked via rustup. Pure plugin (C) has no real precedent for compiled-language toolchains. Tradeoffs: A = one install, tooling can never disagree with the compiler, bigger binary, no independent patch cadence; B = independent releases + smaller core but version-skew risk and N artifacts; C = max flexibility, runtime ABI surface, no prior art, fights one-source-of-truth. Jet-specific: fmt/lint/lsp all need the real lexer/parser/sema (I2/I3), so under B/C they must link the same front end as a shared lib and stay version-locked anyway — getting separation's costs without its benefits. Prior art + that constraint both point at A, reserving the LSP as the one piece that could become a separate artifact later. Full table added to the D-TOOL-SPLIT card in docs/ballots/decision-ballots.md.

questions.text: I still have absolutely no clue what this means. Give me a user story with example code so I can learn what you mean
questions.answer: Ratified A (2026-06-20). Not a language feature — a naming clash inside our own spec docs. Two ratified decisions both coined "Layer 2": S26 (derive ladder: built-in derives) and S60 (capability tier: compile-time pure eval + data embedding). A keeps both numbers and adds one cross-reference sentence on S60 so the next reader can tell them apart. No code, no rename. Compile-time embedding work files under S60.

questions.text: I am leaning B but want to understand the practical tradeoofs of going with B & C respectively
questions.answer: Ratified B (2026-06-20). B (stdlib Guard value: scope.guard(() => {…})) delivers ~95% of C's value — cleanup on every exit path including the ? early return — for zero new syntax and zero ratification, running on existing Drop + lambda machinery, and keeps Jet's one-cleanup-story (RAII) intact. C (a defer keyword) adds a second cleanup mechanism plus the Go leak-by-omission bug class S63 was chosen to avoid; its only unique win is errdefer-style partial rollback, not yet proven. B doesn't foreclose C — add the keyword later on evidence. defer (C) stays declined (D-SUGAR5); user-definable Drop remains the long-term roadmap item.

questions.text: 1) Isnt sharing not supportable with the borrow checker? Wouldnt that be a mutable borrow which can only have 1, but immutable can have many? I dont get the point, refresh me on the memory capability model. How does it play into the borrow checker system? What is auto inferred for beginners but can be specified for experts?
questions.answer: `share` is shared *ownership* (Rc/Arc), not a shared mutable borrow — so the borrow-checker rule still holds: mutable XOR shared. The four capabilities map onto it directly: `view` = `&T` (many readers ok), `edit` = `&mut T` (exactly one, exclusive), `take` = move (ownership transfer), `share` = `Rc<T>`/`Arc<T>` (many owners, READ-only — no mutation, so no conflict with the one-mutable rule). `share` exists for graph/tree shapes where a single owner is awkward; it buys multiple readers by giving up mutation, exactly mirroring &T. Beginners write none of this — the compiler infers the narrowest capability from how the value is used; experts annotate it to pin intent or widen sharing. Full capability↔borrow-checker table is on the D-CAP2 card.

questions.text: How is a supportive of the experts? That is one of the major points for jet -> a beginner friendly automagical side & an expert exposed full control side
questions.answer: Reframed so it serves experts directly: ship BOTH. A (scope-inferred regions) is the beginner default — the compiler places allocations automatically. B (`region r { … }`) is the explicit expert tier — you name a region and allocate into it deliberately, e.g. two arenas live side by side and you choose which one each value lands in. The beginner never sees a region; the expert gets full manual placement. Now RATIFIED (D-REGION1 = A+B together, 2026-06-21). Worked two-arena example is on the card.

questions.text: I'm leaning towards A, but how is bloat/buildup addressed? For large codebases, how will users be able to avoid 3k lines of code that are just migrations?
questions.answer: Bloat is bounded by published-API surface × support window, NOT codebase size, via four bounds: (1) only `#PublishedSchema` types accrue migrations — internal types never do; (2) migrations live in `migrations/`, are build-tier, and cost zero at runtime; (3) you keep migrations only back to your declared support floor; (4) `jet schema squash` collapses old chains into a fresh baseline snapshot. So a large codebase with a few published types stays tiny. Now RATIFIED (D-MIGRATE1 = A) and the rename-only slice is implemented end-to-end + verified green; the squash/baseline tooling and other ops are tracked as follow-on D-MIGRATE2.

questions.text: Please reform the ballot using a2 & c beta (#context) as the baseline. Give me grammar options to pick from using those two choices. That is what I want to pick but need to ensure I like the syntax/grammar
questions.answer: Reformed and now RATIFIED. A2+Cβ fixed as the baseline; the grammar pick resolved to G2 — `#context(field: value) { … }`, reusing Jet's single `name: value` spelling (S61/S29), with `=` staying reassign-only. No single-field shorthand; bundle-spread deferred. Shipped as the c74 Smart Context feature.

questions.text: Option D but I dont want to defer the full implementation if avoidable. We are close to epoch 3 anyway, so what should we do to get this working? Propose a new approach in this decision.
questions.answer: Proposed Option D+ so nothing is deferred: an interpreter seam now (Phase 1) plus a Cranelift JIT this Epoch-3 (Phase 2, tiered — interpreter tier-0, Cranelift tier-1). I6 still holds because Cranelift is runtime-side, never in Source/. This needs your approval of the runtime-side Cranelift dependency (same posture as the regex dep). Recommendation: D+. Decision still open pending your call on the dep.

questions.text: How does this interplay with experts that will want to use low level memory controls like references and pointers?
questions.answer: The tiers compose rather than conflict. `view`/`edit` ARE the safe references an expert wants (`&T`/`&mut T`) — capabilities are the safe-reference surface, not a wall in front of it. The drop below that layer is a raw `Ptr<T>` via `use core.mem` inside a `#Unsafe`/`#Audit` region, where the guarantees are explicitly suspended. The two bridge at the function boundary: public params stay safe capabilities, and the raw-pointer work is a localized `#Unsafe` block inside. Worked `checksum(buf: view [U8])` example added to the D-CAP3/D-CAP2 card. Decision still open.

questions.text: How is this affected when no type is written (inferred type)?
questions.answer: Capabilities are a parameter concept and parameters carry types, so an omitted capability is simply inferred — there is no token to place when no type is written, and the capability rides the type. Rule: no type written ⇒ capability inferred too; you never get a dangling capability. This reinforces option A (type + capability written together in one place). The only spot you'd write an inferred-type parameter is a lambda, where you write the type alongside precisely to pin a capability. Decision still open.

questions.text: I think the $ is fine for me, but what about people trying to use the language globally? Is having such a commonly needed symbol an issue? What if people dont have that symbol? How likely is that? Is it a reasonable concern or not a big deal
questions.answer: Not a blocker. `$` is plain ASCII and universal on physical keyboards; Jet already left the ISO-646-invariant subset behind by depending on `# @ { } [ ]`, so `$` adds nothing new. Programmers type `$` constantly (shell/PHP/JS) and no mainstream language uses it as a binding operator, so no conflicting habit. Answered in the D-BIND2 card; rec stands at A (`$=`); decision stays open for your pick.

That harms reproducibility, allows ambient side effects during builds (fs/env/process/net/secrets), forces the comptime interpreter to duplicate runtime behavior, complicates supply-chain policy, and creates machine-dependent compile failures. The recommendation stays B: deterministic pure whitelist now; explicit build-time IO/sandboxed recipe tier later.

The shortlist is `$=`, `::`, `~=`, and `=:`; the card still recommends `$=` because it is unused, two characters, contains `=`, and is visually far from mutable `:=`.

The card now focuses on what each prefix teaches: `::` reads anchored/address-like, `::` reads marked/metadata-like, and `$=` reads value-centric without borrowing meaning from another Jet sigil family. Recommendation remains `$=` because it keeps `=` in the binding family, stays visually far from `:=`, and does not overload Jet's existing `@` or `#` semantics.

questions.text: For generics, we use <T> -> can we use that?
questions.answer: Two things were colliding on the brackets. `[Particle]` is Jet's *list type* ("a list of Particle"), NOT a generic parameter — generics stay `<T>` and are untouched by this card. The old gist's `columnar [T]` just meant "the keyword in front of a list type," where T was the element. So the real question is the *spelling* of the per-container form, and yes — a generic-style `Columnar<Particle>` is now a real option (B) alongside the prefix keyword `columnar [Particle]` (A). The difference: A reads as a storage modifier on the same list type (no new type, same API, just a layout hint), while B (`<T>`-style) makes layout part of the type identity — `Columnar<Particle>` becomes a distinct container needing conversions and its own impls/trait bounds, like `Map<K,V>`. Recommendation stays A: a layout is how a value is *stored*, not a type parameter, and the prefix keyword keeps one word (`columnar`) across both the struct attribute and the per-use form. `<T>`-style is available as B if you'd rather layout live in the type system. questions.text: What are the downsides of recommendation A? In practice does this cause friction? How do new users know what to do? Will this make it harder to use the system for simpler projects or beginner projects?
questions.answer: Honest answer: A's only real cost is key custody, and it lands entirely on PUBLISHERS — never on consumers, never on beginners, never on simple projects. (1) Consuming a package (the common case + every beginner): zero friction — `jet add` verifies the signature silently and only ever speaks on a MISMATCH (a normal Jet diagnostic, not crypto). Strictly better than checksum-only for the same effort. (2) Simpler/local/unpublished projects: nothing changes — signing is only on the registry-publish path; path/git/unpublished deps are never signed or asked about. (3) Publishing (the one place friction exists): mitigated by the dual-facet rule — `jet publish` auto-generates+stores a keypair on first publish (no separate keygen on the magic path), then prints one line nudging `jet key backup`. The beginner's required action is the command they were already running. What stays genuinely hard is key LOSS/THEFT/ROTATION — the inherent cost of authenticity. Prior art is a warning: PyPI REMOVED GPG signing in 2023 (nobody verified, so publisher pain bought nothing); npm/Go/crates.io all moved authenticity OFF author-managed keys; Maven Central's mandatory GPG is the canonical 'publishing is painful' complaint. Lesson: never make key management mandatory or visible on the magic path. Bearing on the decision: this argues for A as an OPT-IN / non-blocking layer with SHA-256 checksum (B) as the always-on floor — `require_signed` stays an org policy, OFF by default — not a hard gate that refuses unsigned packages. That keeps A's unique win (offline authorship proof) while spending friction only on publishers who opt in. Full Owner Q&A block added to the D-PKGSIGN1 card.

questions.text: What is really the issue with full jai? Build systems allow arbitrary code execution, but this just keeps it within the language. Play devil's advocate & tell me what we would lose out on by going with option a vs full jai. Consider every level of use case (beginner/college student/enterprise/etc.)
questions.answer: Full writeup is on the D-METADEPTH1 ballot card as Owner Q5. Steel-manning C: one language/debugger/syntax (no second toolchain) and a genuinely higher ceiling — rewrite decls, schema-driven codegen, DSLs — that A (read + derive) gives up. BUT 'inside the language' only removes a TOOLCHAIN seam, not Jai's two real costs: (1) local reasoning dies — if any macro can rewrite any decl you can't read code and know what it does; grep/go-to-def/'what did it expand to' all degrade (the proc-macro tax), bending I3/I8 and D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters sema, never injected). (2) It's still arbitrary build-time code execution + non-reproducibility — identical whether in-language or in build.rs; keeping it in-language removes the very seam you'd sandbox/audit it through, so it makes supply-chain RISK worse, not better. By use case: BEGINNER loses ~nothing (and C only adds footguns — a struct no longer trustworthy at face value); LEARNER trades metaprogramming exercises for the guarantee that reading code = understanding it (A wins for learning the language, C only for learning metaprogramming); POWER USER loses custom rules/DSLs/schema-codegen — the genuine cost, mitigated by S56 derives + blessed first-class rules (#(net) effects enforce 'no panic in net', typestate enforces state rules) + the B rung (rejection-lint); ENTERPRISE flips entirely — frictionless idiomatic compile-time exec is exactly the xz/SolarWinds/npm-postinstall attack surface, so a Jai-style Jet gets banned or heavily sandboxed and reproducibility (D-CTEFFECT1) dies. Decisive point: A⊂B⊂C is a LADDER. A is the floor, not the ceiling — we can vote UP later (B for rejection rules, C only post-self-host) with no redesign, because nothing in A forecloses them; the reverse is impossible (you can't un-ship macros — the ecosystem locks you in, see Rust). So A is the only rung that is safe-by-default for beginners, auditable-by-default for enterprise, AND forward-compatible. Recommendation stays A; the live decision is how far up the ladder v1 goes (Owner Q1/Q2: ship B's rejection-lint now or defer).

questions.text: How does jai handle this? Show me a detailed comparison between jet & c3 so I can see what this looks like in practice. What about jai's "#run" directive? How do we do that in jet? How can we scope to a code block?
questions.answer: Full writeup on the D-CTMARKER1 ballot card as Owner Q3 (with a Jet↔C3 table and the Jai #run breakdown). Jai's #run does two jobs: (a) bake a compile-time value into the binary (X :: #run f();), and (b) a free-standing #run { … } block of arbitrary build-time statements that can even generate source via add_build_string — and it is UNGATED (any I/O, no reproducibility wall). Jet already has (a): a `comptime` binding IS #run-for-a-value (`comptime ICONS = pack(@embed("icons/"))`), but GATED — comptime runs only the curated pure-Core whitelist (D-CTCORE1), and world-touching effects are hashed-reproducible (Tier 1 @embed/find/fetch(…,sha256:)) or behind #Impure (Tier 2) per D-CTEFFECT1. Jai's source-generating add_build_string is exactly what D-CTCODEGEN1=A (generated code re-enters lexer→parser→sema, never injected) and D-METADEPTH1=A (reflection/derives only, no user macros) deliberately fence off — so Jet gives you #run's POWER (compute at build time, derive code) without #run's FOOTGUNS (ungated RCE + post-sema injection). C3 vs Jet in practice = the same program with C3's `$` sigil vs Jet's `comptime` keyword: $crc/comptime crc, $if/comptime if, $foreach/comptime loop — identical for everything EXCEPT a build-time statement BLOCK, which Jet does NOT have today (only comptime bindings + comptime if; 'no comptime blocks'). That is the genuine gap and the real thing to add. Sharpened recommendation: add a keyword-spelled `comptime { … }` block (Jet's gated equivalent of Jai's free-standing #run {}, consistent with comptime if) and reserve `$` for the metaprogramming SPLICE site only (rec C: $name = a comptime value woven into runtime/generated code) — Jai's full reach behind Jet's reproducible-by-default wall, no $if/comptime-if I8 fork. Added Owner Q4 to the card to pick the block form. Decision stays open.
